en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the middle section of the Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Śāṃśapāyana said:
The first quarter has been mastered by you; let the second be completed through its connection.
Now, proceed with the third quarter in detail, together with its introductory context.
Sūta said:
O brahmins, I shall proclaim to you the third book in detail, along with its introductory narrative; listen to me as I recite it according to its collection of verses.
O twice-born ones, listen now to the detailed and sequential account of the creation of this present Manu Vaivasvata, the high-souled one.
Indeed, it was previously calculated by the hosts of great gods, along with the sages and the Dānavas, as being seventy-one times four yugas.
Together with the Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and great serpents,
as well as humans, animals, birds, and even the stationary beings.
Having paid homage to Vivasvat, I shall describe the creation of the Vaivasvata Manvantara, beginning with Manu and ending with the future [Manus], accompanied by many narratives.
In the first Manvantara that has passed,
there were seven other great seers who initiated the process of creation during the previous Svāyambhuva interval.
When the interval of Cākṣuṣa had passed and the Vaivasvata [Manvantara] had arrived again,
[there was the lineage] of Dakṣa and of the sages of great splendor, such as Bhṛgu and others.
Due to the curse of Maheśvara, there was the manifestation of the great-souled ones;
thus, the seven mental sons were born once again as the Seven Sages.
And they were themselves appointed as sons by the Self-born One;
and by those high-souled ones, who brought about the continuity of progeny, offspring were produced.
The creation was set in motion again, just as before and in due order;
I shall now describe the progeny of those whose actions were purified by knowledge.
Through the conjunction of both concise and detailed methods, in due order and as it truly is:
by those whose lineage produced this one [Being], this entire world, including all that moves and is stationary,
was once again filled and adorned with planets and constellations.
The sages said:
"O best of beings, tell us how the seven mental-born sages (Saptarṣis) were first produced, and how they were conceived as sons."
Sūta said:
Those seven ṛṣis who were previously mentioned during the Svāyambhuva interval, it is said,
reappeared upon reaching the Vaivasvata interval of Manu.
Pierced by the curse of existence, they did not then attain the fruits of their asceticism;
instead, they were reborn in the world of men as those who return but once (sakṛdāgāmins).
All those great seers in Janaloka always said to one another:
"These highly fortunate ones [were present] at the sacrifice performed by Varuṇa."
"We are all born during the interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa; we are all the sons of Pitāmaha. Therefore, that will be for our welfare."
Having spoken thus, they all, during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu,
were sent by Bhava for the purpose of creation during the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu.
Having returned here from Janaloka,
they were indeed born again at the sacrifice of the Great God, who was assuming the form of Varuṇa.
As Brahmā was offering his pure essence into the fire out of a desire for progeny, the Ṛṣis were born from his long [breath]; this we have heard as the second [creation]. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 2.1.20)
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Marīci, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Atri, and Vasiṣṭha— these eight are the sons of Brahmā.
Likewise, at his extensive sacrifice, all the gods assembled,
as did all the components of the sacrifice and the *vaṣaṭ*-call personified.
And the Sāmans and Yajus by the thousands appeared in embodied form, as did the Ṛgveda there, adorned with its various recensions.
And the Yajurveda stood there, rich in its meters, radiant with the syllable Oṃ upon its face,
joined with the purpose of sacrifice, and possessing the Sūktas, Brāhmaṇas, and Mantras.
And the Sāmaveda, rich in its meters and preceded by all that is to be sung,
was gathered together with the Gandharvas, such as Viśvāvasu and others.
Then the Brahmaveda, accompanied by formidable rites and the applications of the Pratyāṅgirasa mantras,
became the head of his second body.
The characteristics, the expansions, the praises, the etymologies, the musical modes, the divisions, the locus, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, as well as suppression and grasping; BndP_2,1.27.
The goddess Ilā of radiant form, the quarters along with their presiding deities, the celestial maidens, their wives, and likewise the Mothers; BndP_2.1.28 //
All these indeed arrived at the sacrifice of the sacrificing god,
possessing embodied forms known for their beauty, bearing the very body of Varuṇa.
Having seen those self-existent objects, his semen fell upon the earth;
there is no doubt that this was for the sake of ordaining the future state of the Brahman-sages.
Having taken it up and grasped it with both hands using the *sruva* ladle, the Grandfather offered it as an oblation; he poured the flowing stream of ghee while reciting the sacred mantras.
Then that Prajāpati produced the multitude of beings;
from him, moreover, was born the fiery nature within the worlds belonging to the realm of light.
Just as goodness (sattva) is to be remedied by darkness (tamas), so too is passion (rajas);
and he indeed offered his own semen as an oblation, taking it up in a vessel for clarified butter.
Then, at that very moment when Śukra appeared, great sages manifested there,
blazing with physical form and endowed with their own radiant qualities and powers.
When the semen was offered into the fire once, the Sage emerged from the flame;
seeing him, Hiranyagarbha [perceived him] as he had issued forth, having pierced through the blaze.
"Since you have said, 'You are Bhṛgu,' therefore he is indeed Bhṛgu. Having thus emerged, Mahādeva, seeing Brahmā, spoke.
"O Lord, O God, this son was first born to me while I was consecrated for initiation and desiring a son; therefore, let him become my son. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.1.37)
"So be it," having been thus authorized by the Self-born One, Mahādeva then adopted Bhṛgu as his son.
From that [seed] the Bhṛgus were born of Varuṇa; thus he, the lord, was their offspring.
Then the lord offered the second seed into the embers.
O Aṅgiras, because his limbs were gathered together within the embers, he became known as Aṅgiras;
seeing that birth of his, Vahni spoke to Brahmā.
"O Retodhā, let this second one be mine," he said to him;
and having been told "So be it" by Brahmā, Sadasaspati likewise spoke.
We have heard that Agni was born from Aṅgiras as the son of Agni;
however, he was created six times again by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, through Śukra.
When that [sacrifice] was completed, they became the Brahmas, according to the Śruti;
among them, Marīci arose first from the rays of light.
In that sacrifice, Kratu was born; because he was born from that, he is indeed called Kratu.
"I am the third," said Atri; therefore, he is celebrated as Atri.
Because he was covered with matted hair (keśa), he is remembered as Pulastya;
because he arose with long hair (keśa), he is therefore remembered as Pulaha.
Born from the midst of the Vasus, he himself was both self-controlled and possessed of wealth;
therefore, he is called Vasiṣṭha by those who know reality and by the exponents of Brahman.
Thus these six great sages, the mind-born sons of Brahmā,
are the progenitors of the world, by whom these creatures were increased.
The sons of Brahmā are recited as being thus called Prajāpatis;
others, known by the name Pitṛs, were born from these very same great seers.
The hosts of gods were produced, renowned throughout the seven worlds;
and the seven invincible hosts were likewise renowned throughout the seven worlds.
The Mārīyas and the Bhārgavas, as well as others who are Aṅgirasas,
the Paulastyas, the Paulahas, and the renowned Vāsiṣṭhas.
The Ātreyas are declared to be the hosts of the Pitṛs who increase the world;
these have been described in brief, and there are three other hosts besides them.
They are immortal, unmanifest, luminous, and renowned;
their king is this god, whose sins have been destroyed by the Yamas.
Furthermore, the ascetics Kaśyapa, Kardama, Śeṣa, Vikrānta, and likewise Suśravas, being unwearied, protected those subjects.
Bahuputra, Kumāra, Vivasvat, he of pure vows (Śucivrata), Pracetas, Ariṣṭanemi, and Bahula were the Prajāpatis.
Thus, there were many other lords of creatures as well,
such as the Kuśoccayas, the Vālakhilyas, along with the Bhūtas and the supreme ṛṣis.
They became swift as thought, omnipresent, and possessed of all enjoyments;
others, born from the ashes, were honored by the hosts of Brahman-sages.
The hosts of Vaikhānasa sages, devoted to austerity and sacred learning, were born from his nostrils;
and from his two nostrils were born the Aśvins, renowned for their beauty.
From the dust of his birth-star Vidura was born, and likewise from the movement of his eyes;
other lords of creatures were born from his various apertures.
From the pores of his skin arose the sages, as well as sweat and impurities;
from him came the solstices, the seasons, the months, the half-months, and the junctions of the fortnights.
Those days and nights are the years; bile is the fierce light.
They call it the terrible red, and red is remembered as gold.
That is declared to be Taijasa; the smoke is known as the Paśus;
those which are its flames are the Rudras, as well as the Ādityas who have attained prosperity.
The divine and human rays of light have arisen from the embers;
you are Brahmā, the primordial source of this world, born from Brahmā.
Saying "It grants all desires," and thus uttering these words,
Brahmā, the preceptor of the gods, was there propitiated by the deities.
These very lords of the progeny shall generate all creatures;
they are all masters of progeny and all are likewise practitioners of austerity.
"By your grace, may these people sustain these worlds and these sacred rites;
may they perpetually increase your lineage and augment your splendor."
May they all be learned in the science of medicine and likewise masters of speech;
may they all be upholders of the Vedas and mantras, born from Prajāpati.
May they take refuge in the truth of Brahman and in the supreme austerity on earth;
for all of us, as well as these others, O Lord, are indeed your offspring.
Brahmā and the Brahmās, as well as the world with its moving and unmoving beings,
beginning with Marīci, along with the gods and the sages.
"Thinking of them as our offspring, we desire those children;
in that sacrifice, O highly blessed ones, are the gods and the sages. (Bṛhaddevatā 2.1.69)
These, born of your lineage and presiding over their respective stations and times,
shall establish these subjects in that very form of yours.
"O twice-born ones, let them also establish [the rites] that mark the beginning and end of the ages.
Then the Teacher of the World spoke, addressing him as "Supreme": ||| BndP_2.1.71 |||
Having ascertained this very point, I created these great seers who are born into your lineage; of this there is no doubt.
Of them, I shall first proclaim in detail and in due order the lineage of the high-souled Bhṛgu, the foremost of the Prajāpatis.
Hiraṇyakaśipu had two incomparable wives of noble lineage and auspicious nature; one was the daughter of Bhṛgu, renowned by the name Divyā.
And Pulomā, the daughter of Puloman, was a woman of excellent complexion;
she, being divine, bore to Bhṛgu a son who was the best among those who know Brahman.
Śukra, the preceptor of the gods and asuras, the best of sages and a planet, is eternally Uśanas; for this reason, he is also known by the name Kāvya.
The illustrious Gaurī, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs who drink Soma, was the wife of Śukra; she gave birth to four sons.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Varatrī, and both Śaṇḍa and Marka—
these were all like the sun in brilliance and equal to Brahmā in their power.
Rajata, Pṛthuraśmi, the learned Bṛhadgirā,
and Varatriṇa— these were indeed the sons [of Vasiṣṭha], most devoted to Brahman and performers of sacrifices for the Daityas.
For the purpose of destroying the dharma of sacrifice, they approached Manu and caused him to perform a sacrifice;
seeing that dharma being cast aside, Indra spoke to Manu.
"But by these very means, I shall certainly bring you to the performance of the sacrifice.
Having heard those words of Indra, they departed from that place.
When they had vanished, Indra released Manu’s wife from his grasp once she had become unconscious, and then he pursued her.
Then, seeing those wicked sages who had returned and were striving for Indra’s destruction, Indra laughed.
Then, enraged,
he began burning them on the southern half of the sacrificial altar while they were being tormented there by jackals.
Those heads fell down and then became date-palms;
thus were the sons of Varatrin slain by Indra in ancient times.
On the Jayantī day, Devayānī became the daughter of Śukra;
and Triśiras Viśvarūpa was born as the great son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Born of Yaśodharā, there was Vairocana of great fame;
and he who is known as Viśvakarman was the younger brother of Viśvarūpa.
From Bhṛgu, O Lord, the twelve divine Bhṛgu-sages were born as his sons;
and from Divyā was born a daughter who was the younger sister of Kāvya himself.
Bhuvanobhāvana, Antya, Antyāyana, Kratu, Śuci, Svamūrdhan, Vyāja, and he who is Vasuda.
Prabhava and Avyaya are remembered as the twelfth lord;
thus these twelve Bhṛgu deities are remembered as those worthy of sacrifice.
Paulomī gave birth to a son, a twice-born man most devoted to Brahman and self-controlled;
yet in his eighth month of gestation, he was devoured by a cruel Rākṣasa.
He was called Cyavana because of his falling, and Pracetas because of his consciousness;
as Pracetas, he was Cyavana by nature, for out of anger he had burnt the man-eaters.
Together with Bhārgava, he begot two sons upon Sukanyā:
Āpravāna and Dadhīca; both of them were highly esteemed by the virtuous.
Sārasvata was born to Dadhīca by Sarasvatī;
and the highly fortunate Ṛcī was the wife of Apravāna, the son of Nahuṣa.
From her was born the highly illustrious sage Aurva, after he had split her thigh;
and from Aurva came Ṛcīka, blazing with a splendor equal to fire.
Jamadagni was born to Ṛcīka through Satyavatī; formerly, due to the exchange of sacrificial porridge between Bhṛgu and Cyavana, there arose the powers of Rudra and Viṣṇu.
From the sacrificial fire Vaiṣṇava, Jamadagni was born;
and from Jamadagni and Reṇukā was born [Paraśurāma], whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra.
She gave birth to Rāma, who was composed of the essence of Brahman and Kṣatriya and possessed immeasurable splendor; and Orva had a hundred sons, headed by Jamadagni.
From them, O son, thousands of Bhārgavas arose among one another;
indeed, many Bhārgavas are recorded as being outsiders among other sages.
The Vatsas, Vidas, Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, Yaskas, Vainyas, Śaunakas,
and Mitreyus— these seven should be known as the branches of the Bhṛgus.
Listen to the lineage of the wise Aṅgiras, the son of Agni,
in whose progeny the Bhāradvājas and Gautamas were born.
And the gods, headed by the Aṅgirasas, were radiant and possessed of great power;
likewise were Surūpā, Mārīcī, Kārdamī, and Svarāṭ.
Pathyā and Mānavī were the two daughters [of Manu]; thus there were three wives of Atharvan.
From them were born the descendants of Atharvan, the upholders of the lineage.
And Svarāṭ, whose self was purified by great asceticism,
begot Bṛhaspati upon Surūpā, the daughter of Gautama.
Ayāsya, Vāmadeva, and likewise Utathya and Uśij;
Dhṛṣṇi was the son of Pathyā, and Saṃvarta was her mind-born son.
Kitava was the son of Ayāsya, and Śaradvat was the son of Utathya;
likewise, Uśija Dīrghatamas was born of Vāmadeva, as was Bṛhaduktha.
The son of Dhṛṣṇi was Sudhanvan, and from Sudhanvan came Ṛṣabha;
the gods known as the Ṛbhus are remembered as the chariot-makers.
From Bṛhaspati was born Bharadvāja, who was renowned and possessed of great fame;
Svarāṭ begot Gautama upon Surūpā, and he [Gautama] begot Bṛhaspati.
The sons of Aurva-Aṅgiras were born of Surūpā:
Ādhāri, Āyu, Danu, Dakṣa, Dama, and likewise Prāṇa.
Haviṣya and Haviṣṇu, Ṛta and Satya—these were ten;
as well as the Ayāsyas, the Utathyas, the Vāmadevas, and the Auśijas.
The Bhāradvājas, Sāṃkṛtis, Gargas, Kaṇvarathītaras,
Mudgalas, Viṣṇuvṛddhas, Haritas, and likewise the Kapayas.
Likewise, Rūkṣa, Bharadvāja, Ārṣabha, and Kitava—
these fifteen are to be known as the branches of the Aṅgirases.
Indeed, among the other sages, many outsiders are recorded as belonging to the lineage of Aṅgiras;
now I shall also describe the supreme person who is the division of Marīci.
In whose lineage the world of moving and non-moving beings was produced;
Marīci, desiring offspring, performed austerities while meditating upon the waters.
"May a son endowed with all virtues and possessed of progeny be born to me"—
thus did the lord, purified by austerity, unite his soul.
Then all the waters were struck together,
and into them that Lord, having fixed his self within them, produced one [being].
Marīci, devoted to austerity, intensely heated his son Atri— who was peerless and known by the name Ariṣṭanemi, a lord of creatures— in the waters.
Desiring a son, he stood in the forest meditating upon truthful speech for seven thousand years; thereafter, he became peerless.
Kaśyapa, the knower of Savitṛ, equal in splendor to Brahmā,
is born in all Manvantaras as a portion of Brahmā.
Having been addressed harshly by Dakṣa on account of his daughter, the Lord became enraged;
he then drank the *kaśya*, which is here called liquor (*madya*).
Laughter is to be known as *kaśi*; that which is harmful to speech and mind is called *kaśya*.
Intoxicating liquor is remembered by the Brahmins as *kaśya*, and Kaśyapa is the progenitor of those who consume *kaśya*.
Because he uttered a cruel word with his voice, saying "Kaśa," and because he was cursed by Dakṣa in his anger, he became known as Kaśyapa.
And because he had been told this by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, Dakṣa,
the son of Pracetas, bestowed those maidens upon Kaśyapa.
All are expounders of Brahman, and all are indeed mothers of the world;
he who knows this meritorious creation of the Ṛṣis belonging to Varuṇa [attains great merit].
The long-lived, meritorious, and pure one attains eternal happiness;
by either retaining this in memory or even by hearing it, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of the Sages," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said: When the creation of progeny under Cākṣuṣa had indeed ceased during the sixth [Manvantara],...
Dakṣa himself was commanded by the Self-born One to "create offspring."
The Lord first created all beings, both moving and stationary;
he first brought forth the beings born of his mind.
The sages, gods, and gandharvas; humans, serpents, and rākṣasas;
yakṣas, bhūtas, and piśācas; as well as birds, domestic animals, and wild beasts.
When those creatures created by his mind did not multiply,
they were looked upon with displeasure by the wise Lord Mahādeva.
Desiring to create various offspring through the act of sexual union,
he took Asiknī, the daughter of the patriarch Vīraṇa, as his wife.
She was born endowed with great austerity and is the sustainer of the world;
by her all this universe, both the stationary and the moving, is upheld.
In this regard, they also cite these two verses concerning the descendants of Pracetas, when Dakṣa was formerly marrying his wife Asiknī, the daughter of Viraṇa: BndP_2.2.7 //
A million serpents, skillful and full of pride,
followed behind their lord as he moved through rivers and mountains.
Seeing him, the sages declared: "The progeny shall indeed be established;
he is the first here, and Dakṣa is the second, for he is a Prajāpati."
Then, at the proper time,
the skillful son of Pracetas plowed the land where the rivers Asiknī and Vairaṇī had been abandoned by millions.
Then the lord Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, begot a thousand sons of immeasurable splendor upon Asiknī, the daughter of Viraṇa.
Seeing them, the highly resplendent Nārada, the son of Brahmā, who delights in conversing with celestial sages, desired to increase the population of living beings.
Then Parameṣṭhin, who was born as the son of Kaśyapa, spoke these words for his own destruction, uttering a curse against them.
Due to the power of Dakṣa’s curse, he was born again as a mind-born son of Kaśyapa;
thus, he became Kaśyapa’s second mind-born son.
For Nārada was indeed born first from Parameṣṭhin;
by him, the sons of Vṛkṣa were known as the Haryaśvas.
"All have been destroyed for the sake of dharma by destiny; of this there is no doubt.
Then Dakṣa, the lord, became enraged and prepared to utter a curse.
Having placed the brahman-sages at the forefront, he was entreated by the Supreme Lord;
thereupon, Dakṣa indeed entered into an agreement with the Supreme Lord.
"In the maiden [Kāmyā], Nārada shall become your son.
Then Dakṣa gave his beloved daughter to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
From him, that sage Nārada was born again, fearing the consequences of the curse.
Śāṃśapāyana said:
How indeed were those sons of Prajāpati formerly destroyed by the celestial sage Nārada? I wish to hear this according to the truth.
Sūta said:
The sons of Dakṣa, the Haryaśvas, being desirous of increasing their progeny, assembled together;
those of great prowess were addressed by Nārada.
"Alas, you are indeed foolish; you do not know the surface of the earth, nor what is within, above, or below—how then will you create living beings? (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 2.2.21)
But even upon hearing those words, they fled in every direction;
nevertheless, they did not turn back, like rivers flowing into the ocean.
Then, when they had perished, the lord Dakṣa,
the son of Pracetas, again begot a thousand sons from Vairaṇī alone.
Desiring to increase their progeny, those Śabalāśvas were indeed made to hear again that speech which had been spoken previously by Nārada.
They all said to one another, "The sage himself has spoken correctly;
we must follow the path of our brothers, there is no doubt about this."
Having truly understood the extent of the earth, we shall create subjects who are radiant,
composed in mind, and properly instructed according to the law.
They too have set out along that very path in every direction;
even today they do not return, for they desire to reach the farthest extent.
From that time forward, a brother who is intent on searching for his brother perishes quickly; therefore, a wise man should not do such a thing.
When the dappled horses had vanished, the powerful Dakṣa, filled with rage, cursed Nārada, saying: "Go to destruction! You shall dwell within a womb! (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.2.29)
Then, when they too had perished, that high-souled lord Dakṣa indeed begot sixty daughters upon Viraṇī alone, who were renowned by name.
Then Kaśyapa accepted those daughters as wives,
as did Dharma, the lord Soma, and other great ṛṣis.
He who knows this entire creation of Dakṣa according to its true nature becomes long-lived, famous, fortunate, and possessed of progeny.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Prajāpatis," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
[Tell us] concerning the gods, the Dānavas, and the Daityas in their entirety.
Tell me in detail, indeed, about their origin during the Vaivasvata interval.
Sūta said:
I shall now proclaim the origin of Dharma itself; listen to it.
Arundhatī, Vasu, Jāmala, Lambā, Bhānu, and Marutvatī—these were his wives.
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and likewise Viśvā—
these ten wives of Dharma, Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave in marriage.
Twelve Sādhyas were born to Dharma by Sādhyā;
those supreme gods, the knowers of the divine, call them the Sādhyas.
The Brāhmaṇas were indeed created from the mouth, as were the gods, through the desire for progeny;
all of them possess bodies of mantra and have appeared here throughout the Manvantaras.
The New Moon sacrifice and the Full Moon sacrifice, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara [Sāmans], acquisition and the means of acquisition, intention and the act of intending. // BndP_2.3.6 //
The knower, the known, and likewise the mind as the sacrifice—
these indeed are the celebrated names of those sacrifices.
By the curse of Brahmā, they were born from the splendor [of the gods] and were again conquered during the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara];
they were the Tuṣitas in the Svārociṣa, and the Satyas in the Uttama Manvantara.

In the Tāmasa Manvantara, the gods known as the Haris were born from Vaikuṇṭha during the interval of Revata; they were the Sādhyas, who in the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara were born as the gods called Chandajas.
The highly fortunate sons of Dharma, who are the twelve Sādhyas and immortals,
were formerly well-regarded during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
In the past Svārociṣa Manvantara, those gods of great splendor who were known as the Tuṣitas spoke thus to one another during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara.
When only a small portion of that [time] remained, the gods of the Tuṣita heaven indeed said: "Let us enter this very illustrious Sādhyā. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.3.12)
"We shall exist during the Manvantara; that will be for our welfare.
Having spoken thus, they all [remained] during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
From that self-existent Dharma, twelve were born again;
indeed, Nara and Nārāyaṇa were born there once more.
Vipaścit Indra and Satya Hari—
these two were formerly the sons of Tuṣita during the Svārociṣa Manvantara.
But among the Tuṣitas, when they are to be propitiated, these names are recited:
Manas, Anumantṛ, Prāṇa, Nara, and the vigorous Apāna.
Vitirnaya, Haya, Haṃsa, Nārāyaṇa,
as well as Vibhu and Prabhu— the twelve Sādhyas were thus born.
In the previous Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, these names existed; then, in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, they were once again theirs. Now learn those names of the Tuṣitas.
Prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna;

for his birth was from a man (nara), and the Lord himself possessed a human form (naramūrti).
Therefore, that Lord is indeed sung of as Narasiṃha by the exponents of the Vedas;
the All-pervading One stood upon the shore of the ocean, elevated in his ascetic power.
O Lord, the body of that god was indeed composed of divinity;
he was known by the name Sudarśana and was renowned for his great strength.
Then, enraged and thinking "my claws must not be wet, they must be dry," he tore that mighty lord of the Daityas with his nails in a hand-to-hand struggle.
The five sons of Hiraṇyākṣa were valiant and possessed of great strength:
Śambara, Śakuni, and likewise Kālanābha.
Mahānābha, Suvikrānta, and likewise Saṃtāpana—
these were indeed the sons of Hiraṇyākṣa, who were difficult even for the gods to overcome.
Their sons and grandsons, the Daityas together with their hosts,
numbering hundreds and thousands, are recorded as having been slain in the Tārakāmaya war.
Hiraṇyakaśipu had four sons of great strength; Prahlāda was the eldest among them, and Anuhrāda was the next.
Understand that Saṃhrāda and Hrāda were the two sons of Hrāda;
likewise, Sunda and Nisunda became the two sons of Hrāda.
Those two great heroes were slayers of Brahmins, while Mūka was a bringer of joy;
Mārīca, the son of Sunda, was born of Tāḍakā.
Then he was slain at Daṇḍaka by the more powerful Rāghava;
and Mūka was also struck down at Kairāta by Savyasācin.
In the lineage of the Daitya Saṃhrāda, the Nivātakavacas were born;
they were themselves purified by great ascetic penance.
Jambha, Śatadundubhi, Dakṣa, Sura,
and Caṇḍa— these four were the enemies of the gods and leaders of the Daityas.
These are indeed the sons of Bāṣkala; now hear of the sons of Kālanemi:
Brahmajit, Kratujit, Devāntaka, and Narāntaka.
"O subjects, hear this: these are indeed the sons of Kālanemi;
furthermore, Rājaja and Goma are proclaimed to be the two sons of Śambhu."
And Virocana’s son was the powerful Bali;
a hundred sons were born to Bali, and all of them were kings.
Among them, four were preeminent—valiant and possessed of great strength;
the most excellent was the powerful King Bāṇa, who had a thousand arms.
Kumbhagartta, Dayo, Bhoja, Kuñci, and others;
Śakunī and Pūtanā—these two daughters of Bali are thus remembered.
The sons and grandsons of Bali, numbering in the hundreds and thousands,
were renowned as the groups known as the Bāleyas, possessing heroic prowess.
And from Bāṇa, Aindradhanvan was born of Lohinī;
Diti, having obtained sons, indeed gratified Kaśyapa.
Then Kaśyapa, with a serene soul, having been duly propitiated, invited her to choose a boon; and she then chose a boon from him.
Then the Blessed One, being requested again, granted her a boon;
but when the boon had been spoken, Diti, not yet satisfied, addressed him.
Then the goddess, with palms joined in reverence, addressed her husband Mārīca Kaśyapa:
"O Blessed One, I have been deprived of my sons by your sons, the Ādityas."
"I desire a son who has been earned through long asceticism and who shall be the slayer of Śakra;
therefore, I shall practice penance—you ought to conceive a child."
"You ought not to give me a son who is intent on slaying Indra.
Having heard those words of hers, Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, then [replied].
The one of great splendor, being deeply distressed, replied to Diti:
"So be it; however, O lady rich in asceticism, remain pure while you are pregnant."
"You shall give birth to a son who will slay Śakra in battle,
provided that you remain pure for a full thousand years."
"You shall give birth to a son, Manmatha, the most excellent in the three worlds.
Having spoken thus, the one of great splendor then became composed.
Having taken her, the venerable ṛṣi went to his own abode;
when her husband had departed, that queen Diti was exceedingly delighted.
Having reached Kuśaplavana, he performed most rigorous penance;
meanwhile, the lord Śakra, having overheard that conversation between the two of them, [approached].
Having arrived at Kuśaplavana, he addressed Diti with these words:
"I shall perform service for you; you should deign to grant me permission."
"I shall bring sacrificial fuel, as well as flowers and fruits;
however you deem best, my child, remain devoted to service. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.5.57)
"Skilled in all actions, practice what is beneficial for yourself.
Having heard those words of his mother, Śakra was greatly delighted.
Though his inner self was turbid, Śakra remained devoted to service; indeed, he served her at all times, ever-vowed to her.
Taking fruits, flowers, and sacrificial fuel, he who is firm in his vows likewise provides a massage to the body at the proper time to remove fatigue.
Śakra attended upon Diti at all times;
when her vow was nearly completed, the goddess, being pleased, spoke to Śakra.
"I am known to you, O best of gods; ten years have passed, my son.
Ten remain—blessings upon you—and after that, you shall see your brother."
O son, for your sake I shall bear that seeker of victory;
O son, you shall indeed enjoy the conquest of the three worlds together with him.
"O son, I do not recognize you as one whose mind is devoted to me," having spoken thus to Śakra, Diti [fell asleep] when the sun had reached the meridian.
Overcome by sleep, that goddess placed her head upon her knee,
drew her hair down to her feet, and fell fast asleep.
"Whatever is below the navel is indeed considered entirely impure;
therefore, having recognized her as impure, he thought of another."
Having seen all the reasons for this, his intellect arose [with this thought]:
"One must indeed destroy the queen's fetus; for that fault is clearly visible here."
Then the bull indeed entered Diti's womb through her private parts;
and having entered, Indra beheld that embryo of great power.
Terrified, he split his own enemy, the embryo, into seven parts;
yet that embryo, while being split by the hundred-jointed thunderbolt, [remained unharmed].
Trembling again and again, he wept with a loud and terrible cry; "Do not weep! Do not weep! Śakra addressed the embryo.
Having divided that embryo into seven parts, and each of those again into seven, Indra split them with his thunderbolt; then Diti awoke.
"He must not be killed, he must not be killed!"—thus Diti spoke;
then the wielder of the thunderbolt emerged from there out of respect for his mother's word.
With palms joined in reverence and holding his vajra, Śakra addressed Diti:
"O Goddess, you have fallen asleep in an impure state, with your hair trailing down to your feet."
"Having reached his vital spot in battle, I have pierced this embryo of yours in many places; you ought to forgive me."
When that embryo had thus become fruitless, Diti, overcome with supreme sorrow, spoke these words with conciliation to the invincible thousand-eyed one: BndP_2.5.75.
"O Lord of Gods, O mighty son, if this embryo of yours has been rendered fruitless through my fault, there is no fault of yours."
"There is no fault in slaying the enemy, nor should you fear him, O Lord;
however, I desire to do what is pleasing, for what benefit could there be for my child?"
"May there indeed be seven stations for my sons in heaven;
let these seven winds move about as my sons."
Those Maruts are renowned; they departed in groups of seven each:
the first division on earth, and the second in the sun.
The third is to be known among the constellations, the fourth among the planets, the fifth among the planets indeed, and the sixth in the circle of the seven sages.
"May these seven sons of mine, as well as the seven layers of the wind-spheres (vātaskandha), wander today through the firmament (dhruva) from time to time."
"May my sons wander about having become lords of the wind-spheres—
the first sphere upon the earth, which brings [the rain] from the clouds."
"Let my seven sons who are in the first group proceed; and from the second group, Megha, Āsūrya, and Pravaha shall likewise go. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.5.83)
The second group of those who move about is to be known as the Vātaskandha;
it is situated above the sun and below the moon, and it is indeed remembered as the Udvaha wind.
The third is the host of winds (vātaskandha), a group of sons who move about;
above Soma and below the stars is the fourth, which is Saṃvaha.
O Lord, the fourth group of my sons who roam is that which extends upwards from the bears as far as the planets, numbering twenty-four thousand.
The fifth group of sons wandering there is Vātaskandha;
and the sixth is Anuvaha, who is above the planets and the Ṛṣis.
There, as I was formerly wandering among my ancient hosts, I beheld the Vātaskandha,
which is proclaimed as the seventh region above the Ṛṣis and below the Ādhruva.
"Let my sons dwell there in the Vātaskandha wind-circulation;
let all these offspring of mine move about within it at various times."
"O Śatakratu, let these Maruts indeed have names derived from you; therefore, let the names of my sons be yours. BndP_2.5.90.
Know that through such various actions, there are indeed distinct [beings]:
Śakrajyotis, as well as Satya, and another, Satyajyotis.
Citrajyotis, Jyotiṣmat, Sutapas, and Caitya—this is declared to be the first group; now learn the second.
Ṛtajit and Satyajit, as well as Suṣeṇa and Senajit, Sutamitra, Amitra, and another, Suramitra.

Dhātṛ, Dhanada, Ugra, and likewise Bhīma.
And Varuṇa is the third; listen as they are described by me:
the Abhiyuktākṣikas and the Sāhvāyas are recorded as the [two] Gaṇas.
Such is this one, and likewise another; there are the Samaridruma, Vṛka, and Kṣaka; and also the Mitas, the Samitas, and the fifth group.
Such a man, and no other, who is of like mind,

Having performed sacrifices, they all praised [him], as did the other human tribes;

These forty-nine Maruts are indeed recorded by name;
they were then enumerated by both Diti and Śakra.
Having bestowed these names upon them, Diti said to Indra:
"Let these brothers, my dear sons, roam as the winds."
"And may my sons wander with the gods; may prosperity be yours.
Having heard those words of hers, the thousand-eyed Purandara [responded].
Having joined his palms in reverence, he said: "O Mother, let it be so;
all this that you have spoken shall come to pass, there is no doubt."
Such high-souled princes, esteemed by the world,
shall become sharers of your sacrifices along with the gods, O son.
Therefore, all those Maruts, the gods, and the excellent younger brothers of Indra,
as well as all the powerful sons of Diti, are to be known as immortals.
Having thus made their resolve, the mother and son went to the forest of asceticism;

Whoever hears or recites this auspicious account of the birth of the Maruts attains victory in debate and, moreover, becomes one who has realized the Self.

there were the sons of Danu, great Asuras renowned in their lineage."
Those leaders, headed by Vipracitti, possess inconceivable prowess.

Those who were mighty, swift, most devoted to Brahman, and maintainers of the sacred fires—

Dvimūrdhan and Śambara, as well as the powerful Śaṅku,

Ayomukha, Maghavan, Kapila, Vāmana, Maya, Marīci, Asipa, Mahāmāya, Aśirā, and Bhṛśin. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.6.5)
Vikṣobha, Suketu, Ketuvīrya, Śatāhvaya,

Thus, these Asuras—the Daiteyas and Dānavas—are so called; the Daityas are known as those who drank the soma, while the sons of Danu are those who did not drink it.

Śala and Śalabha, as well as Savyasācin;
Ilvala and Namuci, and Vātāpi together with Supuñjika.
Rahukalpa, Kālanābha, Bhauma, and Kanaka—

Prabhā was the daughter of Svarbhānu, Śacī was the daughter of Puloman,

Likewise, there were fourteen other cities belonging to the inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura—

Those who were invulnerable to the gods were slain by Savyasācin;

Māyāvī and Dundubhi, as well as his son Mahiṣa,

Araru, Balavṛtra, Vijvara, and likewise Vṛṣa;

most terrible ones were born to Vṛtra while he was fighting with Indra.
The Rākṣasas known as Bakas are said to be of great strength;
they are recorded as numbering one hundred thousand, and are followers of Mahendra.
All are knowers of Brahman, gentle, righteous, and subtle in form;

Krodhā gave birth to sons who were peerless and the best among singers:

Brahmacārī is the hundredfold [son], Suparṇa is the seventh,

Sūta said:

And Bhīmasena and Ugrasena, as well as Suparṇa and Varuṇa.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gomān, and likewise Sūryavarcas.
Patravān, Arkaparṇa, and likewise Prayuta.
Bhīma, Citraratha— who is renowned as the subduer of all living beings—

Miśrakeśī, as well as Asiparṇinī, Alambuṣā,

Adrikā, Lakṣmaṇā, Kṣemā, Divyā, Raṃbhā, Manobhavā,

Haṃsā, Sarasvatī, Sūtā, Kamalābhayā,

The hosts of Apsarases are renowned as fourteen meritorious groups:
the Āhṛtyas, the Śobhāvatyas, and likewise the Vegavatyas.
The Ūrjas, the Yuvatis, the Sruks, the Kuravas,
the Varhayas, the Amṛtas, the Mudās, the Mṛgavas, and the Rucas.

Then the youngest was indeed remembered as the third Arundhatī;

Akarṇa, Hastikarṇa, Pijara, and Aryaka,

Guhyaka, Śitikaṇṭha, Mahāpāda, and Mahāmukha—

At the end of the night, she gave birth to his second younger brother,

With hair standing upright and a greenish beard, firm as a rock in his build,

With reddish-brown upturned eyes, matted hair, and a body marked by the signs of the pairs;

Immediately upon being born, those two grew up through negligence and remained with bodies capable of employing weapons.

At birth, a son becomes equal to his mother, and a daughter likewise;

"All beings are indeed diverse, and likewise through the power of their renown.

Ten billion nāgas were stationed against each of those ten powers,
as were all the monkey armies stationed throughout the seven continents.
Residing in Kiṣkindhā, Vālin was the king, the scorcher of his enemies;
that one of great strength concealed [his body] in battle with his left arm.
Having steadied himself by bracing his sides and remaining absorbed in meditation,
he moved with the speed of a moment, touching the four corners of the earth.
Having become one whose movement was like that of mind or wind, Vālī, free from all impediment, traversed the southern, eastern, western, and northern oceans.
Having conquered Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out, that hero of great valor, Vālī,
released him from his arms as he was overwhelmed and deprived of consciousness.
And having placed him at the foot of a tree,
Balotkaṭa sprinkled him with very cold water from the soles of his feet up to his head.
Having restored him to consciousness,
the lord of monkeys stood in amazement and spoke to that lord of the Rākṣasas, Raṇacaṇḍa.
O King of Rākṣasas, you whose prowess is equal to that of Mahendra,
having conquered in battle the countless forces of Yama along with his ministers!
And Varuṇa, Kubera, Śaśin, and likewise Bhāskara;
the host of Maruts, as well as the Rudras, Ādityas, Aśvins, and Vasus.
The Daityas and Kālakeyas, the Dānavas of immense strength,
as well as the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Bhujaṅgas.
He likewise [saw] the foremost of birds, the planets, lunar mansions, and stars,
as well as bhūtas and piśācas, who were arrogant due to their increased strength.
How is it that you, possessing such qualities as these, have become equal to thought and wind in speed among hundreds and thousands of human kings?
O crusher of Mēru, you are capable [of this], being as difficult to conquer as Kṛtānta;
having routed all the heroes throughout the worlds, you are a conqueror of enemy cities.
Having leveled the mountains with his thunderbolt-like arrows and having agitated the seven oceans seven times, that great chariot-warrior [acted].
Unchanging, desiring victory, smiling, and powerful by nature,
he was overcome by me, who am weak, especially by a monkey.
"For what reason was one such as you—powerful and difficult to conquer—cursed?
O Brahmin, tell me by what cause you became a preeminent Rākṣasa? (Bṛhaddevatā 2.7.261)
"I grant you safety; have confidence, for you shall have no fear.
Having heard Vālin's words, the powerful Ten-necked one [replied].
Agitated by fear, he spoke these words preceded by conciliation:
"Without doubt, all the gods and asuras have been conquered by me in battle."
"Yet, I have never encountered such a powerful being anywhere;
therefore, I desire a friendship with you that is free from fear."
"O hero, may the field of battle never be yours;
thus addressed, Vālī said, 'These words of yours shall indeed come to pass.'"
Having established Vālī in his place according to the agreement, Rāvaṇa formerly departed for Laṅkā with his retinue, his inner soul filled with joy.
Having conquered the lord of the Rākṣasas at Puṣkara, the powerful Vālī seized many sacrificial offerings provided with food and drink.
With sacrificial fees increased by the hundreds and thousands,
he performed Agniṣṭomas, Aśvamedhas, Rājasūyas, and Nṛmedha sacrifices.
Having also performed many *sarvamedha* sacrifices, endowed with every kind of gift,
he then gratified the gods and the Lord of the Gods (*devendra*) with numerous offerings.
Having gratified Brahmā and offered oblations into the fire for many years,
he lived happily together with his younger brother Sugrīva.
Having protected the kingdom of the monkeys, he— fearless from any quarter,
devoted to Brahman, dedicated to the Supreme Brahman, a bridge of dharma, and intent on sacred rites— [ruled].

In sacrifice, invocation, giving, speed, or even prowess,
there is no one equal to Vālin, who wears a golden garland, in the three worlds.
Śāṃśapāyana said:
"Oh, how truly of great splendor is the mighty son of Mahendra,
Vālī— the performer of thousands of sacrifices, most difficult to conquer!"
O one of great wisdom, you have described the universal monarch Vālī; but tell us, O Lord, how the state of being Mārtaṇḍa is traditionally explained for the Sun—
explain its etymology according to the truth, O observer of noble vows.
Sūta said:
Then, while all beings were being created, Prajāpati himself [acted].
Then, having extracted that supreme splendor which is beyond the three worlds, those who were encompassed by great yoga caused it to enter the heart of Āditi.
The Blessed One first created an egg within her womb;
indeed, the powerful embryo developed there within that egg.
As Vardhamāna grew excessively, the gods became devoid of luster;
perceiving that the embryo was fashioned from all sides, they were stripped of their splendor.
Terrified, they said to Prajāpati: "O Lord, how will this come to pass for us?
The strength and splendor of this one who has been created will be superior."
"Alas, what will become of us? Truly we are lost forever, O eternal one, along with all beings here, both the stationary and the moving. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.7.281)
O best of the twice-born, those [powers] which you have established as splendor and strength within the *iḍā* will undoubtedly be consumed before long. (Bṛhaddevatā 2.7.282)
Therefore, reflect upon this and withdraw it, so that what may be for our welfare shall come to pass;
for the power and majesty of the Veda will otherwise instantly consume everything on all sides.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed Lord Prajāpati then cast [the seed] into the egg and infused power into it; thereafter, the infant was within the interior of the egg.
That which is without punishment they call strength; that which is splendor is considered the child.
But that [child] has emerged from the womb like a lump of dead matter.
Then Prajāpati, having seen that egg, split it in two;
having established himself upon the two halves, he beheld [the world] within one of them.
Having once lifted up that embryo, which was endowed with a state of weakness yet filled with splendor,
he rose and placed it upon the lap of Aditi.
And because he possesses the radiance of the sun and is indeed remembered as being within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa),
the Sun is therefore called Mārtaṇḍa by the wise.
And the Great-Grandfather fashioned for him even greater splendor;
those two shells of the cosmic egg are considered his supreme strength.
Having established them separately at his navel, the Lord gave them to Irāvatī;
desiring their birth, he caused them to enter her womb.
From Irāvatī were likewise born four world-renowned kings who were exceedingly powerful elephants, the mounts of the gods.
Then Airāvaṇa, Kumuda, Añjana, and Vāmana;
furthermore, I shall later describe them to you in detail.
He who is the preeminent one in this world, possessing immeasurable splendor,
is the Lord Sun himself, who illuminates all with his rays.
O twice-born ones, this world is without light, situated beyond the Lokāloka mountain;
it is entirely enveloped in external darkness, and that is its full extent in every respect.
O best of the twice-born, all this has been related by me exactly as it is,
having been heard from the venerable Vyāsa, the high-souled son of Parāśara.
In ancient times, this was indeed proclaimed by Sanatkumāra and formerly by Vāyu;
it was reflected upon in many ways by him, and subsequently by others individually.
Having heard this meritorious nectar of the Purāṇa, which accomplishes all goals,
Abhaya indeed wanders about, having passed through hundreds of other births.
Know that he in whose house this birth of Mārtaṇḍa is established,
or for whom the story of it is told, is not equal to anyone else.
And his children never die prematurely at any time;
for the sister of Ṛkṣa is the protection of even the most powerful monkey.
From the presence of Prajāpati, she gave birth to the king of bears, Jāmbavān, who was of great wisdom, illustrious, and protected by Śūra.
To him was born a daughter named Jāmbavatī from Vyāghrī;
that lotus-eyed girl was given by her father to Vāsudeva.
Likewise, other sons of great strength were born to the king of the bears:
Jayanta, Sarvajña, Mṛgarāj, Saṃkṛti, and Jaya.
Mārjāra, Balibāhu, Lakṣaṇajña, Śrutārthakṛt,
Bhoja, Rākṣasajit, Piśāca, and Vanagocara.
Śarabha, Śalabha, Vyāghra, and likewise Siṃha;
their sons and grandsons were by the hundreds and by the thousands.
The host of bears alone was worshipped by gods and dānavas;
and from Mārjāra were born the cats, his sons of great strength.
There were hundreds of thousands of teachers of the beasts of prey and other such creatures, all endowed with heroism and great majesty, including the śarabhas.
Those who eat spotted deer and the like, as well as mice and birds, are endowed with agility and the ability to leap; they cause the exhaustion of all living beings.
In villages, in groves of trees, in hollows and in caves,
in houses and within the inner chambers of houses— those who rely upon dwelling in homes [are thus described].
Those who move through various realms of existence are virtuous, dwelling in the domain of the village;
likewise, those who roam the forest remain established in their own true nature.
They roam at night, during the day, and at the twilights;
they have the color of dark clouds, or are tawny, squinting, and reddish-brown.
Some were black in color, others tawny, and still others variegated with various markings;
they were terrible, with claws and fangs as their weapons, and spoke with voices like those of peacocks.
Two sons were born to Saramā, Śyāma and Śabala; they were both heroes, extremely difficult to withstand, and are remembered as the attendants of Yama.
Their sons were invincible, accompanied by their own sons and grandsons;
thus the lineage of Śrutimāpta always remained among the Sārameyas.
Now, those of the same kind as that— terrible in form and possessed of great strength—
cause distress to all men of every caste.
Moreover, for those who hear this account of the birth of the fanged ones, or who cause it to be heard, their very dwelling shall be attached to a village.
He has no fear of fanged beasts, nor of thieves, nor from anything else;
it is the firm conclusion that his death occurs at that very moment.
He incurs neither bondage, nor birth in a wrong womb, nor a mixed caste;
he attains the dharma practiced by sages, which is based upon the forest-dweller's stage of life.
Endowed with divine wealth and strength,
he does not fall away from knowledge and is born among the hosts of gods.
Leopards, śarabhas, lions, tigers, blue hyenas, bears, wild cats, iron-colored beasts, monkeys, and likewise māyavas; 2,7.319.
These are considered the eleven races of monkeys;
the powerful King Vālī was the leader of them all.
In the conflicts between the gods and the asuras, he was the constant slayer of those who were ever-proud,
forcibly destroying the fierce and powerful asuras.
Having reflected upon the destruction of the arrogant power [of the demons],
the Great-Souled One designated this faction as the allies of Mahendra.

Then Bhauvana, having brought together the two halves of the sun’s egg and grasping them with his hands, sang the Rathantara hymn.
While the *sāman* was being chanted, that son of Bhuvana departed immediately;
he bestowed [the boon] upon Chadirāvatī for the sake of a son.
Because he was the son of Irāvatī, he is known as Airāvata;
and because he is the mount of the king of the gods, he is considered the foremost among the lords of elephants.
The glorious elephant Airāvata has four tusks and shines like a white cloud;
he is a golden-hued elephant with a single root-tusk as dark as collyrium.
Of that powerful Bhadra, who had six tusks and was indeed a royal mount, there were three sons: Añjana, Supratīka, and Vāmana.
Padma was the fourth, and Hastinī as well as Abhramu; these were the mighty elephants of the quarters, and Abhramu led them toward the waters.
Bhadra, Mṛga, Manda, and Saṃkīrṇa were his four sons;
for that Saṃkīrṇa was Añjana, who became the mount of Yama.
The elephant named Bhadra, who is well-proportioned, belongs to Apāmpati;
while the pale elephant named Mandapadma belongs to Ailavila.
The elephant Mṛgaśyāma was the mount of Pāvaka;
Padmottama, Padmāgulma, Vātagaja, and Gaja were his [other] elephants.
Capala and Ariṣṭa were his [names]; eight sons were born to him, and they were born endowed with noble disposition within his lineage.
Elephants with white young tusks and tawny eyes are considered to be rain-bringers;
now I shall describe the Sāmajā elephants and other types of elephants in their proper order.
From Rathantara were born two sons of equal renown, Kapila and Puṇḍarīka; by them were begotten Supratīka and Pramardana.
Elephants born of that lineage are known to be brave, with thick heads and tusks, as well as clean hair and nails; they are powerful and yet full of suspicion.
Puṣpadanta, Bṛhatsāman, Ṣaḍdanta, Padmapucchavat, and Tāmraparṇa were his sons; they moved in groups and possessed tusks.
And in his lineage are born elephants with long lips, handsome to behold,
with dark skin, mouths, and trunks, and with thick, elongated tusks.
Vāmadeva was born from Sāman as Añjana, who was dark-complexioned;
his wife was Aṅganā, and his two sons were Nīla and Vallakṣaṇa.
Fierce, with beautiful heads and necks, broad-chested, and swift,
those elephants born in his lineage are closely bound and exceedingly powerful.
Supratīka, however, attained a form resembling that of the Sāman through his transformation from a Vairūpa;
he had three sons: Prahārī, Sampāti, and Pṛthu.
In his lineage are born elephants that are tall, with long palates and lips, possessing well-proportioned hair, and yielding soft enjoyment.
From Añjanā was born Añjana; from him was born Jāñjanāvatī. Two sons were born to them as well, who are remembered as the Pramāthis.
With well-proportioned heads, resembling smooth clouds,
they were handsome, well-built, lotus-hued, and perfectly symmetrical.
In his lineage were born brave elephants with faces dejected from hunger;
and from Sāman, the son of Candra, was born Kumuda, who possessed the luster of a white lotus.
By Piṅgalā were born his two sons, Mahāpadma and Ūrmimālin— excellent, powerful, and highly intelligent, resembling mountains and clouds.
Know that those elephants born in his lineage are fond of elephant-combat;
in the war between the gods and the asuras, the gods took them up for the sake of victory.
Having accomplished their purpose, those previously mentioned were dismissed and departed in all directions;
and the gods bestowed well-disciplined sons born in their lineages.
From Aṅga came Lomapāda; from Sūtrakāra came Dvipa;
from Dvirada came Radanadvaya; from Hastin came Hasti; and from Kara came Karin.
He is a *vāraṇa* because he wards off [enemies], a *dantī* because of his tusks, and a *gaja* because of his trumpeting;
he is a *kuñjara* because of his movement through forest thickets (*kuñja*), and a *nāga* because that which is unapproachable (*nagamya*) belongs to him.
He goes intoxicated, thus he is a *mātaṅga*; he is known as a *dvipa* because he drinks with two [trunks];
he is a *sāmaja* because he is born from a *sāman*—such is the sequence of etymological definitions.
Indeed, it is said that their tongues were turned back due to the curse of Agni;
as was their lack of virility and their condition of having hidden testicles.
Both of these [conditions] among elephants are to be known as arising from the curses of gods;
[the same applies to] gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rakṣasas.
From those maidens were born various beings by the Dignāgas, and from them came elephants;
likewise, their origin, their birth, and the etymological explanation of their names [are described].
This should be known as the domain of these elephants; their king is Abhrama. For [the region] from the Kauśikī river to the ocean, and that which lies north of the Gaṅgā, belongs to them.
That region of Añjana with its single root is to be known as dense;
it lies both to the north of Vidhya and to the south of the Gaṅgā.
To the west of the Śakas at Gaṅgodbheda is the city of Supratīka;
and likewise, to the west of the Kāverīs is Utkala.
This forest of Vāmana is remembered as belonging to the son of Ekasūka;
moreover, there is another [forest] called Lauhitya, situated to the west of the ocean.
This forest of Padma was declared to be situated right by Anuparvata; there Bhūtā gave birth to the Bhūtas, who are the attendants of Rudra here.
Some were stout, some lean; some tall, some dwarfed, and some short;
some had drooping ears, some protruding lips, some long tongues, and some slender bellies.
Some had one eye and were deformed; some had pendulous buttocks and thick calves; some were blackish-white, others blue, and yet others white with red faces.
They were tawny, brindled, smoke-colored, and variegated;
their hair was like *muñja* grass, their body hair was visible, and they all wore sacred sacrificial threads.
Some had many heads and no feet, some had a single head, and others were headless;
they were fierce, hideous, and even two-tongued, having been thus fashioned.
They were shaven-headed and those with matted hair, as well as hunchbacks, the crooked, and dwarfs;
they frequented excellent lakes, oceans, mountains, and riverbanks.
Those with one ear, those with large ears, those with ears like spikes, and those without ears; those with fangs, those with claws, those without teeth, and those without tongues.
Some had one hand, some two hands, some three hands, and some were even handless; some had one foot, some two feet, some three feet, and some had many feet.
[He saw] great beings of great yoga, well-disposed and possessed of great power,
who have reached the state of being all-pervading and unimpeded, who possess the knowledge of Brahmā, and who can assume forms at will.
[He saw beings] who were terrible, cruel, and pure, those pure with liquor, and very righteous;
those with false tusks, large tongues, disheveled hair, and distorted faces.
Some had hands [for weapons], some had mouths [for weapons], some had heads [for weapons], and others carried skulls;
likewise, there were those armed with bows, those bearing mallets, and those carrying nooses and tridents.
They were naked or wore variegated garments, adorned with diverse garlands and ointments;
some ate food, others ate flesh, and likewise some drank wine while others drank soma.
Some are fierce night-stalkers who roam at twilight, while others are gentle beings who roam by day;
those night-stalkers are terrible, possessing a harsh touch.
With their minds directed toward the god Bhava as the Supreme, they all became detached;
for none of them had wives or sons, as they were all perpetual celibates.
Those hundreds of thousands of beings who are self-yogis are indeed the attendants of Bhava; all these are proclaimed to be Bhūtas.
And from Kapiśā, the Kūṣmāṇḍas were born again and again;
and through union with one of a tawny complexion, the Piśācas were produced.
Because they were tawny (kapiśa), they were called Piśācas, and all of them were eaters of raw flesh (piśitāśana);
the first sixteen pairs [of Manus] have passed, and the present one belongs to that lineage.
I shall declare them by name and according to their forms and lineage:
Chagala and Chagalā, as well as Vaktra and Vakramukhī.
Duṣpūra, Pūraṇa, Sūcī, Sūcīmukha,
Vipāda, Vipādī, Jvālā, and likewise Aṅgāraka.
Kumbhapātra and Kumbhī, Pratunda and Pratundikā,
Upavīra and Vīrā, as well as Ulūkhala and Ulūkhalī.
Akarmaka, Karmakī, Kuṣaṇḍa, and Kuṣaṇḍikā;
Pāṇipātra, Pāṇipātrī, Pāṃśu, and likewise Pāṃśumatī.
Nitunda and Nitundī, Nipuṇa and likewise Nipuṇī,
Bālāda and Keṣaṇādin, Praskanda and likewise Skandikā.
Sixteen hosts of sixteen Piśācas have been declared:
those with goat faces, those with sheep faces, Pūraṇa, and likewise Skandina.
The Vipādāṅgārikas, the Kumbhapātras, the Pratundakas,
the Upavīrolūkhalikas, the Arkamarkas, and the Kuṣaṇḍikas.
The Pāṃśavas, the Pāṇipatras, the Naitundas, the Nipuṇas,
and those who eat the remnants from the mouths of others— these sixteen are the Kalās.
Thus, these who were born are proclaimed as the Kūṣmāṇḍas;
they were Piśācas and Piśācīs, born together with their kinsmen.
Repulsive and of deformed appearance, with sons, grandsons,
and attendants— therefore, learn the characteristics of those Piśācas.
Those Piśācas have hair on their entire bodies, round eyes, fangs, and claws;
they are animals with limbs turned sideways, givers of harshness, and indeed have the faces of goats.
For those Kuṣaṇḍika-piśācas are indeed earless, hairless, and unclothed, wearing only skins; they are always fond of food and constantly crave meat.
Those Piśācas who have crooked limbs, hands, and feet, as well as crooked conduct and minds, should be known as the "crooked" ones; they move crookedly and can assume any form at will.
Those Piśācas have pendulous bellies, protruding mouths and noses, short bodies, heads, and arms; they are pot-bellied, eat sesame seeds, and are fond of blood.
Having the forms of monkeys, they are talkative and move by leaping;
those Piśācas are sun-worshippers, dwelling in trees and fond of eating food.
With arms upraised, hair standing on end, and eyes bulging from their sockets like their dwellings, those Piśācas shed dust from their limbs; indeed, they are made of dust.
Resembling female bees, afflicted with dry coughs and pains, clad in rags,
and acting as attendants, those Piśācas always have their abodes in cremation grounds.
With fixed eyes and large tongues, those wicked ones were licking their very mortars;
they wore mortars as ornaments and were streams of jewels.
Those Piśācas have their hands as their bowls; they feed upon the offerings set out for them.
They have heads as large as those of elephants and camels, with sunken and protruding calves.
Those Piśācas with pot-shaped heads consume food unseen;
yet others, subtle, hairy, and tawny, wander about both seen and unseen.
Those clever Piśācas wander here among the unrighteous;
their mouths are gaped open to their ears, and they have long eyebrows and thick noses.
Those Piśācas known as Pūraṇas are fond of empty dwellings;
they are stout, with their snouts pressed down by their hands and feet, short in stature, and their gaze fixed upon the ground.
Indeed, Piśācas attend upon the lying-in chamber from childhood;
they follow behind with their hands and feet, moving with the speed of the wind.
Those Piśācas are full of despair; in battle they feed on blood;
they are naked, homeless, with pendulous penises and testicles.
The Piśācas are the sons of Skanda; indeed, others subsist on leftovers and the like.
These sixteen classes are proclaimed to be the types of Piśācas.
Seeing such miserable piśācas,
Brahmā, out of compassion for those of small intellect, granted them a boon out of mercy.
Indeed, [the powers of] invisibility among living beings and the ability to assume any form at will,
as well as movement during both twilights, their respective abodes, and their means of livelihood.
Those houses which are broken, empty, and deficient in water; those which are dilapidated and inhabited by those who do not follow proper conduct.
The royal highways, side streets, pleasure gardens, and crossroads were unswept, unstrewn with offerings, and devoid of all human embellishment.
The gates, watchtowers, exits, and bridges;
the roads, rivers, and sacred fords; the sacred trees and the great highway.
Indeed, Piśācas are settled in all these places;
the gods have ordained that unrighteous people shall be their sustenance.
The castes and stages of life will become mixed; likewise, artisans and craftsmen will employ deceitful means, while thieves and betrayers of trust will abound.
With these and many other means, even those acquired through unjust means, rituals are undertaken; in such cases, the Piśācas are the presiding deities.
With honey, meat, and boiled rice; with curd, sesame flour, and spirituous liquors;

Black garments, incense, and inexhaustible flowers—

The *mīnāmīnā*, the *vṛttā*, the *parivṛttā*, and likewise the *anuvṛttā* are to be known; hear now of their offspring.
Sahasradaṃṣṭras, makaras, pāṭhīnas, timis,

The crocodiles are to be known as fourfold:

She produced many various transformations of aquatic creatures,

Likewise, she gave birth to transformations of mother-of-pearl, of cowries,

The transformations of Kālakaṇṭha and the metamorphoses of the leeches—

They say that even without a [visible] cause, there is generally an extensive lineage of species,
such as the various transformations born from moisture, according to how they come to be.
O twice-born ones, from bodies moistened by sweat arise lice, nits, and other such creatures;

Various swarms of ants, many-legged insects,
and the various forms of shells and stones, as well as pegs and coverings.
In this way, there are many terrestrial groups born from moisture,
just as [insects arise] from water heated by the summer sun or from raindrops.
These creatures do not all arise from the bodies of deer;
likewise, there are flies, slimy regions, and small partridges.
Blue lotuses and many other kinds of water-born flowers arise from impurity;
likewise, these living beings are born as aquatic creatures and as those born from sweat.
The insects known as kāśatoyajaka, nalada, bahupādaka,

This and other such groups are known as those born from water and sweat;
likewise, worms are produced from beans and mung beans by means of *śimbis*.
And from fruits such as those of the *bilva*, mango, and *pūga*, as well as from *mudga* beans, *panasa* fruits, and likewise from rice grains, living beings [are produced].
For indeed, they arise from hollows that have dried up after being filled, and they are born from other sources as well; for they do not always exist within those [sources] for long.
Living beings arise from horses and the like, as well as from poisons and such,
and they are likewise produced within cow dung that has been left for many days.
O Brahmins, worms are born from wood in every way,
and scorpions are born from the moisture of dried cow dung.
For from cows, buffaloes, and likewise other creatures,

And thus the Vaikārika [beings] are born, as well as herds of elephants,

Likewise, from pigeons, kurara-birds, and others, subtle thorns arise;

For the most part, the various species of mosquitoes and likewise bees dwell in this place, which is a mire of leftover water.
From the cows are born seven sons of the puttikās;

For this [state] is declared to be produced by the power of past karma when expressed in a compound;

Saramā gave birth to two sons, Dullolaka and Laloha.

These descendants of Kaśyapa, both stationary and moving, have been described;

This single part of one portion of creation has been described by me;

It is not possible to describe them in detail even in hundreds of years;
Aditi was of virtuous character, and Diti was likewise of powerful character.

Surabhi was devoted to austerity, Danu was devoted to illusion, Gandhaśīlā was likewise [devoted to her nature], Muni was devoted to [her own] state, and Krodhādhyāyanaśīlinī was devoted to wrathful meditation.

Overpowered by rajas, sattva, and tamas, both righteous and unrighteous,

Gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
piśācas, domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, and creeping plants.
Since these were born here among human women of the Dakṣa lineage,
they therefore recognize gods and others as being of human nature.
And since the entire origin of the gods occurs here among humans during all the Manvantaras, therefore human beings are indeed superior.
Human beings are indeed the achievers of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
from there, those of the downward stream (arvāk-srotas) arise, namely the gods and the asuras.
They are born again and again among human beings for the sake of accomplishing their tasks;
thus has this origin of the lineage been recounted in detail.
Of the gods and the asuras, as well as the gandharvas and apsarases;
of the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas; and of the suparṇas, uragas, and birds.
Of serpents and peacocks, and of medicinal herbs in every respect;
of worms, insects, moths, and small aquatic creatures.
For both animals and for illustrious Brahmins, this [work] is characterized by merit;

It should be constantly heard and grasped by those who are free from malice.

obtains abundant offspring and beloved wealth, and after death, attains a glorious state.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Descendants of Kaśyapa," in the third section (Upodghātapāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
