In all things established, whether moving or stationary.
Having consecrated their chiefs in positions of sovereignty, Prajāpati then proceeded to assign the kingdoms in due order.
He consecrated Soma in the sovereignty over the twice-born, the plants, and the constellations together with the planets, as well as over sacrifices and austerities.
He appointed Bṛhaspati, the lord of the Aṅgirases, as the leader of the Viśvedevas,
and he consecrated Kāvya as the sovereign of the Bhṛgus in their kingdom.
Furthermore, among the Ādityas he is Viṣṇu, among the Vasus he is Pāvaka,
among the Prajāpatis he is Dakṣa, and among the Maruts he is Vāsava.
Then [he saw] Prahrāda, the son of Diti, as the king of the Daityas;
Nārāyaṇa as the lord of the Sādhyas; and the bull-bannered Rudra as the lord of the Rudras.
Then he appointed Vipracitti as the king of the Dānavas,
Varuṇa as the king of the waters, and likewise Vaiśravaṇa as the king of kings.
He consecrated Yama, the son of Vivasvat, in the sovereignty over the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, the kings, wealth, and the ancestors.
Of all spirits and piśācas, he is Giriśa, the wielder of the trident;
of mountains, Himavat; and of rivers, the ocean.
Likewise, he consecrated Citraratha as the lord of the Gandharvas,
and he anointed Uccaiḥśravas as the king of horses.
Then [he saw] the tiger among beasts, the humped bull among cattle,
and Garuḍa, the best of all winged creatures who fly.
He is the foremost among the powerful, the wind that possesses strength equal to fragrances, the winds, the elemental spirits, and even those beings who are bodiless.
Of all fanged creatures, he appointed Śeṣa; of the nāgas, Vāsuki;
and of the reptiles, snakes, and pannagas, Takṣaka.
He consecrated Parjanya as one among the Ādityas, [the lord] of the oceans, the rivers, and the rain showered by the clouds.
And likewise Kāmadeva, the lord of all the hosts of Apsarases;
as well as the seasons, the months, and the monthly periods.
And [he knows] the movement of the Yakṣas, the adversaries, the Muhūrtas, the Parvans,
the measures of Kalās and Kāṣṭhās, as well as the two solstices (Ayana).
Then, in the eastern direction, he established the lord Saṃvatsara, renowned as the son of the pure-souled Prajāpati Virajas, as the master of calculation and yoga.
He consecrated his son Sudhanvan as king over the southern quarter of the world, belonging to the Prajāpati Kardama.
He consecrated his son named Śaṅkhapada as king;
likewise, he installed Acyuta, the son of Rajas, in the western quarter.
He consecrated the high-souled Ketumān as king,
and likewise Hiraṇyaroman as the son of Parjanya Prajāpati.
In the northern direction, he consecrated Durddharṣa’s son upon the throne;
he made Vaivasvata Manu the sovereign of human beings.
By them, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its cities—
is even today protected according to their respective regions through righteousness.
In the previous Svāyambhuva Manvantara, these kings were consecrated by Brahmā;
indeed, those who become Manus are likewise consecrated as kings.
For when the past Manvantaras have passed away, these kings have likewise gone;
thus, others are consecrated again when a new Manvantara arrives.
All the lords of the Manvantaras, both past and future, are remembered;
and by them, Pṛthu, the best of men, was consecrated in the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having procreated these sons for the sake of the continuity of his lineage, the powerful sovereign performed the rites according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Furthermore,
the illustrious lord Kaśyapa, the master of creatures, desiring a lineage, performed supreme austerity.
While the high-souled Kaśyapa was thus reflecting, "May these two sons be the founders of my lineage," [the two were born].
Afterwards, two sons of great splendor, Vatsāra and Asita, both speakers of Brahman, were manifested as partial incarnations (aṃśau) of Brahmā.
From Vatsara were born Nidhruva and Rebha, who was possessed of great majesty; Raibhya is to be known as the son of Rebha—now learn of the descendants of Nidhruva.
From Cyavana and Sukanyā, Sumedhas was born;
he was the father of Nidhruva, whose wife was the mother of Kuṇḍapāyin.
From Asita, upon Ekaparṇā, was born the most excellent of the Śāṇḍilyas, the illustrious and highly renowned Devala, who was most devoted to Brahman.
The Nidhruvas, Śāṇḍilas, and Raibhyas were his three lineages; the Kāśyapas, Vajrin and others, were his gods; and these creatures are his progeny.
When four yugas had passed during the eleventh Manvantara of the Lord,
and when that [period] was concluded, the Dvāpara age commenced.
The son of Marutta was Nariṣyanta; his son was Dama, it is said.
Rājyavardhana was his son, and Sudhṛti was his son; his son was Nara.
From him [Bandhumān] was born Kevala, and from him Vegavān;
from him was born Budha, whose son was the lord of the earth, Tṛṇabindu.
At the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, he became the third king. His daughter was Celavilā, born from the womb of Alambuṣā.
Born of her was Viśravas, the enhancer of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha;
and the preceptor of the gods, renowned for his vast fame, is celebrated as Bṛhaspati.
He married his daughter named Devavarṇinī,
as well as Puṣpotkaṭā and Vākā, the two daughters of Mālyavat.
Listen now to their offspring:
the fair-complexioned Kaikasī bore to Mālin the eldest son, Vaiśravaṇa.
Endowed with divine methods, the traditional methods of the sages, and the methods of the Vedas,
as well as the form of a Rākṣasa and the strength of an Asura.
He had three feet, a very large body, a thick head, and a great jaw;
he had eight tusks, a tawny beard, spike-like ears, and was deep red in color.
He had short arms and long forearms, was tawny-hued, and most terrifying;
he was the perfectly awakened one (saṃbuddha), endowed with the knowledge of retrogression, arisen from the source of existence.
Seeing him, his father himself said, "This is Kubera.
In the word *kubera*, the sound *ku* denotes contempt, while *bera* refers to the body. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.8.44)
Because of his deformed body, he was marked by that very name Kubera;
and because he was the offspring of Viśravas, he was like Viśravas himself due to their resemblance.
Therefore, he shall be known by the name Vaiśravaṇa;
and Kubera begot upon Ṛddhi the highly renowned Nalakūbara.
Kaikasī gave birth to four sons, of whom Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā, and Vibhīṣaṇa were the fourth.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Daśagrīva, Piṅgala, and Raktamūrdhaja—
four-footed, twenty-armed, massive-bodied, and possessed of great strength.
Resembling a collyrium made from the finest minerals, with fangs and a crimson neck,
he was endowed with the vital power of a *rākṣasa*, as well as with beauty and strength.
Rāvaṇa was one who caused others to cry out with his harsh emissions; yet he, Rāvaṇa, was the one who put them to flight, having conquered beings and their intellects with his very strides.
In a previous birth, Hiraṇyakaśipu was indeed Rāvaṇa;
that Rākṣasa remained king for thirteen cycles of four yugas.
O twice-born ones, those five crores of years are calculated by number as sixty-one million years, indeed reckoned as such.
And for sixty thousand years, that Rāvaṇa indeed kept the gods and the sages awake with his terrible deeds.
In the twenty-fourth Tretā Yuga, Rāvaṇa, through the exhaustion of his ascetic merit,
met his destruction along with his hosts upon encountering Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
Mahodara, Prahasta, Mahāpārśva,
and Khara were the sons of Puṣpotkaṭā, and Kumbhīnasī was their daughter.
Triśiras, Dūṣaṇa, Vidyujjihva along with the Rākṣasa,
and Kanyānupālikā are known as the offspring of Vākā.
Thus, these ten Rākṣasas of the Paulastya lineage were performers of cruel deeds;
all were of a terrible nature and difficult to overcome even by the gods.
All were heroes who had obtained boons, accompanied by their sons and grandsons;
this included all the Yakṣas as well as the Rākṣasas of Paulastya’s lineage.
Of the cruel Brahmarākṣasas of the lineages of Agastya and Viśvāmitra,
who are devoted to the study of the Vedas and practice ascetic vows and observances.
Among them, Aiḍaviḍa was the king; he was a descendant of Pulastya, left-eyed and tawny-hued.
The others, who were devoted to sacrifice, were indeed three groups of Rakṣasas.
The Yātudhānas, the Brahmadhānas, the Vārttas, and those who roam by day—
these four classes of night-stalkers are recorded by the sages.
The Paulastyas, the Nairṛtas, the Āgastyas, and likewise the Kauśikas—
these seven are indeed known as the clans of those Rākṣasas.
I shall describe their appearance as it is established by its very nature:
they have round eyes, are tawny-colored, possess massive bodies, and have large bellies.
They have eight tusks, ears like spikes, and their body hair stands erect;
they have hair reaching to their ears, are greenish-yellow, and their hair on the crown of the head is as thick as muñja grass and smoke-colored.
They had thick heads and a white luster, with short thighs and arms;
they had copper-colored faces, long tongues and lips, and drooping eyebrows and thick noses.
With blue limbs, red necks, deep-set eyes, and terrifying,
they possessed most dreadful voices and had large, protruding calves.
They are large-bodied with prominent noses, firm with a skeletal structure as solid as stone;
they are of fierce lineage, cruel, and generally performers of afflicted deeds.
Wearing earrings, armlets, and head-ornaments, and bearing crowns and turbans,
they were adorned with various jewels and decorated with diverse garlands, perfumes, and ointments.
They are known as eaters of grain, eaters of flesh, and even eaters of men;
this is recorded by the wise as the commonality of form among the Rākṣasas.
At that time, neither in strength, nor in intellect, nor in battle, nor in the employment of illusions, was he equal to them;
for all the sons of Pulaha were deer, as well as predatory beasts with fangs.
Beings, serpents, and piśācas, as well as sṛmaras and elephants;
monkeys, kinnaras, māyus, and likewise kiṃpuruṣas.
"Even previously, these descendants of Krodhavaśa were traversed by me;
for it is remembered that Kratu was childless during this Vaivasvata interval."
He remained there, having withdrawn his splendor along with his wives and sons;
now I shall proclaim the lineage of Atri, the third Prajāpati.
He had ten beautiful wives who were devoted to their husbands;
indeed, to Badrāśva by Ghṛtācī were born ten sons who were Apsarases.
Bhadrā, Śūdrā, Madrā, Śālabhā, Maladā,
Balā, and Halā— these seven are known as the Gocapalās.
Likewise, there were Tāmarasā and Ratnakūṭā;
among them, he who was the founder of the lineage was named Prabhākara.
When Sūrya was struck by Svarbhānu and falling from the great sky, he begot upon Madri a glorious son, Soma.
When this world was overwhelmed by darkness, he by whom light was set in motion—
may there be well-being for you— so addressed, the Sun himself fell here.
At the word of that Brahmarṣi, he did not fall from heaven to earth—
he who, of great ascetic power, established the most excellent lineages of the Atris.
He begot sons equal to himself through those [wives], for whom the gods had established the sacrifice that never ends.
The Lord, indeed, having been purified by great austerity, produced ten [sons] known as the Svastyātreyas, who were sages who had reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Among them, two were renowned for their fame, most devoted to Brahman, and possessed of great luster:
Datta was the eldest and highly esteemed, and Durvāsas was his younger brother.
Their youngest daughter was a weak woman who spoke of Brahman;
regarding this, the experts in ancient lore cite this verse from of old: BndP_2,8.83.
Those who know the Purāṇas regard Dattātreya— the high-souled son of Atri, whose nature is tranquil and free from blemish— as the very embodiment of Viṣṇu.
From his lineage four renowned clans were born upon the earth:
the Śyāvāśvas, the Mudgalas, the Vāgbhūtakas, and the Gavi-sthiras.
Among these, four of great power are remembered as the companions of the Atris:
Kāśyapa, Nārada, Parvata, and likewise Arundhatī.
Understand this: these were indeed born as the mind-born sons of Arundhatī;
Nārada then bestowed Arundhatī upon Vasiṣṭha.
In ancient times, during that Tārakāmaya war between the gods and the asuras, Nārada, who possessed great luster and had his vital energy drawn upward, [was affected] by the curse of Dakṣa.
When the world was struck by drought and agitated by the curse of the gods,
the wise Vasiṣṭha restored the subjects to life through his ascetic power.
Causing various medicinal herbs with many fruits and roots to grow,
he, out of compassion, revived them by means of that medicine.
Vasiṣṭha begot a son, Śakti, upon Arundhatī;
and Śakti begot Parāśara upon Adṛśyantī, his own daughter.
In the morning, the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana was born from Parāśara;
and from Dvaipāyana, Śuka, endowed with all virtues, was born of Araṇī.
These six sons of Śuka were born of Pīvarī:
Bhūriśravas, Prabhu, Śambhu, Kṛṣṇa, and Gaura as the fifth.
And Kanyā Kīrtimatī, firm in her vows and the mother of Yoga,
was the mother of Brahmadatta and the wife of Aṇuha.
The Śvetas, the Kṛṣṇas, the Pauras, the Śyāmas, the Dhūmras, the Caṇḍinas,
the Ūṣmādās, the Dārikas, the Nīlas, and the Parāśaras.
These eight lineages of the high-souled Parāśaras have been declared;
hereafter, learn from me the origin of Indrapramati.
From Vasiṣṭha and Kapiñjalī, the daughter of Ghṛtācī,
was born he who is known as Kuṇī and is called Indrapramati.
Vasu was the son born to Pṛthu’s daughter;
his son was Upamanyu, from whom these Aupamanyavas indeed descend.
The sons of Mitrāvaruṇa are renowned as the Kuṇḍineyas;
likewise, there are others known by the name Vasiṣṭhas, who trace their lineage to a single ṛṣi.
These eleven branches of the Vasiṣṭhas are indeed remembered;
thus these eight renowned sons of Brahmā are known as the mind-born (mānasa).
The brothers were most highly blessed, whose lineages remain established,
supporting these three worlds which are crowded with hosts of gods and celestial sages.
Their sons and grandsons, by the hundreds and thousands,
pervaded the three worlds just as the rays of the sun pervade all things.

Bṛhaspati said:

A vessel made of silver, or one coated with silver, is said to be the vessel for the ancestors; even a mere conversation about silver, or the sight of it, or its gift [is beneficial]. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 2.11.1)
It is said that giving shines eternally and inexhaustibly in heaven;
by this act of giving, virtuous sons indeed deliver their ancestors.
For in ancient times, the earth was milked by them into a vessel as their own offering (svadhā);
O dear one, whatever is given there by those kings becomes an inexhaustible offering.
The proximity to, the sight of, and the gift of a black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) destroy demons,
bestow Vedic luster, and rescue one's cattle and sons.
A vessel of gold or silver, a daughter’s son, a leather bag, sesame seeds—these are purifying objects; or else, the yoga of the triple staff (tridaṇḍī) itself.
This eternal, Vedic rite is the most excellent for the performance of ancestral offerings (śrāddha);
it increases longevity, fame, progeny, sovereignty, wisdom, and lineage.
In the south-eastern direction, one should designate the site for the altar;
it should be one cubit on all sides, square, and well-proportioned.
I shall duly describe the place ordained by the Pitṛs,
which bestows wealth, long life, health, and increases strength and complexion.
In that regard, three pits should be made for the bodies, and three staffs made of khadira wood, one cubit in length,
should be fashioned and adorned with silver.
Those pits, one span in length and four finger-breadths wide on all sides,
should be made facing east or south, stable and without holes.
Being pure, one should constantly purify oneself with water joined with a strainer;
likewise, purification may be performed with milk—either goat's or cow's—and indeed with water alone.
For this is indeed a constant gratification, and through it, eternal satisfaction arises for one who has mastery,
whether in this world or the next, being endowed with all desires.

Thus, he who, having bathed at the three daily junctures, worships the ancestors with self-restraint according to the rule and with the proper mantra, shall duly obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
On the new moon day, one should establish those pits, each four finger-breadths deep;
these sacrifices, numbering twenty-one, are that by which the three worlds are sustained.
For him there is nourishment, as well as sovereignty, long life, and progeny;
he shines with splendor in heaven and attains liberation in due course.
Indeed, one obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, which removes evil and is purifying;
for this fruit of the Ashvamedha is honored when consecrated by the twice-born.
Therefore, I shall declare the mantra, the nectar created by Brahmā,
for the gods, the ancestors, and the great yogis.
Salutations to Svāhā and to Svadhā; this indeed occurs eternally.
At the conclusion of the funeral rite (āddha) and at the end of the Śrāddha, one should always recite [this] three times.
Or, while offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one should recite this with a concentrated mind;
the ancestors will quickly arrive, and the Rākṣasas will flee.
Furthermore, this mantra pertaining to the ancestors saves [the deceased] at the three times when it is constantly recited during a śrāddha by self-restrained exponents of the Veda.
One who desires sovereignty should constantly recite this mantra without indolence;
it increases vigor, heroism, wealth, strength, blessings, longevity, and intelligence.
I shall proclaim the auspicious *Saptārcis*, which grants all desires, by means of which recitation and observance the ancestors are pleased. (BndP 2.11.22)
I always bow down to those ancestors of radiant splendor, both formless and embodied, who are meditative and possess the eye of yoga.
I bow to those bestowers of desires, who are the leaders of Indra and the others, as well as of the ten Marīcis, the seven Ṛṣis, and the Pitṛs.
And having paid homage to all those leaders of Manu and the others, as well as to the Sun and the Moon, and indeed to all those who possess the ancestors in the ritual injunctions.
With palms joined in reverence, I always pay homage to the constellations and the planets, to wind and fire, to the ancestors, and to heaven and earth.
I pay homage to the Grandfathers, the leaders of the celestial sages, who are honored by all the worlds and are the protectors of all living beings.
With palms joined in reverence, I perpetually bow down to Prajāpati, to the cows, to Agni, to Soma, to Yama, and to the Lords of Yoga.
Salutations to the seven groups of ancestors in the seven worlds;
and salutations indeed to the Self-Existent Brahmā, whose eye is yoga.
And this has been declared: it is served by the hosts of Brahman-sages, the seven-rayed one;
for it is supremely purifying, glorious, and the destroyer of diseases.
A man who is engaged in this rite obtains three boons;
on earth, the ancestors bestow food, long life, and sons.
Endowed with supreme devotion, full of faith, and having conquered his senses, he who,
being always composed, recites the Saptārcis mantra, [attains success].
He shall become the sole sovereign over the earth with its seven continents and oceans;
whatever food, whether solid or soft, is cooked in his house, [he shall enjoy].
One should never eat in that sanctuary without having first made an offering.
Hereafter, I shall describe in due order the vessels for the bali offerings.
Listen as I declare what fruit has been proclaimed for each:
through the *palāśa* one attains the splendor of Brahman, and through the *aśvattha* the realization of the Vasus.
Sovereignty over all beings is eternally ordained for the Plakṣa tree;
nourishment and progeny are found in the Nyagrodha, as are intelligence, wisdom, fortitude, and mindfulness.
A vessel made of *kāśmarī* wood is said to destroy disease and bring fame;
supreme good fortune in this world is found in one made of *mādhūka*.
One who performs [this rite] with vessels made of *phalagu* wood shall obtain all desires,
as well as supreme splendor and especially great renown, like that of the sun.
Likewise, one obtains Lakṣmī, as well as wisdom and constant longevity,
in fields, gardens, tanks, and indeed in all crops.
Parjanya rains incessantly into bamboo vessels;
he bestows the finest of food without remainder into these very excellent vessels.
He who, being devoted to that, always offers flowers, garlands, and fragrances to the ancestors, shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
One who is engaged in ritual action should always give; like the sun, he shines brilliantly, as does he who offers incense such as guggulu and other fragrances to the ancestors.
One devoted to the ancestors, having offered incense endowed with the quality of fragrance combined with honey and clarified butter, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
And he obtains excellent protections both here and in the hereafter;
thus, one should always, without sloth, give offerings to the ancestors.
He who, being self-restrained, always offers a lamp to the ancestors,
obtains from that a beautiful state and incomparable vision.
By means of splendor, fame, beauty, and strength,
he becomes renowned upon the earth and shines resplendent in the third heaven.
Surrounded by apsarases, he rejoices at the forefront of the celestial chariot with perfumes,
flowers, incense, and indeed with muttered prayers and oblations.
Having performed worship for the ancestors with fruits, roots, and prostrations while being self-restrained and pure,
one should afterwards honor the twice-born with an abundance of food.
At the times of the ancestral rites (śrāddha), the ancestors, having become like the wind, invariably enter into the most excellent twice-born; therefore, I say this to you.
One should honor the best of the twice-born with garments, gifts of jewels, as well as foods and drinks, and likewise with cows, horses, and villages.
The ancestors become pleased when the twice-born are honored;
therefore, one should always worship the twice-born with effort according to the prescribed rules.
O twice-born ones, with his right and left hands, he should perform the scraping;
thereafter, he should perform the sprinkling, remaining vigilant during the rite of śrāddha.
The wise man should offer to each individual a gift of darbha grass, funeral cakes (piṇḍas), various kinds of food, flowers, perfumes, and ornaments.
Having properly ground the collyrium for each of them in succession,
one should perform an anointing with three blades of *darbha* grass according to the prescribed rite.
And keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should offer excellent collyrium;
having knelt down, he should offer either a cloth or even a thread for all of them.

O twice-born one, the breaking, sprinkling, and likewise the scraping for the gods and ancestors should be performed once; however, for the ancestors alone, it is said that these three acts should be performed thrice.
Having given a single purifier (pavitra) with his hand to all the ancestors once each with the *caila* mantra, he should offer it to the *piṇḍas*, as well as a mirror and a piece of antelope skin.
Devoted to the ancestors, he should place three balls of food mixed with ghee and sesame seeds upon the ground,
having placed his left knee on the earth.
Having invoked the fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers,
they should diligently offer to the ancestors facing eastward by means of the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.
One should properly circumambulate the funeral cakes, moving from right to left without sloth,
using primarily various kinds of food, edibles, and diverse sorts of snacks.

Some men, however, desire that for the maternal grandfathers there should be three separate rice-balls (piṇḍas), offered in successive order, with the thumb pressed against them, which increase prosperity.
One should carefully offer the rice-balls between one's knees in the proper sequence,
using the left and right hands for support while reciting the mantra.
Saying "Homage to you, O fathers, for nourishment," one who is entirely free from sloth should first release the rice-ball with both hands toward the south.
Reciting thus with vigilance, "Obeisance to you, O Pitṛs,
who are gentle," he should, with his left hand placed over the right, attentively offer the water-oblation according to the sacred law.
Upon the line of the mortar, one should pour out a vessel of water and offer a new thread made of linen,
hemp, or cotton.
One should avoid garments made of bark-fiber, woven silk thread, and silk;
one should also avoid the skin of a yak at a sacrifice, even if it is from an unbleached cloth.
These do not please [the ancestors], and it would even be harmful for the donor;
however, they say that the collyrium from Trikakuda is always the best.
And from the black [sesame seeds], oil was carefully and well-protected;
likewise both sandalwood and agallochum, as well as tamāla, uśīra, and padmaka.
Guggulu incense is the best, as are turuṣka and white [incense];
white jasmine flowers are excellent, as are lotuses and water-lilies.
And there are forests entirely filled with fragrant flowers,
such as the *sumana*, the *nāḍī*, the *rūpikā*, and the *kurunda*.
In the performance of the Śrāddha rite, flowers should always be avoided—
those that are devoid of fragrance as well as those that have a pungent odor.
One who desires prosperity should always avoid certain flowers;
likewise, the twice-born, being self-restrained, should remain facing the north.
The sacrificer, facing the south, should perform the worship according to the rules;
facing them, he should carefully offer balls of *darbha* grass.
By this rite, the grandfathers are directly worshipped;
they become green, tawny, nourished, glossy, and composed.
The best kuśa grass for the purpose of a seat is remembered as being one cubit (ratni) in measure, with three blades spread out, and dark-blue at their bases.
Likewise, śyāmāka, nīvāra, and dūrvā grass have been declared [as suitable];
formerly, the Prajāpati Aśva was the most excellent among those possessed of fame.
His hairs fell to the ground and turned into kāśa grass;
therefore, kāśa grass, which is honored in rites for the ancestors, should always be offered.
One who desires prosperity should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍanirvapaṇa) upon them;
[thereby] offspring shall be endowed with nourishment, luster, wisdom, fame, and beauty.
They become eternally radiant, free from sin, and devoid of evil;
one should spread out the rice balls for the ancestors only once, facing the south.
Restrained, he should follow the prescribed rule, which he will also describe here:
neither dejected, nor angry, nor with a distracted mind, a man should perform the śrāddha with a concentrated mind, fixing his attention on a single point.
I shall destroy everything that is impure; all the gods and dānavas have been slain by me, as well as the rākṣasas, yakṣas, hosts of piśācas, and all the yātudhānas.

With this mantra, the wise man, self-restrained and desiring firm and auspicious intelligence, should once scratch that altar and, having gone toward the north, cast [the clod] twice toward the northeast.
Thus, all the Asuras here avoid that person by whom the ancestral mantra has been seen;
and in whatever place this mantra is recited, the Rākṣasas indeed avoid that place.
A man who looks upon impure and unwholesome kinds of food, or gives them even while touching them,
and who does not keep his hands pure— indeed, such a person does not enjoy the fruit of his actions.
Whoever always performs the Śrāddha rite daily according to this method,
whatever they desire in their mind, that very thing the ancestors shall grant them.
When the śrāddha has been performed in this manner with constant effort, the ancestors become joyful in mind and the rākṣasas become dejected.
In śrāddha rites, one must always avoid the milk of a Śūdra woman, as well as balvaja grass, stones, viraṇa grass, utu-vāla grass, and laḍva.
One should avoid such improper sacrifices as these, as well as grasses,
collyrium, ointments, perfumes, and likewise the wearing of sacred threads.
One shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice by [giving] *kāśa* grasses that have regrown;
for those *kāśa* grasses that have regrown are indeed like the feathers of a peacock and its tail-feathers.
Thus these ancestors are gods, and the gods are again the ancestors;
this is declared to be the mantra for those adorned with flowers and perfumes.
Having diligently brought forth the Dakṣiṇāgni for the purpose of the oblation,
or even the common worldly fire for other purposes, one should offer the sacrifice for the successful completion of the rite.
Then, having placed fuel sticks inside, the fire is kindled;
with a concentrated mind, one should lead the fire all around.
Svadhā to Agni Kavyavāha, the Aṅgiras;
again, svadhā to Soma Pitṛmat, the Aṅgiras. BndP 2.11.93.
"Yamāya vaivasvatāya svadhā namaḥ"—this is for Dhruva;
these are the oblation mantras for the three [deities] in their respective order.
One should always offer oblations to Agni on the south, likewise to Soma on the north,
and always to Vivasvat between these two.
The offering, the utterance of *svadhā*, as well as the scraping,
the fire-oblation, the recitation of mantras, the salutation, and especially the sprinkling— these are prescribed.
Likewise, when the fire has been well-kindled with abundant sacrificial fuel,
one should perform the application of collyrium and ointments, as well as the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
And this yields the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice when performed by the twice-born in a consecrated fire;
one should perform all the prescribed rites with diligent effort.
When the fire has been well-kindled with abundant fuel, and especially when it is smokeless and flickering, one should offer oblations for the successful accomplishment of the rite.
"Whether the sacrificial fire is unkindled or already kindled, the sacrificer who offers oblations therein shall become dull-witted in the hereafter; so indeed have we heard."
If the fire has little fuel, is dry, emits sparks in all directions,
and its flames and smoke move counter-clockwise, that fire leads to failure.
Where the earth is particularly foul-smelling, blue, or black, one should know that defeat is imminent.
Radiant, with a compacted crest, resembling ghee or collyrium,
smooth, and moving clockwise— such a fire portends the accomplishment of one's purpose.
He receives eternal worship from hosts of men and women;
by him, the ancestors and the sacred fires become worshipped and inexhaustible.
The leaves and fruits of the Bilva and Udumbara trees, as well as their fuel-sticks,
are especially great purifiers and sacred for use in a Śrāddha ceremony.
O best of the twice-born, this sacred rite is for the purification of births and actions;
the fruit that has been declared by me regarding the vessels in the performance of the śrāddha ceremony [is hereby concluded].
All that should be known in its entirety and in due order regarding the sacrificial fires;
having composed my mind, I shall indeed perform the rite pertaining to Agni.
Having been granted permission with the words "Do so" by those best of the twice-born,
he should take ghee in a vessel and offer it into the sacrificial fire.
The palāśa, plakṣa, nyagrodha, plakṣa, aśvattha, vikaṅkata, udumbara, bilva, candana, and those trees which are fit for sacrifice; BndP_2,11.109.
The Sarala, the Devadāru, the Śāla, and likewise the Kadira—
these trees are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel (samidh).
Village-grown trees, as well as thorny ones and whatever others are fit for sacrifice— these, when honored for the purpose of sacrificial fuel, act according to the word of the ancestors.
Listen as I describe the fruit of that rite for one who offers oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks of the ṣaṭphalī tree. BndP 2.11.112.
For that indeed yields inexhaustible fruit equal to the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), fulfilling all desires;
[the trees] śleṣmāntaka, naktamāla, kapittha, and likewise śālmali [are used].
The *nīpa*, the *vibhītaka*,
the *cirabilva*, as well as the *kola* and the *tiduka*, are all censured for use in the performance of *śrāddha* rites.
The *balvaja* and *kovidāra* trees are to be avoided on all sides;
one should also avoid those trees that serve as dwellings for birds.
One should likewise avoid all other such things that are unfit for sacrifice. Just as "svadhā" is the utterance for the mantras of the ancestors,
so too "svāhā" is prescribed for the deities in the performance of sacrificial rites.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Fuel-Sticks," in the Śrāddha-kalpa, within the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 11 //
Sūta said:
"The gods and the ancestors are traditionally held to be mutually dependent;
this is the rule of the Atharvans," so spoke Bṛhaspati.
One should first worship the ancestors and immediately thereafter the gods;
for even the gods worship the ancestors first with great effort.
The daughter of Dakṣa was renowned by the name Viśvā; ten sons known as the Viśvedevas were born to her from Dharma according to the sacred law.
Renowned throughout the three worlds and honored by all people,
those great-souled ones together performed intense and supreme penance.
Then, on a delightful peak of the Himalayas frequented by hosts of divine sages,
the Pitṛs, pleased with their pure minds, spoke to them.
"Choose a boon; we are pleased. What desire shall we grant you?"—when the ancestors had spoken thus, the Creator of the Three Worlds [replied].
Brahmā said: "O you of great splendor, I have been gratified by your asceticism. I am pleased by this penance; what desire shall I fulfill for you?"
Thus addressed then by Brahmā Viśvakarman,
they all together spoke to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
"May we have a share in this *śrāddha*; this is the boon we desire.
Then Brahmā, who is honored by the thirty gods, replied to them:
"Whatever boon you have desired shall indeed come to pass in this very way;
and your ancestors have likewise said 'So be it'—this is so, there is no doubt."
"We ourselves must eat whatever is seen here; for in this Śrāddha prepared by us, you indeed have the right to partake. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.12.11)
"This shall come to pass among men; we speak this as the truth:
he will honor you first with garlands, perfumes, and likewise with food. (12.12)
"Having first given [the offering] to you, he will then give it to us;
furthermore, our dismissal shall take place first, and that of the deity afterwards."
And the protection of the *śrāddha* and the two-fold rule for hospitality—
these pertain to the ritual acts for all beings, the deities, and the ancestors.
"When this has been done, all of this will truly come to pass.
Having thus granted them this boon, Brahmā, together with the hosts of the ancestors, [departed].
The God who bestows forgiveness and grace performed [the sacrifice] as it has been declared;
in the Veda, five great sacrifices are proclaimed for human beings.
A man should constantly perform these five great sacrifices;
learn now that place where donors shall abide.
He attains the state of Brahmā, which is fearless, free from passion, devoid of sorrow, and without pain or fatigue, honored by all the worlds.
These five [rites] must also be performed by a Śūdra, though devoid of mantras;
however, he who eats otherwise incurs a perpetual debt.
That evil-minded person who cooks for his own sake alone eats only debt;
therefore, a wise man should always perform the five great sacrifices.
One should offer the bali-oblation toward the north-east, and likewise at the edge of the water;
one should prepare the bali well and cast it up high, even higher than that.
One should offer the horn of a black antelope, cow’s urine, an oblation, and thread;
the funeral cake (piṇḍa) intended for those ancestors who are still living should be presented with these.
One should feed [the ancestors] with desirable food and edibles according to the prescribed rules;
for some desire that even those who are living be offered [food] with effort.
"For these high-souled ones are indeed the gods of gods and also the ancestors;
some teachers, however, desire that the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas) be performed afterwards."
"Bṛhaspati, who was skilled in the matters of dharma and artha, said: 'The worship of Brahmins must indeed be performed here constantly, even before [other rites].'"
One should first present the rice-balls (piṇḍas) and afterwards feed the Brahmins;
for the ancestors are great-souled beings whose nature is yoga and who are born of yoga.
These ancestors, established in yoga, cause the Soma to swell;
therefore, one who is pure and devoted to that [yoga] should offer rice-balls to those who are absorbed in yoga.
For this would be as if an oblation were offered directly to the ancestors themselves,
if one were to cause a thousand Brahmins established in yoga to consume it.
It would carry across the waters, like a boat, both the sacrificer and those who enjoy the fruit; yet where there is the promotion of the wicked and the humiliation of the virtuous, [it is lost].
A terrible punishment ordained by fate falls immediately upon him who,
having killed one of my own followers, provides a meal for a fool.
Abandoning the initial rite, the donor perishes therein;
therefore, a man seeking enjoyment should always first offer the funeral ball (piṇḍa) into the fire.
One desiring offspring should diligently offer the middle [portion] preceded by mantras;
one seeking supreme beauty should always offer it among the cows.
One who desires long life bestows wisdom, glory, and fame upon the waters,
and offers [these] to the crows.
Furthermore, seeking extreme delicacy, one offers [the food] to chickens;
thus has the fruit of offering the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa) been described.
One may also cause [the offering] to go into the sky or into the water, facing south;
for the sky is the station of the ancestors, and the southern direction is indeed their quarter.
Furthermore, some Brahmins said: "The extraction of the *piṇḍas* should come first;
once permitted by those Brahmins, let the object of desire be extracted. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.12.36)
Having set aside the first portion of all flowers, fruits, and edible foods, as well as from the cooked rice, one should offer them into the sacrificial fire.
Having offered into the fire food that is fit to be broken, as well as drinks, roots, and fruits, he should then offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) while facing south.
Having offered oblations to Vaivasvata and Soma and having presented the funeral cakes (piṇḍas),
one should perform the pouring of water and afterwards feed the Brahmins.
Then, O Brahmins, he should gradually satisfy them with foods and edibles according to his ability— succulent, warm, fragrant, and even with flavorful juices.
A man who attends upon [the deity] with one-pointed mind, being self-restrained, standing with palms joined in reverence,
devoted and full of faith, attains his desires.
The ancestors bestow upon them freedom from meanness, gratitude, courtesy, refined speech,
austerity, sacrifices, and charity.
Henceforth, listen as I declare to you the gentle rite prescribed in due order for when the twice-born have finished their meal.
Having sprinkled the ground and first cleared it, one who is devoted to the ancestors should then scatter the food according to the rite prescribed by rule.

Then, having caused the Brahmins to pronounce "svadhā" according to the rules and having given them abundant sacrificial fees, he should ask permission regarding the remnants of the food and honor those most excellent of the twice-born.
With palms joined in reverence and self-restrained, one should follow him and then bid him farewell.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Śrāddha," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Bṛhaspati said: "The immutable ancestors, who are yogic in nature, great-souled, free from sin, and possessed of great splendor, become pleased when honored even once."
And after death, for the sake of the heavenly world, they grant many desires upon earth;
or else, in those [states], they bestow grace so that liberation is attained in due course.
O gentle one, I shall describe those lakes and rivers,
as well as the sacred fords, the regions, the mountains, and the hermitages.
For Amarakaṇṭaka is ever meritorious in the three worlds;
it is the most excellent of mountains, holy, and frequented by those who have attained perfection and by sages.
There, in ancient times, the venerable Aṅgiras performed extremely difficult austerities for thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of years.
Where there is no passage for death, nor likewise for asuras or rākṣasas,
there shall be neither fear nor misfortune as long as the earth endures.
By his ascetic power and splendor, that best of mountains shines eternally upon the peak of Mālyavat like the Saṃvartaka fire.
Soft, fragrant, golden-hued, and pleasing to behold,
these peaceful blades known as *kuśa* grow along the southern bank of the Narmadā.
In ancient times, the illustrious and highly radiant Aṅgiras saw an excellent blade of kuśa grass intended for the strewing in the agnihotra sacrifice, which appeared like a staircase to heaven.
I shall describe the fruit that accrues to that wise man who, even once, offers rice-balls upon those Darbha grasses on Mount Marakaṇṭaka.
That śrāddha becomes inexhaustible and increases the satisfaction of the ancestors;
moreover, having reached that sacred field, they always attain invisibility [liberation].
There, on the auspicious festival days, the meritorious Jvālāsaras lake is seen;
and for beings pierced by arrows, there is the river Viśalyakaraṇī that removes the shafts.
O best of beautiful women, that pond has a clockwise whirlpool extending toward the southeast;
it is located on the western half of Kaliṅga, at the peak of the mighty Mālyavat mountain.
O best of sages, regarding that which is declared on earth as the supreme field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra), esteemed by both gods and daityas, Uśanas also sang this verse: BndP_2.13.14 //
Blessed are those men in the world who, having reached Amarakaṇṭaka,
being devoted to their ancestors, shall satisfy the manes with śrāddha offerings.
By performing austerities there, they will undoubtedly attain perfection;
even if worshipped but once, they shall go to heaven at Amarakaṇṭaka.
The Mahendra mountain is holy and delightful, frequented by Śakra;
having ascended it, one becomes purified, and a śrāddha performed there yields great fruit.
Having ascended the peak of Vailāṭa, his divine vision is activated;
invincible to all beings, he traverses the earth like a god.
By bathing at Saptagodāvara, Gokarṇa, and Tapovana,
and by giving gifts there, one shall thereafter obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having reached Dhūtapāpasthala, a man becomes purified by bathing there;
it was there that Rudra, the God of gods, Maheśvara, performed his ascetic penance.
This was established by the gods at Gokarṇa as a warning for atheists:
the *sāvitrī* of one who is not a Brahmin perishes if he recites it.
Having ascended the peak of the mountain, which is the abode of divine sages and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
you two shall then go from there to heaven.
It was adorned with divine sandalwood trees and other plants,
and from there, waters mixed with sandalwood flowed forth constantly.
From those two, a river flows forth by the name Tāmraparṇī;
it goes from the great region of Candana to the southern ocean.
And from that river Tāmra, as it is carried into the great ocean,
there arise conch shells and mother-of-pearl oysters, within which pearls are produced.
Having performed the water-rite accompanied by conch shells and pearls,
they are liberated from both mental afflictions and physical diseases and go to Amarāvatī.
According to the sacred scriptures, conch shells produced from sandalwood trees, or pearls,
deliver even ancestors who have committed sins.
At Candratīrtha, at Kumārī, at the source of the Kāverī,
at its confluence, at the holy sites of Śrīparvata, and likewise on Mount Vaikṛta;
On Mount Auśīra, where trees are seen gathered in one place—
palāśas, khadiras, bilvas, plakṣas, aśvatthas, and vikaṅkatas.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, it should be understood that this is pierced by two circles;
having abandoned his limbs in this place, a person quickly goes to Amarāvatī.
Rites performed at the sacred site of Śrīparvata, as well as on the Vaikṛta mountain,
succeed during the periods of cosmic manifestation and dissolution.
Indeed, even when poorly applied, [rites] toward the ancestors become well-applied;
for Narmadā, the daughter of the Pitṛs, is meritorious and the best among rivers.
In that sacred forest of Māṭhara, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, the ancestral offerings (śrāddha) bestowed there indeed become inexhaustible.
Having ascended that great mountain, they departed by means of invisibility;
and on the holy Vindhya mountain, they beheld the manifestation of dharma and adharma.
The wicked do not see the blade; the virtuous see the blade.
Therein, that blade is seen by some who have performed evil deeds.
On Kailāsa is the tank of Mataṅga, which destroys all sins;
having bathed in it, birds go to heaven, moving at will.
Likewise at the Śaurpāraka tīrtha, on Mount Pālamañjara,
at Pāṇḍukūpa, at the edge of the ocean, and similarly on the bank of Piṇḍāraka.
And having attained an inexhaustible resolve at Vimala, Vipāpa,
Śrīvṛkṣa, Citrakūṭa, and Jambūmārga, [one should worship] constantly.
On the holy mountain of Asita, the wise teacher of yoga,
there too, as well as at the Asitā, a faithful offering made constantly yields infinite merit.
At Puṣkara, a śrāddha offering and ascetic practice yield inexhaustible and great fruit;
one should point out that it is exactly the same at Mahodadhi and Prabhāsa.
In the Devikā river, there is a well named Vṛṣa, frequented by the Siddhas;
its waters always rise up at the sound of cattle.
I shall describe the fruit for him who offers a śrāddha on that day, which is always frequented by the lords of yoga and is excluded from all sins.
The Śrāddha performed there with all desired offerings becomes inexhaustible and truly gratifies the ancestors; for there exists the Jātavedas stone, which is Agni himself in his eternal form.
One should always perform ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and fire-rituals (*agnikārya*) there during the period of waning;
he who enters the fire there rejoices upon the vault of heaven.
That which is given there at Agniśānta, where he was born again, becomes inexhaustible;
likewise at the Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha and at the Pañcāśvamedhika Tīrtha.
There is no doubt that these sacrifices yield the fruits as they have been described;
the sacred ford known as Hayaśiras bestows boons immediately.
A śrāddha performed there is always inexhaustible, and the donor rejoices in heaven;
a śrāddha should be offered at Sunda and Nisunda, which destroys all sins.

It is declared that at that auspicious holy site of Jatuṅga, ancestral rites (śrāddha), recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and ascetic penances (tapas) become inexhaustible; one should constantly offer libations to the ancestors there.
Where the shadow of the celestial dwellers is always seen during the lunar phases,
there stands the Viraja tree, where what is given becomes inexhaustible upon the earth.
I shall describe the fruit for him who offers a śrāddha on that day, which is always frequented by the lords of yoga and is free from all sins.
By him, the ancestors are indeed always directly honored;
he shall be self-controlled in this world and, after death, is exalted in heaven.
There is generally the holy Madravā, as well as the lake named Śiva;
there also is the meritorious Vyāsasara and the divine Brahmahrada.
There is the holy mountain Ūrjjanta, where the abode of the Lords of Yoga is located;
right here is the sacred hermitage of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
The *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas as their heads, with the *Kapotas* and those called *Puṣpas*,
and the *Ākhyānas* as the fifth— these Vedas were indeed created by the Self-born One.
Having gone there, a twice-born man is released from sin by taking refuge in the fire;
furthermore, at these [sites], ancestral rites (śrāddha), recitation (japa), oblations (homa), and austerities (tapas) yield infinite results.
At the great tīrtha Puṇḍarīka, the fruit is equal to that of a white lotus;
at the Brahmatīrtha, O highly wise one, the fruit is equal to all sacrifices.
Likewise, there is merit at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean, as well as at Pañcanada-kṣaya,
at Virajā, and on Mount Madravā.
A śrāddha should be offered at Saptanada or especially at Mānasa,
as well as at Mahākūṭa, Ananta, and likewise at Mount Trikakuda.
And at twilight, a great marvel is seen upon the great river:
it does not approach one who lacks faith, yet it approaches him who is firm in his vows.
Resorting to that single [tree] alone at the time of sunset every day,
one should always offer a śrāddha there for the ancestors who desire imperishability.
There, a man is recognized as either one who has cultivated his self or one whose self is uncultivated;
that sacred ford (tīrtha) is named Svargamārgaprada, which immediately bestows boons.
But those rags which the Seven Sages cast off there and ascended to heaven can still be seen today, for they have become objects of enjoyment in the waters.
Having bathed in that most excellent sacred ford, a man attains heaven;
there is also a famous sanctuary there, frequented by the Siddhas, belonging to Nandin.
That form of Nandīśvara is not seen by those who lack proper conduct;
rather, golden pillars are seen like rays at the rising of the sun.
Having circumambulated them, they go joyfully to heaven;
and everywhere is Kurukṣetra, but especially so at the excellent holy ford (sutīrtha).
The merit of the high-souled Sanatkumāra, the lord of yoga, is proclaimed:
by giving sesame seeds to the ancestors, it indeed becomes eternally inexhaustible.
It has already been stated that the śrāddha performed in service of Dharmarāja is inexhaustible;
likewise, a śrāddha offered on the new moon day according to the prescribed rule and in due order [is likewise inexhaustible].
But for a man who has visited Kurukṣetra in particular,
having worshipped the ancestors there, he becomes free from debt toward his son.
At the confluence of the Sarasvatī, at Vinaśana, likewise at Plakṣapraśravaṇa,
at Vyāsatīrtha, at the Dṛṣadvatī, and especially at Tripalakṣa.
One who desires that their *śrāddha* be inexhaustible should perform it at the Devasaṃmohana, at the Oṃkāra-pavana,
at Śakrāvatāra on the Gaṅgā, and at Maināka, the best of mountains.
At the source of the Yamunā, one is liberated from all sins;
the presence of water that is both extremely hot and extremely cold is the sign of this.
Puṣyā is the auspicious sister of Yama and the daughter of Mārtaṇḍa;
there, a Śrāddha performed at all times is declared by the ancestors to be inexhaustible.
Having bathed in the Brahmatuṇḍa lake, a Brāhmaṇa becomes endowed with true compassion;
furthermore, a Śrāddha performed there, as well as recitations, burnt offerings, and austerities, yield infinite merit.
There, the great ascetic Vasiṣṭha moved about like an immovable pillar;
even today, trees with jewel-like bark are seen there.
But there, O Brahmin, the scale is seen as the indicator of dharma and adharma,
according to which the supreme fruit of the sacred fords is weighed by the wise.
The daughter of the Pitṛs, renowned as Gandhakālī through her yoga,
was born from the fourth portion of Brahmā in the lineage of Parāśara.
The wise and great sage will indeed divide the Veda into four parts;
she shall give birth to Vyāsa, the high-souled one of great yoga.
There is a lake named Acchodaka, where Acchodā was born;
she was born again in the womb of a fish due to a specific cause and by the power of destiny.
In her first hermitage, which is meritorious and frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds,
it is declared that even a Śrāddha offering given but once becomes inexhaustible.
The application of yoga at the river bestows simultaneous spiritual emergence;
likewise, at Kuberatuṅga and Vyāsatīrtha, it destroys all sins.
On the meritorious altar of Brahmā, a śrāddha offering is held to yield infinite results;
it is constantly frequented by the perfected ones who have mastered their selves.
But on the Nandā, to the northeast of the altar,
is the field of perfection (siddhikṣetra) frequented by the gods, reaching which one does not return.
The wise Mahādeva set foot upon the Mahālaya mountain out of compassion for all beings and as an example for the nihilists.
At Virajā, the Śrāddha is inexhaustible; it is likewise so at Mahālaya, and similarly at Nandā, at Virajā, and at Mahālaya.
In this world, they deliver themselves, as well as ten ancestors and ten descendants;
at Kākahrada, one gains the memory of past births, gold, and immeasurable splendor.
And there is the meritorious Kaumāra lake, protected by the coils of the Nāgas;
having bathed at Kumāratīrtha, a human being goes to the third heaven.
Having performed difficult penance on a single foot in the temple of the gods,
Umā’s husband remained blazing, without food, for a divine yuga.
At Umātunga, at Bhṛgutunga, at Brahmatunga, and at Mahālaya—
there, one who desires eternal imperishability should always offer śrāddha rites.
The ancestral rite (śrāddha) performed at Śālagrāma is always inexhaustible on every side;
yet, the evil deeds of those of undisciplined self are seen there in plain sight.
For there is a prohibition against the unrefined, and especially against the refined;
therein lies the holy Devahrada, where the pure Nāgarāja Brahmā resides.
For the virtuous always accept alms-food, whereas the wicked never do;
it is impossible for food to be consumed by snakes that are excessively inflamed with venom.
The Dharma is visibly seen at these two sacred fords:
at Kāravaṭī and Śāṇḍilyā, as well as in the cave of Vāmana.
Having gone there, one becomes purified; moreover, one's recitation, fire-offerings, austerity, meditation, and whatever other merit may exist, become truly inexhaustible.
Those who observe celibacy and maintain devotion to their guru for a hundred years,
and by bathing in whom— the best of rivers— there is liberation from sin; likewise,
Kumāradhārā is seen right there, where sin is destroyed.
The meditation seat of Vyāsa is still seen there even today;
it is a mountain situated to the northeast, near Kāntipurā.
There is a meritorious lotus pond there, guarded by hosts of Kirātas;
having bathed in it even once, O Brahmin, one obtains eternal desires.
Invisible to all beings, he traverses the earth like a god.
The great sacred site of Kāśyapa is known as Kālasarpis; one who desires imperishable merit should always offer funeral oblations there.
Whether in the Devadāru forest or at the Nidardana of Dhārā,
the sins shaken off by those of virtuous soul are seen to vanish.
At Prayāga on the Bhāgīrathī, it is said that [the merit] is eternally inexhaustible;
likewise at Kālañjara, Daśārṇa, Naimiṣa, and Kurujāṅgala.
In the city of Vārāṇasī, one should diligently offer the śrāddha;
for Yogeśvara is eternally present there, and what is given in that place becomes inexhaustible.

Having gone there, one becomes fulfilled by these acts; the *śrāddha* offering becomes truly inexhaustible, as do speed, fire-offerings (*homa*), meditation, and whatever other merit may be performed.
In the Lauhitya, at the Vaitaraṇī, and likewise on the Svargavedī,
that goddess is indeed seen at the edge of the ocean under various names.
At Gayā, at Dharmāraṇya, at the lake of Brahmā,
and likewise at Gṛdhravaṭa in Gayā, a śrāddha offering bestowed is of great fruit.
And snow falls there from all sides for five yojanas;
that forest is remembered as most sacred, within the holy hermitage of Bharata.
There, Mataṅga’s forest is seen by all human beings;
it was established as the entirety of Dharma, a demonstration for this world.
That meritorious Daṇḍaka forest, frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds,
contains the sacred ford known as Viśalyā, which is said to provide immediate evidence [of one's purity].
Likewise, those people who are doers of evil emerge from their state by means of scales, measures, and various treatises, as well as by means of auspicious planetary conjunctions.
Likewise, a śrāddha offered on the third lunar day at Pāda, at Nirādhāya, at Maṇḍala, at Mahāhrada, or at Kauśikī, yields great fruit.
The wise Mahādeva set his foot upon Muṇḍapṛṣṭha after performing intense and most difficult penance for many cycles of gods.
Even in a short time, a man devoted to dharma here casts off his evil quickly, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.
It generates joy for the perfected ones (siddhas) and strikes terror into the wicked;
it is guarded by exceedingly terrible, licking great serpents.
Known by the name Kanakanandī, it is a sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the world;
situated to the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, it is frequented by hosts of Brahmanical sages.
Having bathed there, human beings go to heaven in their own bodies;
furthermore, a funeral offering (śrāddha) performed there is declared to be eternally inexhaustible.
Then, having bathed there, a man redeems his body from the three debts;
having bathed in the Mānasa lake, he should thereafter perform the Śrāddha rite.
On the shore of that lake is a great temple of the God;
having climbed there and reciting prayers, one who has attained perfection (siddha) goes from there to heaven.
Having gone to Uttaramānasa, one attains unsurpassed success;
having bathed in that best of lakes, a great marvel is beheld.
Having descended from heaven, the highly fortunate goddess Gaṅgā, who flows through the three paths, shines resplendent in the intermediate space, having fallen from the foot of Viṣṇu.
There in the sky, a meritorious archway, resembling the sun and made of Jāmbūnada gold, was seen, as vast as the gateway to heaven.
Then, once again, there proceeds the *Sarvasāgaramaṇḍikā*,
which purifies all beings, especially those who possess knowledge of the Dharma.
The Candrabhāgā and the Siddhu, both originating from the auspicious Mānasa lake,
flow toward the western ocean as the divine and excellent river Sindhu.
There is a mountain named Himavat, adorned with various minerals;
it extends for many thousands of yojanas.
Crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas and frequented by hosts of divine seers,
there is a delightful lotus pond there known by the name Suṣumṇā.
One who bathes there lives for ten thousand years;
furthermore, a funeral offering (śrāddha) performed there becomes infinite and yields great prosperity.
And one should always deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants at a *śrāddha* ceremony;
the Himavat mountain is meritorious everywhere, and the Gaṅgā is meritorious on all sides.
All rivers flowing to the ocean and the oceans themselves are meritorious on every side;
a wise person should perform a śrāddha at such places and others like them.
Having bathed, offered oblations, and likewise given gifts, one indeed becomes pure on the ridges of mountains,
on their peaks, in mountain clefts, and in caves.
Likewise on the slopes and ridges of mountains, at waterfalls,
on the sandy banks of rivers, and similarly at their sources.
In the great ocean, in a cow-pen, at confluences, and in forests—
places that are well-swept, strewn with offerings, pleasant, and fragrant.
One should always perform the śrāddha according to the prescribed rules in these secluded houses that have been smeared with cow dung.
Having gone toward the south-eastern direction with the desire to accomplish all his wishes,
he should thus perform the *śrāddha* for all these [ancestors] without weariness.

But by means of these very things— performed in the proper place according to the rules prescribed for the three castes, and observed by those devoted to their respective social classes and stages of life— an intelligent person shall attain the perfection of Brahman.
By renouncing all, one attains the station of Kausasthāna and the worship of the ancestors;
thus the hero, full of faith and composed in mind, should visit the sacred fords.
Even one who has committed sin would be purified, how much more so one who performs virtuous deeds;
he shall not go to the womb of an animal, nor shall he be born in a wretched land.
A Brahmin indeed becomes a denizen of heaven and finds the means to liberation;
whereas one who lacks faith, whose life is devoted to evil, who is an atheist, and whose doubts are not severed [attains neither].
These five, being intent upon the cause, do not share in the fruits at other sacred sites;
at the sacred site of the Guru, there is supreme perfection—the highest state among all sacred sites.
Meditation is a supreme sacred ford; therefore, the eternal sacred ford of Brahman is superior even to fasting. Meditation is the withdrawal of the senses.
For by means of the very vital breaths bound by fasting, again and again,
having brought the prāṇa and apāna under control, the senses are likewise brought under control.
Having restrained the intellect within the mind, know that the withdrawal of all [senses] is the practice of pratyāhāra, which is undoubtedly the means to liberation.
The mind is the most formidable among the senses; it is the turning away from the intellect and other faculties.
Without food, it goes to its destruction; know that fasting is austerity.
When the intellect and the mind have been subdued, no other thought arises;
when all defects have been exhausted, and the senses themselves have been extinguished.
The pure self enters final nirvāṇa, like a fire that is without end,
having completely withdrawn from causes, from the qualities (guṇas), and from both the manifest and the unmanifest.
The knower of yoga, through his practice, unites the Knower of the Field with those [objects];
yet for him there is no movement or station anywhere, whether in the manifest or the unmanifest.
He is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; he abides as nothing at all.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Auspicious Places," in the Śrāddha-kalpa, within the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 13 //
Bṛhaspati said:
Hereafter I shall declare the fruits of all gifts,
as well as those things which are pure for the rite of Śrāddha and those which are to be avoided.
During a fall of snow, one may either bring forth snow from there or take it away;
this Agnihotra is conducive to long life, purifying, supreme, and beneficial.
One should avoid performing a śrāddha at night, except when there is a sighting of Rāhu;
indeed, upon seeing Rāhu, it should be performed immediately, even at the cost of one’s entire wealth.
He who does not perform [this rite] during an eclipse sinks like a cow in the mud;
but by performing it, he crosses over sin, just as a virtuous boat crosses the ocean.
The meat of the rhinoceros is the supreme oblation for both the Vaiśvadeva and the Soma rites;
yet, out of envy, we destroy the rhinoceros, sparing only its horn.
In ancient times, the husband of Śacī, while dwelling in the midst of the earth, drank Soma as the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, together with the high-souled Lord of the Gods who was acting as the sacrificer.
There, the *śyāmāka* grains were produced for the sake of his ancestors by Aparājita;
likewise, from his two nostrils, drops [of sweat] adhered, which became sugarcane.
Sugarcane is phlegmatic, cooling, unctuous, and sweet; likewise, offerings of śyāmāka grain and sugarcane fulfill all the desires of the ancestors.
He who performs the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice shall quickly attain success;
for two kinds of śyāmāka grain are prescribed for this sacrifice as it is remembered in tradition.
Because they were created by that very deity, they are remembered as imperishable:
the *prasātikās*, the *priyaṅgus*, the green *mudgas*, and likewise others.
These are also equal to śyāmāka grains in their qualities; however, black beans and sesame seeds are likewise excellent, while barley and śāli rice are the best of all.
Large barley, *niṣpāva* beans, as well as *madhūlikā*,
black grains, and red rice (*annaloha*) are to be censured in the rite of *śrāddha*.
Likewise, other *rājamāṣa* beans should be avoided with great effort;
so too *masūra* lentils, *puṇya* seeds, and *kusumbha*, the abode of prosperity.
During the rainy season, barley is always excellent, as are vṛṣaka and vāsaka;
likewise, bilva, āmalaka, mṛdvīkā, panasa, āmrātaka, and pomegranate.
Tavaśola, yātākṣaudra, dates, mangoes, khaśeru, kovidāra, tālakanda, and likewise lotus root; Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 2.14.15.
Tamāla, śatakanda, madvasūcā, antakāndikī, kāleya, kālaśāka, bhūripūrṇā, and suvarcalā.
Māṃsākṣa, duviśāka, bubucetā, and likewise kuru;
kaphālaka, kaṇā, drākṣā, lakuca, and cocam as well.
The gourd, the neck-vessel, the vīra, that which is called the honey-karkandhū,
the vaikaṅkata, the coconut-born, the śṛṅga, and the pakarūṣaka.
Long pepper, black pepper, pointed gourd, the fruit of the *bṛhatī*,
fragrant meat, and all astringent decoctions as well.
And other such excellent and sweet items should be offered here, as well as ginger and long-rooted ginger.
The bamboo, the karīra fruit, the surasa plant, the sarjaka tree, and bhūstṛṇa grass—
these I shall declare as things to be always avoided in the performance of the śrāddha rite.
Garlic, leeks, as well as water from puddles,
and other inferior things such as *karambha* and the like, which are deficient in taste and smell.
The things to be avoided in the rite of *śrāddha* and the reason for this will now be explained.
Long ago, in the war between the gods and the asuras, Bali was defeated by the gods.
From his body, mangled by arrows, drops of blood fell;
from those, all these things, such as garlic and the like, were born in every way.
Likewise, red exudations, salts from saline soil,
and women who are menstruating are to be avoided during the performance of a śrāddha rite.
Where the water is foul-smelling, frothy, or from a mere puddle, where the cow does not find satisfaction, or that which is hidden at night; [in such places one should not perform the offering].
A wise person should avoid the milk of sheep, camels, and all animals with uncloven hooves, as well as that of buffaloes and yaks.
Henceforth, I shall declare with diligence those regions that must be avoided,
as well as those by whom the *śrāddha* should not be witnessed, and the entirety of purity and impurity.
One should perform the śrāddha with faith using forest roots and fruits as food;
thus one attains royal status and indeed imperishable heaven. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.14.29)
In the performance of the śrāddha rite, one should avoid ground that is unpleasant to the ear, crowded, frequented by living beings, turbid, or foul-smelling.
The rivers extending as far as the ocean have their gateway to the southeast;
one should avoid the entire region of Triśaṅku for twelve yojanas.
To the north of the Mahānadī and to the south of the Vaikaṭa [mountain],
the regions known as Triśaṅku are indeed to be avoided for the performance of śrāddha rites.
The Kāraskaras, Kaliṅgas, and those regions further north of the Sidhu river—
countries where the duties of the stages of life have perished— should be avoided with great effort.
Naked ascetics and others should not see the Śrāddha rite as it is being performed;
for if seen by these, [the offerings] do not reach the fathers and grandfathers. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 2.14.34)
Śaṃyu said:
"O Blessed One, please explain correctly to me, who am asking you, about those who are naked and the rest.
Bṛhaspati replied:
For all beings indeed, the triple Veda is traditionally held to be a covering.
Those who abandon her out of delusion are indeed people such as the naked ones (the Jainas) and others;
for in her the Bull (Dharma) dissolves, and upon the Bull he stands without support.
He who, having abandoned the Bull, seeks liberation elsewhere— indeed,
he who does not properly perceive that Bull, which is the Vedic stage of life (āśrama).
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, there is no doubt that he is such;
for in ancient times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, the asuras were likewise defeated.
O dear one, those heretics have indeed been created; their progeny is thus produced:
the Vṛddha-śrāvakas, the Nirgranthas, the Śākyas, the Jīvakas, and the Kārpaṭas.
Those who do not follow the Dharma are indeed people such as the naked ones;
he who is a twice-born man who is naked is vainly matted-haired, vainly shaven-headed, and vainly naked.
Those who observe vows in vain, those who mutter prayers in vain—they are indeed people such as the naked ones (nagnas) and others;
they constantly transgress the dharma of their lineage, and their livelihoods and wives are in vain.
These directions for performing rites are proclaimed to be evil paths;
indeed, a śrāddha offered or witnessed by these goes to the Dānavas.
A killer of a Brahmin, an ungrateful person, an atheist, one who violates the teacher’s bed,
a robber, and a cruel man— one should exclude these from the description.
One should avoid all those fallen ones of cruel deeds who speak ill during disputes between deities and sages.
He who reviles the gods, the brahmins, and the sacred tradition (āmnāya),
as well as the asuras and the yātudhānas, goes to them once he has seen them.
The Kṛta Yuga is declared to belong to the Brāhmaṇas; the Tretā is the age of the Kṣatriyas;
they say the Dvāpara belongs to the Vaiśyas; and the Kali Yuga is remembered as that of the Śūdras.
In the Kṛta age the ancestors were worshipped, and likewise the gods in the Tretā;
in the Dvāpara age there were constant wars, and in the Kali age there are heretics.
A cock, a village pig, and a dog— when driven away by contempt—
destroy a *śrāddha* ceremony entirely by their mere sight.
It must never be seen by those mixed with dogs or pigs, nor by those afflicted with chronic diseases, nor by the fallen (patita) or the impure (malina).

If these [persons] should look upon food that is unfit for offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya), it must be discarded by those intent on the primary purpose; however, the consecration (saṃskāra) itself would serve as a remedy against calamity.
One should avoid sacrificial offerings that have become congealed even before they are used;
however, sprinkling with consecrated water is prescribed for them.
Or one should perform a protective rite using white mustard seeds and black sesame seeds,
or else diligently seek the sight of Jupiter, the Sun, fire, and water.

Food that has been placed upon a seat, that which has been stepped over by the feet, that which has been looked upon by impure moving creatures, that which is dry, and that which is stale; ||| BndP_2,14.53 |||
That which is undercooked, burnt, or licked by fire;
that which contains grit, insects, stones, or hair; and that which has been brought forth [from the fire] improperly—[these are forbidden].
Oil-cakes, curdled milk, as well as sesame, barley, and the like,
and whatever foods have been prepared that have been seasoned with visible salt— [these are forbidden].
Having seen those who are afflicted by such defects, as well as those struck by calamity,
and those who have shaken off [their impurity] with a cloth— these are to be avoided at the rite of Śrāddha.
There are some who, out of pride in their own learning, act in contradiction to the Vedas;
they are called non-sacrificers, and they perish like dust.
One should avoid curd with vegetables as food, as well as anything devoid of medicinal herbs; one should exclude eggplant from the śrāddha, as well as all fermented liquors,
and likewise rock salt and salt produced from Lake Mānasa.
For these two are indeed the supreme purifiers;
even when they have been twisted [into loops], one should cast them into the fire and, having diligently washed both hands, take them up.
One should likewise cause the water to reach the head; that is indeed remembered as the *brahmatīrtha*.
The sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of ritual materials (*dravya*) must be performed, and likewise their immersion (*avapana*) again.
Having placed them there, one should sprinkle them with water; likewise, one should deposit stones, roots, fruits, sugarcane, ropes, and even hides within that dwelling.
For all items made of split bamboo, purification is prescribed as before;
likewise, there is the scraping away of impurities for objects made of ivory, bone, wood, and horn.
For all objects made of clay, re-burning is prescribed;
likewise for gems, pearls, corals, and all things produced from water.
Furthermore, the cleansing of all children and of all sheep should be performed using a paste of white mustard seeds or a paste of sesame seeds.
For all bipeds, purification is prescribed with earth and water;
however, at the beginning and end of purificatory acts, the rule is that washing must be done with water alone.
Likewise, it is declared that for cotton cloths, purification is by means of ashes;
and for fruits, flowers, and leaves, immersion in water is prescribed.
Sprinkling with water, smearing the ground, scraping the earth,
pouring [water], the treading of cows, burning, and digging— these are held to be the means of purification for the ground.
For one who has departed from a village on a journey, the earth is purified by the wind;
for men and quadrupeds, purification is prescribed by means of earth.
In this very way, the supreme rule for purifications has been declared;
now listen as I speak that which has not yet been specified.

In the morning, having gone from the house toward the southwest for a distance of about one arrow-shot, he should indeed void his excrement while covering his head; he must never touch his head with his hand.
Having well-covered the ground in a secluded spot with white grass, straw, leaves, or bamboo slips, and having concealed the earth, [he should proceed].
Having drawn out water and taken earth, remaining silent,
one should perform the rite facing north during the day, and indeed facing south at night.
Then, having taken the water-pot with his right hand,
he should perform purification with his left hand by applying three applications of clay to the anus.
One should also slowly apply ten [applications] to the left hand in succession,
or alternatively, one may apply seven applications of clay to both hands together.
Having washed his feet with earth and having sipped water according to the rule,
[he should know that] the three beginning with the waters— namely the deities of the Sun, Fire, and Wind— are present.
He should always keep two flawless water-pots close at hand;
he should perform the washing of his feet properly with water alone, as if it were the water of the *haṃsa*.
There shall be a second sipping of water (ācamana) for the rite of the gods, and another thereafter;
furthermore, one who has been released from a defilement must observe a fast for three nights, as prescribed by the authorities.
For distant [offenses], a difficult penance is prescribed;
having touched a dog or an outcaste (śvapāka), one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.

Having touched human bones, one must fast for three nights for the sake of purification; if they are smeared with fat, it is said that one night is sufficient, otherwise [if not smeared], it is the same.
The Kāraskaras, the Kaliṅgas, as well as the Andhras, Śabaras, and others,
having drunk the water from the bow and having reached the Dvāpara Yuga, attained the state of being ashes on the earth.
A man [should avoid] the region up to the northern limit of the ocean, as well as the northern interior,
and whatever sinful lands there may be inhabited by people of evil deeds.
Indeed, for those who have been shunned by the learned Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
no sin attaches to them as they proceed, driven by passion and delusion.
Having traveled to impure regions, one incurs the full measure of sin;
but by ascending Bhṛgutuṅga and going to the holy Sarasvatī, one attains merit.
And the delightful river Āpagā, the goddess Gaṅgā, the great river,
those rivers originating from the Himavat, and whatever other rivers are praised by the sages.
Having gone to all the lakes, sacred fords, rivers, and springs,
one is liberated from sins and attains heaven eternally.
Impurity on account of death or birth is declared to last ten nights for a Brāhmaṇa,
while for a Kṣatriya it is ordained to be twelve days.
For a Vaiśya it is half a month, and for a Śūdra it is indeed one month;
however, a woman in her courses becomes pure after four nights for all castes.
Having touched a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a dog, an outcaste (antāvasāyin),
those who are naked, and those who carry the dead, purification is prescribed.
Having bathed with his clothes on and purified himself with twelve applications of clay, the twice-born becomes clean;
this same purification applies likewise after sexual intercourse and vomiting.
A man should wash his hands with clay and perform purification;
then, having bathed and washed [himself] with water, he should again wash his hands with clay.

Having performed the purification of the twelve extremities three times, it should be as if there were an actual smearing; such is the rule for purification seen to be required at all times in all ritual acts.
One should apply three lumps of earth for each foot and for the rinsing of the feet;
this is the purification in the forest. Hereafter, I shall describe that which pertains to village life.
There are fifteen types of impure earth, particularly for the hands and other limbs;
one should apply an excess of earth, and at the end of each application, one should likewise wash with water.
In these cases, purification with water is prescribed in its entirety;
likewise, one who has covered his throat or head, or even one who has gone onto a road or a marketplace [is purified].
Without having performed the purification of the feet, one remains impure even if one has sipped water (ācamana);
having washed the vessel and set it aside, one should sip water and then perform the sprinkling (abhyukṣaṇa).
One should then perform sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) in that same manner for other substances;
likewise, one should perform sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for flowers and the like, for grasses, and for sacrificial oblations (*havis*).
After placing aside materials that have been purchased, one should sprinkle them with water;
O faithful one, one should not touch anything that has not been consecrated by sprinkling, whether for a rite to the ancestors or for a rite to the gods.
One should bring the materials with the left hand and set them down with the right;
