however, in all śrāddha rites, the sacrificer should perform the collection in a secluded place.
There may be a reversal regarding the remnants of food, as well as in rites for the gods and the ancestors;
with the right hand, however, one should touch the southern altar.
With both hands alone, one should likewise perform the *vikara* for the gods and the ancestors,
as well as the discharge of semen during dreams, and likewise the voiding of urine and feces.

Likewise after spitting, after anointing the body, after eating, after changing one's clothes, upon touching those who are impure from food, and likewise after pouring water over the feet; ||| BndP_2,14.101 |||
Nor should one speak with someone who is impure from food remnants, nor with one who has not yet purified himself after eating;
and in all cases of doubt, as well as when the topknot is untied, [one must likewise refrain].
Without the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), one would touch that [water] in vain;
likewise upon touching a camel or a donkey, or upon seeing those who speak what should not be spoken.
Having touched it with the tongue, or likewise while it is stuck [to the teeth], or making a sound with the fingers, or looking at what has fallen [on the ground]. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya 2.14.104)
If one who is standing should sip water out of delusion, even though he has sipped, he remains impure;
therefore, having sat down in a clean place, self-restrained and facing either the east or the north, one should perform the rite.
Having washed his feet and hands, he should touch water while keeping his hands between his knees;
being pure, restrained, and well-composed, he should drink water three times.
One should perform the wiping twice and then the sprinkling once;
likewise, one should sprinkle the apertures, the head, oneself, the hands, and the feet.
One should then sprinkle whatever has been examined for him;
thus, for one who has sipped water in this manner, the Vedas, sacrifices, and austerities [are perfected].
Indeed, acts of giving and the observance of vows become fruitful only for him who performs rituals here with a pure mind;
but for the nihilist who acts out of delusion, they are fruitless.
For his actions—whether pure in speech, body, or intellect, untouched and blameless—are indeed in vain; of this there is no doubt.
These are to be known as pure; in the opposite case, they are impure.
Mind, speech, body, fire, time, and even the act of scraping [the ground]—these are the factors to be considered.
The proclamation of purifications is either always ignorance itself;
for he who, out of delusion, acts otherwise than this, brings about a confusion of purification.
One who lacks faith in purity undoubtedly goes to the state of a Piśāca or a Yātudhāna; indeed, such a person is born among the Mleccha tribes. (14.113)
Even a man who has not performed sacrifices, who is sinful, or even one born as an animal,
shall become a dweller in heaven if he practices purification for the sake of liberation.
For the gods are indeed desirous of purity; this has been declared by the gods themselves:
the deities always avoid those who are loathsome and impure.
Those who perform auspicious deeds practice the three purifications according to the rule;
[he] comes to one who is devoted to Brahman, who is intent on begging, who is endowed with purity, and who is wise.
O twice-born ones, to him who is devoted to his father, self-controlled, and compassionate,
the gods and the ancestors— who increase one’s prosperity—
bestow the desires he longs for in his mind, even those most excellent in the three worlds.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Rules for Impurity," in the Śrāddha-kalpa, within the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the Middle Portion of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as proclaimed by Vāyu. 14.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, oh, blessed is this ritual for the Śrāddha ceremony proclaimed by you!
We have heard the rituals for the Śrāddha as they were proclaimed by the ancient seers."
For this has been described in great detail,
O highly wise one, according to the complete opinion of that seer, without exception.
Sūta said:
O brahmins, I shall proclaim to you that which was the opinion of that most fortunate ṛṣi regarding the śrāddha; listen to that from me in detail.
I have previously described the ancestral rite (śrāddha) and the procedure for the performance of that rite;
now I shall declare the remaining portion, which is the examination of the Brahmins.
Brahmins are never to be scrutinized, for they are the supreme purifiers;
indeed, it is heard that such examination is strictly required only in matters concerning the gods and the ancestors.
One in whom faults may be observed should indeed be avoided in all affairs; or, by observing him through living together, one should know his character and avoid him with great effort.
A wise man should not examine an unknown twice-born man at a śrāddha;
for perfected beings wander this earth in the form of brahmins.
Therefore, one should go out with palms joined in reverence to meet a guest who is approaching;
one should honor him with the arghya and pādya offerings, as well as with ointments and food.
These gods, who are always masters of yoga, move about in various forms across the vast earth bounded by the oceans, enjoining all creatures to righteousness.
Therefore, a self-controlled man should always give gifts after having duly honored his guest.
Now I shall describe the side dishes (vyañjanas) as well as their respective fruits.
One may indeed obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma through milk, and likewise the fruit of the Uktha through milk-rice;
with clarified butter one obtains the fruit of the Ṣoḍaśin and Satra, and likewise the fruit of the Atirātra through honey.

Likewise, a man who has faith shall indeed obtain all his desires; he who feeds the Brahmins enjoys the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice, which grants all goals and provides hospitality to all Brahmins, eternally.
But him who disregards a guest arrived at a funeral rite (śrāddha) or even at a rite for the gods (daiva),
the gods indeed cast out, just as Parāvasu was struck down.
The gods and the ancestors themselves, having entered that very hidden twice-born one, will deliver the brahmin for the sake of showing grace to the worlds.
If unhonored, he burns; if honored, he bestows desires.
Therefore, one should always honor a guest even with one's entire possessions.
A forest-dweller, a householder, one who has arrived as a guest of the virtuous,
a Vālakhilya, and an ascetic should always be recognized as a guest.
One who has arrived unexpectedly is a guest (*atithi*) who moves about seeking food; he is called *apāvaka*.
He is declared to be the guest of guests, and that is said to be the yoga of the guest.
Neither one who lacks vows, nor one who is of mixed caste, nor one who is ignorant, nor one who does not know the distinctions,
nor one who is bound by worldly continuity, nor a goddess, nor a serpent is a guest.
To one who is thirsty, weary, wandering, and extremely hungry,
one who desires the fruit of sacrifice should give with due respect.
O Brahmin, one should never say to a hungry person, "There is nothing here";
rather, one should always give to him with due respect, for he is indeed a source of honor.
One should always feed those who are untainted, free from blemish, disciplined, of simple livelihood, non-solicitous, steadfast in their conduct, and wise among the faithful.
That evil-minded person who says, "I will not give it," shall not be liberated from his sin even after passing through a hundred births.
That man who feeds Brahmins with shared food in a single row—
whether they are formally appointed or not— removes the sins of the entire row.
Sin is quickly seized by him, and his merit from sacrifices and charitable works perishes;
such a man becomes the foremost among all Brahmins. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 2.15.24)
O best of the twice-born, that person who has studied the five Vedas along with the Itihāsas should,
once he has mastered Yoga, be appointed by the wise man to this task.
Immediately after him was one learned in three Vedas, after him one learned in two Vedas, after that one learned in a single Veda, and after that the upādhyāya.
I shall now proclaim those who are enumerated here as purifiers;
listen, for all these who were previously specified shall be described in their proper order.
One who knows the six-limbed yoga of meditation, one who likewise follows all the Tantras,
and the Yāyāvara— these five should be known as the purifiers of the row.
In the Śrāddhakalpa, he who has assembled there is indeed purifying—
one who has reached the further shore of even a single one of the fourteen branches of knowledge.
And all those who abide according to their true nature are purifiers of the assembly;
without doubt, these include the followers of Suparṇa, the five Agnis, and the chanters of the Sāman hymns.

O Brahmin, that twice-born man who would practice continuously for twelve years according to the rule, as well as one who has mastered the three Nāciketas fires and is learned in the three Vedas, and he who recites the Dharmas; [these are equal].
Any twice-born man who has mastered the great treatise of Bṛhaspati— all such Brahmins, when invited, purify the rows of diners.
If a twice-born man, having been invited to a śrāddha, indulges in sexual intercourse with a woman,
his ancestors lie upon that food for that entire month.
One should give to one who is devoted to meditation, compassionate, and wise;
or one should feed either a *yati* or a *vālakhilya* during the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.
He who honors a forest-dweller is satisfied by that mere act of worship;
furthermore, he who feeds a householder has effectively honored the Viśvedevas.
By the forest-dwellers the ṛṣis were honored, by the Vālakhilyas Purandara was honored,
and by the ascetics Brahmā himself was directly worshipped.
The fifth stage of life, which is of a mixed nature, is impure;
however, the four [other] stages of life are to be honored both at a śrāddha rite and likewise in rites for the gods.
One should not cause offerings to be given at a *śrāddha* for those who stand outside the four stages of life (*cāturāśrama*),
even if such a person should subsist on air alone while remaining outside the four stages of life.
One who does not belong to any stage of life (anāśramin) yet performs penance should not be invited there;
likewise, one who exerts no effort and a proponent of liberation—these two are defilers of the row according to the Śruti.
Endowed with fierce austerity, possessing great knowledge, and eloquent in speech, they all revile the twice-born; such are the defilers of the assembly.
Those who observe fasts, as well as the Sāṃkhyas, atheists, revilers of the Vedas,
and whoever else censures meditation— all of them are defilers of the assembly.
One should avoid those who wear their hair shorn in vain, those with matted locks, and all such pilgrims; as well as those who are merciless, those of broken conduct, and those who eat everything.

One should not feed at offerings to gods or ancestors those who follow the livelihoods of artisans and the like, those of improper conduct, those excluded from the world and the Vedas, or those who sing about the contents of the Vedas.
He who subsists by these [means] goes to the dark-colored realm;
he who eats together with a Śūdra—all such persons are defilers of the row.
Attraction, the destruction of living beings, agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing,
and even service to one who is not a guru or an enemy— these are indeed always improper actions for the twice-born.
One should avoid all those who harbor false intentions and are arrogant,
as well as those who speak falsely, those who revile others, backbiters, and hypocrites.

Those who are joined with minor offenses (upapātaka) and especially with major sins (pātaka), who grant injunctions regarding the Veda while seeking the fruits of greed and delusion; ||| BndP_2,15.47 |||
One should indeed avoid those who sell the Veda at the performance of a Śrāddha rite;
he who imparts the Vedas for a fee is a doer of evil.
The speaker falls away from the fruit of the Veda, and likewise the giver from the fruit of the gift;
so too does he who teaches for wages, and he who is taught by one for wages.
Those two are not worthy of the śrāddha offering, nor are they true Brahmins, being buyers and sellers;
for buying and selling for the sake of livelihood are indeed censured.
This mode of livelihood belongs to a Vaiśya, but for a Brāhmaṇa it is a sin;
he should acquire the Vedas through service and live by means of the Vedas.
Neither of those two deserves to partake in the Śrāddha: the husband of a daughter appointed as a son (putrikā), he who approaches his wife in vain, and he who performs sacrifices with futile rites.

Neither an Arhat, nor a twice-born man who is a usurer, nor those whose inner nature is stained by passion for women, nor those who are devoted to the wives of others, are worthy of the funeral offering (śrāddha).
One should not feed those who delight only in wealth and sensual pleasure at śrāddha rites,
nor those who act in opposition to the duties of their social class (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama), or to all prescribed actions.
A thief, one who officiates at sacrifices for all [including unworthy persons], and all those who defile the row (paṅktidūṣaka)—
as well as that twice-born man who eats like a pig and he who eats from the palm of his hand— [are excluded].
The ancestors do not eat at that time when one consumes what should not be spoken of;
one should certainly not cause food given by a woman or a Śūdra to be eaten as the remnants of a śrāddha offering.
That which one gives out of delusion does not indeed reach the ancestors;
therefore, no food that is leavings should be given during the śrāddha rite.
Furthermore, the remnants of curd and clarified butter should be given to one's son and not otherwise;
however, food and other items should especially be given as leftovers.
Or, satisfied even with flowers, roots, and fruits, they may depart at the very end—
before the food has been cooked and while it still retains its heat.
The ancestors eat only so long as [the offerer] eats while restraining his speech;
this applies to what is given, the acceptance of gifts, the fire-oblation, the meal, and even the bali-offering.
Likewise, the water for washing the feet should be offered with the thumb so that it does not reach the Asuras;
and all these gifts, especially, [should be given in this manner].
In the same manner, the sipping of water (ācamana) should be performed while sitting with the knees tucked between the thighs.
In the performance of śrāddha rites, one should avoid those who are shaven-headed, those with matted hair, and those wearing saffron robes.

But those great-souled ones who are always established in right conduct, who possess knowledge and are likewise absorbed in meditation, and who are devoted to the gods— they purify even by their mere sight.
One should cause [these] to be given to the Śikhins, those dyed with mineral pigments, who carry the triple staff;
for the three worlds are indeed pervaded without interval by the Lords of Yoga.
Therefore, having brought under their control everything that exists in the world— both the manifest and the unmanifest, as well as that which is supreme beyond all— they perceive it all.
Whatever has been seen as both real and unreal, and that which is eternally real, by the Great-Souled Ones—
all forms of knowledge, beginning with liberation, were created by those Great-Souled Ones.
Therefore, one who is always devoted to them obtains the highest fruit.

He who knows the Ṛg-verses knows the Vedas; he who knows the Yajus-formulas knows the sacrifice; he who knows the Sāman-chants knows the Brahman; he who knows the mental [self] knows all. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.15.68)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Examination of Brāhmaṇas," in the Śrāddha-kalpa, within the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 15 //
Bṛhaspati said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the gifts and their fruits,
which provide a means of deliverance for all beings and bring happiness on the path to heaven.
Whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to oneself—
all that should be given to the ancestors by one who seeks their favor, acting under their very command.
The giver of food obtains an imperishable, divine celestial chariot made of Jāmbūnada gold, radiant as the sun, and filled with divine apsarases.
But he who gives unsoiled [cloth] along with its fringe during the rite of ancestral offerings (śrāddha) obtains long life, renown, sovereignty, and auspicious beauty.
If one who knows the sacrifice gives a sacred thread at the time of a śrāddha,
that is a purifier for all brāhmaṇas and yields the fruit of a gift of the Veda.
He who offers a water-pot filled with honey, milk, clarified butter, and curds to Brahmins at the time of a śrāddha ceremony stands by the donor [to grant him his desires].
And he who gives a water-pot pierced by a discus at the time of a śrāddha ceremony obtains a divine cow that yields milk and bestows happiness.
And he who gives sandals filled with cotton during the performance of a Śrāddha rite obtains a splendid vehicle, and his feet will experience increasing comfort.
By giving a fan made of palm leaves to a Brahmin with due honor,
one obtains all kinds of flowers that are fragrant and soft.
For by always giving sandals to the Brahmins at a Śrāddha ceremony,
the wise man likewise obtains a divine, new vehicle yoked with horses.
Furthermore, he who gives an umbrella adorned with flower garlands at a śrāddha ceremony,
that excellent palace follows after him as he departs.
Having given a shelter filled with jewels, along with bedding and food,
to ascetics at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*), the wise man is glorified in the vault of heaven.
He gave garments of fine silk and beryl, various kinds of jewels,
and divine vehicles by the millions and tens of millions.
He obtains an imperishable, divine celestial chariot that travels through the vast sky, is meritorious, endowed with all objects of desire, and resplendent like the moon and the sun.
Surrounded by Apsarases, traveling at will and as swift as thought, he shall dwell upon the pinnacle of a celestial palace, being praised from every side.
The wise say that covering [the altar] with divine flowers is the supreme among gifts;
one should cause vessels that are very smooth and golden to be given at the śrāddha.
Flavors, food,
and good fortune attend him who bestows sesame seeds and sugarcane upon the twice-born at a śrāddha.
He who gives a beautiful vessel made of metal along with meals for the śrāddha ceremony obtains friends in this world as well as good fortune among women.
He who gives a vessel made of silver or even gold during the performance of a śrāddha becomes a vessel for desires, as well as for beauty and wealth.
Through giving, however, one obtains desires, renown, and wealth;
likewise, he who gives a cow at a śrāddha—one that has calved for the first time and yields a jar of milk—[attains great merit].
Cows and prosperity likewise attend that man who diligently provides a fire with plenty of wood during the cold season.
A man who gives fuel to the twice-born at the onset of the cold season attains radiance of the body, brilliance, and good fortune.
He is eternally victorious in battle and is born endowed with prosperity;
likewise, he receives fragrant garlands and sweet-smelling perfumes.
Having honored the worthy recipients at the śrāddha, one should respectfully cause them to receive perfumes,
garlands, and various comforts for that high-souled being.
To the giver attend young women devoted to their husbands,
as well as beds, seats, vehicles, lands, and mounts.
He who should give these at the ancestral rites (śrāddha) shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha),
provided that a virtuous Brahmin is present at the time of the śrāddha.
He who gives a desired object obtains memory and intelligence;
one should respectfully cause vessels filled with clarified butter to be given at a Śrāddha ceremony.

By giving at a śrāddha as much as desired of many cows that have recently calved, whose udders are full, and who are first-time mothers, one enjoys the fruit; by giving them, one obtains the fruit of the puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
By giving a forest endowed with flowers and fruits, one enjoys the merit of the Gosava sacrifice;
likewise by giving wells, groves, tanks, fields, cow-pens, and houses.
Having given a well-spread bed adorned with jewels during a śrāddha ceremony, they rejoice in heaven as long as the moon and stars endure.
His ancestors are gratified, and he attains the heavenly world;
moreover, in this world, he shall possess abundant prosperity and a chariot with excellent steeds.
One is honored here with eight [gifts] and increases in wealth and grain;
likewise, there are garments of leaf-fiber, silk, woven cloth, wool, as well as cloaks and blankets.
Having fed the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule, one should give them an antelope skin, gold, a silken cloth, a woolen blanket, or a garment made of deer-hair.
A man who possesses faith attains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice:
he gains many wives of beautiful form, sons, servants, and attendants.
All beings in this world abide under his control, free from affliction;
likewise, [he masters] silk, linen, cotton, fine cloth, and thick woolen fabric.
Whoever offers these at a *śrāddha* obtains unsurpassed desires;
these destroy misfortune just as the rising sun destroys darkness.
It shines at the forefront of the celestial chariot like the moon among the stars;
for this garment is sacred to all the gods and is praised by all the deities.
Without clothing, there is no ritual action, nor can there be gifts or ascetic penances;
therefore, garments should always be given at the time of a śrāddha ceremony.
A man who gives all these at a *śrāddha* obtains them;
likewise, he who, being self-restrained and devoted to that goal, should give at the daily *śrāddha*.
He obtains all desires, as well as sovereignty and heaven;
he enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which every desire is fulfilled.
One should prepare various kinds of food, well-prepared with auspicious designs and the like, along with sugar,
as well as kṛsara, honey, clarified butter, milk, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
He who gives food that is predominantly unctuous,
as well as cow's curd unmixed with anything else and various kinds of edible foods, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having given at a *śrāddha* during the rainy season and under the *Maghā* asterisms, one does not grieve;
one should feed the Brahmins with clarified butter and pour clarified butter upon the ground.
Having offered rice, milk-rice, clarified butter, honey, roots, and fruits in the shade of an elephant, one does not grieve because of the śrāddha. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 2.16.44)
Having given various kinds of food, one rejoices both in this world and in the next;
for *pṛthuka* grains mixed with sugar and milk are eternally inexhaustible.
Affection may last for a year through vegetables, meat broth,
as well as barley meal, parched grain, cakes, and boiled grains with condiments.
One should prepare all these foods, making them smooth with ghee, and serve them with curd;
he who offers these at Śrāddha ceremonies obtains a treasure like a lotus.
One who, having honored them with effort, gives fresh grains at a śrāddha,
attains all enjoyments and, having gone to heaven, is worshipped there.
Having offered the best of foods— those to be chewed, swallowed, drunk, sucked, and licked—
to his guests at the head of the meal, he stands with palms joined in reverence.
For he obtains the unsurpassed fruit of all sacrifices and rituals;
he should quickly give food that is very hot and unspoiled to one who is hungry.
Having respectfully and diligently honored [the recipient] with devotion, offering food that is well-prepared and richly seasoned,
one attains a celestial chariot resembling the rising sun, drawn by swans.
The giver of food constantly obtains ten million daughters;
indeed, there exists no gift whatsoever superior to the gift of food.
From food all beings are born, they live by it, and through it they flourish;
there exists no gift whatsoever superior to the gift of life.
Upon food all worlds are established; that is the fruit of the gift of food.
Food is Prajāpati himself; by it all this [universe] is pervaded.
Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to food—
be they the jewels upon the earth, vehicles, or women.
That man who is devoted to his ancestors quickly attains all of that,
as does he who, with palms joined in reverence, provides shelter to guests.
The gods welcome him with thousands of divine guests;
he who gives all these [gifts] shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
Through three, two, or even one act of giving, one shall become happy;
for giving is the supreme dharma, honored with reverence by the virtuous.
For sovereignty over the three worlds is established as certain through giving alone;
even one who is not a king obtains a kingdom, and one without wealth obtains supreme wealth; and a man who is always devoted to his ancestors recovers his life when his lifespan has been exhausted.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Praise of Giving," in the Śrāddha-kalpa, within the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the Middle Part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as narrated by Vāyu. // 16 //
Bṛhaspati said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim that which is honored in the rite of Śrāddha—
the optional, the occasional, and the perpetual— constantly in the performance of the Śrāddha ceremony.
There are indeed three Aṣṭakās caused by [the memory of] sons and wives;
those in the dark fortnight are the most excellent, for their presiding deity is the ancient Indra.
The second [offering] should be dedicated to Prajāpati, and the third to the Viśvedevas;
the first should always be performed with cakes, and the other should always consist of meat.
The third [day] should be performed with potherbs; such is the rule regarding the materials.
Herein, the desired [offering] for the ancestors is indeed ordained as a constant duty.
And whatever other fourth [lunar day] there may be, one should perform it especially;
on these days, a wise man should always perform the *śrāddha*, even at the cost of his entire wealth.
For he quickly attains the highest good and rejoices both in this world and the next;
at the times of the lunar festivals (parvan), the ancestors [are gratified], and at the times of the lunar days (tithi), the deities [are gratified].
All men go to their downfall like cows to the slaughter;
at the end of each month, they shall surely depart [from this world] if they have not been honored during the Aṣṭakā festivals.
The hopes of those atheists are entirely in vain, both in this world and the next;
for the worshippers there is exaltation, while for the atheists there is a downward path.
Those who give go to the world of the gods, while those who do not give go among the animals;
[the giver attains] nourishment, progeny, memory, intelligence, sons, and even sovereignty.
Performing worship on these [days], one attains everything in its entirety;
on the first lunar day (pratipad), there is the gain of wealth, and what has been acquired does not perish.
He who performs [the rite] on the second day shall become a sovereign lord of bipeds;
the third day, however, destroys enemies and annihilates the sins of those seeking boons.
One who performs [the rite] on the fourth lunar day perceives the vulnerabilities of his enemies;
and one who performs it on the fifth lunar day attains great prosperity.
One who performs śrāddha rites on the sixth lunar day should be honored with great effort;
and that man who constantly performs śrāddha rites on the seventh lunar day [attains the same].
The man who performs [this rite] on the eighth day attains the status of a great lord, becomes the sovereign of the Gaṇas, and achieves complete prosperity.
One desiring sovereignty and women should perform the *śrāddha* on the ninth day;
however, by performing it on the tenth day, a man shall attain the prosperity of Brahmā.
One shall obtain all the Vedas and attain equality with the Brahmins;
likewise, on the eleventh day, there is supreme giving and constant sovereignty.
On the twelfth day, one obtains victory, sovereignty, long life, and wealth;
as well as increase of progeny, cattle, intelligence, independence, and supreme nourishment.
One who desires long life and sovereignty should perform the Trayodaśī rite;
it should be offered for those young people who have died in one's household.
And for those who have been killed by a weapon, one should offer [the oblation] on the fourteenth day;
being ever pure, one should diligently perform the Śrāddha rite on the new moon day.
One obtains all desires and enjoys infinite heaven;
likewise, [this applies] in every respect to those born under inauspicious signs and to twins.
One should offer the śrāddha on the new moon day; one shall obtain all desires.
Performing śrāddhas under the Maghā asterisms, one shall obtain all desires.
At that time, the ancestors become as if directly worshipped by him;
because the Maghās are like the ancestors (pitṛdaivata), an imperishable [merit] is recorded for offerings made under them.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Tithi-Śrāddha," in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the third Upoddhāta-pāda, in the middle section of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 17 //
Bṛhaspati said:
Listen to me as I describe those śrāddha rites which Yama proclaimed to Śaśabindu, to be performed individually according to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
The man who constantly performs the *śrāddha* during the conjunction with Kṛttikā,
having established the sacred fires, shines in heaven, firm in his vows.
One desiring offspring should perform a śrāddha under Rohiṇī; under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), one becomes radiant;
and generally, one performing cruel deeds should perform a śrāddha under Ārdrā.
A man who desires a daughter should perform a śrāddha under Punarvasu so that she may become an heir to the family estate;
furthermore, a man desiring prosperity should perform a śrāddha under Tiṣya.
By worshipping the ancestors under Āśleṣā, one obtains heroic sons;
by performing the Śrāddha rite under Maghā, one becomes the most excellent among one's kinsmen.
A man who worships the ancestors during the Phālgunī constellations attains good fortune;
he who is inclined toward giving and performs the rite under the Uttarā constellation gains offspring.
He becomes preeminent in assemblies and, having honored the ancestors with offerings in his hand,
he who performs [the rite] under Citrā shall behold handsome sons.
One who performs [a śrāddha] under Svāti shall obtain profit in trade;
however, a Mālava seeking a son should endeavor to perform the śrāddha under Viśākhā.
A man who sets a wheel in motion while the moon is in Anurādhā will attain supreme sovereignty; likewise, he who does so constantly while it is in Jyeṣṭhā shall do the same.
By performing [the rite] under Mūla, one desires health; under Āṣāḍhā, great fame;
and by performing it under the Uttarās, a man shall become free from sorrow.
By merely hearing [this], one shall attain the supreme goal among the worlds;
under Dhaniṣṭhā, one becomes a sharer in kingship and shall obtain abundant wealth.
One who has conquered the worlds through ancestral rites (śrāddha) shall obtain the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches;
and by performing [the rite] under the Varuṇa constellations, one shall attain success as a physician.
By performing [the rite] under the former *proṣṭhapadās*, one obtains many means of livelihood;
by not transgressing the *uttarā* ones, one indeed obtains cattle by the thousands.
One who performs the Surevatī rite obtains wealth consisting of many base metals;
one devoted to Aśvayuj obtains horses; and the most excellent of virtuous beings, by performing the Bharaṇī rite, [obtains] the best of men.
Performing this rite of faith, Śaśabindu, having obtained this entire earth by his might, ruled over it without exertion.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Śrāddha for the Lunar Mansions" (Nakṣatra-śrāddha), within the Śrāddha-kalpa, in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 18 //
Śaṃyu said:
"O best of speakers, what indeed is given that brings satisfaction to the ancestors?
What might endure for a long time, and what is fit for infinity?"
Bṛhaspati said:
"Listen to me regarding all those oblations which those learned in the ritual of the śrāddha know to belong to the śrāddha procedure, as well as their fruits exactly as they are."
Indeed, by means of an ancestral offering (śrāddha) given with sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, as well as roots and fruits,
the grandfathers are gratified for one month.
With fish one gratifies [the ancestors] for two months; with the meat of the black antelope (hāriṇa) for three months;
with the meat of the hare (śāśa) for four months; and with the meat of birds one gratifies them for five months.
The boar-skin [vessel] lasts for six months, the goat-skin for seven months,
and that which is made from the skin of the mountain goat (*pārvataka*) is said to last for eight months.
The grandfathers (pitāmahas) are pleased by the raurava meat for nine months;
however, satisfaction from the meat of the gavaya lasts for ten months.
O twice-born ones, mutton provides satisfaction for eleven months,
while cow’s milk provides satisfaction for a full year at a śrāddha ceremony.
Likewise, the meat of a rhinoceros offered at the ancestral rite (pitṛkṣaya) leads to infinity;
so too does milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee, when offered in the shade of an elephant.

With the flesh of a black goat, there is eternal satisfaction. Regarding this, those who know the past recite the verses sung by the ancestors: BndP_2,19.9: "With the flesh of a black goat, there is eternal satisfaction. Regarding this, those who know the past recite the verses sung by the ancestors."
I shall proclaim those [rites] to you; understand them correctly from me:
"May he who would give [this] on the thirteenth lunar day go to our lineage. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.19.10)
With the sacrifice of a goat, or with all types of metal, during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism,
one should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them should go to Gayā;
or one should marry a Gaurī wife, or release a bull or a barren cow.
Śaṃyu said: "O father, tell me, who am asking you, the fruit of Gayā and the other sites;
and tell me in its entirety what merit belongs to those who give gifts there."

Bṛhaspati said: "O son, at Gayā, śrāddha, recitation, oblations, and austerities are indeed inexhaustible because it is the abode of the ancestors; therefore, they are remembered as being eternal there."
When the *pūrṇā* [oblation] is performed, a son is produced who belongs to Gaurī;
it is remembered that his fruit is that one should offer the *mahāmahā* sacrifice.
I shall now declare the fruit of the *vṛṣa* [sacrifice]; listen as I speak. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.19.14)
One who releases a bull for sacrifice purifies ten generations preceding him and ten generations following him.
Whatever water one who has entered the river stream touches,
that is declared to be inexhaustible for the ancestors when the rite of releasing a bull is performed.
Whatever water he touches with his tail or other limbs, all of that becomes inexhaustible for his ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever ground a bull constantly scratches with its horns or hooves,
for that person, streams of honey indeed become inexhaustible for his ancestors.
Just as the satisfaction of the ancestors through a pond measuring a thousand nalvas is according to the sacred tradition, that same satisfaction is indeed accomplished here by means of a bull.
Whoever gives sesame seeds mixed with jaggery,
or honey, or honey mixed with curd, at a śrāddha ceremony, all of it becomes inexhaustible.
One should not examine a Brahmin; for gifts must always be given by men.
However, it is heard in the tradition that examination is indeed required regarding rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors.

Those twice-born who have bathed after completing all Vedic vows and are purifiers of the assembly, as well as those who are conversant with the vernaculars and those devoted to grammar; ||| BndP_2,19.22 |||
He indeed studies the Purāṇas as well as the Dharmaśāstra;
he has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, maintains the five sacred fires, knows the Sauparṇa hymns, and is learned in the six Vedāṅgas.
He was the son of Brahmadeva, a singer of the Chandoga hymns and a chanter of the Jyeṣṭhasāman;
he had performed his ablutions at sacred fords and observed his vows.

Those who have performed the ritual ablutions at the conclusion of all sacrifices, those who are ever devoted to the vow of truth, and those who are constantly intent upon their own duty; ||| BndP_2,19.25 |||
One should invite those who are free from anger and devoted to the absence of greed to the śrāddha rites;
what is given to these becomes inexhaustible, for they are indeed the purifiers of the row.
Those who are worthy of the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and are firmly established in the vow of yoga—by honoring them, he has honored all three: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
The man who honors these worlds together with the ancestors becomes the most purifying of all purifiers and the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
The first is declared to be the yoga-dharma among all dharmas;
I shall now proclaim those who are excluded from the assembly—listen as I speak.
A gambler, a drunkard, a cattle-herder, one who has been expelled from his caste, a village servant, a usurer, a shopkeeper, and likewise a merchant; BndP_2,19.30 //
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, an outcaste who performs sacrifices for a village,
a professional archer, one who eats from a *kuṇḍa*, a honey-gatherer, and a seller of *soma*— [these are those by whose touch one must bathe].
One who is separated by the ocean, a servant, a slanderer, a false witness, one disputing with his father, and he in whose house lives a paramour; BndP_2,19.32.
Likewise, one who is falsely accused, a thief, one who subsists by a craft, a florist, a cook, and one who reviles friends; BndP_2,19.33 //
One who is one-eyed, one who is lame, an atheist, one devoid of the Vedas,
one who is insane, as well as a eunuch, a killer of an embryo, and one who violates the teacher’s bed.

One who lives as a physician for profit, one who subsists on food obtained by begging, one who consorts with another's wife, and one who sells the Vedic vows as well as religious observances; // BndP_2,19.35 //
What is given to an atheist is lost; what is offered to one who has broken his vows is cast away;
and that which is given to a trader shall avail neither in this world nor in the next.
As well as one who misappropriates deposits, an ungrateful person, one devoid of learning, a gambler, and a craftsman who has abandoned the dharma.
For he who buys goods that should not be sold, sells them, or praises them—
unless there is another justification for his action— a merchant does not deserve to receive an ancestral offering (*śrāddha*).
An offering given by a twice-born man to a son of a remarried woman is like a libation poured into ashes;
a one-eyed man [destroys] sixty, a eunuch a hundred, and one afflicted with leucoderma five hundred. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 2.19.39)
One afflicted by a foul disease destroys a thousandfold the fruit of the donor;
indeed, that foolish giver falls away from that very fruit.
Whatever one eats with one's head covered, whatever one eats facing south, whatever one eats while wearing shoes, and whatever is given without due respect; BndP_2,19.41 //
Brahmā assigned all of that as a portion for the lord of the Asuras;
neither a dog nor a slayer of a Brahmin should ever look upon it under any circumstances.
Therefore, one should give food surrounded by sesame seeds and scatter sesame seeds as well;
for sesame seeds are said to belong to the Rākṣasas, and likewise, those surrounded [by them] belong to the dogs.

A pig destroys [the merit] by its mere sight; a cock, by the wind from its wings; and one who is angry and bestows [the gift], as well as by the touch of a woman in her menses. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-smṛti 2.19.44)
On the delightful banks of rivers, by streams and lakes,
and in secluded places, the ancestors here rejoice at what has been given.
One should not let the left knee touch the ground, nor should one utter speech while engaged [in the rite];
therefore, having circumambulated here according to the rules with darbha grass in hand—
The propitiation of one's parents must be performed; in this way, one pleases the ancestors.
Having first obtained the permission of the twice-born, one should perform the *argha* offering according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer to the ancestors on the ground, or upon the sun, or on a bed of darbha grass;
one should perform the śrāddha according to the prescribed rule during the bright fortnight and in the forenoon.
During the dark fortnight, one should certainly not cross the Rauhiṇa [river] on the afternoon;
thus did these high-souled ones, great yogis of immense power, [declare].
The ancestors are indeed always to be honored when the proper place and time have arrived;
through devotion to the ancestors alone, a person attains that yoga which is difficult to obtain.
Indeed, by means of meditation one shall go to liberation, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma;
for the sake of sacrifice, he extracted that [karma] and likewise deluded the world.
O best among those who know yoga, having extracted the secret nectar from within the cave by means of yoga, the high-souled Kaśyapa established that Brahman there.
This supreme secret of the gods and the ultimate refuge of the sages, the great station of Brahman, was proclaimed by Sanatkumāra.
Having attained that through devotion to the ancestors and diligent effort,
those wise ones have summarized it for one who is devoted to his father and who honors his paternal lineage.
One shall indeed attain all this without effort; of this there is no doubt.
Bṛhaspati said: To whom the śrāddhas should be given, that which, when given, yields great fruit,
and those sacred fords (tīrthas) and caves in which the śrāddha becomes inexhaustible.
I have explained to you in summary those [rites] by which one attains heaven;
yet that man who, having heard this ritual for the ancestral offerings (śrāddhakalpa), does not perform it, [is lost].
That nihilist shall sink into a terrible hell shrouded in darkness;
therefore, one must not engage in slander, especially against yogins.
Having become a worm due to his disparagement, he revolves right there;
for he who disparages the yogas of those meditators who long for liberation, [suffers this fate].
He who hears this [slander] shall undoubtedly go to a terrible hell;
that entire hell, which is dreadful to behold, is shrouded in darkness.
Due to reviling the lords of yoga, a human being does not go to heaven.
He who hears the words of the masters of yoga who are self-restrained even from a distance of one krośa,
shall undoubtedly sink for a long time in hell;
he is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells and has his tongue cut off again and again.
Just as a clod of earth sinks in the ocean, so do those men sink;
therefore, one should avoid hatred in all yogic practices through mind, deed, and speech.
Through love, one enjoys infinite fruit, both in this world and hereafter—of this there is no doubt.

One who has not reached the further shore does not find the Supreme Self; wandering within the three worlds by means of one's own actions, even if one has mastered the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas along with their ancillaries, one perishes without attaining this immutable reality.

He who has reached the further shore of transformation and the further shore of primordial nature; he who has gone beyond the qualities of the three Vedas and the further shore of the triad of qualities; he who has reached the further shore of the twenty-four principles—he is one who has reached the further shore, not merely one who has reached the further shore of Vedic study.
He who, devoted to that, attains to its entirety as it truly is, and likewise again to the dissolution of his own self,

and who does not withdraw from the path of yoga— that twice-born man has not reached the further shore of all, nor does he range within the scope of those who have crossed to the other side by gradual stages.
The knower of yoga attains that which is to be known from the Veda and that which is to be realized;
indeed, those who know the Vedas call him a knower of the Veda, and they call him one who has reached the further shore of the Veda.
Having truly understood both the Veda and that which is to be known as they really are,
those who know the Veda thus speak to another who has indeed reached the further shore of the Veda.
One who is devoted to the ancestors obtains sacrifices, the Vedas, as well as desires, various forms of austerity, long life, and progeny; of this there is no doubt. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.19.68)
But he who, being self-restrained, recites this Śrāddhakalpa with faith,
obtains all these as well as the fruits of visiting sacred fords and making gifts.
He shall indeed be a purifier of the assembly and the foremost eater among the twice-born;
and having caused the twice-born to hear [the sacred texts], he shall then attain all his desires.
And the twice-born who would constantly hear this and cause others to hear it—
free from malice, having conquered anger, and devoid of greed and delusion— [shall attain the highest state].
Having obtained the fruits of visiting sacred fords and all other acts such as giving,
one will undoubtedly attain the supreme means to liberation and the means to heaven; moreover, there is supreme nourishment even in this world— therefore, one should practice this constantly.
Whoever recites this ritual procedure with vigilance and concentration in an assembly on the junctions of the lunar festivals,
shall possess offspring and, through supreme splendor, attain the same world as the dwellers of heaven.
Salutations to that Self-Existent One by whom this ritual manual was proclaimed;
and I am forever bowed down before the great lords of yoga.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Examination of Brahmins," in the Śrāddha-kalpa, within the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the Middle Part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 19 //
Bṛhaspati said:
"These are the Pitṛs, the gods who are even the deities of the gods;
these imperishable Pitṛs are eternally established in seven locations."
For these are indeed the sons of Prajāpati; they constitute the first host of all those great-souled ones devoted to yoga, increasing the practice of yoga.
The second belongs to the deities, the third to the Dānavas and others; the remaining ones are to be known as belonging to the social classes (varṇins). Thus they have all been proclaimed.
The gods indeed worship these [deities] who are established in all forms of knowledge,
and the four stages of life (āśramas) likewise worship them in their proper order.
All four castes perform sacrifices to these according to the scriptures;
likewise, those born of mixed castes and even the Mlecchas indeed perform sacrifices as well.
But he who worships the ancestors with devotion—the ancestors please him;
[they especially favor] one who desires prosperity or, again, one who desires progeny.
The ancestors bestow nourishment, progeny, and even heaven;
thus, the rite for the ancestors is superior even to the rite for the gods.
For the ancestors are traditionally known as the primary source of nourishment for the gods;
indeed, the subtle course of the ancestors through yoga is not understood by men.
Indeed, by means of well-known ascetic power (tapas), what need is there to mention the eye of flesh?
[One should offer] a vessel made of silver for all, or one adorned with silver.
For it is declared by the gods together with the ancestors that this is the supreme purifier for those kinsmen who shall offer three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) according to name and lineage.
When offered on the ground covered with kusha grass according to the rite of the apasavya,
these funeral cakes (piṇḍas), wherever they may be placed, truly gratify the ancestors.
Whatever food a living being may have, that very food becomes his sustenance;
just as a calf finds its mother when she has wandered lost in a cow-pen.
In that same way, the mantra leads the person to wherever he dwells;
they lead him by means of his name, his lineage, the mantra, and the food that was offered.
Even when they have attained hundreds of wombs, satisfaction does not follow them;
such is the condition of these beings belonging to Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
"In the primordial creation of the ancestors who desired imperishable worlds—
thus were these the Pitṛs, as well as the worlds and the daughters."
O sinless one, the daughter's sons and the sacrificer have been mentioned by me;
O son, they indeed are declared by me to be your ancestors in their proper order.
Śaṃyu said:
"O dear one, oh, the divine creation of the Pitṛs has been described by you! The worlds, the daughters, and likewise the grandsons have been heard."
The gifts together with their purifications, the proclaimed fruits,
the state of imperishability, and the twice-born— this entire matter has been declared.
From this day forward, I shall perform all of this exactly as it is.
Bṛhaspati said: "In former times, the lord Aṅgiras spoke this to the ṛṣis;
and when questioned by them regarding all their doubts, he addressed the ṛṣis in an assembly of men."
When that thousand-year sacrificial session had previously been commenced,
Brahmā, the lord of the gods, sat there as the presiding master after having performed his ceremonial bath.
Indeed, five thousand years have passed there;
and here, verses were formerly sung by the seers who discourse upon Brahman.
Formerly, at the sacrificial session (satra) of the consecrated Brahmā, the Supreme Self,
the first portion of food was offered right there by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin for the sake of the welfare of the worlds and for the inexhaustible benefit of the ancestors.
Sūta said: Thus, having been previously questioned by his wise son, Bṛhaspati spoke concerning the creation of the ancestors (pitṛsarga), which has also been fully described.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Śrāddha," in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
And this Śrāddhakalpa is completed.
Vasiṣṭha said:
While the high-souled Jamadagni was conducting himself in this manner, [the following occurred].
O King, several years passed for him of immeasurable splendor.
Rāma also, O tiger among kings, was the best of all upholders of dharma;
he knew the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and was proficient in all the śāstras.
With a humble soul and great intelligence, he performed service to his parents and daily increased their affection through his own conduct.
O King, while conducting himself in this manner, Rāma, the best among the wise, spent several years in the service of his parents.
Once, O King, that highly resplendent one resolved to go toward Guha, the Grandfather, being impelled by destiny.
Pressing his father’s and mother’s feet with his head, that bull among the Bhṛgus spoke these words with humility, his hands joined in reverence.
"O father, I now wish to make a certain request of you and my mother; you both ought to listen to it."
My mind has long been filled with longing to see my grandfather;
therefore, with his permission, I shall now go to his side.
And many times, O dear one, she was summoned with longing by my affectionate grandmother, who desired to see me through her many words.
This manifestation of mine is indeed pleasing to my fathers and even to my grandfather;
therefore, let him grant me permission to go to his side.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words spoken by him in agitation,
the two of them were filled with great joy, and their eyes became filled with tears.
Having affectionately embraced that illustrious one and smelled his head,
they both greeted him with blessings, dear son, and spoke as follows.
"O dear one, go at your pleasure to the house of your grandfather,
for the sake of pleasing and beholding both your grandfather and grandmother."
Having gone there, O child, dwell for some time in their house, devoted to serving them according to the proper rule, for the sake of their pleasure.
Having stayed for not too long a time, they felt a renewed longing for them;
"Come here again, O illustrious one, in safety and with a desire to see us."
"You are not able to remain even for half a moment without seeing your son;
therefore, O Grandfather, you ought not to stay in my house for long."
"Or else, O son, by his command, even though you have gone into the presence of your great-grandfather, return quickly; then, with his permission, you may proceed in due order."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus, the high-minded one circumambulated and bowed to them;
then, having also taken leave of his parents, he departed for the house of his grandfather.
Having gone there, Rāma entered the hermitage of the high-souled Ṛcīka, the best of the Bhṛgus, which was graced by the disciples of the sage.
It resounded everywhere with the vast sounds of Vedic recitation;
it was rich in beings whose enmity had been stilled, and it was enchanting to all living creatures.
Having entered the delightful hermitage, O king of kings, Rāma saw his grandfather Ṛcīka seated upon his throne before him.
Blazing with ascetic power like the sacrificial fire situated upon its altar,
he was attended by Satyavatī as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) attends a rite.
O King, seeing Rāma approaching their presence, those two—
who had previously seen him only by command— reflected upon him for a very long time.
"Who is this mass of asceticism, honored everywhere?
Though he is a child, he appears powerful through his profundity and humility."
While the two of them were thus reflecting with joy and curiosity in their hearts,
Rāma, full of humility, slowly approached their presence.
Having joyfully uttered his own name and lineage, as well as those of his parents, the wise man touched their feet with his head and saluted them with both hands.
Then, having raised up that most excellent being with joyful minds, both of them greeted him individually with blessings.
Embracing him and placing him upon their laps, their eyes overflowing with tears of joy,
they gazed at his lotus-like face and attained supreme delight.
Then, once he was comfortably seated, both the husband and wife inquired after the well-being of that upholder of their own lineage.
"O child, are your parents well, and likewise your brothers? Is your livelihood maintained without hardship, and do you ever fare well?"
Then, O King, he related to them both, exactly as it had been told to him,
all that had occurred regarding his parents and his brothers.
Thus, O Great King, Rāma dwelt in the abode of his father’s parents, being delighted by the qualities born of their true affection for him.
Delighting the minds and eyes of all beings,
he dwelt there for several months, devoted solely to serving him.
Then, O King, having taken leave of those two, the high-minded and eminent descendant of Bhṛgu desired to go to the hermitage of his grandfather’s preceptor.
He was greeted with blessings by those two who were filled with affection,
and he departed toward the hermitage of Aurva according to the instructions they had given him.
Having paid homage to Cyavana according to the prescribed rites, that man of great asceticism,
with joy and having received his permission, departed for the hermitage of Bhṛgu.
Having gone there, he beheld the hermitage circle of Bhṛgu, the foremost of sages, surrounded on all sides by ascetics whose minds were tranquil.
He was delighted by the trees that were covered with very glossy and cool shade, endowed with the qualities of all seasons, and laden with an abundance of fruits and flowers.
It resounded on all sides with the cries of various flocks of birds, which brought delight to the mind and the ear,
and with diverse sounds of Vedic chanting.

By the fragrance of the smoke arising from the oblations of clarified butter accompanied by mantras, which spread throughout the forest interior, the entire multitude of his sins was dispelled in every direction.
O King, it was graced on all sides by charming young ascetics, adorned with staffs, girdles, and deerskins, who were gathering sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass.
It was beautified by groups of auspicious female ascetics moving here and there, with their hands holding vessels filled with flowers and water.

It was occupied by herds of female monkeys from the Sapota trees, who, being free from fear, had entered with confidence to take shelter in the shade of the trees bordering the courtyards of the huts.
The sweet-voiced peacocks began their dance, while being observed by the herds of cows as they ruminated with joyful cries.
Where grains were scattered about, where nearby deer let out their cries, and where heaps of nīvāra grain lay drying, having been reached neither by the sun's heat nor by shade; (2,21.45)
At that time, the sacrificial fire was being kindled, a multitude of guests was being honored,
a flood of Vedic meters was being practiced, and the joy arising from the sacred texts was being contemplated.

The study of all the Smṛti texts being recited, the investigation of the meaning of the Śruti, the performance of sacrifices to the ancestors and gods that had been commenced, and [the sound] that was enchanting to all beings.
Abounding with ascetics, frequented by noble men,
increasing the power of penance, meritorious, and a source of happiness for all living beings.
It brought joy to those whose wealth is asceticism, like another world of Brahmā;
it resounded with the humming of bees wandering about, drawn by the fragrance of flowers.
Beholding that supreme hermitage, endowed with such qualities as these, while being fanned on all sides by various breezes from the sky.
With a disciplined mind, Rāma entered, like a man of meritorious deeds entering the abode of the immortals; having reached the vicinity of his own great-grandfather, he entered.
O King, he saw him surrounded on all sides by hundreds of the sage’s disciples,
seated upon a mat of kusha grass in the midst of the platform for exposition,
adorned with white beard, matted locks, a mustache, and the sacred thread.
He sat with his left knee between his right and left thighs, using his left leg.
The preeminent among sages had his body wrapped in a yogic cloth,
and the lotus of his right palm shone with the gesture of exposition (vyākhyānamudrā).
His left hand, shining brightly, was placed upon his yogic belt;
he [was expounding] the collection of the subtle, essential meanings of the words concerning the true forest-dwelling.
Seeing his father’s grandfather, that storehouse of asceticism, revealing [the truth] to the foremost sages and causing them to hear it, Rāma [beheld] that great-souled one.
O Great King, he approached him slowly;
and perceiving that he had arrived, they were overwhelmed by his power.
O King, all the sages felt apprehension from afar;
meanwhile, Bhṛgu, whose nature is immeasurable, was delighted by their arrival.
Having ceased all other conversation, the king sat gazing at him;
Rāma also approached him, his face bowed low in humility.
Endowed with humility, he saluted Khyāti according to the prescribed rule, just as Upendra salutes the Creator. Having offered his salutations according to the proper custom, he stood before her.
And Rāma honored those sages according to their seniority,
and he was in turn gladdened by the blessings of all of them, who were filled with joy.
The wise one sat down upon the ground with their permission;
then, as Rāma was seated, he was greeted with blessings.
Then, having beheld him, Bhṛgu asked that auspicious question:
"Is all well with you, my child, and is there no ill-health among your parents?"
"And for what purpose have you now come here into my presence— [on behalf] of your brothers, of your father, and likewise of your parents?"
"Have you been sent by someone, or have you come here of your own accord?
Then Rāma, in accordance with propriety, related everything to him without exception.
He related that which was asked by that high-souled one:
the account of his father, his mother, and his noble brothers.
O King, he joyfully related everything with humility— his father’s affection, his mother’s, the sight of Kauśalyā, and those two [parents]— as well as all else concerning Bhṛgu.
He reported his own desire according to the proper custom;
O King, having heard all this that was uttered by Rāma, [the sage spoke].
And seeing him, Bhṛgu was especially pleased and welcomed him,
for he was performing what was dear to him through his own preeminent deeds.
O King, Rāma dwelt in that hermitage for several days;
then, on one occasion, the best of sages [Vasiṣṭha] addressed Rāma in private.
"O child, come here," he called out to him in a secluded spot, O King;
and having approached him as he sat there, he saluted him with palms joined in reverence.
Rāma stood before him with a deeply pleased inner soul;
then Bhṛgu, his mind full of joy, greeted him with blessings.
Looking at Rāma with respect and seeing that his apprehension had vanished, he said:
"Listen, my child, to these words of mine which I shall now speak to you."
"For the benefit of all the worlds, and for yours as well as ours,
go, my son, at my command to the great mountain Himavat."
O illustrious one, having now set your mind upon asceticism,
go from this hermitage to that place and establish a beautiful hermitage there.
Propitiate Mahādeva through austerity and self-restraint;
by means of devotion directed toward no other, you shall produce joy in him after a long time.
You shall attain great excellence; there is no need for hesitation here. Śaṅkara becomes pleased with you through your vigor and devotion.
And he will fulfill for you everything that you desire in your mind,
when that Lord of the World, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, is pleased.
"O son, choose the entire collection of weapons as you desire;
for the sake of the gods' welfare, you must perform what is exceedingly difficult to do."
There exists manifold karma that must be accomplished by means of weapons;
therefore, you should propitiate Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods.
Endowed with supreme devotion, you shall thereafter attain your desired goal.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the third introductory section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 21 //
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus by Bhṛgu, Rāma replied, "So be it," and having bowed down and received his permission, he set his mind on departing.
Having duly circumambulated Bhṛgu and Khyāti and bowed down to them,
he was embraced by them and greeted with blessings.
Having paid homage to those sages and being commended by them all,
he departed from that hermitage, having resolved to practice asceticism.
Then, by the command of his guru, the high-minded Rāma proceeded along the very path he had been instructed, toward Himavat, the best of mountains.
Having passed through various countries, mountains, and rivers,
as well as forests and the dwellings of the foremost sages, he gradually moved on.
Dwelling on the path in various abodes of sages,
or staying at sacred fords and preeminent holy sites, he proceeded slowly.
Having passed through very many delightful regions and beholding them,
he reached the unsurpassed Himavat, the best of mountains.
Having gone to that excellent mountain, which was covered with various trees and creepers,
he beheld it as if scraping the sky with its vast peaks.
It was adorned with various regions variegated by diverse elements,
and beautified on all sides by jewels and medicinal herbs shimmering everywhere.
In some places, fresh [grass] was being fiercely consumed by fire accompanied by wind, which had been produced from the sapless wood rubbed by the friction of the Maruts.
In some places, the forest fires were extinguished by water flowing from melting snow-mountains and bitumen, as the sun blazed with its rays striking the parched earth.
In some places, the forest was ablaze with heaps of crystal, collyrium, base metals, and gold that radiated light, their shimmering reflections striking one another like arrows.
In one place, the forest was illuminated by throngs of perfected beings (siddhas) drenched with frost, who were basking in the sunlight upon the rocky plateaus of the foothills.
In some places, its borders were illuminated by throngs of yakṣas resting upon golden rocks, who, pierced by the rays of the sun, seemed as if they were entering a fire.
In one place, the mountain cave was filled with the distressed cries of herds of deer, agitated by the leaping of hyenas emerging from the mouths of caves.

In some places, the banks of the river were strewn with excellent tigers and leaders of boar herds engaged in combat, while elsewhere the rocky slopes and tree-lined shores had been forcibly stripped away.
In some places, the slopes of the rocky ridges were pitted by the hooves of wild oxen (gavayas) who were pursued by female elephants drawn by the scent of their young.
In some places, the forests and boulder-strewn slopes were pulverized by rut-maddened elephants, grown large in that very region, as they fought one another.
In some places, the ground was trampled by the feet and pierced by the claws of lions who, provoked to fury by hearing that roar, were charging at the elephants.
In some places, the forest was filled with the sound of trumpeting elephants whose heads were being split open by the claws of lions suddenly pouncing upon them.
In some places, the deep caverns of all the rocks were being split apart by the fierce claws of lions whose manes were drawn back by the strength of their eight legs.
In some places, there was a mutual crushing together of many agitated leaders of elephant herds engaged with Śabara hunters, as they broke apart the rocks.
In some places, there were female elephants sporting with their mates in mountain thickets;
elsewhere, the forest was filled with rutting male elephants pursuing their females.
In its dense thickets, hundreds of caves were filled with the wind from the breaths of sleeping lions, while deer wandered about, trembling with heavy fear and apprehension.
The herds of yak-cows wandered very slowly, playing timidly as the hair on their tails was caught and torn by thorns.
The faces of all the quarters were filled with the sounds of cymbals and the songs uttered by kinnarīs dwelling in mountain caves.
And the ground was marked by the footprints of forest deities wandering here and there, their feet stained with red lac-dye.
On all sides, flocks of peacocks with their crests spread wide began to dance, accompanied by songs of sweet melody.
He was being gently fanned by forest breezes that rained down a profusion of various flowers from both water and land and brought delight to his limbs.
The interior of its mango groves was agitated by the cries of intoxicated male cuckoos, who were reveling in the taste of the excellent nectar of the blossoms of the season.
It resounded with the songs of bees intoxicated by various flower-nectars,
while its forests were deafened by the cries of many birds.
The surface of the earth was adorned by clusters of fresh flowers, moist with flowing honey, sparse yet abundant, and scattered by the winds from the edge of the forest.
It was deafened on all sides by the great roars of waterfalls falling from above onto the treacherous, rocky precipices.
With the dense foliage of their many spreading branches and with the shadows of their boughs rising from the ground near the settlement, the *pāṭala* trees stood there.
With kadamba, nimba, hintāla, sarja, bhedhūka, and tinduka;
with kapittha, panasa, aśoka, sahakāra, iguda, and aśana trees.
With *nāga*, *caṃpaka*, *puṇnāga*, *kovidāra*, and *priyaṅgu* trees; with *priyāla*, *nīpa*, *bakula*, *bandhūka*, and *akṣatamālaka* trees.
With grapes, madhūka, āmalaka, jambu, kaṅkola, and jāti;
and also with the trees bilva, arjuna, karañja, mango, and bījapūra.
With *picula*, *ambaṣṭha*, gold, *vaikaṅkata*, *śamī*, *dhava*,
*putrajīva*, *abhayā*, *ariṣṭa*, iron, *udumbara*, and *pippala* [wood], ||| BndP_2,22.38 |||
It was adorned on all sides by various other trees,
whose dense shade kept the heat at a great distance.
Its surface was not reached by the rays of the sun on all sides,
and it was filled with monkeys moving with great speed, nourished by the strength gained from tasting various kinds of ripe fruits.
It was crowded with hundreds of forest rows that were startled and overwhelmed as they were traversed,
and here and there it was graced by exceedingly beautiful rock caves from which [water] issued forth.
O King, it was being diminished by hundreds of rivers made treacherous by its heat,
as well as by vast lakes adorned with white and blue lotuses.
Having reached that lord of mountains, the peak cool with frost, which was adorned on all sides by the warbling of various flocks of birds.
Filled with joy, Bhagaśreṣṭha swiftly ascended it;
having entered that dense forest, the high-minded Rāma [proceeded].
O King, he wandered slowly among the trees at the edge of the village;
as he roamed there in all directions, he was surrounded on every side by does.
Being gazed upon with apprehensive, innocent glances,
he found joy there amidst the forest breezes, fragrant with the scent of flowers.
Being fanned [by the breezes], that descendant of Bhṛgu rejoiced upon beholding the magnificent splendor of the forest and the various trees, having traversed the subtle [upper regions].
Observing various pairs of elements, he reflected thus:
"Aha! This one has been consecrated to the sovereignty over all mountains."
He was established in his proper place by Brahmā as a partaker of the sacrifice;
his sovereignty over the king of mountains is clearly evident.
The forest was made sweet by the sounds of kīcaka reeds,
while the slopes of the hips were covered with clusters of frost.
It was as if dawn had broken, with a pure white cloth spread over it,
while a dense mass of frost rested thickly upon its surface.
He appears as if his limbs were draped in upper garments of various colors,
and he is adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron, and other such substances.
O serpent, your body, adorned with ornaments, clearly appears like that of a playful elephant, with [gems] fallen from the frontal globes of lordly elephants slain by the king of beasts.
This mountain shines on all sides with heaps of large pearls,
its hair adorned with various trees, creepers, vines, and flowers.
Adorned by a canopy formed by a dense and curved mass of clouds,
his body variegated with various minerals and embellished with all kinds of jewels.
He was resplendent with a white parasol shining under the guise of Mount Kailāsa,
and was surrounded on all sides by herds of elephants and horses with faces like those of beasts.
His palace was a cave-chamber formed by great door-stones on the Jewel Island;
he took his seat upon a lion-throne situated in the midst of a secluded, deep cavern.
Seeing it slowly surrounded on all sides by trees and cane thickets,
it was unapproachable by people, like a great king of kings.
He moved about while being fanned by the radiant chowries of yak-tail fans,
with peacocks dancing nearby and kinnaras singing.
Served by many beings born of the *sattva* quality, he shines resplendent,
clearly established in the position of supreme sovereignty over the lords of mountains.
"Having overpowered the entire earth, he enjoys its splendor through his own prowess"—
thus did he reflect while staying in a forest thicket of the Himalayas.
Filled with supreme joy, Rāma,
the foremost of the Bhṛgus, wandered for a long time and reached that vast forest.
O Great King, there was a vast lake of pure water,
adorned with clusters of kumuda, utpala, and kahlāra lotuses.
It was adorned on all sides with lotuses and water lilies— red, yellow, white, and blue— as well as other aquatic flowers.
It was also filled with hundreds of swans, cranes, dātyūhas, and kāraṇḍavas,
as well as throngs of jīvajīvaka birds, cakravākas, kuraras, and bees.
It resounded on all sides, was fanned by a gentle breeze,
and was filled with shoals of *śapharī* fish moving here and there.
The best of the Bhṛgus reached that supreme lake, which seemed to be dancing on all sides with the waves generated within it.
Having established a vast and auspicious hermitage on its shore, he made the surrounding regions sweet with the various warbling of birds.
Rāma, the best among the wise, set his mind upon asceticism; subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, he remained disciplined and with senses restrained.
Having fixed the Lord of Gods within his own mind,
he performed penance with supreme devotion, following the path instructed by Bhṛgu.
O King, with one-pointed mind he worshipped the Lord of Gods;
homeless during the rains, he took refuge in the water during the cold season.
In the summer, standing amidst five fires, he practiced asceticism for a long time in this manner,
having conquered his enemies such as desire and having shaken off the six waves [of the senses].
With an intellect unperturbed by dualities, undisturbed by the defects of suffering,
his body purified by restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), he remains composed.
The great sage, a silent ascetic with a steady mind who had mastered the lotus posture, brought the vital breath moving within his body under control through *prāṇāyāma*.
Devoted to the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), he brought his senses under control;
and the self-possessed one, by means of concentrations (dhāraṇās), made his flickering mind steady.
Through meditation, with his internal organ composed, friendly, and free from all afflictions, he beheld the Supreme Lord, the God of gods.
Having beheld the Teacher of the World within meditation, he meditated upon the Lord of Gods; with his mind and self established in the object of meditation, his senses and body became motionless.
He remained there for a time without limit, like a lamp sheltered from the wind,
muttering prayers and meditating upon the Lord of the Gods according to his own understanding.
The one of immeasurable soul propitiated the Lord who dwells within all beings;
thereafter, he beheld the fruitless, stainless form of the Lord.
The supreme light is inconceivable, that which is to be meditated upon by yogis, unsurpassed,
eternal, pure, ever-peaceful, beyond the senses, incomparable,
consisting of pure bliss, immovable, and pervading all that is moving and unmoving.
The descendant of Bhṛgu meditated upon that form of the God of gods—
eternal, pure, ever-peaceful, beyond the senses, and incomparable.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Performance of Austerities by the Son of Jamadagni," within the *Arcunopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Arjuna) in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Sagara, in the third section (*upoddhātapāda*) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, while Rāma was an ascetic, single-minded in his being,
devoted to solitude in a secluded place, self-restrained, and firm in his praised vows—
Having heard that, all the sages— whose impurities had been washed away by austerity, who were great men advanced in knowledge, action, and age, and whose vows were highly praised— [approached him].
Desirous of seeing him and filled with curiosity, O King, they gathered together, proclaiming the supreme ascetic power of that high-souled one.
Bhṛgu, Atri, Kratu, Jābāli, Vāmadeva, and Mṛkaṇḍu—
these sages, esteemed by the elders, honored Rāma.
Those great sages, dwellers in that holy field, came from afar to the hermitage of Rāma, who was performing intense ascetic penance.
"Penance is most weighty in all the worlds, as is supreme knowledge";
having thus praised him, they all departed for their respective hermitages.
O best of kings, as Rāma was thus proceeding, the blessed Śiva became exceedingly pleased in his heart.
O King, desiring to test his devotion toward himself, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara assumed the form of a hunter and went into his presence.
Resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, with long eyes whose corners were red,
he was tall, possessed a body as firm as a diamond, was young, and carried a bow and arrows.
With prominent jaws, arms, and shoulders, and with tawny beard and hair,
he was foul-smelling due to the flow of flesh and was a harmer of all living beings.
His body was scarred by wounds from contact with thorny creepers,
and he repeatedly chewed pieces of flesh right before his companions' eyes.
With his neck bent down by the weight of two loads of meat he was carrying,
he violently broke trees in great numbers with the force of his thighs.
Like a mountain moving on foot, he approached that region;
having reached the shore of that lake, which was lined with flowering trees.
He placed his monthly load at the foot of a certain tree and sat down there for a moment, taking refuge in the shade of the tree.
He saw the descendant of Bhṛgu standing on the shore of the lake;
then, rising quickly and approaching his presence, he [prostrated].
With his two hands, which held the arrow and the bow, he offered a salutation with joined palms to Rāma,
and with a voice as deep as the roar of a water-laden cloud.
He spoke to that tiger among the Bhṛgus with a voice resonating through the interior of the cave:
"I am a hunter who lives in this great forest, raining down showers of contentment."
"I am the lord of this land, including its living trees and creepers;
with a mind and self equanimous toward all beings, I wander about, subsisting on various creatures as my food."
I am equal toward all beings, and even my father and others are not, in any respect, objects of my desire for forbidden food, improper sexual conduct, drink, or similar things.
Deprived of the discerning intellect required for the rules of what ought and ought not to be done,
I have taken refuge with no one, neither seeking their approach nor even their shelter.
I have no doubt that even by the power of Śakra,
they would recognize this place as my refuge, just as everyone else knows it.
"Therefore, no one comes here without my permission;
thus has this account of mine been told to you in its entirety."
And you, tell me in truth and in its entirety your own history:
who are you, from where have you come here, for what purpose do you stand here,
are you prepared to go elsewhere, or what is it that you intend to do?
Vasiṣṭha said:
