Having been addressed in this manner by him, the immensely radiant Rāma laughed;
after remaining silent for a moment as it were, he reflected with his face slightly cast down.
Who is this, so difficult to assail, with a voice like the roar of a water-laden cloud,
who speaks words whose meanings, phrases, and syllables are exceedingly clear?
However, my body indeed gives rise to a great suspicion regarding him;
for, by virtue of his reliance on a different species, even his arrows are so beautiful.
As he was reflecting thus, auspicious omens indeed appeared both upon the earth and within his body, fully granting him his desired object.
Then, having reflected many times with his mind, that bull among the Bhṛgus spoke these words, consisting of truthful syllables, slowly to the hunter: BndP_2.23.28.
"I am the son of Jamadagni; may you be blessed. I am Rāma by name, a descendant of Bhṛgu, who has now come here at the command of my preceptor to perform austerities."
"However, for a long time I have been striving to propitiate the Lord of all worlds through austerity, devotion, and self-restraint."
Therefore, [one should worship] Śaṅkara, the Lord of all, the refuge of all, the bestower of fearlessness,
the three-eyed one, the subduer of sin, who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Resorting to strict discipline in this hermitage on the shore of the lake, I shall propitiate the omniscient destroyer of Tripura through ascetic penance.
"Until the Lord Hara, who is compassionate toward his devotees, comes into my direct perception, I shall remain right here; this is my resolve. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.23.33)
Therefore, it is appropriate for you to depart from here this very day to another place,
provided that there is no loss to me of my own merit or my religious observance.
Moreover, I am worthy of your honor as a guest from another land who has come to his own dwelling,
being both an ascetic and a sage.
"Your dwelling in my absence would lead only to sin for me;
likewise, your attendance upon me would result in unhappiness for you as well."
Therefore, by abandoning wandering and other such activities in the vicinity of my hermitage, may you become happy for the sake of both worlds.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words of his, he, his eyes copper-red with rage, spoke this reply to Tāmrākṣa, that bull among the Bhṛgus.
"O Brahmin, why do you reproach me so excessively for dwelling near you, as if I were ungrateful? (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.23.39)
What harm have I done to you, or to anyone else in this world? Who would ever despise one who is self-controlled and innocent of offense? ||| BndP_2,23.40 |||
O best of Brahmins, if [you wish to avoid my curse], you must avoid keeping me in your presence—
whether it be by seeing me, living with me, or even conversing with me.
"O long-lived one, you must depart from this hermitage this very moment; having abandoned my own refuge, where shall I go, famished as I am? (BndP 2.23.42)
"Having abandoned my own dwelling, how can I go elsewhere as you have commanded?
I shall not go far from here, especially so."
"Go elsewhere, or stay here as you wish;
I cannot be moved from this place by any means whatsoever."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard those words of his, filled with a touch of anger,
that descendant of Bhṛgu spoke these words again to him, O King.
This hunter caste is cruel, bringing fear to all living beings;
always delighting in wicked deeds, it is despised by all creatures.
O evil-minded one, you were born from her as a most wicked person who harms all living beings; how could such a person not be abandoned by virtuous men?
Therefore, O untroubled one, knowing yourself to be of inferior birth, depart quickly from here to another place; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Out of compassion for the protection of your body, you do not approach [the fire], just as you feel pain through intolerance of thorns and the like. (BndP 2.23.49)
Understand it thus: for all embodied beings, life is dear;
yet for those who are struck down, there is suffering, which is otherwise for you.
"Non-violence toward all living beings is the eternal dharma;
because of conduct contrary to this, one is constantly censured by the virtuous."
For the sake of protecting your own life, how can you kill all living beings? You will incur the reproach of the virtuous.
Therefore, O lowest of men, depart quickly from my presence;
for by your presence, the destruction of the fault of my deed will not occur.
"You shall not go from here by your own will, nor even by force;
I shall clearly instill in you the thought of retreating."
O sinful one, even for half a moment your dwelling here is not for your welfare;
how can one who constantly acts in opposition and is an enemy of Dharma attain peace? (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.23.55)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard Rāma’s words, though pleased, he spoke these words to him like one enraged— the wielder of the Pināka bow in the form of a hunter.
"I consider all this resolve of yours to be in vain;
for how can you be the first knower? How can there be Śambhu? And how can there be austerity?"
Why do you, O fool, afflict yourself with that austerity?
For Śaṅkara is certainly not pleased with one who has engaged in such a false practice.
Śambhu acts contrary to worldly custom for his own satisfaction;
O dull-witted one, who else but you, a foolish mortal, would torment him? BndP_2,23.59.
Or rather, it has come to pass today that this is undoubtedly fitting:
the union of Śambhu and you, both of whom are skilled in honoring and being honored.
He alone, who is devoted to the world, is worthy of being worshipped by you;
you too are a fit worshipper of him—of this there is no doubt.
Having severed the head of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, the grandfather of the worlds, Śambhu again incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O twice-born one, you have likely been instructed by Śambhu, who was himself overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin; for how else could you have acted in such a way?
O Sage, because of your identity with him and the union of your qualities with Rudra’s, you have now attained perfection in austerity in a very short time.
Having slain your mother today, you have been rejected by all the worlds;
under the pretext of asceticism, you now wander in the deep, uninhabited wilderness.
And you perform penance for the expiation of the sin arising from the murder of a preceptor’s wife or the killing of a Brahmin;
yet that sin is not destroyed by this penance.
"Indeed, although there are expiations for other sins,
know that for those who betray their mother, there is truly no atonement anywhere."
O Rāma, if in your view dharma is characterized by non-violence in all the worlds,
how is it that you have cut down your mother with your own hand?
Having committed the terrible murder of your mother— an act censured by all the world—
you have now become righteous and, out of desire, you revile others.
Beholding this in vain while laughing, and being unaware of my own fault,
I am not capable of scrutinizing the faults of another.
If I were to live having abandoned my own duty out of fear for both families,
then you may indeed censure me after deliberating upon it yourself with your mind.
"Only for the sake of supporting my mother, father, children, and others,
do I take the lives of living beings as my own duty."
Day after day, I support myself and my family with the material gains resulting from my own duty;
that means of livelihood was ordained for me by the Creator in the past.
If I were to kill more than that amount of meat which would ensure the constant nourishment of my father and others, then I would indeed be joined with sin. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 2.23.74)
"As long as we do not become objects of reproach by the destruction of our nourishment,
having reflected upon this, you may either censure me or praise me."
Whether an action be good or evil, whatever was ordained for one in the past, that alone must be performed by him, even in times of distress, by any means possible.
Examine with your own intellect the difference between yourself and me;
for I am devoted to supporting friends and others with my whole being.
Having abandoned your aged father and having slain your mother,
you have now become righteous and have come here to practice asceticism.
But for those who know the root, their vision is perfectly clear; herein, it is not possible even by speech to describe it as it truly is.
But I know your conduct completely and accurately;
therefore, enough of this fruitless austerity for you, O descendant of Bhṛgu!
If you desire happiness, O Rāma, abandon this asceticism that causes bodily suffering; go elsewhere, to a place where people do not know you.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, in the third introductory section (upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O protector of the earth, having been addressed thus by that wise one, Rāma, the best among the intelligent—
Having reflected upon him further with his mind, he spoke to him who was greatly amazed:
Rāma said:
"Tell me, O illustrious one, who are you? You are certainly no ordinary man;
your form appears to possess the majesty of Indra himself."
With its diverse meanings, noble phrasing, and the qualities of profundity and elegance,
your speech is heard to be most enchanting, belonging only to the Omniscient One.
Indra, Vahni, Yama, Dhātṛ, Varuṇa, or the Lord of Wealth;
Īśāna, Tapana, Brahmā, Vāyu, Soma, Guru, and Guha.
It is likely that you are one of these;
indeed, your majesty stirs doubt in my heart regarding your birth.
The Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, is heard to be a master of illusion;
tell me, who are you that have approached me in this form?
Or rather, he is the Lord of the worlds, the omniscient Supreme Lord,
the Supreme Self, born of himself, delighting in the self, and eternal.
The Lord Śiva, who moves according to his own will and consists of the entire universe,
ought to become united with you through this very body.
In this world, no other person possesses a body endowed with such power,
nor a voice characterized by the excellence of its birth and meaning, and graced with magnanimity.
I believe that out of affection for his devotees, Hara has assumed this form and appeared before my eyes to test me.
"You are not merely their physician; they do not possess such a form as yours.
Therefore, salutations to you! Reveal your true, beautiful form."
Revealing a form commensurate with Your own majesty, be gracious,
so that the manifold doubt in my mind may be dispelled.
Be gracious toward me with your whole being; now, utterly destroy my delusion of intellect by means of the apprehension of your true nature alone.
"O highly fortunate one, having bowed my head to you again and again, I entreat you:
who are you? Show yourself to me; here I join my palms in reverence to you."
Having spoken thus, O illustrious one, that scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage, desiring to know him,
sat upon the ground and remained absorbed in meditation with a concentrated mind.
Seated in the bound lotus posture, observing silence, with his speech, body, and mind restrained,
and having stilled the movement of his vital breaths, the noble-minded one meditated for a long time.
Having restrained the collection of his senses and having fixed his mind within his heart,
he meditated upon the Lord of Gods, the Teacher of the World, with the vision of dhyāna.
And with the eye of self-realization, he beheld the Lord of the World,
who bestows grace upon his devotees, appearing in the form of a hunter.
Then, opening his eyes and rising quickly, Bhārgava beheld the God standing before him in that very same form.
O great king, having seen him who is the refuge for all and who is affectionate toward his devotees, manifested for the sake of favoring himself, Rāma was filled with agitation.
With his entire body covered in horripilation and his eyes overflowing with tears of joy,
the high-minded one fell upon the ground at his feet in devotion.
O King, with a voice faltering and agitated by agitation, he said to him repeatedly: "Be my refuge, O Śarva! O Śaṅkara! (BdP 2.24.22)
Then Śambhu, assuming his own form and gratified by that devotion,
raised up Rāma, who was prostrate on the ground in salutation.
Raised up by the Sustainer of the World with his own two hands, the descendant of Bhṛgu stood before the Lord of the Gods and, with palms joined in reverence, offered praise.
Rāma said:
Salutations to you, the God of gods, to Śaṅkara, the primordial form;
salutations to Śarva, the peaceful, the eternal—salutations again and again.
Salutations to you, O Blue-throated One; salutations to you whose form is blue and red.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Beings; salutations to you who dwell among all beings.
Salutations again and again to Mahādeva, the bountiful giver, whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, who is Śiva, the multiformed, and the three-eyed one.
O Śarva, Lord of the Universe, be the refuge for me who am devoted to you;
for those who have no other shelter, you alone are indeed the ultimate resort.
O Lord Śaṅkara, whatever harm I have done to you, or whatever harsh words I have spoken,
O Blessed One, since I did not know you, you ought to forgive me for that.
O Lord of All, who else but you could truly know the existence of one whose form is unknowable by any other, were it not for you? (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 2.24.30)
Therefore, O Śaṅkara, be gracious toward me with your whole being;
I have no other refuge but you. Homage to you, again and again, homage! Homage!
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus being praised, the Blessed One, whose soul is serene and who pervades the universe, spoke to him who stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
The Blessed One said:
"I am pleased with you now, my son,
because of this asceticism and your unwavering devotion, O best of the Bhṛgus."
And at every sacrifice, I shall grant you whatever is desired and chosen by you;
for you are exceedingly devoted to me—there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Everything has been understood by me alone; it dwells within my heart and remains there even today.
Therefore, do without hesitation whatever I tell you.
"O child, you no longer possess the power to wield these fierce weapons;
therefore, once again perform severe austerities. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.24.36)
Having traversed the entire earth and bathed in all the sacred fords in due order,
you, with your body purified, shall obtain all the divine weapons.
Having spoken thus, O King, the omnipresent Lord, who ordains the portions of worldly existence, vanished in that very form in an instant while Rāma was looking on.
When the Lord of the World had vanished, Rāma, having bowed to Śaṅkara and circumambulated the entire earth, set his mind upon bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha).
Then, having traversed the entire earth in due order,
that self-possessed man performed his ablutions at all the sacred fords according to the prescribed rites.
At sacred fords, in the principal holy sites, and likewise in temples,
he tirelessly offered libations to the ancestors and the gods according to the prescribed rites.
Performing virtuous deeds such as fasting, austerity, fire-offerings, recitation,
and ritual bathing according to the prescribed rules at sacred fords, he wandered over the earth.
O King, having thus bathed in the sacred fords in due order and having slowly circumambulated the earth, he became purified in body.
Having thus traversed the earth by the command of Śambhu, the descendant of Bhṛgu returned once more to that place where he had previously dwelt.
Having gone there, O King, and remaining right there, he worshipped the Lord Umāpati with devotion, through austerities and religious observances as well.
At that very time, O King, there occurred between the gods and the asuras a long-lasting battle that caused the hair to stand on end.
Then, having defeated the gods in battle, the exceedingly powerful asuras attained the sovereignty of the immortals in its entirety, free from fear from any quarter.
Defeated in battle by their enemies and stripped of their sovereignty, all the gods, led by Vāsava, sought refuge with Śaṅkara.
Having gratified the Lord of the World with prostrations, victories, and hymns of praise,
the gods requested the wielder of the Pināka bow to slay the asuras.
Then, O King, having promised the slaughter of those Dānavas to the gods,
Śambhu, the granter of boons, spoke to Mahodara.
On the southern side of the Himavat mountain, a son of a sage named Rāma, a man of great asceticism and exceeding splendor, is performing penance directed toward me.
Having gone there this very day and having delivered my command,
O Mahodara, bring him here without delay while he is performing austerities.
Having said "So be it" to the command, Mahodara prostrated before the Lord and departed with the speed of the wind to where Rāma was stationed.
Having reached that place and beheld the great sage Rāma performing austerities, he spoke these words with humility: *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa 2.24.54*
"O best of the Bhṛgus, Śambhu desires to see you; by his command I have come. Therefore, come now into the presence of his lotus feet."
Having heard those words of his, Bhārgava rose quickly,
and honoring his command with his head, replied, "So be it."
Then Mahodara, filled with haste, quickly brought Rāma to the presence of Śambhu on Kailāsa, the best of mountains.
Accompanied by all the elements and by the immortals headed by Indra,
the best of the Bhārgavas beheld Śaṅkara, who is compassionate toward his devotees.
He was being praised by sages such as Nārada and others whose wealth is austerity,
while being sung to by Gandharvas and accompanied by throngs of Apsarases who were dancing.
The Lord of Gods was being worshipped, wearing an elephant hide as his garment,
with all his limbs smeared with ashes, possessing three eyes, and having the moon as his crest-jewel.
He bore a mass of matted locks of tawny hue, was adorned with the weight of serpents,
possessed long-hanging lips and arms, and was gentle with a serene lotus-like face.
O King, as he sat upon a golden seat in the assembly of the gods,
the best of the Bhṛgus approached the Lord of the Gods with palms joined in reverence.
With his body thrilled by horripilation arising from the vision of Śrīkaṇṭha,
he approached the presence of Hara with his frame drenched by a flow of tears.
With devotion and agitation, speaking repeatedly with a voice faltering from joy, she cried out in indistinct syllables, "Salutations to you, O God of gods! (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.24.64).
He fell, touching with his head the feet of the enemy of Tripura,
in the midst of the hosts of gods who were watching the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Having raised him up, Śiva, pleased and with a face like a lotus in full bloom,
spoke to Rāma with sweet words, laughing and showing great respect.
"Overrun by these hosts of Daityas and fallen from their own domain,
the gods, being unable to slay them, have come to me."
Therefore, O Rāma, by my command and out of a desire to do what is pleasing to the gods, slay all the hosts of Daityas; for in my opinion, you are indeed capable.
Then Rāma, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words with humility to Śarva while all the gods were listening: BndP_2,24.69.
O Lord, what is unknown to you, the omniscient soul of all?
Nevertheless, please attend to these words of mine as I address you.
If all the gods, beginning with Śakra,
are unable to slay the enemies of the immortals, how could they possibly be slain by me alone?
"O Lord of Gods, I am ignorant of weapons and unskilled even in battles;
how shall I slay all the enemies of the gods while being unarmed?"
Thus addressed by him, the Lord of Gods gave to that great-souled one a white, fiery energy consisting of the Śiva-weapon, which possessed the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction.
Having given his own axe, which overcomes all other weapons,
Rāma, with a serene soul, spoke while the gods were listening.
O gentle one, by my grace, may you possess the power to slay all the enemies of the gods,
making you invincible to every foe.
"With this very weapon, go and fight with your enemies;
you yourself know, as it truly is, the skill required for battle."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus by Śambhu, Rāma then bowed to him and,
intent on slaying the enemies of the gods, took up his axe, which belonged to Śiva.
Then that Rāma, born from a portion of Viṣṇu’s splendor, shone forth,
endowed with devotion to Rudra like the great radiance of the sun with its own brilliance.
Permitted by the three-eyed god and accompanied by all the deities,
he went forth, having resolved to wage war in order to slay the asuras.
Then, O King, there occurred once more a most terrifying battle between the gods and the asuras, who were intent on conquering the three worlds.
Then, in that most terrible battle, the mighty-armed Rāma,
filled with wrath, struck down the great asuras with his axe.
Striking down thousands of Daityas with blows resembling thunderbolts,
Rāma moved through the battle like another enraged God of Death.
Having slain all the Daityas, Rāma, the best among strikers, gladdened all the gods and destroyed them in an instant.
While all the Daityas and Dānavas were being slain by Rāma,
those who remained after the slaughter, filled with fear, saw Rāma everywhere.
When the hosts of asuras had been utterly routed and fled,
the gods took leave of Rāma and returned once more to the third heaven.
Rāma, too, having slain the sons of Diti and having granted leave to the immortals,
returned to his own hermitage with his mind intent on ascetic penance.
Having fashioned an image of Śambhu as a hunter,
that high-minded and self-controlled man worshipped it with devotion in that very hermitage.
With fragrances, flowers, pleasing food offerings, prostrations,
and hymns of praise, he brought her supreme delight through devotion according to the prescribed rites.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Episode of Arjuna," in the third section (the Introductory Section) of the Middle Part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said: Then, through the power of his devotion, that Lord of the World, with a pleased soul,
appeared before him in person along with all the hosts of Maruts.
Having seen that Lord of the gods, the three-eyed Śambhu who bears the moon upon his crest,
who has the king of bulls as his vehicle, and who is accompanied by ten million spirits;
Rising up in agitation, his eyes clouded with joy,
Bhārgava prostrated himself on the ground with devotion before Śarva.
Rising up again and again, bowing his head repeatedly to the Lord of Gods,
Rāma, with palms joined in reverence, praised the Lord of the Universe.
Rāma said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord;
salutations to you, O Protector of the world; salutations to you, O Destroyer of Tripura.
Salutations to you, the presiding lord of all; salutations to you, who are affectionate toward your devotees;
salutations to you, the sovereign of all beings; salutations to you, whose banner bears the bull.
Salutations to you, Lord of all; salutations to you, O mine of compassion;
salutations to you, abode of all; salutations to you, Nīlalohita.
Homage to the wielder of the trident, the destroyer of the hosts of all the enemies of the gods;
homage to you, the bearer of the skull, the sole protector of all the worlds.
Homage always to the dweller in the cremation ground, homage to the dweller on Kailāsa;
homage be to you, the wielder of the noose, the consumer of the kālakūṭa poison.

Homage to you, the self-existent one, the source of all, who are worthy of being saluted by the immortals in their various states of existence; homage to Śambhu, who has become the witness to the karma of the entire world.
Salutations to Śiva, the Supreme Self, who dwells at the confluence of the three paths, who shines with the crescent moon upon his crest, and who wears the great lord of serpents as a necklace.
Salutations to you whose body is covered with ashes; salutations to you whose eyes are the sun, fire, and moon;
salutations to you, the one with matted hair, the crusher of the Asura Andhaka.
Salutations to the destroyer of Tripura, to the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
salutations to Him whose great chest is stained with the saffron from the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Obeisance to Mahādeva; obeisance to you, the one clothed in a hide;
obeisance to Śiva, whose true nature is meditated upon by yogis and whose splendor is inconceivable.
Salutations to You, who abide in the center of the pericarp of the lotus-heart of Your own devotees, and whose very form is the essence of the established conclusions of all the Āgamas.
Homage to Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self, whose nature is nectar, who awakens all the lords of yoga, and whose majesty pervades everything.
Salutation to Śarva, the peaceful one, to Brahman who possesses all forms,
who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, eternal, and whose form is unmanifest.
Salutations to Him whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, whose self is both gross and subtle;
salutations to Him who is known through the Vedānta and whose form is the supreme consciousness of the universe.
Homage to Śrīkaṇṭha, the sustainer of the world and the creator of the universe, whose feet are worshipped with flowers from the crowns of the hosts of gods and demons; salutations again and again!
Salutations to you, whose nature is the quality of rajas, the ordainer of the creation of the universe,
who takes the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, and who is the destroyer and the origin of the world.
Homage to the Self of the Universe, who effects the maintenance of the world;
to the Supreme Inner Self, whose nature is pure being and consciousness.

Salutation to the one who brings about the dissolution of the universe through the transformation of the quality of darkness (tamas), who assumes the form of Rudra at the end of the kalpa, and who knows that which is both supreme and non-supreme.
Salutation to the changeless and eternal one, whose nature is both being and non-being;
salutation to the awakening of the intellect, who is the transformer of the intellect and the sense organs.
Salutations again and again to Him, by whose māyā the gods— divided into the Vasus, Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, Rudras, and Aśvins— possess minds split asunder.
That which is unchanging, unborn, eternal, subtle in form, and incomparable—
even yogins who are ever-pure do not know that which belongs to You.
Indeed, even Brahmā and the other gods, failing to know you who are difficult to comprehend, truly wander in the cycle of existence; they are certainly not, for long, masters of their own karma.
As long as one does not approach your feet, which destroy ignorance,
so long does one wander in saṃsāra, whether one be a scholar or even a fool.
He alone is skillful, he is successful, he is a sage, and he is a scholar,
by whom the intellect has been made steadfast in the lotus-feet of Your Lordship.
Your true being, consisting of the three Vedas, is profound due to its extreme subtlety;
how can it be known by me, a fool, even by those who possess wisdom?
Since I am dull-witted and lack the capacity for perfect knowledge, I am currently unable even to praise you properly, O Mahimna, because you transcend the range of words and speech.
Therefore, whether out of ignorance or indeed through devotion alone, I have offered praise; be pleased, O Lord of Gods, for you are surely compassionate toward your devotees.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus praised then by Rāma with devotion, Śaṅkara spoke to him in a voice as deep as a thundercloud, as if smiling.
The Blessed One said:
"O Rāma, I am well-pleased with you because of your glorious fame,
your asceticism, your devotion to me, and especially because of this hymn."
"Choose a boon, therefore, whatever you desire in your heart;
I shall grant all of that to you in its entirety and without remainder."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, O King, that scion of Bhṛgu bowed to him and,
with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words.
"O Lord, if you are pleased with me, and if I am worthy of this boon,
then I desire from you the complete knowledge of all weapons."
By your grace, may there be no one in the worlds superior to me in missiles, weapons, and sacred scriptures, nor shall there be a conqueror of me in the art of slaying.
Vasiṣṭha said: Having replied, "So be it," Śambhu, being well-pleased, then bestowed all his missiles and weapons, along with their mantras, upon Rāma in due order, O King.
With a gracious countenance, Śaṅkara caused Rāma to master the fourfold collection of missiles, together with their preliminary applications and methods of withdrawal.
Śaṅkara gave to Rāma an unsurpassed chariot with unimpeded speed, white horses, and a splendid banner, along with two quivers containing inexhaustible arrows.
An unbreakable, undecaying, divine bow with a firm string, victorious and capable of enduring all weapons; and a wonderful, highly precious armor.
O lord of men, he also possesses invincibility in battles, peerless valor on earth,
and the power to sustain his life-breaths at his own will.
He bestowed upon the descendant of Bhṛgu great power of asceticism, as well as universal renown under that very name, which was merely a seed.
Having bestowed upon himself and upon Rāma the appropriate devotion due to a king,
the moon-crested Lord, accompanied by all the celestial beings, departed.
In that very form, Śambhu, the Sustainer, quickly vanished;
then Rāma, having obtained everything he desired, felt his purpose was fulfilled.
When Śarva had become invisible, he said to Mahodara:
"O Mahodara, for my sake, you must carry out all of this in its entirety."
"For now, you ought to preserve your chariot, bow, and other equipment;
when I have need of them, then you shall be remembered by me.
Send all of these—the chariot, the bow, and so forth—to my presence."
Vasiṣṭha said:
When Mahodara, the best of the Bhṛgus, had departed after saying "So be it," he,
having accomplished his purpose, desired to go to see his elders.
Then, as he was traveling, Rāma, impelled by his future destiny, entered a cave within a forest thicket of the Himalayas.
There he saw a young son of a brahmin, still breathing but pursued by a tiger, crying out in extreme terror.
Seeing this, his heart filled with compassion and anxious to protect him, he pursued the tiger while calling out loudly, "Stay! Stay! (BndP 2.25.51).
Having pursued him with speed for what seemed like a long time, the descendant of Bhṛgu encountered a terrible and most fearsome tiger in the forest.
Pursued by a tiger, that son of a brahmin also fled into a forest thicket; terrified and afflicted by the fear for his life, he fell down.
Rāma, his eyes red with anger, desiring to recover the brahmin’s son,
took a blade of grass and consecrated it with the *kuśāstra* mantra.
Then the powerful Tarakshu,
seeing the fallen bird, rushed toward it and roared most fiercely, as if making heaven and earth tremble.
Having burned the attacking tiger with the fire of his weapon,
he quickly released that twice-born man, who remained entirely unscarred.
That evil one, his body consumed by the fire of Brahmā,
assumed a celestial (gāndharva) form in the sky and spoke respectfully to Rāma.
"O Bhīma, formerly I attained the state of a jackal due to the curse of a brahmin;
now, liberated from that curse by you, I am going to heaven."
When he had departed after saying this, Rāma, filled with wonder,
rushed forward with speed and compassionately rescued that fallen son of a brahmin.
"Do not fear," saying these words from nearby, O King, he gently touched the limbs of the son of the twice-born, reviving him.
Thus awakened by Rāma, he opened his eyes and,
looking about, beheld the best of the Bhṛgus standing before him.
Seeing that Śārdūla had been reduced to ashes, he was filled with wonder; free from fear, he said: "Who are you, sir, and how have you come to be here?"
"By whom has this terrifying hyena, whose form is like another Death personified, been reduced to ashes as he prepared to slay me? (BndP 2.25.63)
O Mahāmati, even now my mind is utterly bewildered by fear;
though he has been slain, all the quarters of the sky appear to me as being filled with him.
I consider you alone to be my father, mother, son, kinsman, and teacher;
for you are sustaining me while I am fallen into the greatest of calamities.
There was a certain excellent sage named Śānta, a man of great asceticism;
I am his son, and seeking sacred fords, I have come to Śālagrāma.
Therefore, having set out with the desire to see Mount Gandhamādana,
he went to the holy hermitage of Badarikāśrama, which is frequented by various hosts of sages.
Desiring to go, I left the path and entered a delightful thicket on the Himalayas, agitated by the sight of its various regions.
Having set out toward the eastern direction, I traveled for the distance of a *krośa*;
then, by the power of fate, I fled, tormented by fear.
"Having fallen, you were now raised up from the ground by me,
just as a son is by a most compassionate father through exceeding love;
thus has this account of mine been related to you in its entirety."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus questioned by him at that time, O king of kings, Rāma related his own history to him in its entirety and in due order.
Then, having stood for a short while conversing with one another in a state of mutual affection, he desired to depart.
Then, followed by him, Rāma emerged from the mouth of that cave and,
filled with joy, set out for the dwelling of his parents.
Akṛtavraṇa himself was struck down to the ground by a tiger,
but he was protected by Rāma, who slew the tiger.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, that very name became famous on earth for that son of a brahmin; such was Akṛtavraṇa.
From that time forward, O King, she became Rāma’s exceedingly dear friend in all circumstances, following him upon the earth like his own shadow follows the sun.
Followed by him, O King, he reached the presence of Bhṛgu;
having seen Khyāti, he approached her and saluted her with humility.
Honored with blessings by those two who were pleased with him,
he dwelt there for several days, desiring to do what was pleasing to them.
Then, with the permission of those two and of the great sage Cyavana,
he proceeded toward the hermitage, which was surrounded by throngs of disciples.
The high-minded [king] also paid homage to his wife Sukanyā, whose internal organ was restrained and whose mind was perfectly tranquil.
And Rama, greeted with affection by those two,
proceeded to the hermitage of Aurva, desiring to see that treasure of asceticism.
Having saluted him and being greeted by him in return,
O King, the wise man dwelt there for several days out of affection for him.
Dismissed by him, the illustrious descendant of Bhṛgu set out joyfully and slowly for the abode of Ṛcīka, accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa.
Having bowed down separately at the feet of his father’s parents, he paid them homage;
and they, O King, joyfully greeted him in return with blessings.
And being questioned by those two, O king of kings, he of noble intellect related his entire life story in due order, exactly as it had occurred.
Having stayed there for some days with his permission,
he went to the home of his parents, filled with supreme joy.
Having approached his parents, O King,
the descendant of Bhṛgu sat down in that most excellent hermitage and duly prostrated at their feet.
Having respectfully raised him up as he bowed down at their feet,
they embraced him and, rejoicing, drenched him with the tears from their eyes.
Having greeted him with blessings and placed him upon their laps, they gazed repeatedly at his face; as they examined his limbs and touched them, they experienced great joy.
And they asked Rāma:
"O son, what have you done with all this play? Who is this, and where have you come from?"
"How did you remain here together with him, or how did you come here?
My child, tell us both the whole truth of this matter."

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Deeds of Bhārgava" within the "Episode of Arjuna," in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the Middle Part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 25 //
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, having been thus questioned by the two of them, Rāma, with palms joined in reverence,
related to them everything that he himself had performed.
Indeed, by the command of his family preceptor, he performed penance for himself;
and by the command of Śambhu, he traveled through the sacred fords in due order.
By his command alone, for the sake of the immortals, there was the slaughter of the Daityas;
and by the grace of Hara, even here, the sight of Akṛtavraṇa occurred.
Rāma related all of this in its entirety, as well as whatever else he had done himself, to his parents who were filled with joy.
O King, having heard all that he had related concerning that deed in detail, both of them experienced yet another surge of joy.
In this manner, O Great King, that bull among the Bhṛgus performed service to his parents,
keeping himself under their command, and likewise toward his brothers without distinction.
At that very time, however, the lord of the Haihayas once set out for a hunt, accompanied by his fourfold army.
The sky was becoming suffused with reddish rays on all sides— rays as crimson as the bandhūka flower, which stole away the luster of the clusters of stars.
The morning breeze blew gently, carrying the fragrance of rows of swaying ketakī groves and touching the beds of night-lotuses.
And birds, dwelling in nests upon the trees on the banks of the Narmadā,
uttered their various cries, bringing delight to the mind and the ear.
Having descended to that holy ford on the banks of the Narmadā, which removes all sins,
he entered its waters while hosts of sages were chanting the eternal Brahman.
When the chief sages, performers of ritual acts, had performed their rites of friendship according to rule and returned from the riverbank, they were proceeding toward their hermitage.
While each of the heroes' wives was busy with household chores, and while the cows—resembling sages—were being milked for the sake of the fire-oblation; ||| BndP_2,26.13 |||
It was indeed fitting that while the young sons of sages were leading him away,
the world became filled with the performance of the Agnihotra sacrifice, bringing happiness to all living beings.
While the lotuses were blooming, the bees were singing, and the birds, having emerged from their nests, were warbling on all sides; ||| BndP_2,26.15 |||
At a time when the limbs were refreshed by a gentle breeze, and when the elephants, horses, and chariots moved without excessive agitation.
And as they approached the vicinity of the hermitage, carrying flowers and water,
there were many wearing deerskins as garments, engaged in the recitation of sacred texts with numerous Vedic syllables.
While various mantras were being correctly employed, while the ritual calls (praiṣas) were being uttered, and while oblations were being poured into the fires; (BndP 2.26.18).
Just as when the rituals prescribed in the *van-mantra-tantras* are extensively performed,
there arises a heat that dispels darkness, appearing like the crest of a blazing flame.
Having struck down all directions and laid bare the earth,
as the sun rises, the nocturnal darkness perishes.
When the stars had vanished and the quarters were clear,
the king, the lord of the Haihayas, having performed the preliminary rites of loving-kindness and so forth, went out on a hunt.
Accompanied by his family priest and all his assembled forces— including horses, chariots, and elephants— he departed from that city.
Accompanied by his ministers and glorious kings of his own age, he pressed down upon the surface of the earth with a vast burden of troops.
The king made all directions resound with the roar of his chariot,
as the dust from the earth, trampled by the stamping feet of the flood of his own troops, rose up on every side.
He proceeded, covering the sky which was crowded with hundreds of celestial chariots,
having entered the formidable Vindhya forest with his vast hosts of troops.
Surrounding that forest on all sides with his own troops, that best of kings caused it to tremble violently.
He struck down various kinds of predatory wild animals with sharp arrows—
those keen shafts released by warriors drawing their bows back to their ears.
Some tigers, their bodies mangled by the feet and swords of those with fierce speed, fell to the earth with their limbs severed.
Some leaders of boar herds, their heads pierced by spears discharged from fierce spearmen, went to the earth, drenched in blood.
Multitudes of deer fell upon the earth like mountains;
lions, bears, śarabhas, and other beasts had all their limbs pierced by iron arrows.
Drenched in blood, they were scattered all over the earth;
likewise by some who were still clutching their nooses, whether falling or already fallen.
With some being pursued by dogs and others likewise fleeing as deer,
they were seized while crying out, terrified and overcome by the fear for their lives.
At the end of the age, the forest appeared exceedingly agitated,
filled with boars, lions, tigers, hyenas, hares, and rabbits.
Many camaris, rurus, jackals, gavayas, bears, and wolves; black antelopes, leopards, and red rhinoceroses, he beheld.
He saw various other deer with variegated limbs, as well as antelopes of every kind— calves, sucklings, the young, the old, pairs, and herds.
The soldiers indeed struck down with sharp weapons those troops who were to be slain by weapons;
thus they slaughtered all those terrible beasts, which were mostly predatory, leaving none remaining.
The king’s soldiers became exhausted by great toil;
when the sun had reached the meridian, the king then proceeded with his army.
Tormented by the heat of dharma and thirsting for water, he went slowly to the Narmadā;
then, having descended into her waters along with his army and vehicles, [he drank].
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, the king entered that auspicious place;
having bathed and drunk her pleasantly cool water, he was refreshed.
And having sported for a long time in the water, the king, together with his army, emerged and ate the white and delicious lotus sprouts.
And when the sun had reached its setting place, adorned by groves of trees, the king, together with his army and his followers, took rest upon that shore.
He set out from the forest thicket of the Vindhya mountains to go to the city;
as he was traveling, he beheld [a place] situated on the bank of the Narmadā.
Then, having turned back from there and stationed his armies at a distance, the king [proceeded] to the hermitage of the high-souled Jamadagni, who was of virtuous character.
Accompanied by a few attendants and joined by his domestic priest, he then went to that delightful hermitage.
Having approached the tiger among sages, the king bowed his head;
Jamadagni, for his part, greeted that best of kings with a blessing.
He honored her according to the prescribed rites with offerings of water for the feet, water for the guest-offering, a seat, and so forth;
and the sage, having accepted that worship thus performed, [proceeded].
The illustrious one sat upon a seat before that great sage; and as the best of kings was seated there, the sage, himself sitting upon a mat of kusha grass, [addressed him].
The best of supreme sages, conversing with that king, inquired after the welfare of his sons, friends, and kinsmen.
After staying for not too long a time, he invited him for the purpose of hospitality;
then that king, being well-pleased, spoke to Jamadagni.
"O Great Seer, grant me permission; I shall go to my own city, for I am accompanied by my entire host of vehicles and forces, O Great Sage."
"Hospitality cannot be performed by you in this forest while subsisting on wild fare;
or rather, you must perform hospitality for me today through the power of your asceticism."
"You are indeed able to go to the city; you ought not to disregard me.
Otherwise, O best of sages, [the city] will be overwhelmed by the wicked armies."
"There would be suffering for the ascetics, causing the destruction of their religious observances.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed in this way, that sage said to him, "Please wait a moment."
"I shall provide every hospitality for you and your followers," he said;
having spoken thus, he summoned the milch-cow and said, "This is my guest."
"Therefore, let hospitality be shown today by you.
Thus addressed by the sage,
that milch-cow quickly yielded for the king, out of respect for the sage, all the provisions suitable for a guest.

Then that hermitage of the bull among the Bhṛgus became like the abode of the king of the gods; through various manifestations of its splendor, it possessed an inconceivable form, unattainable by others due to the power of Surabhi.
It was high and encircled by garlands shining with gold variegated by many jewels;
within, it was surrounded by clusters of palaces whose peaks were joined by clouds as white as the full moon.

It was illuminated by many dwellings made of bell-metal, brass, tin, copper, gold, and base metals, as well as stone, clay, wood, and earth— some distinct and others mixed— which were pleasing to both the eyes and the mind.

It was intensely beautified by golden altars blazing with precious gems, by pinnacles, staircases, small chambers, and gables; and by scales, door-panels, bolts, walls, thresholds, inner rooms, halls, and courtyards.

With porticos, verandas, side-chambers, and lofty archways, with spacious quadrangles and other such structures, and with pillars and walls resplendent with various paintings of divine jewels; BndP_2,26.60.
With various excellent jewels, diverse golden lion-thrones and pedestals,
and with foods such as hard and soft delicacies, along with vessels filled with drinks and other provisions, [he was honored].
With houses endowed with every prosperity befitting the immortals and delightful to the eye and mind,
his hermitage shone like a great city, filled with charming women.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Episode of Arjuna," in the third section (the Introductory Section) of the Middle Part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said: In that city, whose splendor equaled that of Indra’s city, the cow of the best of sages subsequently created dwellings and the multitude of men and women suitable for them.
Their bodies were adorned with various garments, ornaments, flowers, perfumes, and fine cloths;
they were radiant together with him, endowed with noble gestures and the qualities of splendor, loveliness, and beauty.

With the splendor of their moon-like faces illuminated by the network of rays from their gently shimmering teeth, with voices made charming by the weight of fresh youth, and with glances of side-long looks languid with love; ||| BndP_2,27.3 |||
With hearts radiant with joy, delighting in the splendor of their pleasure, adorned with the flowers of the wish-fulfilling tree of love,
they were captivated by forms as sweet as desire, possessing beauty, grace, and fortune equal to those of celestial nymphs.
By those women whose waists were bent under the weight of their two beautiful, full breasts resembling cups of refined gold;
and whose feet and ground beneath them were reddened by the juice of lac-dye, as if from the exhaustion of supporting the burden of their hips.

Adorned with armlets, necklaces, gems, bracelets, golden neck-threads, and spotless jeweled earrings; with masses of hair kissed by garlands of flowers, and with the tinkling of their girdles and anklets; BndP_2,27.6 //
In matters such as the touching away of anger, conciliation, jesting, laughter, fond conversation, reproach, and wrath—
states in which they were skilled at capturing the king’s own beloved fortitude and then utterly robbing him of it— all these were brought about by the goddesses of Death.

They spoke with voices as sweet as the deep, charming, and gentle songs of the Gandharvas, resembling the sound of lute strings; their fingers were skilled upon the surface of the lutes, and they were eager for the pleasure of making profound, circular, and flattering sounds.
By women who were exceedingly languid with intoxication, possessed of an extremely bold disposition, and who had agitated the minds of their lovers;
who were skilled in the application of amorous arts, endowed with no lack of wealth, magnanimity, beauty, virtue, and good character.
It was surrounded on all sides by female attendants who, though constantly occupied with household chores, were beyond counting,
as well as by men of resplendent beauty who were worthy of his multitude of virtues and who moved about within the house.

It was surrounded on all sides by the citizens, whose every desire was fulfilled and who possessed all wealth and virtues, as they occupied the royal highways, marketplaces, palaces, mansions, staircases, temples, and courtyards.

With countless and incomparable multitudes of diverse palaces resplendent with many jewels, and with numerous mansions suitable for chariots, horses, elephants, donkeys, camels, cattle, and goats; BndP_2,27.12 //

[He saw] the houses of the king’s vassals, cavalrymen, infantry, foot-soldiers, army commanders, and leaders; likewise those of the Brahmins and others, the charioteers and their drivers, and the bards and panegyrists.

With its secluded streets, marketplaces, and wonderful squares; with numerous transactions of buying and selling goods; and with the bright houses of courtesans, well-constructed with costly furnishings.

With lofty gate-towers blazing with precious jewels, together with dwellings for dogs and vultures where flocks dance, and with variegated banners, white flags, and elevated pavilions; BndP_2,27.15 //

And with ponds, pools, and lakes filled with water, made delightful by the various cries of cakravākas, haṃsas, kurarīs, bakas, and sārasas, and scented by the pollen of white, yellow, and blue lotuses; and with lotus-pollen-scented [waters].
It was adorned with mango, priyāla, panasa, āmra, madhūka, jambu, and plakṣa trees, as well as young saplings for which basins had been prepared;
and it was surrounded by delightful groves of nāga, ketakī, punnāga, and campaka planted along its borders, frequented by birds.
It was beautified by trees bearing various flowers and fruits such as the *mandāra*, *kunda*, *karavīra*, lovely *yūthikā*, and *jāti*,
and by the bees in the surrounding groves that appeared to be filled with delight— possessing forms that inspired wonder throughout the world.

O Lord of Men, this city possesses a clearly manifest human splendor, with a breeze blowing very gently, carrying the most excellent fragrance of all seasons, which mocks the time of the Dharma, and with an abundance of enjoyments delightful to both gods and asuras.

"O King, having immediately provided immeasurable enjoyment of good fortune, may this sacrificial cow of the sage bestow it upon him at once. Then, O Lord of Men, the excellent sage, recognizing that the beautiful hospitality had been accomplished by the twice-born’s sacrificial cow, [accepted it].
O King, having summoned a certain virtuous disciple of his own, he dispatched him immediately;
and having gone swiftly into the presence of the lord of the people, that son of the sage addressed him with great humility.
"The hospitality we have prepared must be promptly accepted by the King; this is the command of our family preceptor.
Thereupon, having been granted permission by the eminent sage, the king entered that excellent city which had been built for his sake.

Accompanied by those whose strength was undiminished, that best of kings entered the city and beheld its splendor, which was the abode of every enjoyment, indicative of the power of the sage’s sacrificial cow, and enchanting to all the world.
With a face radiant with joy, the powerful and wise donor was then filled with great wonder as he went forth,
his beautiful form worthy of being the sole vessel for the eyes of the hosts of celestial women.

That lord of the Haihayas sported upon the royal highway like Śakra in the abode of Kubera amidst a host of immortals; as he set out from the main road, the women of the city surrounded him on all sides with [hands] sprinkled with sandalwood water.

The women on the palace rooftops, with eyes as lovely as those of their sons, incessantly showered handfuls of flowers and parched grain; these pure showers of lājās fell from the lotus-like hands of the city’s beloveds, who were eager to honor the arriving guests.
We were being strewn at every step with heaps of white flowers from the Nandana grove made fragrant by the mud of kālīya, with the songs of swarms of bees,
and even with the finest collyrium, gems, and pearls belonging to the women of that city.
The lord of the earth shone on all sides with his pure [splendors], like Mount Mandara with the mass of the cool-rayed moon’s beams;
he possessed the inconceivable glory of Brahmanic asceticism, which is exceedingly rare in the worlds and possesses a beauty that is longed for.
Beholding that abundance of the city, O King, the lord of the people praised it highly in his mind as if with words;
and the lord of the Haihayas thought, "This royal prosperity, so exceedingly charming and honored, is indeed difficult to find on earth."

Beholding the splendor accumulated by the citizens in the midst of the city, he— along with the family priest, ministers, and their retinues— realized that even the grace of the Brahmins was not capable of approaching even a hundredth part of this [splendor] worshipped by the gods.
As he proceeded, his palace revealed its splendor to those walking by his side, and being honored by the city folk, the king attained great joy;
thereafter, let him, along with his retinue, receive here a reception prepared by the best of sages that is worthy of himself.
Thus, having turned back without fatigue, the king proceeded toward his own palace, which he had already reached;
meanwhile, on the road, he was surrounded on all sides by the citizens who met him with various offerings in their hands and joyfully formed añjali-gestures.

Honored at every step by the resounding cries of "Victory! and the blasts of musical instruments that deafened the quarters of the sky, the king slowly passed through three inner courtyards, each attended by chamberlains in a state of hurried agitation.
Delighted by the respectful reception of his ministers, he entered the residence, which was crowded with common folk stretching out their hands from afar;
there, it was made magnificent by the city women with lamps, curds, mirrors, perfumes, flowers, dūrvā grass, unbroken grains, and other offerings.
Having emerged gracefully from the interior of the royal palace, the delighted king, with great respect,
quickly entered that [palace] which was occupied by those women and shone with a network of luster from various excellent jewels.

O King, in that palace, the group of his wives ascended that golden couch, which was covered with a fine upper cloth, possessed of great renown, and beautiful in its middle; there the monarch quickly seated himself and honored them with various offerings.
With musical instruments and other offerings, and with ornaments, perfumes, flowers, garments, and various decorations, he spread forth the highest joy;
having completed all the duties appropriate for the entire day according to his own tradition, the lord of the Haihayas [proceeded].

The king spent the entire day fully engaged in various kinds of playful sports and diverse amusements with his wives; then, having performed the duties appropriate for the time of day's end, he was followed on all sides by his ministers and counselors.
He quickly entered the assembly hall, where the thick darkness was dispelled by the mass of lamps held in the hands of nearby servants;
there, he sat upon his throne, attended by hundreds of priests, ministers, vassals, and leaders.
He sat in the royal assembly, delighted by various diversions, like the Lord of the Gods surrounded by the hosts of deities;
thereafter, for a long time, there ensued a succession of laughter and conversation centered on the performance of various musical instruments, amusements, and dances.
Thus the lord of men sat for a long time with Āniśā, his mental state delighted by the pleasures of jesting, laughter, and amorous play,
experiencing many various riches of recreation.
Having remained there and dispatched even the subordinate kings to their own dwellings, he himself proceeded to his own residence;
and that entire royal army settled in their quarters according to the power, majesty, and excellence of their own prowess and valor.

Those armies of the king became exceedingly joyful with garments, garlands, ornaments, and other costly items suited to their respective status; they were likewise gratified by various kinds of food, drink, fine snacks, hard foods, honey, meat, milk, clarified butter, and so forth.
All the inhabitants of that king’s city dwelt in contentment, enjoying every pleasure just as hosts of gods do in heaven;
thus, those followers of the monarch were then satisfied by the experience of various appropriate delights.
They said to one another: "What is to be accomplished by means of houses, wealth, and the like? Let us all dwell right here.

Then the king, having made arrangements for the night and retired to his excellent bedchamber, lay down upon a bed most comfortable with heaps of jewels; and the lord of men, feeling confident, enjoyed a long and blessed sleep.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Episode of Arjuna," in the third section, the Introductory Section (*upoddhātapāda*), of the Middle Part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said: At the end of the night, the charioteers, bards, and panegyrists approached the sleeping king and, remaining unperturbed, sang aloud to awaken him.
It was accompanied by the soft sounds of lutes and flutes mixed with the rhythmic clapping of hands,
possessing a sweet and praiseworthy tone that was pleasant to hear for all the senses.
With melodious throats, they sang a captivating song, clearly indicating the *mūrcchanās*, *grāmas*, and accompanied by high,
low, and rhythmic tempos.
And the bards and panegyrists spoke various words to that high-souled king as he slept, desiring to awaken him gently.
Behold, this moon of the lord of kings is setting, utterly defeated by the ever-increasing splendor of your lotus-like face.
O Lord, as if eager now to behold the lotus of Your face,
the sun has indeed reached its rising, piercing the darkness.
O King, crest-jewel upon the crown of the entire lunar dynasty, O one of great intelligence, enough with sleep; awaken now!
Hearing these words of theirs, the lord of the earth awoke,
just as the lotus-eyed one [Viṣṇu] awakes from his sleep upon Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk.
Rising with eyes free from sleep, he performed his daily duties with devotion; being fully attentive, he properly completed the rites for victory and so forth in their entirety.
Having paid homage to his chosen deity, adorned with divine garlands, perfumes, and ornaments, and having taken hold of *dūrvā* grass, collyrium, a mirror, and auspicious objects; BndP_2,28.10 //
Having given gifts to those who sought them, and having bowed down to cows and Brahmins,
he departed from that city and worshipped the Sun.
Then all the ministers, vassal chiefs, and leaders approached;
with palms joined in reverence, O King, they bowed down before that best of monarchs.
Then, surrounded by them, he approached that treasure of asceticism and bowed at his feet with his crown, which possessed the brilliance of the sun.
Then, having greeted the king with blessings, that bull among sages spoke to him with gentle words as he stood bowed in humility: "Please, be seated."
When the king was seated, the great seer, with a joyful mind, said to him:
"O King, has your night passed happily?"
O Indra among kings, for us who live by forest produce in the forest, it is possible to subsist on anything whatsoever, as we share the nature of wild animals.
But for city-dwellers, staying in the forest is utterly unbearable;
for indeed, O King of kings, everything that is unaccustomed is difficult to endure.
That you, along with your followers, have repeatedly undergone the hardships of dwelling in the forest is surely due to that exalted pride of yours toward me.
Thus addressed by that sage, the king, with feelings of affection and as if smiling, replied to him once more with these words.
O Brahman, what indeed is the use of this speech? Have you seen that great majesty of ours by which the entire world has been struck with wonder?
O great sage, my soldiers, their minds overcome by the power and majesty produced by your presence, do not wish to depart from here.
O Lord, by the power of the austerities of those such as you, the worlds here are surely sustained at all times; the splendor of Brahman is indeed inconceivable.
O Lord, it is not at all surprising that you, by means of your ascetic power,
are able to establish the three states of the worlds in their proper sequence.
"Your great ascetic perfection, honored by the world, has been well-beheld by me.
O Brahmin, I shall go to my city; may you grant me leave."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus by Kārttavīrya with respect, the sage honored him greatly and replied, "So be it."
Permitted by the sage, he then departed from that hermitage and,
surrounded by all his armies, set out toward the city.
As he was traveling along the road, the king reflected in his mind:
"Aha! How marvelous is the perfection of this asceticism, which causes wonder in the world!"
"Since by her I have obtained such a cow, the best among all those that milk every desire,
what need have I for an entire kingdom or even for great supernatural power?"
Since this cow, who is like a jewel among cattle, stands before the best of sages,
it is certain that even the prosperity of those who dwell in heaven has been produced by her.
I consider even the manifest station of Indra, which is prosperous and honored by the three worlds,
to be not worth a sixteenth part of this cow.
Then, as the king was reflecting in this manner, the minister Candragupta approached him from behind and spoke with his palms joined in reverence.
O tiger among kings, for what purpose will you go back to the city?
What fruit do you have for a kingdom or a city that has been protected?
O Lord, that which is like a precious jewel to the king—half of which we do not even move—is your kingdom; yet even half of it does not belong to you, for your realm is empty.
Moreover, O King, listen to another marvel that I have seen:
beautiful palaces and likewise beautiful women.
Palaces of various forms and wealth whose depletion was never seen—
while I was looking on, all that dissolved in an instant within her.
O best of kings, that very place was now a penance grove;
for one who possesses such power, what could possibly be difficult to attain?
Therefore, as a being worthy of jewels, you must indeed accept this cow;
for if this deed is approved by you, it should be announced to your dependents.
The king said:
"It is improper for me to say, 'I too do not know her.
My mind suspects that this might be the property of a Brahmin, which must not be seized."
To the king who was speaking thus, the family priest Garga—the best among the wise—spoke these words as if censuring him, O lord of the earth: BndP_2,28.39 //
The property of a Brahmin must not be seized under any circumstances, even in times of distress; there is nothing in this world as difficult to digest as the property of a Brahmin.
Poison kills only the one who consumes it, O Haihaya;
but the fire from the wooden drill-stick of a Brahmin’s property burns the entire family to its very roots.
"O King, this poison of a Brahmin's property is unavoidable in this world; it is difficult to digest, yields its fruit only at the end through sons and grandsons, and is bitter in its ripening."
For what indeed will the mind of those with an unreal nature— not deceived by the eyes— fail to do when it is deluded by power and intoxicated by its own abundance?
O best of kings, who else besides you, apart from giving, would ever contemplate taking from Brahmins? Indeed, no one other than you would desire such an act.
O mighty-armed one, do not perform such an act that is censured by the virtuous; for it would bring about the destruction of your fame in the worlds.
Born into a great lineage of generous donors, do not now,
through this action, bring your fame under the power of others.
Alas! Servants, puffed up by their master's favor, being intent on misconduct, cause their lord to sink somewhat into an ocean of calamity.
Displaying his power through prosperity in matters of human action that are inconceivable, yet himself devoid of consciousness,
the king immediately falls into despair when he follows the course of their opinions.
A minister who is ignorant of the sages would, through his own wicked intellect, cause the king to sink in the ocean of misfortune, just as a wooden boat sinks with its occupant.
Therefore, O tiger among kings, you ought not to follow the opinion of this dull-witted and foolish man regarding the path of policy.
While he was speaking these words, which were for the welfare of his master, the minister interrupted the king and spoke this further: BndP_2,28.51 //
This Brahmin considers only the welfare of his own kind;
the great affairs of state cannot be understood by the twice-born.
The king alone should understand the affairs of state by his own intelligence;
indeed, without taking food, a Brahmin does not find the means to perform his duty.
A Brahmin is never to be despised; he is always to be saluted and is worthy of receiving gifts, for there is nothing superior to him anywhere.
Therefore, O King, accept that cow and depart for your own city;
otherwise, abandon your kingdom and go to the forest to practice austerities.
O King, forgiveness is the duty of Brahmins, while punishment is that of the Kṣatriyas; even if you take [this] by force, no unrighteousness shall befall you.
O King, if you perceive a fault in taking [the cow] by force,
then let the Ṛṣi’s cow be taken after giving him a price in cattle, horses, and other goods.
Indeed, you must accept that cow, for you are entitled to a share of the jewels;
for how could those whose wealth is asceticism have any regard for the accumulation of jewels?
O King, that ascetic, whose wealth is his penance, is peaceful and well-disposed toward you;
therefore, when requested by you, he will certainly grant you the cow in every way.
Or else, having gathered together abundant wealth such as cattle, gold, and whatever else is desired, he will give that cow back to him.
"A great jewel must not be disregarded by a king who desires prosperity;
such is my conviction—what do you think? (BndP 2.28.61)
The King said:
"O counselor, go yourself to that Brahmin, propitiate him especially,
and having given him whatever he desires, bring that cow back."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been thus addressed by the king, that minister, impelled by destiny,
turned back and quickly departed for the hermitage of Jamadagni.
When that king had departed, Rāma, accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa, also set out for the forest in order to fetch sacrificial fuel.
Then that minister, accompanied by his forces, having reached that hermitage and bowed to the tiger among sages, spoke these words:
Candragupta said:
"O Brahmin, it has been commanded by the king that the king is the possessor of jewels on earth;
and this cow is a jewel on earth, the most excellent among all milk-yielding creatures."
Therefore, having stated the appropriate value for a jewel or gold,
you ought to give me this cow, who is a jewel among cattle.
Jamadagni said: "This sacrificial cow belongs to me; she must certainly not be given to anyone.
How can that generous king desire the property of a Brahmin?"
The minister said:
"The king does not desire the cow for himself, but wishes to share in its jewels;
therefore, you ought to give it to him in exchange for ten thousand cows."
Jamadagni said:
"I am never, under any circumstances, a participant in buying or selling;
therefore, I cannot readily give away this vessel for the oblation."
The minister said:
"O Brahmin, whether with half the kingdom or even with the whole of it, give this one cow to the king; that will be for your own welfare."
Jamadagni said:
"O evil-minded one, even for Vāsava himself, I will not give [it] while I am alive;
what need is there to speak again of the king’s request to my preceptor?"
The minister said:
"Out of friendship, you yourself should give the cow to the king by your own will;
for what will you do when she has been taken away by force?"
Jamadagni said:
"Even if that king, as a donor to the twice-born, shall bring [the wealth] here,
what shall I, a brahmin, do without the granting of it according to my own will?"
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed in this manner, that evil-minded minister became enraged and began to forcibly carry off the sage's milch-cow.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as spoken by Vāyu. // 28 //
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Jamadagni, filled with wrath, spoke to him once more:
"The property of a Brahmin must not be seized by a man who possesses knowledge."
"O evil-minded one, you shall incur sin by forcibly seizing my cow;
I know that your life is nearly exhausted, unless you do this [to restore it]."
"O King, whatever you desire to take away by force cannot be accomplished by any means;
or if she should go of her own accord, the king will perish."

Who else, desiring to live and possessing a hundred years of life, would wish to seize the property of Brahmins and ascetics without it being given? Who other than Arjuna would do so? ||| BndP_2,29.4 ||| From: Bhaviṣya Purāṇa 2.29.4.
Thus addressed by him, that minister, incensed and impelled by Time (Kāla),
bound the cow with firm ropes and, endowed with strength, dragged her away.
Then Jamadagni, impelled by his past karma and overcome with anger,
resisted him as he was dragging away the milch cow to the best of his power.
"I will not release this cow while I am alive," the great sage, filled with indignation, said, and he seized her firmly by the neck with both his arms.
Then Candragupta, his soul overcome with rage and exceedingly cruel, commanded his own soldiers: "Drive him away!"
By the king's command, the royal servants forcibly surrounded that ṛṣi on all sides, he who was most invincible in the world.
Beating her with sticks, whips, cudgels, and their fists,
they drove the cow very far away from their presence.
Even while being struck in such a manner, he was not pained, for he was endowed with patience; he did not give way to anger, for freedom from anger is the supreme wealth of the virtuous.
He was capable of destroying or even protecting the entire world by means of his own ascetic power; yet, contemplating its destruction, he did not become enraged.
Having been excessively provoked by his former anger, that great ascetic was then constantly appeased by Rāma for the sake of his mother, and became forever tranquil.
Being struck most violently, his joints and bones crushed to powder,
that one of great splendor fell to the earth, deprived of consciousness.
When that sage had fallen, that evil-minded one became apprehensive and swiftly commanded his servants to bring the cow back by force.
Then, O King, having bound that cow along with her calf with firm ropes,
they struck her with whips and dragged her, desiring to lead her away.
Being dragged by many with whips and even sticks,
and being struck severely by them, the milch cow grew enraged.
Distressed by the blows of that exceedingly harsh curse and filled with great wrath,
she drew out her very firm nooses and freed herself.
Her bonds and fetters released, she was surrounded on all sides by forces;
uttering cries of "huṃ," she fell down everywhere in a rage.
Striking from all sides with the tips of his horns, hooves, and tail, he,
filled with indignation, put the entire army of the king’s ministers to flight.
Having swiftly put all the *kiṅkara*s to flight, the milch-cow,
while all beings were looking on, ascended into the sky.
Then, their resolve shattered and their bodies broken and wounded,
those utterly merciless men forcibly bound that dear child and departed.
Having seized the milch cow without her calf along with his servants,
that wicked man quickly approached the presence of the king.
Having approached the king and bowed down to him with words of praise, he,
filled with trepidation, related the entire account of those events in their entirety.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Story of Arjuna," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard all this, including the slaughter of Jamadagni and the rest, the king,
his mind deeply agitated, reflected in many ways.
Alas! For me, who have spoken such pleasant falsehoods, there is a desire to seize the property of a Brahmin in both worlds; and that is a most despicable act, as it involves the taking of his life.
"Alas! Had I not heard these words from this wise Brahmin, then, being deluded in soul and devoid of shame, I would have abandoned her."
Reflecting thus with a grieving heart,
he then returned toward his own city, accompanied by his army and followers.
O King, when that king had departed for the city along with his retinue, Reṇukā suddenly emerged from the hermitage.
Then he beheld his husband on the ground, motionless and surrounded, with all his limbs wounded and drenched in blood.
Then, perceiving her husband to be struck down and deprived of consciousness, she fell to the ground in a swoon, as if struck by a thunderbolt.
As if rising from the earth after a long time, she, being exceedingly distressed,
fell down and then rose again, weeping most piteously.
And she, covered in the dust of the earth, her face flooded with tears, wretched and fallen into an ocean of grief, lamented most piteously.
Alas, O Lord, beloved knower of Dharma, ocean of the nectar of courtesy!
Alas, fie! O you who are utterly tranquil, one such as you would never have desired this.
Having suddenly departed from the hermitage, where have you gone, O giver of honor, after casting me, helpless as I am, into a bottomless ocean of calamity?
"Since friendship with the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together, I have been stolen away by you;
where you go alone, there you ought to take me."
O illustrious one, seeing you in such a state, my heart does not shatter; indeed, women are hard-hearted.
Lamenting thus and weeping again and again, she, overwhelmed by intense sorrow, cried out, "Rāma! Rāma! in great distress.
Meanwhile, Rāma also, accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa and carrying a load of sacrificial fuel from the forest, returned to his own hermitage.
Seeing many omens foreboding fear,
the powerful lord, his heart agitated, quickly reached the hermitage.
Seeing him approaching, Reṇukā, weeping and deeply distressed, wailed aloud once more, as if overwhelmed by grief.
O King, before Rāma, tormented by the calamity that had befallen her husband,
she struck her belly with both hands.
On the road, having learned the news, Samyagrāma also, seeing his mother afflicted with grief like a female osprey, fell into a state of sorrow.
Having summoned his fortitude, the wise man, overwhelmed by grief and sorrow,
stood upon the ground with his face cast downward, his eyes filled with tears.
Beholding that Tathāgata, Akrūra said to Rāma:
"What is this, O tiger among the Bhṛgus? This is not worthy of you."
But men like you, O highly fortunate one, do not grieve excessively anywhere;
for the steadfast and great do not allow sorrow to cause their ruin.
For grief causes the complete withering of all the senses;
abandon your grief, O mighty-armed one, for such as you are not a fit vessel for it.
Grief is surely the absolute obstacle to goals pertaining to both this world and the next; how then can you allow it entry into your heart?
Becoming a man whose wealth is fortitude, console your mother as she weeps, her consciousness stricken by the calamity of widowhood.
There is no returning here for a thing that has already passed away;
therefore, having abandoned everything of the past, reflect upon what must be done.
Thus being consoled by him,
Rāma, though filled with grief, gradually steadied himself by his own power.
Overwhelmed by grief and sorrow, Reṇukā, weeping repeatedly,
struck her belly with both hands twenty-one times.
Then Rāma, approaching her with tearful eyes, consoled his weeping mother, saying, "Enough, O Mother! (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.30.29).
He spoke to her, who was overcome with grief for her husband and whose suffering had been dispelled:
"Since this chest of yours has been struck twenty-one times."
"I shall slay every last one of that number of Kshatriyas throughout the entire earth; I tell you this truth."
Therefore, casting aside your grief, maintain your fortitude now;
for that which has passed away has truly never come into being.
Thus addressed by him, Reṇukā, though deeply overcome with grief, summoned her fortitude with great difficulty and replied, "So be it."
Then the mighty-armed Rāma, together with his brothers,
began to honor his father’s body in the fire according to the royal rites.
Renukā, whose body was overcome with grief for her husband, though firm in her vows,
summoned all her sons and spoke these words:
Reṇukā said:
"O sons, I desire to follow here my father, who has gone to heaven and was of virtuous character; you ought to grant me permission for that."
How indeed shall I, deprived of that husband and censured by all, endure this unbearable and ill-fated widowhood?
Therefore, I shall follow my beloved husband,
so that I may be with him eternally, both here and in the next world.
Having entered this very blazing fire as if after a long time,
I shall become a beloved guest in the world of my father, who was my husband.
"O sons, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, you must not speak there in that matter except as a mere repetition, acting as guarantors."
Having spoken these words, Reṇukā, firm in her resolve,
entered the fire and set her mind upon following her husband.
At that very moment, however, a disembodied voice, exceedingly profound, addressed Reṇukā together with her sons.
"O Reṇukā, listen attentively to my words along with your sons;
do not act rashly, O blessed lady, for I shall speak what is pleasing to you."
No rash act should ever be committed by anyone who desires their own welfare;
you must not die, for everyone who lives beholds auspicious things.
Therefore, becoming one whose wealth is fortitude, wait for the appointed time,
O lady of pure smiles, having made some mere pretext an intermediary.
"Before long, O beautiful one, your husband will regain his senses; with your life restored, you shall surely obtain your desire and become for a long time a vessel for many blessings."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard those words, Reṇukā took recourse in fortitude,
