and your sons also attained joy out of respect for her speech.
Then, having led their father’s body into the interior of the sage’s hermitage and laid it down in a windless spot, they sat down all around it.
As they sat there with their hearts and minds devoid of joy,
many great and auspicious omens appeared.
Then those bulls among sages, their minds somewhat comforted,
sat down together with their mother, longing for the life of their father.
In the meantime, O King, a wise sage belonging to the lineage of Bhṛgu arrived there by chance through the power of destiny.
He was the direct authority for the Atharvans, one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
a wise man who knew the meaning of all the scriptures, and one honored by all the Asuras.
He who knows the *mṛtasaṃjīvinī* lore, which is difficult even for sages to attain,
can raise up like slain dead the Dānavas who have been killed by the gods.
The treatise of Śukra, which bestows the fruit of sovereignty upon kings, was composed by him;
even today, all monarchs here subsist according to it.
Having reached that hermitage, the great sage entered within and beheld them all in that state, overwhelmed with sorrow.
Then, upon seeing Bhṛgu, the progenitor of their lineage, they rose up with joy and,
having honored him, offered him an excellent seat.
And that great sage, having greeted them all with blessings, asked, "What is this event that has occurred? and they reported everything to him.
Having heard that, Bhṛgu, the knower of mantras, quickly took water and, with humility, sprinkled him with the *saṃjīvinī* mantra while uttering this: *BndP_2,30.58*
If there is merit for me from this sacrifice and from my ascetic penance,
by that power may he live quickly, as if rising from sleep.
When these auspicious words had been spoken by Bhṛgu, the performer of virtuous deeds,
Arcīka then rose up like another manifest Bṛhaspati.
O King, having seen his venerable grandfather Bhṛgu standing there,
he bowed with devotion and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke.
Jamadagni said:
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and my life is fruitful."
"O Blessed One, I behold today your feet, which are saluted by gods and asuras; O giver of honor, what service may I perform for you now?"
"O Lord, purify your own lineage with the drops of water from your feet!
Having spoken thus, he joyfully accepted the *arghya* offering brought by Rāma.
With his neck bowed in devotion, he placed that water at the sage’s feet;
the high-minded one, together with his family, then received it upon his head.
Then, having honored Bhṛgu, he, filled with humility, asked:
"O Blessed One, what sinful deed was committed by that wicked king?"
O high-minded one, what did that evil-souled man do after I had properly honored him as a guest with a virtuous intent?
Vasiṣṭha said: Thus questioned, the wise Bhṛgu, the omniscient lord,
having meditated for a long time and reflected upon the cause, spoke, O King.
Bhṛgu said:
Listen, O dear one, O highly fortunate one, to the seed of this action,
which you, O sinless one, have indeed committed against the omniscient one.
"O fool, because of your offense against a twice-born, that lord of the earth was cursed long ago by Vasiṣṭha for the sake of his destruction: 'Your virility shall perish.'"
How then could the word of that sage prove otherwise? "This Rāma shall forcibly overcome the preeminent king of great heroism. (Bṛhaddevatā 2.30.71)
"O mighty-armed one, he will fulfill the vow he made long ago,
because my mother's chest was struck by you in my presence."
Indeed, twenty-one times, being overwhelmed by intense sorrow,
I shall rid this earth of the kṣatriyas three times sevenfold.
Therefore, O giver of honor, even though he is being constantly restrained by you and his father, he will surely act by force toward this destined purpose.
That illustrious king was a devoted attendant of the elders;
high-minded and having attained awakening from Dattātreya, who is a portion of Hari.
"He is a direct devotee and a great soul; in his killing, there would be sin.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, that wise Bhṛgu, the son of Brahmā, departed as he had come, due to the turning of the future time.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 30 //
Sagara said:
O highly fortunate son of Brahmā, tell me of the deeds of Bhārgava;
for, enraged by the king's action, that one of great heroism performed a certain deed.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When that illustrious one had departed,
Rāma, devoted to his father, spoke in great anger, sighing again and again.
Paraśurāma said:
"Alas! Behold the folly of King Kārtavīrya, who, though a learned man, has set out on a path astray by attempting the murder of a Brahmin."
For I consider destiny to be powerful, by whose influence all embodied beings,
being deluded, perform actions that are either auspicious or inauspicious.
"Listen, all you sages, a vow is being made by me:
having slain Kārtavīrya in battle, I shall settle my father’s enmity."
Even if the king were protected by all the gods, including Indra, and likewise by the Dānavas, I shall still destroy him; it cannot be otherwise.
Having heard these words spoken by Rāma, whose soul was filled with agitation, Jamadagni spoke thus to his son who had spoken so rashly: BndP_2,31.7 //
Jamadagni said:
Listen, O Rāma, I shall proclaim the eternal dharma of the virtuous,
hearing which all human beings become performers of dharma.
Those virtuous ones of great fortune who long for liberation from saṃsāra do not become angry with anyone, even when they are reviled or beaten.
Those who are rich in forgiveness, highly fortunate, self-controlled, and ascetic—
for them, as for those who constantly perform righteous deeds, there are indeed imperishable worlds.
But he who, even when struck by wicked people with sticks and other weapons, or even by words,
does not fall into agitation— he is proclaimed a virtuous man.
He who strikes one who is striking him is not a virtuous man, but a partaker of sin;
we Brahmins are virtuous men who have attained the state of being worthy of honor through our forbearance.
"O dear one, in the killing of a lord of men, a very great sin would arise;
therefore, restrain yourself today, practice forbearance, and perform penance."
Vasiṣṭha said: O prince, having understood what was thus commanded by his father,
Rāma spoke to his father, who was of a forgiving nature and a subduer of enemies.
Paraśurāma said:
Listen now, O father of great wisdom, to my explanation; you have pointed out the path of tranquility belonging to the virtuous and high-souled ones. (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 2.31.15)

One should cultivate a sense of reverence toward virtuous and humble beings as if they were lords; however, one should not practice equanimity toward those of wicked conduct, for such equanimity does not bestow happiness.
"Therefore, the slaughter of this Kārtavīrya must indeed be carried out by me.
Grant me permission today from you, who are worthy of honor, so that I may accomplish my own vendetta."
Jamadagni said:
Listen with a concentrated mind, O highly fortunate Rāma, to my words;
you shall do as it is destined to be, for it cannot be otherwise.
"Go from here, my dear, and ask the Brahmins about what is beneficial and what is harmful;
whatever that Lord says, you shall do—of this there is no doubt."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus, that high-minded one, having paid homage to his father,
went to the world of Brahmā, which is inaccessible to ordinary people.
He beheld the world of Brahmā, fashioned from śātakaumbha gold,
joined with golden ramparts and adorned with pillars of jewels.
There he saw Brahmā, of immeasurable splendor,
seated upon a beautiful jeweled throne and adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
He was surrounded by lords of the Siddhas and lords of the Munis intent on meditation,
and he gazed with a smile and joy upon the dancing of the Vidyādharīs.
Meditate with a restrained mind upon the Supreme Brahman— the giver of fruits through austerity, the creator of the worlds, the all-pervading Lord, and the most perfect one.
Seeing that imperishable one constantly proclaiming the secret yoga among the multitudes of devotees, the descendant of Bhṛgu bowed down before him with devotion.
Having seen the humble Rāma and having greeted him with blessings, he asked about his welfare: "My child, how have you come here?"
Thus questioned according to the prescribed rite, Rāma related from the beginning the entire account of his high-souled father, Kārtavīrya.
Having heard all that, O giver of honor, Brahmā— though he already understood the matter—
spoke to the most righteous Rāma words that bring happiness in the end.
"O child, the vow which you have made out of anger is difficult to fulfill;
O boy, this creation could only come to pass through the grace of the Blessed One."
"O dear one, this world was created by me through affliction at his command;
yet you have made a vow to bring about its destruction."
"Because of the fault of one king and through the humiliation of your father, you desire to rid the earth of its rulers twenty-one times."
This eternal creation, consisting of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
has appeared and disappeared again and again from Hari alone.
Your vow shall indeed not be in vain, and by virtue of your former deeds,
the accomplishment of your purpose shall come to pass through whatever effort you exert.
Go to the world of Śiva and receive the command of Śiva;
there are many kings on earth who are servants of Śaṅkara.
Without the command of Maheśa, who indeed would be capable of slaying them,
when they bear armor upon their bodies and possess weapons that are difficult to withstand?
Exert yourself with diligence in employing a skillful means that brings about victory and auspiciousness;
for when a skillful means is undertaken, all undertakings reach fulfillment.
"O child, receive from your guru Hara the mantra and the armor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
the Vaiṣṇava splendor is indeed difficult to overcome, yet Śiva’s power shall prevail."
The armor named Trailokyavijaya is most wonderful;
having petitioned Śaṅkara in whatever manner possible, one obtains that which is difficult to attain.
He, who is gracious through his virtues, compassionate, and affectionate toward the distressed, will surely grant you the divine Pāśupata weapon as well; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 31 //
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard the words of Brahmā and having bowed down to the Teacher of the World, he,
with a deeply serene mind, departed for the realm of Śiva.
Two hundred thousand yojanas above is the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka), which is characterized by two lakṣas;
it is indescribable, accessible only to yogis, and higher than the highest.
Since Vaikuṇṭha is to its south and the world of Gaurī is to its left,
and since Dhruvaloka is beneath it, it is indeed beyond all worlds.
Rāma, through the power of his asceticism, beheld the world of Śiva,
which was beyond all comparison and filled with manifold wonders.
There dwell the lords of yogis, perfected ones, and auspicious Pāśupatas—
people who are peaceful and free from envy, possessing the merit of austerities performed for ten million kalpas.
Adorned with trees such as the pārijāta and with wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus),
it was indeed created by Śaṅkara himself through his yogic power and according to his own will.
In a dream, his preceptor Śilpī, who was free from all worldly activity,
beheld hundreds of divine lakes resplendent with rubies.
It was beautiful and exceedingly delightful, furnished with jeweled altars,
and completely surrounded by a wall constructed of gold and gems.
Reaching far above and touching the sky, it was pure, supreme, and white like milk;
it was provided with four gates and adorned with jeweled altars.
Adorned with red stairways, jeweled pillars, and door-panels,
and beautified by various wonderful and diverse paintings, they were exceedingly enchanting.
In the midst of that, the righteous-souled Rāma, having come together, beheld a delightful palace adorned with a lion-gate, appearing as if it were a marvel.
There he saw two extremely terrifying gatekeepers stationed at the entrance,
with mouths containing large, formidable fangs, and distorted, blood-red eyes.
Resembling two burnt mountains, they possessed great strength and prowess;
their limbs were adorned with ashes, and they were clad in tiger-skins.
Seeing those two blazing with Brahmanic splendor, bearing tridents and battle-axes, he was terrified in his mind and spoke somewhat humbly.
I pay homage to you two lords; I have come to see Śaṅkara. Having received the command of the Lord, you should now give me your instructions.
Having heard those words and received the command of Śiva,
those two attendants of the Lord gave them permission to enter.
Having received that command, the twice-born entered the inner apartments with joy; there he beheld a most beautiful assembly hall, crowded with hosts of perfected beings (siddhas).
Having seen the abundance of fragrance belonging to the Lord, he was filled with wonder;
there he beheld Śiva, peaceful, three-eyed, and moon-crested.
His hand is adorned with a trident; he wears a garment of tiger-skin as his excellent raiment;
his limbs are decorated with sacred ashes, and he has a serpent as his sacred thread.
Delighting in the Self, with all desires fulfilled, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
five-faced, ten-armed, he whose form exists for the grace of his devotees.
He was proclaiming the knowledge of yoga to the perfected ones (siddhas) with the gesture of logic (tarka-mudrā),
while being joyfully praised by the lords of yogis and the hosts of Pramathas.
Seeing him surrounded by Bhairavas, Yoginīs, and likewise by the hosts of Rudras,
Rāma bowed his head with supreme joy.
On the left side [he should place] Kārttikeya, and on the right, Gaṇeśvara;
and before him, Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, and Vīrabhadra.
Having seen Durgā with a hundred arms upon his lap and having bowed down to her as well,
the wise one began to praise the Lord with a faltering voice.
I pay homage to Śiva, the Lord, the all-pervading, the omnipresent, and the imperishable;
he who is fierce, adorned with serpents, and radiant with a garland of human skulls.

I know you, the all-pervading one, the ocean of compassion, who assumes the forms of Brahmā and others as the eldest [of the gods], and who effects the creation, maintenance, and destruction of all worlds.
I bow to Him whom the Vedas are unable to praise, who is beyond the reach of speech and mind, unattainable by knowledge or intellect, and formless.
I bow to that Supreme beyond the supreme, whom Śakra and the other hosts of gods, the sages, the Manus, and the asuras do not know according to reality.
I bow to that one who consists of the universe, by a fraction of whose parts all worlds, both moving and unmoving, are created, and into whom they are again dissolved.
I bow to that supreme Hara, from whose slight anger the fire arises that consumes the entire world above, along with the netherworld below.
Earth, wind, fire, water, ether, the moon, and the sun—these are the eight forms worshipped by the world; I bow down to that sacrifice.

I take refuge in Him who is the embodiment of Time, the primordial creator of the world, its protector assuming distinct forms, pervading the universe, and likewise at the end, the destroyer in the form of Rudra.

Having spoken thus, that descendant of Bhṛgu, the ocean of compassion, being distressed, joyfully fell at his feet; then, raising him up with ease by his left hand, he placed his hand upon the other’s head.
Having greeted him with respect and honored him with benedictions, he seated him to the east of Gaṇeśa;
then, looking toward Umā, who stands to his left, he whose gaze is moist with compassion spoke, for he fulfills all desires.
Śiva said:
"Who are you, O boy, and in whose family were you born? With what purpose have you come here?
Point it out; being pleased by your devotional state, I shall grant you whatever is in your heart."

Thus addressed with respect by the high-souled Hara, the remover of the suffering of the universe, Bhṛgu bowed again to the Lord of the gods, his preceptor who is an ocean of compassion, and spoke quickly.
Paraśurāma said:
O Lord, I am born in the lineage of Bhṛgu as the son of Jamadagni;
known by the name Rāma, I have come to you for refuge—you who are adored by the world.
O Lord, fulfill that very desire which I have come to your presence for the sake of accomplishing; grant my wish, O Ruler of the Universe.
O Lord, even when King Kārtavīrya arrived on a hunt,
my father Jamadagni offered him hospitality.
The dull-witted king, out of greed and by force, caused her to fall;
seeing him dead, that cow went indeed to the world of cows.
Without grieving for my innocent father’s death, the king subsequently departed for his own city; thereafter, my mother wept most bitterly.
Knowing that, our great-grandfather Bhṛgu, who understands the ways of the world, came [to us], O Mahādeva; indeed, I too have come from the forest.
Having comforted my brothers and my mother, who were afflicted by great sorrow,
that knower of mantras restored my father to life.
O Lord, in the future, when Bhṛgu [is born], I was provoked to anger by my mother’s suffering;
then, O God, I made a vow while consoling my own mother.
"Since my mother struck her own chest twenty-one times,
for that same number of times I shall rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas."
"Thus my purpose is fulfilled; the Lord, the Master of the World, is the Great God (Mahādeva). Therefore, O Protector, I have come here into your presence."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words and having seen the face of Durgā,
Hara then became for a moment one whose face was bowed down, reflecting in thought.
In the meantime, O Great King, Durgā laughed heartily in amazement and spoke to Bhārgava, the achiever of enmity.
"O son of a twice-born ascetic, you wish to rid the earth of its kings twenty-one times over out of anger; O young brahmin, this is a great act of rashness."
Desirous of killing the lord Arjuna of the thousand rays while unarmed,
you do not realize that even Rāvaṇa was repulsed by him with the mere play of a frown.
In the past, the armor of Śrī Hari was bestowed upon him by Datta;
how then can you wish to slay him, whose power and valor are exceedingly great?
Śaṅkara is perfected in compassion and is all-powerful to act otherwise;
yet, O son, there is no one other than Śaṅkara who is capable of performing such a noble deed.
Then, having obtained the consent of the Goddess, the omnipresent Śambhu, an ocean of compassion,
addressed the son of Jamadagni with auspicious words.
Śiva said:
"From this day forward, O Brahmin, you shall be equal to Skanda unto me;
O high-minded one, I shall grant you a divine mantra and a protective armor (kavaca)."
By whose grace you shall, with ease, slay Kārtavīrya and render the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara gave him a mantra that is very difficult to obtain,
a most wonderful armor named Trailokyavijaya.
The Nāgapāśa, the Pāśupata, and the exceedingly rare Brahmāstra;
likewise the Nārāyaṇāstra, the Āgneya, the Vāyavya, and the Vāruṇa.
The Gandharva weapon, the Gāruḍa weapon, and the most wonderful Jṛmbhaṇa weapon;
as well as the mace, the spear, the axe, the trident, and the unsurpassed staff.
Having paid homage to Śiva, the peaceful one, as well as Durgā, Skanda, and Gaṇeśvara, he became filled with joy over his entire collection of hand-to-hand weapons and missiles.
Having performed the circumambulation and having mastered the supreme armor-mantra (kavaca) and the mantra spoken by Śiva, Rāma went to the excellent holy site of Puṣkara.
The descendant of Bhṛgu accomplished his entire purpose,
having joyfully slain Kārtavīrya along with his army and his kin; then, having returned, that scion of the Bhṛgus went to his own father’s home.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sagara said:
"O best of sages, O Lord, everything that has been recited by you has been heard.
Now tell me the armor (kavaca) which grants victory over the three worlds everywhere."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the most wonderful armor (kavaca) and the mantra that bestows success and brings constant happiness to practitioners.
One should then utter "to the Beloved of the Gopījana-pada"; this ten-syllabled great mantra, ending with *svāhā*, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Sadāśiva is its seer (ṛṣi), the Paṅkti is declared to be the meter (chandas),
Kṛṣṇa is said to be the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of everything.
Now, for the armor (*kavaca*) of Trailokyavijaya, Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*),
the *jagatī* is the meter (*chandas*), and the deity is Rājeśvara himself.
The application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of victory over the three worlds:
"May the Praṇava protect my head; may it always be 'Obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa'. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.33.6)
May the skull protect me constantly with the mantra "Kṛṣṇāya svāhā";
may "Kṛṣṇa" protect my eyes, and "Kṛṣṇa-svāhā" protect my pupils.
May this mantra "Salutation to Hari" always protect my creeper-like eyebrows;
may "Oṃ Govindāya Svāhā" constantly protect my nose. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.33.8)
"Obeisance to Gopāla"—may this mantra constantly protect my cheeks.
"Klīṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇa"—may the Kalpa-tree protect my ears. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.33.9)
"Śrīṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇa—may this protect my pair of lips eternally; Oṃ, svāhā to the Lord of the Gopīs—may this protect the row of my teeth. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.33.10)
May the three-syllabled mantra "Śrīkṛṣṇa" protect my teeth-gaps;
may "Oṃ Śrīkṛṣṇāya Svāhā" always protect my tongue. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.33.11)
"Rāmeśvarāya svāhā"—may this protect my palate forever;
"Rādhikeśāya svāhā"—may this protect my throat at all times. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.33.12)
Homage to the Lord of the Gopī hosts; may He protect my neck at all times.
Oṃ, svāhā to the Lord of the Gopas; may He always protect my shoulders. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.33.13)
"Obeisance to Him in the form of a youth, Svāhā! May He protect my back. May He always protect my belly; 'obeisance to Mukunda' is the mantra. (Bṛhad-brahma-vaivarta-purāṇa 2.33.14)
Hnīṃ Śrīṅ Klīṅ Kṛṣṇāya Svāhā—may this protect my two hands forever.
Oṃ Viṣṇave Namaḥ Svāhā—may this protect the pair of my arms. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.33.15)
Oṃ hrīṃ bhagavate svāhā—may this protect the rows of my nails.
Namo nārāyaṇāya—may this protect the hollows of my nails. (Bṛhad-nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 2.33.16)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ! May [the mantra] for Padmanābha always protect my navel.
Oṃ sarveśāya svāhā! May it always protect my hair. (BndP 2.33.17)
"Oṃ *namaḥ kṛṣṇāya svāhā*—may this always protect my *brahmarandhra*. Oṃ *mādhavāya svāhā*—may this always protect my forehead. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.33.18)
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ; may Rasikeśa always protect my waist.
Homage to Gopījaneśa; may he always protect my thighs. (Bṛhad-brahma-vaivarta-purāṇa 2.33.19)
"Oṃ, obeisance to the destroyer of the Daityas, svāhā"—may this protect the knees; "obeisance to Yaśodānandana"—may this protect the shanks.
"Oṃ hīṃ rāsārambhapriyāya svāhā"—may this protect my heart;
"vṛndāpriyāya svāhā"—may this protect all my limbs. (BndP 2.33.21)
May Kṛṣṇa, whose mind is ever-compassionate, protect me always in the eastern direction;
may he himself, the Lord of Goloka, protect me in the south-eastern quarter.
May He whose nature is the fullness of Brahman always protect me in the south;
may Kṛṣṇa protect me in the southwest, and may Hari protect me in the west.
May Govinda protect me in the northwest; may Rasikeśvara protect me in the north;
and may he who sports in Vṛndāvana always protect me in the northeast.
May the eternal Lord of Vṛndā’s life protect me from above;
may the mighty destroyer of Bali always protect me from below.
May Nṛsiṃha protect me always in water, on land, and in the atmosphere;
and may Mādhava himself protect me both in sleep and while awake.
"May the all-pervading Lord, the inner self of all, who is untainted, protect me from every side.
Thus, O King, has been told to you that which destroys the entire flood of sins.
This armor known as Trailokyavijaya belongs to the Supreme Lord;
it was heard by me from the mouth of Śiva and must not be spoken of to anyone.
He who, having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rites, wears this armor (kavaca) on his neck or on his right arm, is Viṣṇu himself; of this there is no doubt.
Wherever that practitioner may dwell, if he possesses the armor of accomplishment, he is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
One shall certainly obtain the fruit of worship for ten million years,
as well as the merit of thousands of Rājasūya sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
Even the great gifts and the circumambulations of the earth are not worth a sixteenth part of this *Trailokyavijaya*.
Vows, fasts, and observances, as well as the study and recitation of the Vedas,
and bathing in all sacred fords— all these do not equal even a sixteenth part of this [merit].
Whether it be the state of a Siddha, immortality, or even servitude to Śrī Hari—
if one possesses the perfected armor (kavaca), one certainly attains all of these.
He who recites it ten hundred thousand times shall have his armor perfected;
he whose armor is perfected will certainly be victorious.
O King, a kingdom may be given, a head may be given, and even life itself may be given;
but this armor, my child, must never be given, even in times of extreme peril.
Know this, O Sun of the Clan: that which I have revealed for the sake of their protection and for the fulfillment of my command,
by wearing this armor, you shall become a universal sovereign (cakravartin).
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sagara said:
"O son of Brahmā, O highly fortunate one, you have shown me great favor."
This is the stainless armor that has been revealed to me.
"O Lord, by the grace of Aurva I have become skilled in weapons;
now, through your favor, I have become an object of your compassion."
O Guru, tell me in detail how the heroic King Kārtavīrya was brought to his end by Rāma, the lord of the Bhṛgus.
O Guru, how did those two heroes, Rāma— the object of Śiva’s compassion— and Datta, the king, encounter one another in battle?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the sin-destroying life-story of King Kārtavīrya and of the high-souled Rāma.
Having received the armor and the mantra from the mouth of his guru, that Rāma,
endowed with supreme devotion, performed its propitiation.
O Rāma, devoted to the three daily ablutions and intent upon his meditative practices, Bhūśuṇḍi lived at Puṣkara for a hundred years without weariness.
O King, Akṛtavraṇa brought sacrificial materials such as wood, flowers, and kuśa grass from the forest every day and presented them to Bhṛgu.
Constantly engaged in meditation, Rāma, the best among the wise,
propitiated the omnipresent Lord Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of all impurities.
O Lord of the Earth, as Rāma was thus performing sacrifice,
a hundred years passed while he remained constantly engaged in meditation.
Once, O Great King, the great Rāma went to bathe at Madhyama Puṣkara, where he beheld a most excellent wonder.
A single deer, accompanied by its mate, fled;
having encountered the hunter while on his hunt, it was tormented and deeply afflicted by the heat of the dharma.
Thirsty and eager for a drink of water, O illustrious one,
he arrived at the shore of that lake while Rāma was looking on.
Afterwards, a doe arrived, her eyes wide with fear;
both of them, their minds filled with apprehension, were drinking water there.
Just then, a hunter arrived, bow in hand and with an arrow in his grasp;
he saw Rāma, the delight of Bhṛgu’s lineage, lying there.
Joined with Akṛtavraṇa, he stood with his gaze cast far away;
filled with apprehension regarding the descendant of Bhṛgu, he then began to reflect.
"This Rāma is a great hero, the bringer of destruction to the wicked;
how can I kill these two deer while he watches? (BndP 2.34.17)
O best of kings, the hunter, overcome by these thoughts and with a mind terrified by fear of Rāma, remained right there.
But Rāma, the wise one, seeing those two deer drinking the water from the pool, reflected: "What could be the cause of fear here? (BdP 2.34.19)
Neither Vyāghrasena nor the hunter is to be seen here;
for what reason, alas, do these two have such apprehensive and startled looks?
Or rather, for the species of deer is by nature timid-eyed;
if these two, even while drinking water, have such timid eyes as they look about.
This is not the only reason here; rather, it is because these two appear afflicted by grief and fear, with all their limbs exhausted and trembling.
Having reflected thus, the wise Rāma remained in the middle lotus together with his disciple, as long as those two also remained there.
Having drunk water and then taken refuge in the shade of a tree,
they joyfully engaged in conversation upon seeing the high-souled Rāma.
The doe said: "O beloved, let us remain right here until Rāma has settled there;
in the presence of this hero, no fear shall come upon either of us."
Even here, having arrived at our dwelling, he will indeed strike us;
for as soon as he is seen by the sage, he shall be reduced to ashes.
When these words had been spoken by the doe, who was delighted with Rāma,
the deer, filled with joy, spoke to his beloved.
"In this very way, O illustrious and beautiful lady, regarding what you say,
I too know the power of the great-souled Rāma."
And this disciple of his who is seen by his side, Akṛtavraṇa, is highly fortunate; he too has been rescued from the terror of the tiger.
"O highly fortunate lady, this is Rāma, the younger son of Jamadagni;
having seen his father insulted by Kārtavīrya," ||| BndP_2,34.30 |||
Becoming exceedingly enraged, he made a vow to slay the king;
for desiring to fulfill that vow, he indeed went formerly to the world of Brahmā.
That Brahmā commanded him, "Go indeed to the world of Śiva";
having received his command, he went into the presence of Śiva.
That compassionate Mahādeva, having honored the descendant of Bhṛgu, related the entire account of the king as well as that of his own father.
He gave to Kṛṣṇa an excellent, impenetrable mantra as well as his own armor,
the Pāśupata weapon, and the entire collection of other weapons.
Having joyfully and respectfully given him weapons, he dismissed him;
O auspicious lady, this very person has arrived here, intent upon the practice of mantra-siddhi.
The righteous and wise one constantly recites the armor of Kṛṣṇa;
one hundred years have passed for that great-souled man.
O auspicious lady, for one who seeks to accomplish a mantra, success indeed does not come;
for there is a cause in this matter, which is devotion, and that is considered to be threefold.
O lady with tremulous eyes, there are indeed three types— superior, middling, and inferior—
belonging to Śiva, to Nārada, and to the high-souled Śuka.
Of the royal sage Ambarīṣa, of Rantideva the son of Māruta, of Bali, of Vibhīṣaṇa, and of the high-souled Prahlāda; ||| BndP_2,34.39 |||
O lady of auspicious gaze, the highest devotion belongs only to the gopīs, to Uddhava, and to the lords of sages such as Vasiṣṭha, as well as to Manu and others.
There is indeed only moderate devotion toward other common people;
this Rāma possesses such moderate devotion, being eternally devoted to Him alone.
"She served the Lord of the Gopīs, yet she did not attain perfection.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus, that doe, with a joyful mind, quickly [approached] her beloved.
Again he asked about the characteristic of devotion that bestows love.
Mṛgī said:
"Well said, O beloved, O illustrious one; your words are extraordinary, my dear."
Tell me now: how has this direct knowledge of yours arisen?
The deer said:
"Listen, O beloved and highly fortunate one; knowledge is born from merit."
That merit has been produced today from the sight of this Bhārgava;
for this Bhārgava is a virtuous soul, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, and one who has conquered his senses.

"O beautiful lady, because he was constantly devoted to serving his guru and always respectful toward obligatory and occasional rites, knowledge was born within me this very day through the sight of him."
"Today itself it has become known to me that this great-souled Rāma is the indicator of the auspicious and inauspicious for all beings dwelling in the three worlds."
This account bestows merit and destroys the sins of those who hear it;
furthermore, whatever shall be done [hereafter] will also fall within the scope of knowledge.
That which is declared to be the supreme devotion— without it,
neither the armor nor the mantra will succeed, even in tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years.
O blessed lady, if this descendant of Bhṛgu should indeed receive the grace of Agastya,
[he shall obtain] the hymn named *Kṛṣṇapremāmṛta*, which bestows supreme devotion.
And having understood this, he shall attain the perfection of the mantra and the armor;
that sage, who has realized the true meaning of reality, is compassionate and the bestower of fearlessness.
And he shall indeed instruct him in that knowledge of reality which brings joy,
since it consists of the entire life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa strung together with his names.
From the hymn *Kṛṣṇapremāmṛta*, his great intelligence will be known;
thereafter, O King, the two of them, having attained perfection, [bestowed] armor upon the lord of the Haihayas.
Having slain him along with his sons, ministers, friends, forces, and vehicles,
O dear one, he will render the earth devoid of kings twenty-one times.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to the doe, O King, the deer then became silent;
he had come to understand the cause of his own state as a deer.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sagara said:
O Sage, knower of the supreme reality, skilled in the meaning of meditation and knowledge,
how can there be grace for those whose minds are absorbed in devotion to the Blessed One?
For you too, O highly fortunate one, since you recount these excellent stories,
having heard everything regarding the deeds of Bhārgava from the mouth of the deer.
"O Lord, tell me in detail once more that which concerns the past, the present, and the future, and which is filled with the stories of Nārāyaṇa."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O King, I shall relate the great history of the deer;
as it was asked by her, that knower of truth described it to her.
Having heard the life-story of that high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu,
he again respectfully questioned his beloved regarding the true meaning of the principles of knowledge.
The female deer said:
"Excellent, excellent, O illustrious one! You have achieved your purpose, there is no doubt, since through the sight of him today, suprasensory knowledge has arisen within you."
Therefore, O Lord, tell me also the entire cause regarding ourselves:
by what action have we both attained this birth among the animals?
Having heard these words of his beloved, that deer himself then described his own history, as did the doe.
The deer said:
"Listen, O beloved and highly fortunate one, to how we two came to this state of being deer; in this world, O illustrious lady, one's own disposition is the cause of existence."
Indeed, due to his past good and evil deeds, the soul regained its memory in the Draviḍa country, which was once filled with various prosperities.
I was born into a family of Brāhmaṇas belonging to the Kauśika lineage;
my father was named Śivadatta, who was an expert in the sacred scriptures.
We four were born as his sons, O best of the twice-born:
Rāma was the eldest, Dharma was his younger brother, and Pṛthu was the one born after him.
"O beloved, I was born as the fourth [son], renowned as Sūri;
and the highly illustrious Śivadatta, having performed the initiation ceremony for all of us in due order—"
He taught us the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs and secret doctrines;
there, all four of us were devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Devoted to service toward their guru and dedicated to the pursuit of knowledge,
they went daily to the forest for fruits, water, fuel, kusha grass, and earth.
Having brought him and given him to our father, we then indeed began our studies;
however, on one occasion, we all arrived at a forest on a mountain.
O lady with tremulous eyes, all of them, having bathed at dawn in the great river Audbhida— which is situated on the bank of the Kṛtamālā— with joyful minds, [proceeded].
Having offered the guest-water (argha) and performed their silent prayers (japa), they mounted that best of elephants,
which was surrounded by *śāla*, *stamāla*, *priyaka*, *panasa*, and *kovidāra* trees.
With *sarala* trees, *arjuna*, betel-nut palms, date palms, coconut palms, rose-apples, mangoes, *kaṭphala* fruits, and bṛhatī trees; ||| BndP_2,35.19 |||
It was filled with various other trees that provided for the needs of others, offering pleasant shade and resounded with the joyful calls of diverse birds.
It was frequented by tigers, lions, leopards, musk deer, elephants,
and śarabhas and other beasts dwelling within its caves.
It was surrounded by other fragrant trees— mallikā, pāṭala, kunda, karṇikāra, and kadamba— their pollen stirred up by the wind.
And it was filled with curiosity as its peaks— blue, yellow, white, and crimson, strewn with various clusters of jewels— scratched against the sky.

With waterfalls rising from the caves that resounded with the noise of falling from great heights, it seemed as if the mountain were roaring in close proximity to the beasts of prey, wild animals, and birds.
There, our eyes were so thrilled with extreme curiosity that we brothers did not even remember ourselves, nor did we perceive that we were separated from one another.
In the meantime, O beloved, a certain doe arrived, parched with thirst,
desiring to drink the water falling from the head of the waterfall.
While she was drinking water, a most terrifying tiger arrived there by chance and seized her as she was overcome with fear.
Seeing that seizure, I fled in fear;
because of the extreme height [of the place], I fell down and died, while remembering the doe.
Having died, you were born as a doe, and I, remembering you, was born as a deer, O blessed lady; I truly do not know where my elder brothers have gone.
This conduct of yours has come to my memory through my own power;
listen, O blessed lady, as I speak of what has been and what is yet to be.
Even that hunter who had previously remained at a distance,
clinging to a tree, has now been devoured by the lion out of fear of this Rāma.
Having abandoned his life according to the prescribed rite, he will go to the heavenly world;
meanwhile, we two have drunk water here at the Middle Puṣkara.
This descendant of Bhṛgu has been seen in person, bearing the very form of Viṣṇu;
by him, the sin produced over many births has been brought to destruction.
Having obtained the vision of Agastya and heard the hymn that bestows a [favorable] state of existence,
we two shall go to the auspicious worlds, having gone to which one does not grieve.
Having spoken thus to his beloved, that deer of pleasing appearance,
with a serene soul and his mind fixed intently upon Rāma, became silent.
O Indra among kings, Bhārgava, who was learned and accompanied by his disciples, was struck with wonder upon hearing what was said by the deer, and he likewise resolved to depart.
Bound by his unfulfilled vow, he set out toward Agastya’s hermitage;
having bathed and performed his daily rites, he departed with great joy.
While proceeding on the road, Rāma then saw a hunter who had died from the blow of a lion; the high-souled one was struck with wonder.
Having traveled one and a half yojanas toward Kaniṣṭha Puṣkara,
he bathed and performed the midday twilight rites, filled with great joy.
While he was reflecting on that which had been declared by the deer as beneficial for himself,
a pair of deer arrived, following closely behind him.
Having drunk the water at Puṣkara and sprinkled his own body with the waters,
he went toward the hermitage of Agastya while Bhārgava was looking on.
Rāma, too, having performed his evening rites, went to the hermitage of the Pot-born Sage,
the high-minded one observing Puṣkara fallen into calamity.
Having gone to the footprints of Viṣṇu, the pool where the Nāgas dwell, and the abode of the Seven Sages, he touched the pure water there and proceeded to the retreat of Agastya.
And that Sarasvatī, O King, who is the daughter of Brahmā,
arrived there in order to fill the three basins of the Agnihotra ritual.
There on the bank, the descendant of Bhṛgu beheld the great and wondrous hermitage of the Jar-born Sage, auspicious, meritorious, and frequented by various sages.
It was frequented by deer and lions that had come together with tranquil minds,
and it was filled with *kuṭara*, *arjuna*, *nimba*, *pāribhadra*, *dhava*, and *guda* trees.
Having entered there, which was crowded with *khadira*, *āsana*, and *kharjūra* trees as well as *badarī* trees, Rāma indeed went forth accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa.
He beheld the pot-born sage seated there, his mind tranquil,
resembling a lake of still water, meditating upon the eternal Brahman.
In a bower of creepers, wearing a deerskin that was both auspicious and aphrodisiac,
he prostrated himself before the great king while uttering his own name.
"I am Rāma, the son of Jamadagni; I have come to see you.
Know me as such through my prostration; salutations to you, O Creator of the World! (BndP 2.35.50)
To Rāma, who had spoken thus, he slowly opened his eyes;
seeing him, he uttered a welcome and offered him a seat.
Having brought the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the preeminent sage gave it to his disciple and inquired after his welfare regarding his asceticism and his lineage.
Thus questioned by him, Rāma indeed spoke to the Jar-born one:
"O Lord, by the very sight of you, all is well with me in every respect."
What doubt has arisen within you? Cut it away with the nectar of your own words.
O Lord, I saw a single deer in the middle of Puṣkara.
He related to me his entire history, both past and future;
having heard that, I was filled with wonder and came to you for refuge.
Protect me with compassion, O Lord, as I accomplish this great mantra;
O Guru, protect me with auspiciousness as I practice this armor bestowed by Śiva.
"Indeed, more than a hundred autumns have passed for me while practicing Kṛṣṇa-yoga, yet I have not attained perfection; therefore, please tell me why this is so."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this question of the high-souled Rāma,
O great king, he meditated for a moment and understood in his heart what the deer had said.
When the deer had also arrived at his own hermitage together with the doe,
the sage Bhārgava, having reflected upon the entire cause for hearing that hymn of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa, comforted them with the nectar of his words.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Lineage of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upoddhātapāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said: Having understood all that, Agastya, the jar-born son of Bhṛgu, with a delighted mind, spoke to Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Agastya said:
Listen, O illustrious Rāma, I shall tell you what is for your benefit,
by which you may swiftly attain the perfection of the mantra.
O great-minded one, once a man has understood the characteristics of the threefold devotion,
he who strives toward it shall attain perfection quickly.
Once, desiring to behold the Infinite One,
I arrived at Pātāla, which was graced by the lords of the Nāgas with supreme joy.
There, O illustrious one, I beheld on all sides perfected beings,
such as Sanaka and the others, as well as Nārada, Gautama, Jājali, and Kratu.
"O twice-born one, I am Ṛbhu, Haṃsa, Aruṇi, Vālmīki, Śakti, Āsuri,
and these other great Siddhas headed by Vātsyāyana."
Indeed, those who have approached him for the sake of knowledge should worship the Lord of Serpents,
having paid homage to him along with the lords of the *nāgas*, the *siddhas*, and the great-souled ones.
Seated there, he joyfully listened to the Vaiṣṇava discourses:
"O highly fortunate one, this earth is the sustainer of beings in her own form."
Seated before him, they constantly listened to his discourses;
whatever that Earth would ask, Śeṣa himself would answer directly to the Mountain.
All the sages situated there hear it through His grace;
O child, it was there that I heard the auspicious nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s love.
I shall proclaim to you that hymn for the sake of which you have come here—
the account of the incarnations beginning with the Boar, which destroys all evil.
O child, having heard everything that bestows happiness and liberation, and which is the cause of knowledge and realization, the Earth gazed upon that upholder of the earth.
Bowing down again, she spoke further in order to understand Kṛṣṇa’s activities.
Dharaṇī said:
"The birth of even the inhabitants of Nanda’s Vraja has been rendered glorious."
That god Kṛṣṇa, who assumes a form for his divine play,
possesses numerous names applied according to various conditions of victory.
"O Vāsuki, desiring for a long time to hear the principal names among them,
please tell me those names of Vāsudeva."
"O Vasundharā, O lady of beautiful hips, there exists nothing more meritorious than this in the three worlds; it grants liberation to people," Śeṣa said.
The foremost of all auspicious things, bestowing the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*,
destroying millions of great sins, and granting the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
O Goddess, listen; I shall proclaim the one hundred and eight names which bestow the fruit of all sacrifices of recitation and destroy all sins. BndP_2,36.18
Whatever fruit is obtained by reciting three times the thousands of meritorious names,
a single name of Kṛṣṇa bestows that very same fruit with a single recitation.
Therefore, O beloved, this hymn of one hundred and eight names is even more meritorious than that, for it destroys all sins; I myself am its seer (ṛṣi).
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Yoga, who brings pleasure to Kṛṣṇa;
he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Kamalā, Vāsudeva, the eternal one.
The son of Vasudeva, the meritorious Hari, who assumes a human form through his divine play, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and who is affectionate toward Yaśodā.
With four arms, bearing the discus, sword, mace, conch, and other weapons,
he is the joy of Devakī, the Lord of Śrī, and the beloved son of Nanda the cowherd.
He who checked the current of the Yamunā, the beloved younger brother of Balabhadra,
the taker of Pūtanā’s life, and the breaker of the demon Śakaṭāsura.
He brings joy to the people of Nanda, his very form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
his limbs are smeared with fresh butter, he is a dancer of fresh butter, and he is sinless.
He who subsists on a portion of fresh butter, who bestowed grace upon Mucukunda,
the lord of sixteen thousand women, possessing a triple-bend and a sweet form.
Govinda, the lord of the knowers of the Vedas, who is the moon to the ocean of the nectar of Śuka’s words;
he who wanders about tending the calves and who is the crusher of the demon Dhenuka.
He who treated the Tṛṇāvarta serpent as a mere blade of grass, the breaker of the twin Arjuna trees,
the shatterer of the towering palm tree, and whose form is dark like the Tamāla tree.
The Lord of the cowherds and cowherdesses, the yogi whose splendor equals ten million suns,
the lord of the earth, the supreme light, the chief of the Yādavas, and the upholder of the Yadu lineage.
Wearing a forest garland and yellow garments, the remover of the Pārijāta tree,
the lifter of Mount Govardhana, the cowherd, and the protector of all.
The unborn, the stainless, the progenitor of desire, the lotus-eyed one;
the slayer of Madhu, the Lord of Mathurā, the powerful Lord of Dvārakā.
Wandering within the precincts of Vṛndāvana, adorned with garlands of tulasī,
the stealer of the Syamantaka jewel, he is the very essence of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
The supreme Puruṣa, the master of illusion, wore the garments drawn from the hunchbacked woman;
he was skilled in wrestling with the Asuras Muṣṭika and Cāṇūra.
The enemy of worldly existence, the foe of Kaṃsa, the enemy of Mura, the destroyer of Naraka;
he who is beginningless celibate and the one who draws away those distressed by the misfortunes of Kṛṣṇā.
The slayer of Śiśupāla’s head, the ender of Duryodhana’s lineage,
the granter of boons to Vidura and Akrūra, and the revealer of the universal form.
He whose speech is truth, whose resolve is truth, who delights in Satyabhāmā, the victorious one,
the elder brother of Subhadrā, Viṣṇu, the bestower of liberation upon Bhīṣma.
The teacher of the world, the lord of the universe, skilled in the playing of the flute,
the destroyer of Vṛṣabhāsura, the enemy of Baka, and the one who severed the arms of Bāṇa.
The establisher of Yudhiṣṭhira, adorned with a crest of peacock feathers,
the unmanifest charioteer of Pārtha, and the great ocean of the nectar of the Gītā.
Dāmodara, whose glorious lotus feet are colored by the rubies on the hoods of the serpent Kālīya,
is the enjoyer of sacrifices and the destroyer of the wealth of the Dānavas.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, whose vehicle is the serpent-eater (Garuḍa),
and who stripped the gopīs of their garments while they were engaged in water-sports.
He is of meritorious fame, whose feet are the source of all holy places, who is to be known through the Vedas, and is a treasury of compassion;
he is the embodiment of all sacred fords, the form of all planetary deities, and higher than the highest.
Thus, having formerly heard the nectar of the Gītā from Kṛṣṇa, the devotee of Kṛṣṇa [recited] these one hundred and eight names of Kṛṣṇadeva.
Therefore, I have heard this hymn composed by me, which is dear to Kṛṣṇa and named *Kṛṣṇapremāmṛta*, the bestower of supreme bliss.
Whatever gift, vow, austerity, or pilgrimage has been performed here in this birth, it destroys excessive calamities and suffering, and increases supreme longevity.
For those who read it and for those who hear it, the merit shall be ten million times ten millionfold;
it bestows sons upon the childless and grants a refuge to those without refuge.
It brings wealth to the poor, victory to those desiring victory,
nourishment to children and herds of cattle, and increases merit.
It brings about the pacification of childhood diseases, planetary afflictions, and the like, performing rites of propitiation;
at its conclusion, it grants remembrance of Kṛṣṇa and removes the threefold suffering.
O blessed lady, it accomplishes for oneself what has not yet been achieved through the practice of recitation and other rites;
[it is dedicated] to Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the Yādavas, the yogi who possesses the seal of knowledge.
"O Great Goddess, by chanting this mantra day and night— 'Salutation to the Lord, the husband of Rukmiṇī, the knower of the Vedānta'— " BndP_2,36.49.
He shall become the recipient of favor from all planetary deities, most beloved by all,
surrounded by sons and grandsons, and endowed with the abundance of all spiritual perfections.
"Having enjoyed pleasures even until the end, one shall attain union with Kṛṣṇa.
Agastya said:
"Thus has the Lord Ananta been described; he is the pervasive one whose form is known as Saṃkarṣaṇa."
Having sufficiently instructed the worlds regarding the support of the earth, the bestower of honor, Dharādhara, ceased speaking.
Then all those beginning with Sanaka, who were seated around him and intent upon that discourse,
submerged in an ocean full of bliss, honored that Lord of Serpents.
The sages said:
Salutations, salutations to you, the creator of the entire universe, the imperishable soul who removes the suffering of devoted seekers;
salutations to you, Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth, the ocean of compassion, and the source of the world.

O Lord, the nectar of Kṛṣṇa has been made to drink by us; we have been rendered free from sin by you. O Lord, those like you who are compassionate toward the wretched surely uplift their own who are bowed down in devotion.
Having thus paid homage at the feet of the Lord of Serpents, which fulfill all desires, and having fixed our minds there,
we all circumambulated the Supporter of the Earth and returned to our own dwellings.
Thus has this hymn named *Premāmṛta* (the Nectar of Love) been declared to you, O Rāma;
it is the hymn of Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Rādhā, which bestows spiritual perfection.
O highly fortunate Rāma, this hymn is extremely difficult to obtain;
it was heard directly from the Blessed Śeṣa as he related various stories.
As many as there are nets of mantras, hymns of praise, and protective amulets, [all are contained therein].
"By reciting this hymn, all those [powers] in the three worlds are indeed accomplished for him.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Great King, having thus spoken this hymn, which is the nectar of love for Kṛṣṇa..."
As long as that sage remained there, so long did the celestial vehicle continue to arrive.
Then, accompanied by four miraculous, perfected beings who could assume any form at will and move with the speed of thought,
the man and woman leaped up;
having bowed at the feet of Agastya, they joyfully ascended [the mountain] like two deer.
Having assumed divine bodies marked with the signs of the conch, the discus, and other emblems,
they went to the world of Viṣṇu, which is honored by all the gods,
while all beings— including Bhārgava and Agastya— were looking on.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having witnessed that most wonderful and marvelous marvel, Paraśurāma then related the entire account of the hunter exactly as he had heard it.
Having heard that, the Blessed One Agastya himself, born from a jar,
spoke these words with joy to Bhārgava, who stood before him.
Agastya said:
Listen, O illustrious Rāma, you who are skilled in discerning what ought to be done;
I speak that which is for your benefit today, so perform it with a concentrated mind.
Not far from here is a very great place of Viṣṇu, extremely difficult to attain,
where the footprints placed by that most magnanimous one are seen.
There, from the tip of the foot of that great-souled one as he stepped through the worlds to restrain Bali by his power, the Gaṅgā emerged.
Having gone there, recite this hymn for one month with undistracted mind,
strictly observing the rules and restricting your diet.
That armor which was previously practiced by you while desiring perfection for the sake of subduing enemies— that shall indeed grant you success.
Vasiṣṭha said: Thus addressed by Agastya, Rāma, the destroyer of enemies,
paid homage to the peaceful sage and departed from the hermitage.
O King, he quickly reached that very same path where the celestial river Ganges flows out from the northern step.
Having established his residence there together with Akṛtavraṇa,
he practiced the divine hymn named *Kṛṣṇapremāmṛta*.
O King, Hari became pleased by that constant hymn of praise to the Lord of Vraja,
and He appeared before the sight of that son of Jamadagni.
The lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, the manifest lord of the fourfold manifestation,
shone with a crown the color of the sun and with two earrings.
With his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, wearing yellow garments, and possessing the luster of a cloud,
he was intent on playing the flute, manifesting the very form that enchants the world.
Seeing him, the son of Jamadagni rose up suddenly, filled with joy;
bowing prostrate like a staff upon the ground, he, being self-restrained, praised the Lord.
Paraśurāma said:

Salutations again and again to the Supreme Lord, whose form is the cause of all, the protector of those who have sought refuge, the remover of the afflictions of the gods, and who is praised by Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other deities; to him I bow eternally.

I praise you, the indefinable, the imperishable, the ancient, and the infinite—one whom the lords headed by Īśāna were unable to determine through the various methods of Vedic discourse; O Bhava, be intent on compassion for me.
But He who is the one Lord, the granter of His own desires, assumes various bodies for the sake of wandering in the world, for its protection,
and to remove the burden of the earth consisting of gods, humans, animals, and aquatic creatures.
I [praise] you, who are devoted to your devotees, though utterly detached even from Indirā and the like;
whose mind is bound by love even when they are personally present with hearts corrupted by infidelity.
O Lord, those Asuras who were indeed devoted, as well as gods, humans, Kinnaras, and even those born of animal wombs,
have all attained their own true nature by abandoning their attachment to bodies, wives, children, and possessions.

With devotion, he approached that God of gods— the bestower of desired boons upon those who worship him, who is effortless and devoid of qualities, inconceivable, unmanifest, the destroyer of the flood of sins, free from passion, and a treasure-house of love.
Others, however, torment their own bodies with various forms of austerity and worship with various sacrifices;
yet even in their dreams, O All-pervading Lord, they do not behold Your supramundane form, for their latent impressions are bound to external objects.
Those whose minds are weary of the toil of worldly existence who duly remember your feet, bow down with devotion, worship them, and indeed describe them to one another in assembly; // BndP_2,37.22 //
O Lord, those whose minds are intent on piercing the mire born of a single birth [in this world] take refuge at Your lotus feet;
they cross over themselves and indeed ferry others across as well, for Your nectar, O Master, is truly called the medicine for existence.
O Lord, with my mind bound by desire, I sought to propitiate you, the Noble One, through various efforts;
yet you, O Protector, are all-knowing—what is there left for me to request of you here in this world?
Vasiṣṭha said:
To the son of Jamadagni, who was thus praising him while prostrated before him,
he spoke with unfathomable words, as if bewildering him with his illusory power.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"Ah, O illustrious Rāma, your supreme task has been accomplished;
understand this to be through the power of both the armor and the hymn."
Having slain that King Kārtavīrya, whose mind was arrogant,
and having thus accomplished the vengeance for your father, make the earth devoid of kṣatriyas.
"O best of the twice-born, O giver of honor, Kārtavīrya, my incarnation on the surface of the earth, has indeed accomplished his task; therefore, bring him to an end."
"From this day forward, you shall move about in this world through the descent of a portion of myself; at the proper time, you will act as the self-sovereign Lord, the creator and the destroyer."
In the twenty-fourth age, O child, during the Tretā Yuga, I, the eternal one, shall become known as Rāma, born of the lineage of Raghu, manifesting in fourfold form.
I am the one who brought joy to Kausalyā, born from King Daśaratha;
at that time, having completed the sacrifice of Kauśika along with Lakṣmaṇa.
"O illustrious one, I shall go to the great city of Janaka;
there, having broken the bow of the Lord and having wed the daughter of Videha," BndP_2,37.32 //
"Then, as you are departing for Ayodhyā, I shall take away your intoxicated splendor.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus instructed the son of Jamadagni, that treasure-house of asceticism, Kṛṣṇa departed.
It vanished there even as the high-souled Rāma was looking on.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (the Introductory Section) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When Kṛṣṇa had vanished, the highly illustrious Rāma then considered himself exalted by the power of Kṛṣṇa.
Accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa and blazing like a kindled fire,
Bhārgava arrived at the city of Mahiṣmatī.
There flows the Narmadā, the best of rivers, holy and the remover of sins;
she purifies even sinful living beings merely by the sight of her.
O lord of the earth, in ancient times, even the high-souled Hara, having settled there, made an effort for the destruction of Tripura.
In that regard, O King, what merit can be described for those men who possess the nature of gods,
having beheld the Narmadā, O delighter of the Bhṛgu lineage?
Intent on the destruction of his enemies, he, being well-pleased, paid homage:
"Obeisance be to you, O Narmadā, born from the body of Hara."
"Quickly destroy my enemies; be a granter of boons, O beautiful one! Having thus paid homage to Narmadā, the destroyer of sins, he spoke.
He dispatched a messenger to Kārtavīryārjuna, saying:
"O blameless messenger, you must say to the king what I tell you."
"You must not entertain any doubt; a messenger is never to be bound anywhere.
It was by relying on whose power that the king [challenged] the sage Jamadagni."
"O fool, you have treated him with contempt; his son has come to fight.
Depart quickly, O dull-witted one, and give that battle to Rāma! (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.38.10)
"Having approached Bhārgava, go quickly to the other world.
Having spoken thus to the king and having heard his words accordingly, [the sage departed].
"Come quickly, may it be well with you; delay is not praised here.
Thus addressed by him, the messenger went to the Haihaya king.
That king, who was devoted to Atri and possessed great strength and prowess, caused all of that which had been uttered by Rāma to be heard in the assembly.
Having heard that reproachful speech, he grew angry and delivered this reply to the messenger.
Kārtavīrya said:
"The earth was given by me alone through the strength of my arms, as a gift after gift."
Having forcibly conquered and bound the kings, I have brought them to my own city;
let that army remain with me, and I shall now give battle to you.
Having spoken thus, the lord of the Haihayas quickly dismissed the messenger;
then that best of speakers summoned his commander-in-chief and addressed him.
"O illustrious one, esteemed by heroes, prepare my army;
I shall fight with Rāma of the Bhṛgu lineage. Let there be no delay!"
Thus addressed, the great hero Pratāpana, the commander-in-chief,
quickly made the fourfold army ready and announced it as such.
O lord of the people, hearing that his army was ready, King Kārtavīrya joyfully ascended his own chariot brought by his charioteer.
Then the neighboring lords of the surrounding regions, accompanied by many akṣauhiṇīs, stood encircling that king on all sides.
O Great King, there were tens of millions of nāgas, as well as horses, chariots, and foot soldiers; in that army which resembled the ocean, they were beyond counting.
There are seen kings born of various lineages,
great heroes with massive bodies, skilled in many kinds of warfare.
The kings, skilled in various weapons and missiles, mounted on various vehicles,
adorned with diverse ornaments, intoxicated, and embellished with gifts, [approached].
Indeed, many elephants created by the mahāmātras appear,
as do horses born of various lineages, possessing the speed of the wind.
O protector of the earth, the chariots— long and yoked to swift horses— gleam as they glide along, their riders having been well-trained.
O King, the foot soldiers, bearing swords and shields, shone like clouds in the rainy season accompanied by the rumbling of thunder.
When the army of Kārtavīryārjuna indeed set forth, they were filled with the spirit of "I first! I first! (ahaṃpūrvaka).
Then the sky and the ten directions were shrouded by dust,
along with the sounds of various musical instruments and the neighing of the horses.
O King, the circle of the sky was pervaded by the trumpeting of elephants;
O lord of the earth, the king of kings beheld these portents on the road.
In that battle, there were omens portending his death:
a woman with disheveled hair, her nose cut off, weeping and naked.
He beheld a woman dressed in black garments,
as well as one in tattered rags, one who was fallen, one who was broken, one who was naked, and one clad in saffron robes.
He saw a man with a missing limb whose mind was distressed,
as well as a monitor lizard, a hare, a porcupine, an empty water-jar, and a lizard.
Cotton, a tortoise, oil, salt, and a piece of bone,
as well as a jackal on one's own right side making a terrifying howl— [these are inauspicious].
Even upon seeing a sick man, a Pulkasa, a bull, a hawk, and a bear, he suddenly rushed forward to fight, enveloped by the noose of Time.
Seated in the shade of a banyan tree on the northern bank of the Narmadā, Rāma, accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa, beheld him approaching.
Seeing Kārttavīrya, the best of kings, accompanied by a hundred crore of monarchs and joined by a thousand akṣauhiṇīs, he was indeed struck with wonder.
"Today my long-cherished purpose has reached fulfillment, since Kārtavīrya, that lowest of kings, has come within the range of my vision."
Having spoken thus, he rose up and seized his weapon, the axe;
like an enraged lion intent on destroying its enemy, he stretched out his arms.
Seeing Rāma prepared for the slaughter of the soldiers,
they all trembled violently, like embodied beings facing death itself.
Wherever Bhṛgu, filled with rage, hurled his battle-axe with the speed of the wind,
there the elephants, horses, and heroic men fell, their arms, thighs, and legs severed.
Just as a lordly elephant, intoxicated with rut, crushes a forest of reeds while running in every direction,
even so did Rāma, whose speed was like that of thought, utterly trample the king's army.
Seeing Rāma, the best among weapon-bearers, thus striking with vigor in battle,
the king of the Kīlakas raised his great bow, stood upon his chariot, and having made Sṛñjaya his target, remained firm.
Drawing his arrows, which possessed a brilliance as fierce as fire, he scattered them and approached the descendant of Bhṛgu;
then, seeing him approaching, the high-souled Rāma took up his most formidable bow.
Overwhelmed with rage, he discharged the Vāyavya weapon to ward off the shower of auspicious arrows;
and that exceedingly powerful and high-minded king, in turn, loosed the Parvata weapon at Rāma.

Skilled in the application of weapons, Rāma paralyzed that exceedingly powerful Vāyavya missile with his own; and perceiving that king of the Matsyas to be possessed of great strength, he assailed him there with various multitudes of missiles.

O King, when the Nārāyaṇa weapon was discharged by Paraśurāma for the sake of slaying the monarch, it emitted rays in battle and was released with force, accompanied by the prescribed mantras. (BdP 2.38.46)
Indeed, all the directions blazed intensely with his splendor, and the Lord of Matsya trembled;
then Rāma, observing that trembling, struck down his horses with four arrows.
With a single arrow the high-souled one cut down the banner, and with two arrows he severed the bow;
then, forcibly striking the charioteer to the ground with a single shaft, he shattered the chariot with three more.
Leaving his chariot, he descended to the ground and swiftly struck Maṅgala on the head with a battle-axe;
with his skull shattered and vomiting blood repeatedly, he fell into a swoon and died in an instant.
Then that army, utterly consumed by his weapon, was reduced to ashes in an instant;
for when that king, born of the lunar dynasty, had fallen.
When Maṅgala was the best of kings, Rāma attained great joy.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the king of the Matsyas had fallen,
the immensely powerful King Kārtavīrya, skilled in battle, urged on other lords of kings.
Bṛhadbala, Somadatta, Vidarbha, the lord of Mithilā, the sovereign of Niṣadha, and likewise the sovereign of Magadha; BndP_2,39.2 //
O King, those skilled in various modes of combat arrived at the battle to fight with the son of Bhṛgu,
raining down nets of arrows.
At that time, all those who prided themselves on their heroism acted by the command of the Haihaya;
then Bhṛgu, with the Pināka bow in hand, appeared like a blazing crest of fire.
Having consecrated it with mantras, Druṇa hurled that supreme arrow, the serpent-noose weapon (*nāgapāśa*),
at Bhārgava at the forefront of the battle.
The mighty Somadatta cut [him] down with the Gāruḍa weapon;
thereupon, the illustrious Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, became enraged.
Rudradatta struck Somadatta with a spear,
Bṛhadbala with a mace, and likewise Vidarbha with his fist.
He struck the King of Mithilā with a mallet, the Lord of Niṣadha with a spear,
the King of Magadha with kicks, and the soldiers with a multitude of missiles.
Having destroyed the entire army with the wind of the fire of universal destruction,
the mighty son of Jamadagni pursued Kārtavīrya.
Seeing him approaching to fight, other kings who were great chariot-warriors and experts in discerning what ought and ought not to be done placed the Haihaya at their rear.
The Kānyakubjas by the hundreds, as well as the Saurāṣṭras and Āvantyas, fought with Rāma while displaying their friendship.
And they created nets of arrows all around Rāma;
enveloped by those nets of arrows at the forefront of the battle, Rāma [stood firm].
And at that time, O Indra among kings, he was not seen with his wounds unhealed;
he indeed remembered the deeds of Rāma as they had been told by Hari.
While the sage was thus entreating Hari for the welfare of the lord of the Bhārgavas,
at that very time, Rāma, who was skilled in weapons and missiles, [appeared].
Having shaken off the masses of arrows with the Vāyavya weapon, the knower of mantras rose up,
longing for battle, like the sun emerging from the mist.
For three nights the powerful Rāma fought with them in battle;
there, he of swift prowess destroyed twelve akṣauhiṇīs.
Just as one armed with the excellent weapon of the battle-axe [fells] a grove of plantain trunks,
so did he [fell] all those groups of kings and their great armies.
Having seen her slain by that great-souled Rāma,
the exceedingly heroic Sucandra, born of the solar dynasty, arrived.
Accompanied by a hundred thousand kṣatriyas and joined by seven akṣauhiṇīs,
many great heroes were there, roaring like clouds.
O King, shaking the earth, they fought with the descendant of Bhṛgu;
O lord of the earth, they hurled at him weapons and great missiles.
In an instant, the powerful lord of the Bhṛgus destroyed them,
having taken up his divine axe which resembled the staff of Time or Yama.
Sweeping through the entire army, the descendant of Bhṛgu cut down [the enemy] just as a farmer in a field cuts down both the ripe grain and the weeds.
In that same manner,
Rāma used his sword to utterly destroy that army of a hundred thousand kṣatriyas, which they had not seen torn asunder by Rāma.
O King, Sucandra, the protector of the earth, fought in that battle;
both of them, skilled in various weapons and missiles, were greatly agitated there.
The two great heroes, the lord of sages and the lord of kings, fought each other;
for whatever weapons and missiles Rāma hurled at him, [the sage rendered them ineffective].
Sucandra, skilled in battle, cut all of them down;
thereupon, Rāma became enraged at Sucandra, the lord of the earth, in that conflict.
Knowing him to be one who recognizes both offense and retaliation, he then sipped water and fixed the irresistible Nārāyaṇa weapon upon his arrow.
Then that weapon, possessing the brilliance of a hundred suns, was discharged by the wise Rāma;
Sucandra, immediately rising from his chariot with joy, prostrated himself before it.
Having abandoned him who was thus prostrate— who was worthy of worship by all weapons and had been created by Nārāyaṇa— he went to the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Then Rāma, the slayer of enemies, was struck with wonder in that battle upon seeing that great weapon rendered futile and observing the king remaining composed.
In his wrath, Rāma hurled a spear, a mace, a javelin, a sharp-edged spear, as well as a club and an axe at the head of the king.
Sucandra indeed seized all of them with ease;
and when Rāma hurled Śiva’s trident at the king, [Sucandra caught it].
And that trident became a garland of flowers upon the king's neck;
and he beheld Bhadrakālī, the mother of the world, standing before him.
She wears a garland of severed heads, has a distorted face, and is terrifying;
she is mounted upon a lion, possesses three eyes, and holds a trident and the boon-granting gesture.
Seeing her, he cast aside his weapons and missiles and, having offered salutations, praised her.
Rāma said:
"Homage be to you, the beloved of Śaṅkara, the mother of the world, who is beautifully adorned!"

To her who is adorned with various ornaments, who has exerted herself for the protection of those who have sought refuge, who is the mother of Dakṣa, who dwells on the Himavat, and who is established as half the body of Maheśvara; // BndP_2,39.36 //
Salutations to her who is Kālī, who possesses the digits of the Lord of Digits (the Moon), who is dear to her devotees, and who is the sovereign of the worlds;
to her named Tārā, who is devoted to Śiva, and whose sandals are worshipped by the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Salutations to her who is higher than the highest, the bestower of the supreme state, whose meditation uproots the threefold suffering;
to her who acts for the welfare of the world, who possesses the three cities as her abode, who is the primordial source of all, and who is designated as Tripurā.

Salutations to the Mother of the World, who bestows the exquisite play of all branches of knowledge; who dispels both the beneficial and the harmful; whose face is like a crane; who grants many forms of prosperity; and who has utterly destroyed various asuras and dānavas.
To her whose vine-like arms are adorned with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who is saluted by all the gods,
who wears yellow garments, who moves with the speed of the wind, who bestows auspiciousness, and who is praised by Śiva.

To her who is the enemy of serpents, whose feet are the nine divisions [of the earth], who has the luster of the Blue Mountain (Nīlācala), whose neck shines with radiance, who is swift in her strides, whose name is Lalitā, who is the sovereign of the gods, and who is the mine of salt; // BndP_2,39.41 //
To her of tremulous glance, who is free from dissolution, whose lotus feet are adorned with lac-dye;
to her named Ramā, who is most fond of Rati, who removes disease, and who has fashioned all things.

Salutations, salutations to you who bestows sovereignty; salutations to you who yearns for union; salutations to you who possesses the luster of jewels and radiant garments; salutations, salutations to you from behind and from the front, and salutations, salutations to you from the sides, below, and above.

And always, everywhere, salutations, salutations to you; salutations, salutations to her whose form is the totality! Be gracious, O Queen of Gods; O Bhadrakālī, fulfill the promise you made to me in the past.
"You alone are the mother and you alone are the father even of the three worlds; salutations, salutations unto you!
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus was the goddess Bhadrakālī, the swift one, then praised.
Delighted and celebrating the granting of the boon, Bhadrakālī spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu:
"O child Rāma, O highly fortunate one, I am now pleased with you."
"Choose from me whatever boon is requested by you in your heart.
Rāma said:
"O Mother, if a boon is to be granted by you to me, O lover of your devotees..."
"O Goddess, I have declared that Sucandra shall be victorious in battle and a recipient of your grace; therefore, act with a pleased heart. (BndP 2.39.48)
"O Mother of the World, by whatever means possible, homage be to you!
Bhadrakālī said:
"O Indra among kings, take Sucandra, the lord of men, to my abode by means of the fiery weapon (āgneyāstra)."
"Let him become my attendant this very day; he is exceedingly dear to me.
Having heard these words, Vasiṣṭha said: "Then that lord of the Bhṛgus became intent on doing what was pleasing to the goddess."
Having restrained his breath and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
O King, Rāma then forcefully directed that weapon— which had been employed for the sake of slaying the monarch— toward Sucandra.
Having burned her body composed of the elements, she led it to the world of the Supreme Deity;
then Bhadrakālī, the primordial creator of the universe, was saluted by Rāma.
Then the son of Jamadagni vanished; he stood upon the battlefield, longing for the slaughter of kings.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said: O King, when Sucandra— the crest-jewel of the lords of kings— had fallen,
his son Puṣkarākṣa then came to fight Rāma.
Standing upon his chariot, that hero of great prowess, skilled in all weapons and missiles,
beheld Rāma— who was as fierce in battle as Yama, the god of death.
And he [Rāma] created a web of arrows all around the lord of the Bhārgavas;
for a moment, even the son of Jamadagni was struck down by those shafts.
Then, O great king, having suddenly emerged from that bond of arrows, the mighty lord of the Bhṛgus looked all around him.
Having then beheld that lotus-eyed son of Sucandra,
he summoned his wrath, as if wishing to consume him like fire.
Overcome with anger, he unleashed the weapon of Varuṇa;
from that, clouds arose, thundering with terrifying new sounds.
O King, they rained down torrents of water, flooding the earth;
then Puṣkarākṣa, of great prowess, discharged the Vāyavya weapon.
By that [weapon], those clouds were instantly brought to invisibility;
then Rāma, becoming violently enraged, aimed the Brahmā-weapon there.
The mighty Puṣkarākṣa also dragged him with that very same [weapon];
seeing it applied by Brāhma, he was like a tree struck by a staff.
Taking up a terrible axe and sighing deeply, he rushed at him;
as he was charging there, the lotus-eyed Rāma, wielding his bow, [rushed toward him].
He aimed five arrows that were like blazing-mouthed serpents;
with each single shaft, he struck him in the heart, the head, and both arms.
And having pierced his crest-lock in succession, he struck his mother’s son violently;
thus was Rāma afflicted by the lotus-eyed one in that encounter.
