Having stood for a moment, he rushed forward violently and brought his axe down upon the head;
starting from the crest-lock and ending at the feet, it split Putthakarākṣa in two.
When the fragment fell upon the earth, at that moment, a most great wonder arose among the men who beheld it, as well as among the gods in heaven.
Having torn asunder that mighty Puṣkarākṣa in his wrath, Rāma,
enraged, consumed his army like a fire consumes a forest.
Whithersoever the lord of the Bhārgavas, whose mind was as swift as the wind and who brandished his battle-axe,
rushed forth, thither fell by the hundreds horses, chariots, elephants, and men with their limbs mangled.
There, being struck by Rāma with his exceedingly powerful axe in battle, they were completely pulverized and reduced to ashes while crying out, "O father! O mother! at that time.
And in a mere moment, Bhārgava destroyed that entire army of Puṣkarākṣa—
nine akṣauhiṇīs consisting of many royal lineages, their lords slain, utterly routed, and deeply distressed.
When Puṣkarākṣa had fallen, the immensely powerful Kārtavīryārjuna himself arrived, mounted upon his golden chariot.
The king [ascended] a chariot ten *nalvas* in size, strewn with various weapons, adorned with various jewels, and yoked with a hundred horses.
With his thousand arms bearing various weapons,
he shone like a man of merit ascending to the heavenly world with his body.
His hundred sons, of great heroism and skilled in battle,
stood arraying their armies in the conflict at their father’s command.
But the powerful Kārttavīrya, seeing Rāma on the field of battle— who resembled Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time— proceeded to fight him.
In the battle, intent on victory, he seized five hundred arrows in his right hand and five hundred bows in his left from the lord of the Bhārgavas.
Then, O King, he released a shower of arrows upon Rāma,
just as a cloud, O hero, pours rain upon a mountain.
Honored in battle by that shower of arrows, the descendant of Bhṛgu took up his divine bow and likewise released a shower of arrows.
Then those two, the descendant of Bhṛgu and the Haihaya, both exhilarated by battle, engaged in an incomparable, tumultuous, and hair-raising combat.
And at the forefront of the battle,
that powerful king, wielding all manner of weapons and missiles, aimed the Brahmāstra for the sake of slaying the lord of the Bhārgavas.
Rāma, too, having touched water for purification, fixed his mind upon Brahman;
then, O lord of men, his two arrows remained eternally attached in the sky.
They both grew in power at the edge of the world like blazing fires and the sun;
the three worlds, along with Pātāla, beheld that great wonder.
They considered the withdrawal of his blazing pair of weapons to be a conflagration;
then Rāma, beholding that destruction of the world, remembered what the Dweller of the World had previously spoken.

"Protection must be provided by me today; this restraint must be warded off by one who bears a supreme portion [of divinity],"—having thus resolved, the Lord of fierce splendor then discharged that pair of weapons with his two eyes.
Having drunk [the nectar] excessively and observed the world, the Great-Souled One remained for a moment absorbed in meditation;
then, by the power of his meditation, the pair of Brahma-missiles lost their luster.
Then, at that very moment, he suddenly fell to the ground, and the entire world immediately attained well-being;
for that son of Jamadagni was the greatest among the great, capable of creating, protecting, and destroying.
Nevertheless, the All-pervading Lord,
though he was a wielder of the bow, most heroic, radiant, a leader in the assembly, and a speaker of truth, enacted the ways of the world in order to conceal his own power.
Having exerted effort in the collection of arts, wise in the sciences and scriptures, and knowing the prescribed rules,
he thus proclaims his own nature in the world of men and constantly performs all auspicious deeds.
Indeed, all the worlds were conquered by that Rāma, the slayer of kṣatriyas;
thus did Rāma, whose power was renowned, having pacified that pair of weapons.
Once again, he set out to bring about the destruction of the banner of the Haihaya dynasty upon the field of battle;
having taken a pair of feathered arrows from his quiver and fixed them at the nock upon the bowstring.
Aiming at the king's pair of ears, he who desired to seize the crest-jewel cut them off;
yet that high-souled king, the conqueror of all the world’s great heroes, remained with his ears severed.
His own prowess here considered himself destroyed by Rāma, his soul humiliated by the lord of the earth;
for a moment, the body of the ruler of the earth became pale, its majesty departed.
Like a painting executed by a skilled artist, his body appeared on the surface of that most wretched mind;
then the king [perceived] the majesty of his own prowess, which had attained supremacy over all the world.
Reflecting upon what had been gained from the defeat of Paulastya and other victories, he remained as if grieving for his desire for further conquest;
then, with eyes closed, he meditated again upon that lamp of the Ātreyi clan whom the two kings had bestowed upon him.
When he was favored by the majesty and vital power of that [Lord], he surpassed all the world-protectors;
yet when this Great-souled One was granted a place within his heart, he did not indeed come into his sight.
Then the lord of the earth, being exceedingly distressed, repeatedly returned to the path of meditation;
yet even as he meditated, O King, Datta did not come within the range of his mind.

Thus was the high-souled son of Atri seen by the king— not as an ascetic, most self-controlled, virtuous, and innocent, but rather as a perpetrator of evil deeds— and he did not appear within the range of the king's meditation.
Then, being tormented by extreme suffering, he became possessed by grief and delusion;
to that king submerged in sorrow, the high-souled Rāma, who perceives the minds of all, spoke.
O King, do not fall into a state of grief; the high-souled do not grieve at all.
He who appeared as your boon-granting bull in the first creation is indeed I myself, come for your destruction.
You have arrived here with a resolute mind; at the time of battle, there is no room for despondency.
For every person in the world experiences the results of their own actions—whether auspicious or inauspicious—when that which was wrought by destiny comes to fruition.
O Lord of Men, no one else is capable of reversing this good or evil fortune of yours;
for that great merit accumulated over many births, you are here a worthy recipient of the gift.
"Born today, you must now experience the fruit of the evil deed you have committed here;
since my guru was insulted by you through your lack of respect, therefore your ears shall be cut off."
"Behold what I have done! I shall seize your crest-jewel by force, leaving behind your fame!
Having spoken thus, the high-souled Bhṛgu fixed an arrow to his bow and drew it back.
But he [the king], with great agility, cut the jewel as it was hurled and approached Rāma;
seeing that feat of his son, the sage, Arjuna, the sustainer of the Haihaya lineage, [was amazed].
Once again, he prepared himself for battle, raising his weapons to slay that brahmin, his own enemy,
with spears, pikes, maces, discuses, swords, sharp-edged spears, and javelins.
With various other weapons, he struck the son of the twice-born;
but Rāma, through his very agility, parried those which were hurled by him.
He quickly cut down the spears and other weapons right in the middle with his own arrows;
that king, having touched water for purification, discharged a supreme fiery weapon.
Rāma quickly neutralized that weapon with the Vāruṇa weapon;
the king employed the Gāndharva weapon, and [the other] struck the lord with the Vāyavya weapon.
O King, Rāma cut down with the Gāruḍa weapon the Nāga-weapon that had been given by Datta— a spear bestowed with mantras that was never-failing.
In the battle, the king seized that spear— which possessed the brilliance of a hundred suns and was irresistible even to gods and asuras— in order to slay Bhārgava.
He hurled it toward Rāma with his entire force;
then, O lord of the earth, it fell upon the head of that descendant of Bhṛgu.
O king of kings, afflicted by that blow from the spear, Bhārgava then fell into a swoon and collapsed while remembering Hari.
When Bhārgava had fallen there, all the gods, overwhelmed with fear,
assembled together, placing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara at their head.
Śaṅkara, the great knower and the Lord who is Mṛtyuñjaya himself,
restored Bhārgava to life by means of that vidyā known as Saṃjīvanī.
O king of kings, Rāma, having regained consciousness, beheld the gods before him and bowed with devotion to them, beginning with Brahmā.
Having been praised by the lord of the Bhṛgus, they immediately vanished from sight;
that Rāma, having touched water, then recited that armor-mantra (kavaca).
And having risen, highly incensed and as if burning with his eye,
that descendant of Bhṛgu called to mind the Pāśupata weapon granted by Śiva.

O delighter of the Bāhus, that king Kārtavīrya, who had been granted a portion of Viṣṇu’s food, immediately withdrew his great power; the Sudarśana discus of Viṣṇu entered his body and reduced it to ashes.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Kārtavīrya," in the *Bhārgavacarita* (The Life of Bhārgava), within the third section (*upoddhātapāda*) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 40 //
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having witnessed the terrible slaughter of their father, his hundred sons swiftly warded off the most fierce Bhārgava individually with their own forces.
Each of them was joined by an *akṣauhiṇī* division; all of them, maddened for battle and enraged by the slaughter of their father, waged a tumultuous war.
But Rāma, seeing those sons of his who were heroes skilled in battle,
took up his battle-axe and fought with them in the fray.
The Blessed Lord Rāma, acting with haste, destroyed that army, numbering one hundred akṣauhiṇīs, in the mere space of two muhūrtas.
Seeing their entire army thus effortlessly annihilated by Rāma as if with a mere axe, all those who prided themselves on their heroism fought on.
Striking with various divine weapons, those beings of great splendor formed a circle all around the high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then the powerful Rāma also, standing in the midst of their circle,
shone like the Lord himself, as the hub shines within a wheel.
Dancing as it were, Rāma shone brightly in their midst; and those hundreds, wandering all around him, gleamed like the Gopīs standing in the center of the herd while Kṛṣṇa wanders about them.
Then all the gods, led by Brahmā, having assembled and mounted their respective celestial chariots,
showered from all sides the earth-born Rāma of undiminished prowess with rains of *nandana* flowers and garlands.
That sound which arose from the feet of the weapon, containing the syllable *huṃ* and touching the heavens,
shone like the wounds of arrows from the triple symphony (of song, dance, and instrument), just as the falling of nails and teeth [shines] when they are struck.
With their limbs mangled and wounded by weapons, they cry out yet sing as if they were masters of song;
the gods, their eyes wide with great wonder, behold the circle of the kings’ battle thus engaged.

Then Rāma, desiring to slay the princes in battle with various multitudes of missiles, took up his bow and, having broken their circular formation, the Lord separated those exceedingly powerful warriors from one another.
Then he slew those heroes one by one—one hundred and five—and they fled:
Śūra, Vṛṣāsya, Vṛṣa, Śūrasena, and Jayadhvaja, their courage shattered.

Then, their minds overwhelmed by great fear, those kings, having scattered in various directions through the forests at the foot of the Himalayas, fled in their intense desire for safety; not one among them was seen who was not deeply afflicted.
Rāma, too, having slain the circle of kings who had come to assist the monarch in battle,
returned with Akṛtavraṇa and joyfully bathed in the Narmadā.
Having bathed, performed his daily rites, and fully worshipped the bull-bannered Lord,
O King, he set out to see Śiva, the dweller of Kailāsa.
He also [honored] Umā, the wife of his guru, as well as the two sons, Skanda and Vināyaka;
that high-souled one, Akṛtavraṇa, was capable of traveling at the speed of thought.
Having accomplished his task and filled with joy, he reached Kailāsa at that very moment and beheld there the great city named Alakā.
It was adorned with palaces strewn with various clusters of jewels,
and graced by yakṣas wearing diverse forms and colorful ornaments.
It was endowed with forests and groves filled with various kinds of trees,
and it was adorned with very long oblong ponds and lakes.
It is surrounded on all sides externally by the Sītā and the Alakanandā;
there, it is turned tawny by the saffron released from the bathing of the celestial nymphs.
There, elephants free from thirst drink water with joy,
and everywhere indeed the sounds of musical performances are heard.
O King, having seen her accompanied by Gandharvas and Apsarases as constant companions, Bhārgava was filled with supreme joy.
He went further up to that peak where the supreme abode of Śiva is located;
from there, O king of kings, he beheld a great banyan tree with lush shade.
Below that, he beheld a most excellent and well-frequented residence inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas),
where there was a rampart extending for a circle of one hundred yojanas.
It was beautiful, inlaid with various jewels, possessed four gates, and was surrounded by hosts of attendants—
Nandīśvara, Mahākāla, Raktākṣa, and Vikaṭodara.
Piṅgalākṣa, Viśālākṣa, Virūpākṣa, Ghaṭodara,
Mandāra, Bhairava, Bāṇa, Ruru, and Bhairava himself.
Vīraka, Vīrabhadra, Caṇḍa, Bhṛṅgin, Riṭi, and Mukha;
Siddhendranātha and the Rudras, as well as the Vidyādharas and Mahoragas.
And [he saw] bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, kūṣmāṇḍas, brahmarākṣasas,
vetālas, lords of the dānavas, and lords of yogins wearing matted hair.
Having seen the yakṣas, kimpuruṣas, as well as the ḍākinīs and yoginīs, he entered there with joy, filled with delight.
There he beheld the temple of Śiva, encompassed by the worlds and extending four yojanas in width; there, stationed at the eastern gate, were two [beings].
Having seen Kārttikeya on his left and Vināyaka on his right—
both of whom possessed prowess equal to Śiva— the descendant of Bhṛgu bowed down to those two.
The foremost attendants and the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas) were stationed there,
seated upon jeweled lion-thrones and adorned with jewel ornaments.
O Great King, as Bhārgava was entering the abode of Śiva, Vināyaka said to him, "Wait for a moment."
"For Mahādeva is now asleep with Umā.
Having received this command from Īśvara, I arrived here in an instant.
"O brother, stay here for now; I shall enter together with you.
Having heard this from Vināyaka, the delighter of the Bhṛgus [replied].
Filled with haste, he began to speak to Gaṇeśa.
Rāma said:
"O brother, having gone to the inner apartments and having bowed down to the two lords of the world..."
"O Pārvatī and Śaṅkara, I shall go immediately to my own abode;
so too shall Kārtavīrya and Sucandra, along with their sons, armies, and kinsmen."
Thousands of other kings followed— Kāmbojas, Paṅlavas, Śākas,
Kānyakubjas, and lords of Kośala— all possessed of illusion and great strength.
"All have been slain by me in battle through the grace of Śambhu;
having prostrated before him, I shall now depart for my own home."
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Bhṛgu stood there before Gaṇapati;
then that lord of the Gaṇas addressed these sweet words to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Vināyaka said: "Wait, O highly fortunate one; you shall have a vision [of him].
Today, O brother, Viśveśvara is present together with Bhavānī."
O dear one, he who causes a disturbance of the pleasure of a man and woman joined together while seated on the same seat shall certainly go to hell.
In particular, it is the settled rule that a twice-born man must not look upon his father, his teacher, a king, or one who is seated in private.
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, he who looks upon one intent on sexual union will certainly suffer separation from his wife throughout seven births.
He who gazes upon the hips, the chest, the bosom, or the face of another's wife—
even if she be his mother, sister, or daughter— is the lowest of men.
Bhārgava said:
"Aha! What unprecedented speech has issued from your mouth? Has it emerged through delusion, or was it spoken for the sake of jest?"
This is the illustration from the scriptures concerning those who possess desire and undergo transformation;
however, for this child who is free from transformation, there is indeed no fault whatsoever.
"I shall go to the inner apartments, O brother; why do you remain, O child?
I will do there whatever is appropriate for the occasion, exactly as it has been seen."
In that very place, you have indeed designated your mother and father as Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the worlds.
Having spoken thus, O King, Bhārgava prepared to enter [the earth],
whereupon Vināyaka rose up and quickly restrained him.
A verbal battle and a mutual tugging of hands occurred between them;
seeing this, Sakanda became agitated and then sought to reconcile them.
Having seized them both with his two arms, he cast them apart;
then Bhārgava, the slayer of enemy heroes, enraged at Gaṇeśa,
took up his battle-axe and prepared to hurl it.
Seeing that best of the Bhṛgus hurling [the axe] in anger, Gajānana then swiftly raised his own axe with his trunk for his own sake;
with great force, he brought it through the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and above those, Mahas, Vaṃjana, Tapaḥ, Satya, and even the other world, Vaikuṇṭha.
Pointing upward to Goloka, the realm of the Lord, for Bhṛguvara, the Son of Īśa cast him down through the seven lower worlds and likewise showed them to him;
then, having lifted him up from there, he quickly brought him back to that very place where he stood, as soon as he was cast into the waters of the womb, though terrified and longing for his life.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as narrated by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, thus deluded by the Lord of the Gaṇas, Rāma was overcome with both joy and grief as he reflected upon his own defeat.
Beholding Gaṇeśa standing there unperturbed on all sides,
he became intensely possessed by rage and hurled his own battle-axe at him.
Then Gaṇeśa, beholding the battle-axe given by his father and desiring to make it unfailing, took it up with his left tusk.
But that tusk, severed by the axe, fell upon the earth,
drenched in blood like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
O protector of the earth, when the earth— bearing its oceans and islands— was struck by the fall of his teeth,
it trembled and the worlds were seized with terror.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the gods as they watched from heaven;
Kārttikeya and the others there wailed intensely, overcome with distress.
Then, hearing the tumultuous noise as well as the sound of teeth falling out,
the two lords, Pārvatī and Śaṅkara, arrived there.
Seeing Heramba, who has a single tusk and a curved trunk, standing before him,
Pārvatī asked Skanda, "What is the cause of this?"
Thus questioned by his mother, the commander-in-chief then related the entire account from the beginning to his mother while Rāma listened.
O King, having heard the entire account, Pārvatī, the mother of the worlds, became enraged and spoke to Śaṅkara, the lord of her life.
Pārvatī said:
O Śambhu, this Bhārgava has become your disciple and a son equal to you;
having obtained supreme splendor and armor from you, O Lord, he is a conqueror of the three worlds.
Having defeated the powerful King Kārttavīryārjuna in battle and accomplished his own purpose, he bestowed the sacrificial fee upon you.
"By this very [act] of striking down your son with the axe, you will have accomplished your purpose; of this there is no doubt."
O Śambhu, you must protect this Bhārgava, the most excellent of disciples;
he shall accomplish all the tasks of his true guru.
"O Lord, since you have doubted me in this matter, I shall not remain here;
accompanied by my two sons, I will go to the abode of my own father."
The virtuous honor the son of a servant as they would their own son;
yet you have not shown him even the slightest honor, not even with a word.
"Then, sorrowful for this son of mine, I shall depart.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Having heard these words of Pārvatī, the Blessed Lord Bhava..."
O King, he did not utter a single word, whether good or bad;
instead, he remembered Kṛṣṇa in his mind, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him.

Then, as soon as he was remembered, the Blessed Keśava— the Lord of Goloka, the Master of the Gopīs, skilled in various forms of persuasion, the ocean of mercy, the remover of the distress of those who bow to him, subject to his devotees, and the Lord of all— arrived.
Dark as a rain cloud, with a radiant face, adorned with jeweled armlets and necklaces, clothed in lightning, wearing crocodile-shaped earrings,
bearing a crest of peacock feathers set with clusters of gems, with a slightly smiling countenance, the Lord of the Gopīs, whose fame is well-proclaimed, his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem.
The glorious one was accompanied by Rādhā and was unconquered by Śrīdāmā.
Stealing away the splendors of all with his own radiance, that ocean of knowledge arrived;
then, seeing him approach, Śiva was delighted in his heart.
Having prostrated according to the prescribed rule, he honored the Lord who had arrived;
having led the Lord into the inner chamber together with Rādhā.
He seated him, together with his wife, upon the venerable jewel-throne;
then the goddess Pārvatī arrived there accompanied by her daughter.
Accompanied by her two sons, she joyfully bowed at the feet of the Lord;
then Rāma also went to that very place and, with his neck bent low, paid homage.
With an agitated mind, he fell at the feet of Pārvatī;
yet when she did not welcome that descendant of Bhṛgu as he lay prostrate before her, [he spoke].
Then the Lord of the World, gladdening Pārvatī with his speech, said:

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O lady with a face like the moon, who is praised by the mountains and the quarters, O you of infinite virtues, take this son of Jamadagni onto your lap, offered by your own lotus-hand.

O Goddess who removes the fear of worldly existence, who sports with Śambhu, who destroys all impurity, O You who have entered the water-pot (the womb)—I, though constantly fallen at Your feet and burdened by sin, pray: grant me a boon.
Listen, O illustrious goddess, to my words as declared in the Vedas;
having heard them, you will surely be filled with joy, of this there is no doubt.
Your son Vināyaka is a high-souled being, the greatest among the great.
O beautiful lady, he whom desire, anger, agitation, and fear never enter— at any time— according to the Vedas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Saṃhitās.
I shall proclaim those names of his, which have been taught by the great-souled ones as most meritorious, and which remove all sins in their entirety.
Since he is the lord of those hosts of Pramathas who possess various forms and great strength, he is therefore celebrated as Gaṇeśa.
He in whom all the egg-universes— those that have been, those yet to be, and those that are currently existing— are contained, is indeed Laṃbodara.
He who, by the power of divine yoga, is steadfast and has joined together again what was severed,
is called Gajānana because he was [conceived] by the head of an elephant through divine union.
On the fourth day, the moon rose afflicted, having been cursed by Darbhin;
because it was held upon his forehead by him, he is therefore known as Bhālacandra (the Moon on the Forehead).
Cursed in the past by seven sages, he went to his destruction; thus was Jātavedas kindled, he who has Śūrpa as his instrument of action.
In ancient times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, he was worshipped by the hosts of celestial beings;
because he warded off obstacles, he is therefore remembered as Vighnanāśa (the Destroyer of Obstacles).
"O Goddess, today this Daśana has been struck down by Rāma with his axe; O auspicious one, by divine fate he has been made Ekadanta by him."
Then, in a future age, when Brahmā is beloved by Hara, he shall become "Crooked-snout" (Vakratuṇḍa) because his snout has become crooked; thus he is remembered by the wise.
Thus, O Pārvatī, these names of your son exist,
which remove sins through mere remembrance and remain efficacious throughout the three periods of time.
In a previous tenth kalpa, prior to this thirteenth kalpa,
I granted him a boon regarding the creation and the foremost worship among the gods.
In the purificatory rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others, as well as in the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) and so forth;
in journeys, in trade and similar pursuits, in battle, and in auspicious worship of the gods.
Whoever worships the elephant-faced one during times of distress for the sake of accomplishing desired goals, all his undertakings will indeed be successful; of this there is no doubt.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these words spoken by the great-souled Kṛṣṇa,
Pārvatī, the mistress of the worlds, was filled with wonder, her countenance radiant.
When Pārvatī gave no reply in the presence of Śiva,
then the eternal goddess Rādhā, who is the very form of Śiva, spoke to the goddess.
Śrī Rādhā said:
Prakṛti and Puruṣa, both having their forms mutually dependent upon one another,
appear divided into two ways in this phenomenal world, just as they do.
O Goddess, there is no difference whatsoever between you and me;
you are Viṣṇu and I am Śiva, having attained a state of duality.
Viṣṇu, having assumed your form, resides in the heart of Śiva;
and Śiva, having assumed my form, resides in the heart of Viṣṇu.
O highly fortunate one, this Rāma is a Vaiṣṇava who has attained the state of Śiva;
this Gaṇeśa is Śiva himself, who has established himself in the state of a Vaiṣṇava.
"Even between these two lords, no difference is perceived.
Having spoken thus, Rādhā took the elephant-faced one onto her lap.
Having smelled him on the crown of his head, he touched his cheek with his own hand;
as soon as the cheek was touched, the wound attained complete healing.
Then Pārvatī, being entreated by Rādhā, became well-pleased;
she raised with her own hand Rāma, who had fallen at her feet.
Highly pleased, Pārvatī embraced them and smelled their heads;
thus did she show honor to both Rāma and Gaṇeśa.
Kṛṣṇa drew Skanda toward him and affectionately placed him on his own lap;
then Śambhu also, being pleased, [welcomed] Śrīdāmā who stood before him.
The giver of honor placed me upon his own lap out of love, regarding me as his son.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, while they were thus standing there with hearts full of affection,
Rāma rose from Bhavānī’s lap and joined his palms in reverence.
Having become composed, he offered praise to the one who is without distinction yet possesses distinctions,
who is non-dual yet has entered into duality, and who is without qualities yet consists of qualities.
Rāma said:
To create this entire universe born of primordial nature and its transformations, how great must my majesty appear to be?
May Bhavānī—whose body and name are unknown, who is the singular abode of all desired objects, and whose every wish is fulfilled—protect me.

O Mother, may that Pradhāna protect me today—the source of all existence, the manifestation of manifested qualities, the ordainer of the reckoning of time, which is proclaimed as the primordial cause; from whom, O Father, this entire universe arose, wherein the fall of both the uncreated and the created occurs.
May he who destroys the race of Danujas, who never fails to deliver a written message, who causes the first lineage to flourish, who illuminates all branches of knowledge,
who forcibly bestows fame upon the world, who eats everything offered by his devotees, who has conquered the noose of Māra, and who feeds the six-faced Kārttikeya— may he protect me.
May Kīrtidhāman— who dwells near Haranikaṭa, who delights in the service of Kṛṣṇa, who shines upon those who bow to him, who makes the cowherd girls laugh,
who is highly honored by Hara, who is solely intent on the mistress of the cowherds, and who knows many kinds of knowledge— arise for our two families.
May He, who is guided by His Lord, who has dispelled the obstacles within my devotion, who has destroyed the multitude of my sins, who is intent on bestowing knowledge,
who is most eminent in all virtues, and who rests upon the lap of Rādhikā— may He forgive my profound offense.

May she who is worshipped by people during the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe; who makes known the sound of the Lord’s mouth which is the tasting of the nectar of trickling love;

the Queen of the Rāsa, the Mistress of the Sensitive, whose devotion is fixed on the eyes of her Beloved, who gladdens her own kin, and who is celebrated as Rādhā—may that Leader protect me, who am bowed down before her.

May she, whose womb gave birth to the Ativirāṭ, from whose portion the Virāṭ arose, by whom— through Brahmā born from the lotus of her navel and instructed solely by her— this entire universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving was created, and within whose pores the cosmic eggs shine forth;
may that mother be eternally gracious.

May that Kṛṣṇa, the all-pervading Lord of the moving and unmoving world, the ocean of existence, consciousness, and bliss, who shines manifest with Rādhā blinded by love—may he, the most perfect one whose heart is moistened with compassion for me, be ever present; through him may I become a man of merit, and may my inner self be dissolved in bliss.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus offered praise, the son of Jamadagni ceased;
he who had realized the meaning of all ultimate principles stood with his hair standing on end, as if his purpose were fulfilled.
Then the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, his soul serene, spoke to Bhārgava, who stood before him, bowing with devotion and being a worthy recipient of his grace.
Kṛṣṇa said: "O lord of the Bhārgavas, you have now attained perfection through my grace;
from this day forward, O child, may you be the most excellent in this world."
"O Lord, a boon was granted to you by me long ago in the hermitage of Viṣṇupada;
all of that must come to pass for you in due course over many years."
Compassion should be practiced toward the miserable by one who desires the highest welfare;
likewise, yoga must be mastered and enemies must be subdued.
There is no one equal to you in this world, whether in splendor or in strength, nor even in knowledge or fame; you are the most excellent of all.
Then, having returned to your own home, perform service to your parents;
practice austerities at the proper time, for by that, success will be held in the palm of your hand.
Raising Gaṇeśa from Rādhā’s lap, the Lord of Rādhikā embraced him firmly and established a friendship with him through the rāsa dance.
Then, O subduer of enemies, both of those illustrious lords of Rāma’s hosts became filled with joy at the command of Kṛṣṇa.
In the meantime, the goddess Rādhā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, being virtuous,
with a gracious countenance and filled with joy, granted a boon to both of them.
Rādhā said:
"You two are worthy of worship by the entire world, invincible, and bringers of joy;
you are especially my devotees, and these two are your sons."
Whatever task anyone may undertake after pronouncing the names of you two,
may all that attain success through my grace.
Then Bhavānī, the Mother of the World and beloved of Śiva, said:
"O child Rāma, I am pleased with you; what boon shall I grant you?
O illustrious one, cast your fear far away and tell me that."
Rāma said:
"In whatever thousands of births I may go through,"
"Grant me that I may become a devotee of both Kṛṣṇa and Bhava,
and that I may likewise perceive Kṛṣṇa and Bhava as non-different."
Pārvatī said:
"So be it, O illustrious one! You are a devotee of Bhava and Kṛṣṇa;
by my grace, O observer of noble vows, may you quickly become long-lived."
Then the Lord of the Earth, the Lord of Umā, the Sovereign of the World, being pleased, spoke to that descendant of Bhṛgu, the best of the Bhārgavas, who stood before him bowing and worthy of a boon.
Śiva said:
"O child, you are a devotee of Rāma; whatever boon has been granted to you by me shall come to pass in its entirety. Truth has been spoken, and it shall not be otherwise."
From this day forward in this world,
my dear child, there shall be no one more powerful than you, nor any radiant being who surpasses you.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Kṛṣṇa, having taken leave of Śiva and the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī),
departed for Goloka together with Śrīdāmā and Rādhā.
Then the righteous Rāma, having worshipped and saluted both Bhavānī and Bhava, proceeded to circumambulate them.
O King, having bowed to Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya and having taken leave of them,
he departed from within the house accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa.
As he was departing, O King, Rāma, saluted by the Gaṇas headed by Nandīśvara,
went to his own home with supreme joy.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as narrated by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, thus the wise and righteous Bhṛgu, observing many regions,
arrived accompanied by Kṛtavraṇa.
All the Kṣatriyas, intent on saving their lives, hid themselves here and there upon seeing that descendant of Bhṛgu as he proceeded along the path.
Then, O Indra among kings, Rāma reached his father’s hermitage,
which was filled with peaceful creatures and resounded with the chanting of the Vedas.
There, lions, deer, cattle, elephants, cats,
and mice dwell together in joy, having cast fear far away.
O King, where, upon merely seeing the smoke arising from the *agnihotra* sacrifice, the peacocks cry out and dance; ||| BndP_2,44.5 |||
At that time of evening, when the twice-born cast handfuls of water facing the sun,
the earth becomes turbid with mud.
Where the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Samhitas are constantly studied with joy by disciples who remain steadfast in the vow of celibacy.
Then, O King, Rāma, with a serene soul, beholding the excellence of the hermitage, entered it slowly accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa.
Honored by the sons of the twice-born and the twice-born themselves as they uttered shouts of "Victory! and "Homage!", Rāma attained supreme joy.
Having entered his own dwelling within that hermitage,
Rāma beheld his father Jamadagni, a treasure-house of asceticism.
He fell at the feet of him who sat like Bhṛgu in person, capable of both restraint and grace, with his eight limbs touching the earth in prostration.
"O King," he said, "I am Rāma, your servant," and uttering these words,
that leader of virtuous men duly grasped his feet.
Then, having prostrated at the feet of his mother with palms joined in reverence,
he bowed down and spoke these words, which were the cause of great joy for them both.
Rāma said: "O Father, by the power of your asceticism,
Kārttavīrya— whose strength and mounts were formidable— has been slain in battle."
"O bull among sages, I have forcibly inflicted punishment upon him who committed that offense, instigated by his wicked minister."
Having paid homage to you, I went into the presence of Brahmā;
having saluted him according to the prescribed rites, I reported my own business to him.
Having heard the account from the beginning, the Blessed One said to Samā:
"Go to the eternal world of Śiva for the sake of accomplishing your purpose."
Having heard that, O dear one, I paid homage to my father Mahat and went indeed to the world of Śiva, desiring a vision of Hara.
Having entered there, O Blessed One, Śiva, accompanied by Umā,
was saluted by me— the God who bestows all desired objects.
Before him, my entire life story was related by me with a composed mind; he, though already having heard it all, listened to everything.
Having heard and reflected upon all of that, he, filled with compassion, gave to me the armor named Trailokyavijaya, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Having obtained that [boon] and paid homage to him, I went to Puṣkara;
there, with a joyful heart, I accomplished the rite for the armor.
Having slain Kārtavīrya in battle, he returned once more to the world of Śiva;
there, at the gateway, I beheld those two, Skanda and Vināyaka.
O knower of dharma, having paid homage to him, I was about to enter;
he, seeing me entering the cow-pen with haste, looked at me.
Then he suddenly restrained me, saying, "Now is not the right time. O father, because of that, there was a verbal duel with him and a pulling of hands.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, because of this, supreme security was born;
knowing that, he took hold of me from both below and above.
He whirled him around with his hand and then brought him back again;
seeing that, I was overcome with extreme rage and hurled my axe at him.
Danta fell down,
and then a deity approached him;
at that moment Pārvatī became enraged there, and Kṛṣṇa arrived.
Accompanied by Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa was entreated by him and granted him a boon; then, having established friendship with him, Kṛṣṇa departed.
Then, having bowed down to the two lords of gods, Pārvatī and Parameśvara,
he arrived in your presence accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Rāma of the Bhṛgu lineage became silent;
then Jamadagni spoke these words to Rāma, the destroyer of enemies.
Jamadagni said:
"Overcome as you are by the slaughter of a Kṣatriya, you must first perform an expiation in the proper manner for the sake of pacifying that fault."
Thus addressed, Rāma, the best among the wise, said to his father:
"You ought to prescribe for me that appropriate expiation."
Jamadagni said:
"Wasting your own body through vows and observances,
subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, perform penance for twelve years."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus, O King, that scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage prostrated before him and his mother, and departed for ascetic penance accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa.
Having gone to Mahendra, the best of mountains,
that crusher of enemies established a hermitage there and performed austerities most difficult to practice.
The high-minded Rāma spent several years in that place, engaged in vows, austerities, observances, and the propitiation of the deities.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Account of Bhārgava" within the "Legend of Sagara," in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the Middle Part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 44 //
Vasiṣṭha said: Then, on one occasion in the forest, that hero, accompanied by his fourfold army and by the Śūrasenas and others, went out for the hunt.
Having entered the great forest and slain various kinds of wild animals,
they went toward the Narmadā river at midday, afflicted by thirst.
Having bathed there and drunk the water of the river, their fatigue dispelled,
they proceeded on their way and then beheld the hermitage of Jamadagni.
Seeing the beautiful hermitage on the path as the sages were approaching, they,
impelled by their future karma, asked, "To whom does this belong?"
Having sought supreme peace, the great ascetic Jamadagni dwells here, whose son Rāma is the foremost among those who wield weapons.
Upon hearing that, they became afraid because of the proclamation of Rāma’s name;
yet, recollecting their former enmity, they gave way to wrath and cruelty.
Then they said to one another: "Since our father has been slain by the killer of our father, what vengeance shall we now carry out against the quarters?"
Having spoken thus, with swords in hand, they entered that hermitage and slaughtered the people when the heroic sages had departed in all directions.
Having slain him and taken his head, those wicked ones, like merciless Niṣādas, departed with their forces toward their own city.
Seeing their father slain, O great king, his two high-souled sons surrounded him and wept, emaciated by grief.
Seeing her husband slain and fallen upon the ground, Reṇukā immediately fell down in a swoon, like a creeper struck by a thunderbolt.
Fainting within her own mind and inflamed by the fire of grief,
she was instantly deprived of her life, as if her consciousness had utterly vanished.
When she remained silent, they indeed regained their senses once more;
yet, fainting, they fell to the ground, submerged in an ocean of grief.
Then the other ascetics dwelling in that penance grove,
sharing in his sorrow, gathered together and consoled the sage’s sons.
Though being consoled by the hosts of sages according to the prescribed rites, the sons of Jamadagni,
by their word, cast the bodies of their parents into the fire.
Afflicted day and night by the grief of their parents' death, they indeed performed thereafter whatever was to be done immediately following that.
Then, after twelve years had passed, Rāma returned from his austerities and went to his father’s hermitage together with his friend.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Deeds of Bhārgava" within the "Legend of Sagara," in the middle section of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 45 //
Vasiṣṭha said:
As he was traveling on the road, he heard from the sages the truth from the beginning regarding the prince’s resolve and the departure of his two parents to heaven.
Upon hearing of his father’s taking of life and the severing of his head,
as well as the mere news of his mother’s death, he himself died.
Overwhelmed by pain and grief, the mighty-armed one lamented;
then Akṛtavraṇa, sharing in his sorrow, consoled him.
By means of reasons taught in the scriptures that indicate the power of his own vigor,
and through logical arguments and worldly examples, he completely pacified that grief.
Consoled by him, the wise descendant of Bhṛgu, summoning his fortitude,
set out together with his friend, desiring to see his brothers.
Having seen them and saluted those who were suffering, he himself emaciated by grief and filled with sorrow and distress stood together with them for three days.
Then, as he remembered the death of his father, a most great wrath suddenly arose within him— one capable of destroying all the worlds.
True to his promise, he who was intent on slaying all the Kṣatriyas strengthened in his heart the vow he had previously made for the sake of his mother.
Having resolved, "I shall perform the libation for my parents with the blood from their bodies after slaying the entire lineage of the Kṣatriyas," Bhārgava [set forth].
Having informed all his brothers of his own intention and performed the funeral rites for his father, he departed with their permission.
Then, accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa, he reached Māhiṣmatī;
staying in a grove outside its walls, he called to mind Mahodara.
He suddenly dispatched to Rāma a chariot, a bow, and other equipment, along with horses and all manner of armor.
Rāma, the conqueror of enemies, also mounted his chariot; having equipped himself and taken up his bow with arrows, he blew the conch shell given by Rudra.
Making a loud twang of his bowstring as if shaking heaven and earth,
that best of charioteers suddenly assumed the role of a driver.
Due to the sounds of chariots, bowstrings, and conchs from that man who was indignant at the slaughter of his parents,
the entire city became agitated, as did the men and elephants.
Having learned that Rāma, the destroyer of all kṣatriya lineages, had arrived,
the princes became greatly agitated and made preparations for battle.
Then, O King, five brave warriors, including Śūrasena and others, together with other kings, made a cruel effort to fight against Rāma with five chariots each.
Then those bulls among Kṣatriyas, equipped with a fourfold army,
encountered Rāma like moths encountering a fire.
Having warded off those who were rushing forward with a single chariot, the descendant of Bhṛgu,
possessed of immeasurable prowess, fought in battle against all those kings.
Then once again there was a battle between Rāma and the kings,
wherein the noble-minded one, filled with rage, slew a hundred monarchs.
Then, having slain the Śūrasenas and others along with their armies and vehicles,
he struck down the circle of Kṣatriyas upon the earth with his arrow.
Then those kings, their resolutions shattered and their own forces and mounts slain, fled in every direction as the remnants of the slaughter.
Having thus routed the armies and having slain and conquered them in battle,
he then struck down hundreds of heroic kings with the fire of his excellent arrows.
Then, his soul overcome with anger and desiring to burn the entire city,
Bhārgava discharged a missile whose radiance was like the fire of cosmic destruction.
The fire of his weapon consumed the city, along with its elephants, horses, and men, as it enveloped the entire garland of city walls in a mass of flames.
Seeing the city burning, Vītihotra, intent on saving his life and overcome with fear, quickly departed for the sake of survival.
Having burnt the entire city with the fire of his missiles and having slain his enemies,
he devoured all the worlds like Death himself appearing in person.
Accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa and joined by Sahasrāha,
he departed with the roar of his chariot as if making the earth tremble.
Having struck down all the kṣatriyas and brought peace to the surface of the earth,
Rāma, his mind intent on asceticism, went to Mount Mahendra.
Having returned to that place where the fourfold [evil] had perished, up until the emergence of the Kṣatriya race, he again undertook a vow, bound by initiation for the sake of destroying it.
Furthermore, the twice-born produced the Kṣatriya caste within the fields of the Kṣatriyas;
yet he slaughtered them again upon the earth by the hundreds of thousands.
After once again making the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas over the course of two years,
he performed ascetic penance for another six and four years.
Furthermore, O King, the twice-born produced a Kṣatriya against the fully enlightened one;
he slaughtered him on the earth without remainder, like Death himself appearing in person.
After that period of time had passed, he was born again as a son of the king;
slaying [his enemies], he traversed the earth incessantly for two years.
"Enough with Rāma, O Indra among kings; remember the death of your father!
By him, the earth was cleared of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times."
Because his mother thrice seven times beat her breast out of her own will,
for that reason the Kṣatriyas were utterly exterminated from the earth by Rāma.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Life of Bhārgava," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as narrated by Vāyu.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Then Rāma captured two thousand six hundred consecrated kings of immeasurable splendor alive.
Then, taking those thousands of kings along with the sages,
that one of great splendor went to Kurukṣetra, which was filled with asceticism.
Having caused five lakes to be excavated there, the descendant of Bhṛgu made those bathing-places easy to enter on all sides.
There, the descendant of Bhṛgu indeed purified the impurity arising from the body of the king and filled those five lakes.
Having bathed in them according to the prescribed rule, the powerful son of Jamadagni,
unwearied, gratified his ancestors in accordance with the scriptures.
O Indra among kings, he performed there, together with the Brahmins, the funeral rites for his deceased father and mother in their entirety, exactly as prescribed.
Thus, having overcome all obstacles, he dwelt unwearied in Kurukṣetra, which was filled with austerity,
properly devoted to the worship of his ancestors.
From that time forward, O King, it became the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas),
established by the son of Jamadagni in the penance grove of Kurukṣetra.
The place known as Sasyamantapañcaka is renowned throughout the three worlds;
it is there that Bhṛguśreṣṭha performed sacrifices for the inexhaustible satisfaction of the ancestors.
By means of bathing, giving gifts, ascetic penance, burnt offerings, feeding the twice-born, and libations,
all his ancestors there were greatly nourished by him.
They attained imperishable satisfaction and the eternal world of the ancestors;
[this is] the sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned in the world by the name Samantapañcaka.
It causes the destruction of all sins and is augmented by great merit; for mortals who have gone there, indeed, all their transgressions [are destroyed].
Like dry leaves in a gale,
the wicked mortals here will flee from afar at the mere approach of that field.
O Great King, even in hundreds of births, one can never find the sacred ford of Samantapañcaka in Kurukṣetra, which is so exceedingly purifying.
Having bathed there, a human being becomes as if bathed in all sacred fords;
thus, O Rāma, one has accomplished his purpose, with his desires perfectly fulfilled.
The high-minded one, self-controlled and disciplined, dwelt there for some time;
then, at the end of a year, he departed accompanied by brahmins.
To offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for his ancestors, the son of Jamadagni went to Gayā;
having gone there, the subduer of enemies then performed the śrāddha according to the scriptures.
He gratified the Brāhmaṇas, honoring them in honor of his ancestors;
that supreme Śaiva station there is known as Candrapāda.
There is no field in this world like that which brings satisfaction to the ancestors,
even if they are worshipped there by those born of their own lineage with only a little effort according to their ability.

By means of the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other rites, the ancestors will attain an imperishable state when those twice-born ones have been gratified there with libations intended for the ancestors.
And filled with devotion to his ancestors, he offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) according to the prescribed rites;
thereupon, all his ancestors arrived from the world of the Pitṛs.
Led by Jamadagni, they accepted the worship performed for them;
then, with hearts full of joy, they gathered together around the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then all his ancestors, becoming invisible and moving through the atmosphere, spoke.
The ancestors said:
"O hero, a great deed has been performed by you, which is extremely difficult for others to accomplish."
"You have indeed satisfied us properly according to the prescribed rule;
yet, you do not grant us imperishable satisfaction."
For although he had committed the murder of a kṣatriya, he became one whose deed was completed;
by the power of this sacred field and through devotion to you, he has obtained a vision of you.
"We have arrived and been honored, yet we do not partake in the fruit of imperishability;
therefore, you must indeed perform [this rite] for the pacification of sins such as the killing of a hero."
Perform atonement according to the rule and practice the eternal dharma;
from this point forward, desist from the slaughter of Kṣatriyas.
They have not offended against your father, for the world is not independent;
rather, your father's death was ordained long ago on account of that very [destiny].
Who in this world would be capable of killing anyone, or even of protecting anyone? In both of these matters, everyone here is merely an instrument for another.
Indeed, all beings act in accordance with their past karma;
the world of men is surely subject to the power of time—of this there is no doubt.
"O child, since every living being on earth is capable of acting only through its own karma, no one at all is able to obstruct other beings without the intervention of destiny."
Therefore, releasing your anger toward the kṣatriya and desiring our welfare, attain peace; may prosperity be yours, for he is indeed our supreme strength.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, all the ancestors vanished from the sight of the descendant of Bhṛgu,
and he, in turn, respectfully accepted all those words.
Accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa and filled with supreme joy,
Rāma then departed from that hermitage in the Siddha forest.
O King, having established himself there together with the brahmins, that high-minded and best of the Bhṛgus became one whose resolve was fixed upon asceticism.
Having made an agreement for their return, he then dispatched him along with his chariot, his followers, and his bows and armor.
Then, unwearied, he performed ablutions at all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*s),
having circumambulated the entire earth while worshipping the ancestors, the gods, and others.
In this manner, O king of kings, the descendant of Bhṛgu traversed the earth three times in succession, following the conduct of the world.
Then, O King, surrounded by Brahmins, he went once again to Mahendra, the best of mountains, for the sake of ascetic penance.
O King, that knower of dharma established his own dwelling there, a place frequented by sages and perfected ones for many long nights.
Sages dwelling in all sacred fields,
disciplined exponents of the Veda, gathered together, desiring to see him as he was performing austerities.
The hosts of sages beheld him, his mind intent on asceticism,
like a fire that has been extinguished after completely burning away a thicket of kṣatriya power.
Then, seeing those divine lords of sages who had arrived,
the descendant of Bhṛgu honored them with hospitable rites such as the offering of water for the feet (*arghya*).
Preceded by inquiries regarding their practiced skills, there arose between them and him auspicious, highly exalted,
meritorious, and captivating conversations.
Then, with the consent of those sages of purified souls,
he began to perform the great horse sacrifice, the Aśvamedha.
O King, having gathered all the necessary provisions, he was accompanied by Aurva and others,
as well as Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, Mārkaṇḍeya, and the rest.
Having acted according to their counsel and regarding Kāśyapa as his own preceptor,
O King, he then performed the great sacrifice of the horse (vājimedha).
Kāśyapa was the *adhvaryu* priest for that Rāma of realized self, Gautama the sage was the *udgātṛ*, and Viśvāmitra was the *hotṛ*.
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya performed the office of the Brahman priest for him,
while Bharadvāja, Agniveśya, and others, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, served as priests.
The sages performed other rites in their respective order;
the blessed Bhṛgu, however, was accompanied by his sons, disciples, and grand-disciples.
O King, that bull among the Bhṛgus performed the duties of the assistant priest (sādasya) together with other sages; having completed all the rites along with them, he [concluded the sacrifice].
Having adorned his beautiful daughter Mahī according to the prescribed rites, he duly honored Brahmā along with his preceptor.

Having summoned [the Earth], which was endowed with hundreds of cities and villages, garlanded by the oceans as its garment, and possessed of mountains, forests, and groves— that tiger among the Bhṛgus— addressed her.
Rāma gave that entire, supreme mountain to Kāśyapa, with the exception of one spot;
he reserved it for his own residence.
From that time forward, O Indra among kings, he worshipped [the deity] according to the scriptures with gold, jewels, garments, horses, cows, elephants, food, and other such offerings.
Formerly, having completed the sacrifice at its conclusion and likewise having bathed in the final purificatory rite (avabhṛtha),
he then made a renunciation of his possessions with their consent.
And having granted fearlessness to all beings, the descendant of Bhṛgu began to practice austerities there on that excellent mountain.
Then, having taken leave of him, all the members of the assembly, the officiating priests,
and the sages of celebrated vows departed as they had come.
When they had departed, the Blessed One, accompanied by Akṛtavraṇa,
undertook great austerities and dwelt there happily.
Then the earth belonging to Kāśyapa, at the command of Mārīca, gave birth to many lords of men for the sake of pacifying all suffering.
There, the Earth duly observed the vow known as the Installation of the Lamp, as proclaimed from the mouth of Viṣṇu, and she became liberated from her sufferings.
Thus has this manifestation of the son of Jamadagni been recounted;
by hearing which, a person is liberated from all sins.
The power of Kārttavīrya, whose splendor was renowned throughout the world,
has been correctly described in this context, neither too briefly nor too elaborately.
Such was the power of that King Kārttavīrya on earth; no man like him has ever existed, nor will there be, nor is he heard of anywhere.
From Dattātreya, the Supreme Person, he chose as a boon death at the hands of Rāma,
by which he formerly attained liberation when slain by Rāma in battle.
His fifth son was the famous Jayadhvaja;
O King, his son was the mighty-armed Tālajaṅgha.
He also had a hundred sons who were excellent archers;
they were known as the Tālajaṅghas, of whom Vītihotra was the eldest.
Accompanied by his sons, Vītihotra and the others, as well as kings such as Haihaya,
he dwelt for a long time in the mountain caves of the Himālayas.
O Rāma, Tālajaṅgha, who had previously been fleeing when struck on the back by an arrow,
fell to the ground unconscious and in intense pain.
Vītihotra saw him fleeing as if driven by fate;
having placed him upon his chariot, he became intent on escaping with speed.
Afflicted by fear and having encountered great hardship, they all dwelt there on the Himālaya mountain, subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
Then, when Rāma had attained peace with his mind intent on asceticism,
Jālajaṅgha regained his own kingdom along with his son.
Having once again established his city as it was before, that best of kings,
the subduer of enemies, dwelt there and protected his own kingdom.
O great king, Tālajaṅgha, accompanied by his sons and his army, approached your city, recollecting their former enmity.
Endowed with a fourfold army and as if shaking the earth,
that lord of the earth arrived and besieged the city of Ayodhyā.
Then, having departed from the city, your father Phalgutantu also fought against all those kings, though he was old, as if he were young.
Having destroyed many mothers, elephants, horses, chariots, and soldiers,
the aged king, defeated by his enemies, became intent on flight.
Having abandoned the city, the kingdom, along with its treasury, army, and vehicles,
he entered the forest together with his pregnant mother.
And there, dwelling for not long at all near the hermitage of Aurva,
he was soon overcome by grief and indignation, as well as by his own old age.
O Indra among kings, as you were being watched by your mother, whose throat was choked with tears, you departed from here to the heavenly world like one who is helpless.
Then, O King, his mother, overcome with pain and grief, weeping, placed her husband’s body upon the funeral pyre.
Afflicted by her husband’s misfortune and the suffering of fasting and other penances,
she formed a very firm resolve within herself to enter the fire.
Having heard all of that, the great sage Aurva himself emerged from his hermitage and, seeking to restrain her, spoke as follows.
"You must not die now, O Queen;
for in your womb dwells a son who shall be the most excellent among all living beings."
Having heard those words of his, your wise mother ceased speaking of death; then the sage led her back to his own hermitage,
where she restrained all her sorrows and fixed her gaze upon the lotus of your face.
Desiring to see him, she lived happily near his hermitage;
then, in due time, she gave birth to you in the hermitage of Aurva.
That sage performed for you all the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony;
you were reared in the hermitage of Aurva and cherished by him.
Everything beyond this has been known by you alone, O subduer of enemies;
such was the power of King Kārtavīrya on this earth.
By the power of this vow, you shall become renowned throughout all the worlds;
for it was by those born of your lineage that your father was defeated in battle and sent to the forest.
I have related that entire account to you in its entirety;
and all this has been told to you as the most excellent of vows.
This tantra, together with its mantras, bestows all worldly fruits upon those in the worlds;
for there is nothing in the four aims of human life that cannot be achieved by this king who is its author.
Whatever is desired, even if difficult to obtain in the three worlds, may it be yours.
In brief, I have related to you the vow of the Haihaya king and that of the sage Jamadagnya; what else shall I tell you?
Jaimini said:
Then King Sagara, with his palms joined in reverence, [addressed] the sage.
He said, "O Blessed One, I wish to perform this vow;
grant me your permission for it through your perfect instruction."
"O brahmin-sage, by this deed I have achieved my purpose; of this there is no doubt.
When the king had spoken thus, the great sage replied, "So be it."
He initiated the king according to the very path prescribed in the scriptures;
that best of kings, Sagara, was thus initiated by Vasiṣṭha.
Having brought the ritual substances, the king duly performed the auspicious vow after worshipping the Lord of the World according to that prescribed rite.
Having completed [the rites] as was appropriate and having then taken leave of his guru,
the king made this supreme vow.
"I shall maintain my livelihood with diligence until the end of my life," thought the high-minded one;
then, having taken leave of the king, the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha [departed].
He went to his own hermitage as he followed him back from where he had turned.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Arrival of Vasiṣṭha," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu, within the narrative of Sagara.
Jaimini said:
When that best of sages had departed, Sagara, the most excellent of kings, [acted].
Dwelling in Ayodhyā, he protected the earth.
Endowed with the multitude of all perfections and knowing the true reality of the meaning of all dharmas,
he was like a child in age alone, yet was esteemed as an elder by his deeds.
Nevertheless, remembering [his situation], he does not eat by day nor sleep at night;
with an agitated heart, he constantly sighs long and hot breaths.

Hearing that his own kingdom had been seized by enemies who had defeated his own preceptor, and that he [the preceptor] had gone with his mother to the exceedingly dense forest and passed away there, the King of the Ikṣvāku lineage was overcome with grief and filled with wrath; having made a solemn vow for the total destruction of the entire host of his foes, he immediately made a vow to endure the fire of humiliation.
Once that protector of the earth, having performed the auspicious rites of consecration,
set his mind upon conquering his enemies and all the quarters in succession.
Surrounded on all sides by many thousands of chariots and by troops of elephants, horses, and chariot-warriors, the king emerged from that best of cities.

Then he set out to slay his enemies with his own vast host of leaping horses, which resembled an ocean agitated by a mass of waves; with his sixfold army, which was like the earth's surface together with its ranges of mountains and its herds of intoxicated elephants; and with the multitude of white umbrellas and banners that shone like the moon and the sun.
As that protector of the earth marched forth, the low-lying regions were filled with the dust from the heaps of mountains crushed by the hooves of the vanguard troops;
meanwhile, the ground there became perpetually covered by a cloud of earth-dust produced by the trampling of the multitudes of each of his fourfold armies.
Slaying many arrogant heroes who had shattered the arrays of elephants, horses, and chariots, the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) immediately assumes a splendor while striking down the host of asuras;
even from afar, proclaiming his intent to besiege their cities, he indicates the moment for their swift retreat and bestows courage upon their lives.
A king desiring victory shall march against whichever king occupies his direction.
Having conquered all kings and brought them into submission to his own position, that king will immediately offer obeisance to him, the lord of that realm.
Having appointed some of those who were traveling to the meeting place to the kingdom, the king turned back;
thus did that monarch proceed, dispersing [his followers] toward the various directions while facing the south.
Remembering a former enmity, he marched against the Haihayas;
then, together with kings possessing a full array of chariots and elephants, [he attacked them].
A hair-raising battle took place between the heroic Haihayas and thousands of kings with their armies in that great conflict.
The mighty-armed lord of Kosala, filled with rage,
struck [them] down after having conquered the Haihaya kings, destroyed, and burned their city.
The king, who brought about the end of enmity, rendered [the earth] entirely empty;
he wiped clean the entire surface of the earth with the crushing impact of his complete army.
The Haihayas ruled their entire kingdom as if it were mere dust;
then, having abandoned both their kingdom and their city, they lost their sovereignty and their splendor.
The kings, for the most part slain, fled in every direction;
but the lord of the earth, having pursued those fleeing monarchs, [overtook them].
Intoxicated with power, he struck down his followers like the enraged God of Death destroying living beings;
then Sagara, the slayer of enemies, became filled with wrath toward them in battle.
He discharged the most terrible Bhārgava weapon, which strikes fear into his enemies;
by that weapon, those kings— whose bodies were now utterly helpless as they were being scorched by the intensely fierce, flickering flames of the Bhārgava missile, terrifying to the three worlds—

wandered for a moment with the range of their vision stolen by the mass of darkness from the rising clouds of smoke produced by the Vāyu-weapon, and barely visible beneath the thick dust falling upon the surface of the earth.

Their movements thwarted by the majesty of the Āgneya weapon, their paths unseen, the kings on all sides have lost their ranks; with bodies subject to others and minds thrown into turmoil, terrified, they have cast aside their garments, weapons, armor, and ornaments; with disheveled hair, they most clearly imitate the state of madness before their enemies.
Having conquered all the Haihayas in battle, the powerful Sagara,
who resembled the agitated ocean, turned toward the Kambojas.

Their fortitude shattered by hearing the sounds of various musical instruments and the roar of beaten drums, these enemies— Kāmbojas, Tālajaṅghas, Śakas, Yavanas, Kirātas, and others— abandoned their kingdoms, their own armies, and the throngs of women in their cities, and wandered bewildered in every direction out of fear of his many weapons, having committed numerous offenses against him.
Terrified by that lord of men, some of his enemies, their vision stolen by the flames of the fire of his majesty, abandoned their dwellings, kingdoms, and sons;
pursued by the enemy armies, they reached forest regions, yet even there those foes encountered him as he rose from sleep in a mountain cave.
Having slain the Tālajaṅghas along with their armies and mounts in battle, that king,
the subduer of enemies, gradually destroyed their kingdom.
Then, overcome with rage, he slew the Yavanas, Kambojas, Kiratas, and others in great numbers, as well as the Palhavas and Paradas.
But all those kings, being struck down by him in that battle,
fled in groups in every direction, terrified, as the survivors of the slaughter.
"By you, whose kingdom was seized by many, I, now his son, have come with a vow to slay you by force, seeking to avenge our enmity.
Proclaiming his own history thus aloud in battle, King Sagara—possessing the prowess of a naga, yet his splendor eclipsed by the kṣatriyas who were his enemies—caused them to remember [his lineage].

Seeing that best of kings, who had undertaken the initiation for the total destruction of the host of his enemies, those who were previously the foremost among women and children fled in fear to seek refuge for the protection of their lives.
The Pāradas, Palhavas, and other notorious enemies of the excellent king—born from the seven kings during the Kali ages—fled toward Vasiṣṭha, the family preceptor of the Ikṣvākus.
Approaching Vasiṣṭha, who was dwelling near his hermitage surrounded by sages,
all the kings spoke with their palms joined in reverence.
O Brahman, be the refuge for us who are afflicted and seeking fearlessness,
whose bodies have been consumed by the fire of Sagara’s weapon and who are on the verge of death.
Intent on bringing an end to enmity, he destroys [his foes] without leaving a single one remaining;
it is indeed out of fear of him that we have fled, desiring to preserve our lives.
Having been separated from the prosperity of his kingdom, his wife, children, and kinsmen,
he has come to you for refuge solely for the sake of protecting his life.
For there is no other man in the world, whether by friendship or by power,
who could turn him back and protect us from this great danger.
"You have indeed been chosen as the family preceptor of the kings born of the solar lineage;
such was the power of the monarchs who were the ancestors of that dynasty."
Therefore, even this Sagara today, restrained by profound reverence for his elder,
does not overstep your command, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore.
O All-pervading Lord, you are our friend, father, and mother, and the teacher of the worlds;
therefore, O Illustrious One, it behooves you to protect us.
Jaimini said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha slowly gazed upon those who had come to him for refuge.
Seeing the remaining descendants of the kings, who were mostly elderly women and children, the Blessed One, compassionate toward all beings, felt deep sorrow.
Having observed them for a long time with his mind and having looked upon them with respect, the high-minded one slowly revived them with his voice, saying, "Do not fear."
Then the illustrious one, filled with supreme compassion,
established those kings who desired their lives in the observance of the vow.
Having caused the royal family to be consumed by the fire of mutual anger and deprived of all the religious merit established by their lineage, Vasiṣṭha went to that best of kings himself and,
having gradually consoled him, requested permission for the departure of his enemies alive, so as to fulfill the king's promise.

Although the king was filled with anger, he honored the words of his elders; thus, he abandoned those enemies who had cast aside their duty, their family traditions, and their proper attire, as well as those Brahmins who were devoted to rites divided by the Śruti and Smṛti and who had utterly forsaken their lives—each of these kings he dismissed one by one, treating them as if they were already dead.
He made the Śakas half-shaven, the Palhavas bearded,
the Yavanas devoid of beards, and the Kāmbojas possessed of prominent chins.
In this manner, he made the other royal lineages deformed and devoid of the rites prescribed in the Vedas, and they were abandoned by the brahmins.
Having established them in the observance and while they were still living, he released them;
thereafter, those enemies of his abandoned the characteristics of their own proper conduct.
Having fallen into the state of *vrātyas*, they were despised by all social classes;
they were constantly reviled by everyone, being cruel and shameless.
And in the world, there arose tribes of Mlecchas who were cruel and lived in organized groups.
Then, released by that king, the Śakas, Yavanas, Kirātas, and others immediately abandoned their own customs and dress and took up residence in mountain thickets, caves, and other such places.
Even today, these races, constantly despised by the virtuous, persist in their wicked conduct and evil deeds in this world, fulfilling the promise of the king.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "Sagara’s Fulfillment of His Vow," in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Jaimini said:
Then, having given leave to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, Sagara...
Endowed with a great force, he marched toward Vidarbha.
Then the King of Vidarbha affectionately offered his own daughter, the peerless and suitable girl named Keśinī, to him.
At an auspicious moment, that tiger among kings, the lord of the earth, duly took the hand of Keśinī in the presence of the sacred fire.
Having stayed for some days in his house, being treated with great hospitality,
he consulted with the King of Vidarbha and then prepared to depart.
Then, having been granted permission by him and honored with gifts,
the king departed from that city and proceeded toward Śūrasena.
Then, honored by the Yādavas and his maternal kinsmen,
and gratified by them with floods of wealth, he departed from Madhurā.
Thus King Sagara, having conquered this earth,
compelled all other kings to pay him tribute and even made them attend his royal assemblies.
Then, having taken leave of the kings who were his followers,
the lord of men granted permission for all his attendants to return to their own kingdoms.
Then, accompanied by a great army and his royal camp,
he gradually returned to his own kingdom, causing no distress to the lands along the way.
Being repeatedly honored with numerous offerings from various regions, he eventually arrived at Ayodhyā amidst a great tumult.
Having learned of his arrival, all the people of the city,
eager for the great festival, adorned that city.
Then that entire city was adorned with festive rites and auspicious ceremonies;
its ground was sprinkled and swept clean, and it was filled with hundreds of full water-jars.
It was adorned with hundreds of raised banners and flags,
enriched everywhere by the incense of agarwood, and radiant with various flowers.
Adorned with lofty gate-towers and watchtowers featuring archways of the seven precious gems,
its great highways were beautifully decorated with showers of flowers and parched grain.
The city was filled with great festivals in every house,
and the rows of dwellings for all the local deities were fully awakened.
The city was adorned on all sides by the citizens and countryfolk, filled with joy, who had beheld the king, the conqueror of the circle of directions.
Then all the subjects, as well as those dwelling in the inner apartments,
were accompanied by the Vārakātākas, the Kadabas, and the women of the city.
Then all the ministers and city-dwellers approached him;
having met with them, the king received their blessings and performed the customary rites of hospitality.
The entire circle of the quarters was deafened by the abundant sound of victory,
which was sweet and mingled with the resonance of various musical instruments.
Having honored them according to their merit, accompanied by those joyful ones,
and gladdening all his subjects, he entered the best of cities.
He was greeted by Brahmins with the very sweet sounds of the Vedas,
and was being praised most intensely by Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards.
And with shouts of "Victory! uttered on all sides by people from various lands, mingled with the sounds of lutes, flutes, and cymbals accompanied by the resonance of cymbals and rhythmic clapping.
Followed by singing musicians and dancing courtesans,
he shone, adorned with a shimmering white parasol.
Scattered all around with heaps of *salla* flowers and *jaka* blossoms,
he entered his own city of Ayodhyā like Indra entering heaven.
Purified by his vision, he proceeded along the path of the Brahmins with fragrant incense,
and went through the middle of the city to his glorious and adorned home.
Then, having descended from the vehicle together with his two wives,
he joyfully entered his mother’s house, which was filled with happy and well-fed people.
Approaching his mother as she sat upon her couch, he, filled with humility,
then performed a prostration, touching her feet with his head.
Having greeted him with blessings and a voice faltering with joy,
she rose up in haste and embraced her son.
He joyfully greeted both daughters-in-law with many blessings;
having honored them with conversation, he remained there as if for a long time.
Permitted by her, the king then departed from that abode;
thereafter, the king, accompanied by his followers, was fanned with white whisks.
Resplendent like the king of the gods, he slowly approached the assembly;
having entered that divine hall, which was attended by many kings.
Having bowed to all his elders and being greeted with blessings,
the lord of men sat down upon a beautiful, divine throne.
And being attended by kings who were lords of various realms,
that best of monarchs engaged in various kinds of conversation there.
Having thus fulfilled his vow and conquered the entire circle of the quarters, the king dwelt with his kinsmen, being exceedingly well-pleased.
The noble-minded sovereign of the regions, who had conquered all his enemies through his own power, followed the three aims of life according to the path of righteousness.
Like a bull, he ruled the earth under a single umbrella,
unable to endure the former humiliation of his father who had departed for heaven.
Having perfectly fulfilled that vow upon which he had embarked,
[he beheld] the earth garlanded with the seven continents, oceans, cities, villages, and dwellings.
Having conquered his enemies without exception, he protected the earth;
and as time passed in this manner, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha [arrived].
He approached once more, desiring to see that Lord of Old Age;
and seeing that best of sages approaching, he was filled with agitation.
The high-minded king, accompanied by those princes, went out to meet him with offerings in his hands; having properly honored him with the arghya, pādya, and other rites, he received him.
Filled with devotion for his guru, he prostrated before him;
then Vasiṣṭha, having honored Sagara with blessings, [spoke].
"Please be seated," he said, together with all the lords of men;
thereupon the king sat down upon a supreme golden throne.
Permitted by the Sage, he, together with his wife and the kings, approached Āpava,
the best of monarchs, as he sat nearby in a secluded place.
Vasiṣṭha spoke these words in soft syllables slowly, while the kings were listening: "O King, is all well with you, both in your external and internal affairs?"
Now, by good fortune, all the ministers, the assembly of counselors, and the entire kingdom have been conquered, along with their complete forces and vehicles.
