For it is by good fortune that you, having fulfilled your vow and honoring my word, have indeed subdued your enemies in battles without even an effort.
The enemies who have abandoned dharma and been deprived of life by you— you desire to conquer others again after defeating them, out of a wish for world conquest.
"I have heard the words, 'You have departed with your mounts and army,' but having further heard that you, who have conquered the circle of the quarters, are now stationed in the city."
"O best of kings, I have now come out of affection to see you.
Jaimini said:
Having been addressed thus by Vasiṣṭha, Sagara, the conqueror of the Tālajaṅghas, [replied].
With palms joined in reverence, he replied to the great sage.
Sagara said:
"O Great Seer, there is indeed well-being in all respects; of this there is no doubt."
O Sage, all the deities are constantly oriented toward what is auspicious for you,
since you perpetually contemplate the auspicious with your mind.
"And how is it, O Sage, that such obstacles arise for me?
I have been favored by you and have now been made one who has accomplished his purpose."
O Guru, that you yourself have come here to see me, and that the Blessed One has spoken to me concerning the victory over adversaries and other matters; [all this is due to your grace].
All that was performed accordingly; however, everything has been attained by the favor of you, O rulers of the earth, and through your grace, I consider it all achieved.
Otherwise, what power would I have to slay such enemies?
You have made my resolve bear abundant fruit.
"Even a small fruit would bring joy to one who has climbed the mountain," Jaimini said. Thus was the great sage properly honored by Sagara.
Having granted him leave once more, he returned to his own hermitage;
and when Vasiṣṭha had departed, King Sagara was delighted in his heart.
Dwelling in Ayodhyā, he ruled the entire earth,
accompanied by his two wives who were endowed with beauty, character, virtue, and other such qualities.
Sumati and Keśinī, both with their lotus-faces in full bloom, enjoyed delightful sense-objects according to their desire and as they pleased.
Endowed with the quality of magnificent beauty, possessing full and rounded breasts,
adorned with dark, curly hair, and decorated with all ornaments.
She was endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed the bloom of fresh youth,
was ever dear to him, and constantly delighted in what was pleasing and beneficial to him.
Through their own conduct, disposition, and gestures, the two of them constantly captivated his mind;
and that lord of the earth, too, felt his own self to be fulfilled by the excellence of their maintenance.
He dwelt in the city with those two, enjoying himself as he desired;
moreover, among other kings on earth, the very title of "king" did not even exist.
And by virtue of that great-souled Sagara’s quality,
even a small amount of dharma remained constantly present within his mind.
But for him, although wealth and pleasure were abundant, they were not so [dominant];
with a mind free from greed, he pursued wealth without causing harm to dharma.
For that very purpose, O Indra among kings, I intentionally afflicted those two.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The World-Conquest of Sagara," in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Jaimini said:
Thus that king protected the earth,
consisting of seven islands, according to the prescribed rules, like another Dharma incarnate in person.
Having established the Brahmins and the other castes each in their respective duties according to the law, he protected them with his senses unimpaired.
And the subjects among all the social orders followed their respective superiors;
likewise, the social orders followed one another in due order according to their sequence in worldly affairs.
O protector of the earth, while that elder was ruling the world, death did not approach even a child among any of the social classes.
At that time, all the kingdoms were prosperous and free from affliction;
within them were innumerable districts filled with people belonging to the four social orders.
And while that king was ruling, there were countless hundreds of cities and villages, each with its own divisions, and the lands were mostly inhabited by people.
At that time, there was no twice-born man on earth who did not belong to an āśrama;
among all the social orders, the undertakings of the people were fruitful.
And at that time, human beings undertake only those actions appropriate to themselves—
actions endowed with human effort.
The cities, villages, cow-pens, and mines were engaged in great festivals;
they desired one another's welfare and were endowed with devotion to the king.
Among his subjects, there was no one who was censured, nor anyone falsely accused; nor was there anyone who was impoverished, afflicted by disease, greedy, or even miserly.
The people were delighted by the virtues of others, longing for the company of their own kin;
they were ever bowed before their elders and devoted to their passion for true knowledge.
Fearing slander from others, they constantly delight in their own wives;
by nature they refrain from associating with the wicked and are devoted to dharma.
While he was ruling, all his subjects were entirely devoted to the existence of the higher realms;
thus did Subāhu rule the earth acquired by his own prowess.
O highly fortunate one, the seasons followed their proper times,
and the entire earth was always rich with crops, abounding especially in rice.
While that tiger among kings was ruling over the kingdoms, [this] came to pass.

In which assembly hall, illuminated by the radiance of jewels, there shines forth a splendor like that of Śakra in heaven; for it is intensely occupied by hundreds of consecrated kings of celebrated and great prowess—lords of eighteen circles—who have arrived to serve him and sit individually upon thrones of gems, as if they were gods.

Having accepted the various sites designated for them, all the kings, having established their military camps around the city separately, desired to see the King whom they longed to behold; thus, with their sons, they repeatedly made requests through the gatekeepers that they might dwell for a long time within the inner apartments.
The two feet of that king shine with calluses formed from the excessive rubbing by the rows of crowns on the heads of prostrate monarchs.
Scattered on all sides by the multitude of kings who had come to serve him, his assembly hall shines with jewels like a cave in the moonlight does in the sun.
Thus that king, the crest-jewel of the solar dynasty and subduer of enemies, ruled the earth according to dharma, its sovereignty being subject to no other.
While King Sagara was thus protecting the earth,
the joy arising from beholding the face of his son did not fail to descend upon him.
Without her, he was exceedingly distressed and reflected in many ways:
"Alas, what misery! For I am certainly childless in this lineage."
"Surely our ancestors now go to the flood of funeral cakes;
for it is said that when a virtuous son is born, the ancestors [are rescued] even from hell."
Eager for the performance of the birth-rite, they go to his house with joy,
as if he had attained heaven through great merit.
For the immortals do not open the gate to heaven for one who is sonless;
yet the father [secures] both worlds, and his grandfather [secures] the heavenly world.
"Indeed, they shall both conquer when a virtuous son is born, even though we are of two lineages;
yet, because of my childlessness, may I attain that destination which belongs to those who possess sons."
I shall certainly not attain that [state], for it is indeed exceedingly difficult to obtain;
it is a prosperous and unbroken kingdom, said to be non-different from the position of Indra himself.
Whatever merit of mine was destined to become fruitless here,
this very throne has been occupied by my ancestors alone.
"Because I am sonless, the kingdom will fall into the power of others; therefore, having gone to the hermitage of Aurva, I shall approach that bull among sages."
"Now, together with my two wives, I shall go and propitiate that Great-souled One by informing him of my sonlessness for the sake of obtaining a son."
"Whatever he shall say, all that I will do; there is no doubt in this"—thus did that best of kings, Sagara, reflect within his mind.
Thus, O King, having entrusted the kingdom to his most excellent minister, Aurva, who was skilled in what ought to be done, set out toward the hermitage.
Having ascended his chariot, he set forth joyfully accompanied by his two wives;
he proceeded with the sound of the chariot, which caused those who heard it to suspect it was the roar of a thundercloud.
O King, being observed by peacocks at the edge of the path with their eyes fixed in stillness,
he showed his two beloved wives the deer whose own eyes were likewise motionless.
Seeing the trees, which were capable of facing upwards, yet suddenly intent on fleeing, and laden with flowers and fruits, he became joyful once again.
It was surrounded on all sides by mountains filled with unfading flowers, sweet fruits, and grassy grounds, and adorned everywhere with the lush shade of glossy foliage.
All directions resounded with the cries of cuckoos, their throats made supple by tasting the tender sprouts at the tips of mango trees, producing delight for the ears.
It was endowed with flowers of every season, adorned by swarms of wandering bees,
and its trees were entwined by creepers bending under the weight of clusters of blossoms.
It was surrounded by hundreds of trees occupied by troops of monkeys,
and filled with flocks of birds warbling amidst intoxicated peacocks and deer.
The forest thickets were made enchanting by the songs of Vidyadhara maidens singing, and they shone with pairs of Kinnaris wandering about.
It was surrounded by lakes whose shores were filled with the melodious calls of swans, cranes, ruddy geese, ducks, parrots, and other birds.
The lake, with its masses of lotuses, white lilies, night-blooming water-lilies, and blue lotuses,
slowly filled the quarters of the horizon with a gentle, drifting breeze.
Having entered the penance grove endowed with such qualities,
the king, proceeding by chariot, then attained supreme joy.
Then, with his mind pacified, having reached the circle of hermitages,
that illustrious one, accompanied by his two wives, indeed descended from the vehicle.
Having said to the charioteer, "Let the draft-animals rest," the lord of the earth reached the vicinity of the hermitage of the great seer of purified soul.
Having heard this from the disciples of the sage, he, having performed his daily rites with devotion and being humble in spirit,
then entered the hermitage to see the sage.
The king, together with his two wives, joyfully bowed his head in salutation to the Sage as he sat in the midst of the assembly, surrounded by hosts of seers.
When the king had offered his salutation, the powerful sage Aurva affectionately commanded him and the two others, "Please be seated."
Having properly honored him with offerings of water for the hands and feet and other rites, the great sage gratified him and his wife with hospitality consisting of forest produce.
Then, after the king had rested from his hospitality and was seated before him, Aurva bowed down and spoke these words slowly and in gentle syllables.
Is it not well with you in your kingdom, both in its outer and inner realms? For you protect all your subjects entirely in accordance with righteousness.
Moreover, you strive effectively by means of expedients to conquer the three aims of life;
for indeed, your virtues bear fruit when they are rightly impelled by you.
"By good fortune, O best of kings, all your enemies have been conquered by you;
and by good fortune, the entire kingdom is protected by you in accordance with righteousness."
For those for whom the Dharma itself is their stability, there is no failure in this regard;
does the Dharma protect him who is already protected by himself?
"Previously, I heard that you had conquered the entire earth and,
having taken a wife, had arrived at the city with your army."
The foremost duty of kings is indeed the protection of their subjects;
by that alone they certainly become happy both in this world and in the next.
O King, tell me why you have come into my presence, having abandoned the burden of ruling the kingdom and accompanied by your two wives.
Jaimini said: Having been thus addressed by the sage, Sagara, the best of kings,
joined his palms in reverence and spoke these sweet words to him.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Sagara’s Journey to Aurva’s Hermitage," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 50 //
Sagara said:
"O great seer, all is well with me in every respect;
of this there is no doubt, since you, the best of the Bhṛgus, have taken thought for my peace."
Having been trained in this manner previously in both missiles and weapons,
how could I now be incapable of subduing all my enemies?
"You are my teacher, my friend, my deity, my kinsman, and my sole ally;
indeed, I recognize no one other than you and my father."
"Since all the kings have been conquered by me with the weapon taught by you,
that power is yours, arising from your asceticism."
By means of your ascetic power (tapas), you purify and protect the entire world;
you are indeed capable of both creating and destroying it, of this there is no doubt.
Your ascetic power possesses a majesty that is great and without equal;
even a single portion of it, as seen here, is enough to inspire wonder.
O Brahmin, you see a young fawn that, having approached the lion-throne out of its youthfulness, drinks water slowly and without fear in your penance grove.
Here, out of excessive trust, even a slender doe suckles at [the sage's] breast;
and the ruru deer scratches its temples on the tip of his antler.
Having killed a doe that had recently given birth for the sake of sustenance in the depths of the forest,
that very tigress now nourishes its fawns in the abode of your asceticism.
"Since the lion, having swiftly pursued the elephant, entered this forest,
we two, following him out of fear of you, have come to stay together in one place."
Nakula, however, [is the deity of] the swift cat, peacock, hare, serpent, wolf,
boar, tiger, śarabha, bear, and monkey.
Jackals, gayals, cattle, deer, and likewise buffaloes,
having abandoned their natural enmity in this forest, have attained a state of friendship.
O Brahmin, such power of austerity, which causes wonder to the world, is not seen anywhere; it is difficult to find on earth except in you.
"But by your grace, O brahmin-sage, having conquered the earth along with my enemies, I have returned to my own kingdom."
With my ministers under my control and showing due respect to each member of the three aims of life as was appropriate,
I protected the kingdom properly according to the path taught by you.
O bull among the Bhṛgus, as I was thus engaged and remaining in my kingdom, a desire to see you arose within me, accompanied by a sense of longing.
But today, for me, who am childless,
my protection of the earth has been fulfilled by the very offering of the ancestral funeral cakes (piṇḍa).

This state of mind, which is exceedingly difficult to endure and impossible to restrain, has come upon you with the thought, "This world is mine," and there is no one in this world who can take it away from you.

Thus addressed by Sagara, the venerable Aurva stood for a moment with a troubled mind and spoke these words in accordance with his instructions: BndP_2.51.19: "Thus addressed by Sagara, the venerable Aurva, having stood for a moment with a troubled mind, spoke these words in accordance with his instructions."
"Restrain yourself and dwell here for some time with your two wives;
thereafter you shall obtain your desired goal—do not entertain any doubt in this matter."
And that righteous-souled one dwelt there for a long time, filled with joy, devoted to serving him, and endowed with devotion along with his two wives.
And his two queens, ever vigilant,
displayed boundless affection toward the sage through their humility, proper conduct, and devotion.
Pleased by their devotion and service, the great sage summoned the two wives of the king and spoke these words: (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.51.23).
"O ladies, choose from us whatever boon you desire;
I shall grant it to you without a doubt, even if it should be very difficult to obtain."
Then, having bowed their heads to that great sage, they both respectfully said to him, "O Blessed One, we desire sons."
Then the Blessed One said to them: "Furthermore, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to the king, this desired boon has been granted by me to you both."
"O highly fortunate ladies, by my grace you shall both surely possess sons;
furthermore, listen to these words of mine."
There will be one son born of one [wife], who will not be exceedingly righteous;
nevertheless, his lineage shall endure until the end of the kalpa.
And sixty thousand sons will be born to another [wife],
yet they all, having failed to achieve their purpose, will perish almost immediately.
"Endowed with such qualities as these, you two have been granted boons by me;
however, let that which is desired by her according to her own wish be proclaimed."
When the sage had spoken thus, she chose as her son-in-law the son who increases the lineage of Vaidarbhī, and likewise other sons as well.
Having thus granted this boon to King Sagara, the great sage took leave of him and his wife and dismissed them toward the city.
Permitted by the Sage and having accomplished his purpose,
the lord of the earth mounted his chariot and, together with his beloved, departed swiftly for the city.
Having entered that beautiful city, which was filled with people who were both well-fed and joyful,
he rejoiced with supreme delight, gladdened by the citizens.
At that very time, O King, both queens,
filled with supreme joy, informed the king of their pregnancy.
And their embryo grew like the lord of stars in the bright fortnight,
along with the abundance of contentment of the parents and the citizens.
Then, when that auspicious moment had fully arrived, Keśinī gave birth to a boy of immeasurable splendor, who shone like the fire within its womb.
Having performed for her the birth rites and other ceremonies according to the prescribed rules,
the king gave her the name Asamañjasā.
And at that time, Sumati also gave birth to a miscarriage;
seeing that it had been born and then cast away, the king set his mind [upon the matter].
Knowing this, the Blessed One Aurvā arrived there by chance;
duly honored by the king, he spoke to him with urgency.
"O King, this embryo, which is the seed for your sixty thousand sons, ought not to be abandoned by you. (BndP 2.51.41)
Therefore, having consecrated them with the sakalīkaraṇa rite, one should carefully place them in jars of ghee with their lids on, and they must be preserved separately.
O King, when this has been performed correctly through my grace,
there will undoubtedly be as many leaves as the number previously stated.
Then, when the time was fulfilled, they emerged individually after breaking through the jars;
in this way, O King, those sixty thousand sons were born to him.
Having spoken thus, the omnipresent Lord Aurva vanished right there;
and the king did exactly as he was instructed by Aurva.
Then, when a full year had passed, they were born again from the jar of ghee, bursting forth one after another, day after day, all at once.
O Lord of the Earth, thus born in succession, those sons of yours,
O King, grew up in groups numbering sixty thousand.
Practicing the Dharma without deviation, possessing great strength and prowess,
they became invincible, especially those of a cruel nature.
That king, the best among the wise, did not feel excessive affection for them;
however, he held the son of Keśinī alone in high esteem as his beloved son.
The king had him perform his marriage according to the prescribed rites;
and he, in turn, delighted all his friends with his own virtues.
As Keśinī’s son was thus engaged in his duties,
a glorious son was born to him, renowned by the name Aṃśumān.
Even in his childhood, that wise youth greatly delighted his mother’s heart and his grandfather with his noble qualities.
In the meantime, that king’s son, Asamañjasa,
became possessed by a certain piśāca and lost all his faculties.
In a previous birth, he was indeed a certain Vaiśya who knew the Dharma;
in the realm of a certain king, he possessed abundant wealth and grain.
Once, while wandering through the forests, he saw a supreme treasure; overcome by the greed of a merchant, he began to seize it.
Then the piśāca who was its guardian approached him and said at that time:
"I have been living here for a long time as the protector of this treasure, yet I am hungry."
Therefore, in order to avoid that [sin], give me the meat of the cow;
by my command, accept this treasure according to your desire.
Having heard that from him, [the king] thought, "I shall give it," and with the approval of the Piśāca, he took up that treasure consisting of the flesh of cows.
Then, out of folly, he did not give him what had been promised; O King, I do not believe that he felt any anger arising from the failure to provide what was promised.
Having waited for such a long time like that in his desire for food,
he too, his wealth exhausted, died, tormented by hunger.
The Vaiśya boy, having met his death at the hands of Sagara,
was later born as a son who increased the lineage through Keśinī.
O King, even as a bodiless *piśāca*, remembering his former enmity,
he became like the wind and entered the body of the prince.
Possessed by that [demon], he then became cruel-hearted;
having suffered a derangement of his intellect, he was repeatedly overpowered by it.
That wicked man also brought disorder to the city like a cruel tyrant,
constantly harassing children, youths, the elderly, and women alike.
Having killed them one after another, he cast them into the Sarayū with utter cruelty;
then all the citizens, seeing his wickedness, [were filled with dismay].
Having been repeatedly humiliated by him, they went and informed the king;
and the king, having heard that, summoned him with great effort.
Filled with great sorrow, he tried to restrain him in many ways; yet, although he was forbidden many times by that high-souled father, he did not desist.
And when the water was heated, they became scorched like barley grains;
when the king was unable to turn him away from that sin, [he departed].
Out of fear of public censure, he did not abandon his sense objects at that time.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Abandonment of Asamañjasa," in the Sagara-carita, within the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 51 //
Jaimini said:
Having abandoned his son, that righteous-souled lord Sagara then bestowed upon the infant Aṃśumat, who was of virtuous character, the affection he had previously held for him.
At that very time, O King, all the sons of Sumati grew up together, each devoted to the others.
They will have bodies as hard as adamant, being cruel, merciless, and shameless;
they will be utterly devoted to unrighteousness and exclusively single-minded in their pursuit of it.
Devoted to a single purpose, wrathful, and of deluded minds,
they are unassailable by all beings and cause affliction to the people.
Disregarding the path of discipline and virtuous conduct in every respect,
they oppressed the entire world like asuras acting out of lust.
The world, oppressed by them, had its true path of sacrifice destroyed;
it became especially afflicted, devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of "vaṣaṭ."
While [the world] was being violently destroyed by the oceans swollen with pride,
the gods, asuras, and great serpents fell into the utmost agitation.
Then the earth, though encompassed by the oceans, trembled even though it was not [naturally] mobile;
and a disturbance of their asceticism and meditative concentration overcame the practitioners.
Deprived of their offerings to the gods and ancestors, the deities, together with the Pitṛs,
overcome by great suffering, went to the abode of Viriñca.
Having gone there, the gods, led by Śarva, reported to him in due order the entire conduct of the oceans.
Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds and the best of the gods, remained reflective within his mind for a moment and then spoke.
"O gods, listen; may it be well with you. Pay close attention to my words:
the oceans will perish before long; there is no doubt about this."
Wait for some time; by him everything is governed. Everything else is merely an instrument; he alone is the sovereign lord of all.
Therefore, O best of gods, whatever I shall say for the sake of your welfare must now be carried out by all of you without hesitation.
By a portion of Viṣṇu, the Lord Kapila,
the best among victors and the foremost of the lords of yogins, was born on earth for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Now, in that place where the waters were drunk by Agastya, he remains in a certain secluded spot within the ocean, meditating for the duration of a divine hundred years.
"Having gone, by my command, to the presence of Kapila, the bull among sages,
stay there desiring to obtain the cessation of meditation."
When he has ceased his meditative concentration, bow down to him and speak your entire intention to him; he will provide for your welfare.
O best of the gods, act in such a way that the Sage’s concentration may be broken, just as it was once disturbed by the oceans.
Jaimini said:
Having been addressed thus by him, those gods bowed to the Grandfather and,
approaching that best of the gods with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him.
The gods said:
"Be gracious to us, O best of sages; we have come to you for refuge.
The entire world, being overwhelmed, is perishing by the oceans."
"You are indeed the cause of the preservation and destruction of all worlds;
as a portion of Viṣṇu, you abide upon the earth in the form of a lord of yogins."

O best among those who perform austerities, you have assumed this body by your own will solely for the sake of destroying the suffering of men afflicted by the threefold miseries; you are not merely a performer of penance.
O Brahman, you are undoubtedly capable of creating, destroying, and ordaining the entire universe by your mere will through the mind alone.
You are our supporter and ordainer; you are our teacher and our ultimate refuge. You are our protector; turn back this calamity.
O best of Brahmins, become a refuge especially for the foremost of Brahmins,
and for the inhabitants of the three worlds who are being consumed by the oceans.
Indeed, O observer of noble vows, the conduct of those like you in this world is truly characterized by goodness; therefore, you ought to protect both the worlds and us.
"O Blessed One, if the entire world were not to perish at an improper time," thus addressed by all the gods, Jaimini slowly opened his eyes. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.52.28)
Beholding them, Kapila spoke these truthful words:
"Consumed by their own karma alone, the sons of Sagara shall perish."
When the time arrives, you must protect them for now;
as for me, I shall be the cause of the destruction of those evil-minded ones.
O best of gods, I shall become [the ocean] for the sake of accomplishing your purpose;
the oceans, whose minds are wicked, have been scorched by the fire of my wrath.
"Let them, whose intellects have long been afflicted by Time, become free from fever; therefore, O gods, may the worlds also be free from fear from any quarter."
"Let those of evil conduct quickly go to their destruction;
therefore, you all, becoming fearless, proceed toward your own city."
"Wait for some time; then you shall obtain what you desire.
Thus addressed by Kapila, all those gods, together with Vāsava, [did as they were told].
Having bowed to him, they then departed with joyful hearts toward the celestial realm of Agni;
meanwhile, King Sagara, the lord of the earth, [remained there].
Then, with the approval of Vasiṣṭha, he gathered all the necessary materials and formed the resolve to perform the great sacrifice of the horse (vājimedha).
Together with the Brahmins beginning with Aurva, he was duly initiated;
the king indeed entered the initiation for the purpose of letting the horse roam.
Having summoned all his sons and caused the horse to wander, having traversed the surface of the earth, the highly illustrious one gave them this command.
"O sons, you ought to bring [the horse] back to me quickly.
Jaimini said:
Then, by their father's command, they took that horse.
They caused him to wander throughout the entire circle of the earth;
for that horse had been made to roam upon the ground solely by the impulsion of destiny.
But that lord of the earth had already conquered the entire world long ago, not for the sake of a conquest of the quarters nor for the purpose of collecting taxes.
And by his noble prowess, the kings were made to pay tribute in battle;
then those princes [were cast] into the salt ocean that was devoid of water.
Joyfully, they alighted upon the ground, surrounding the horse.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Release of the Horse," in the Sagara-episode, within the third section (Uddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 52 //
Jaimini said:
While they were seated there, Vāyu, impelled by Vāsava, carried the horse to the subterranean realm (rasātala) in that very instant.
Having carried off the horse unseen by all of them,
O King, the Wind-god led it along that path to the presence of the sage Kapila.
Then, all the princes became distraught when their horse was lost;
wandering over the entire earth, they searched for the steed.
Having searched the earth, including its mountains and forests,
they did not see the sacrificial animal and fell into great sorrow.
Then, having reached Ayodhyā, which was surrounded by sages,
they beheld their father, bowed down, and reported everything to him.
After we had traversed the earth and entered the abode of Varuṇa,
the horse was carried off by someone, even though it was being guarded and watched by us.
Thus addressed by them, that best of kings, overcome with rage, said to them:
"O most unrighteous ones, you shall all depart so as never to return again!"
"How is it that while you were still alive, you have perished, O cowardly ones? Without the horse, there is truly no reason for your coming here."
Then, having come together from that place and set out toward one another, they said:
"The horse is still not to be seen even now; what shall we do?"
The earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, has been searched by us;
yet the horse is not seen, nor is there any news of him anywhere.
Therefore, having divided the earth from the ocean down to the netherworld (pātāla) and having traversed it by means of the sun, we entered the horse in the netherworld.
Having thus resolved their minds, all the Sāgaras, firm in their cruel determination, began digging the earth on every side, starting from the shores of the ocean.
As the earth was being dug up by them, it groaned, utterly overwhelmed;
and all living beings cried out upon seeing their actions.
Then, having dug up the land of Bhārata and compressed it upon the surface of the earth,
they joined it to the ocean for a thousand yojanas of the earth's extent.
While digging into the surface of the earth down to the depths of the netherworld (pātāla),
those sons of the king beheld the horse wandering in Pātāla.
Then, all of them, having gathered together from every side, were greatly delighted; out of contentment some laughed, while others, filled with joy, danced.
And they beheld the high-souled Kapila, blazing with splendor,
aged, seated upon a lotus throne, with his eyes fixed on the tip of his nose.
With his head and neck straight and elongated, and his chest firmly expanded forward,
he was completely filled on all sides by his own radiance as it surged forth.
Shining forth on all sides like a lamp placed in a windless spot,
its form consists of the totality of consciousness illuminated within its own heart.

But with the mind attained through concentration, resembling a tranquil ocean, having ascended to yoga according to rule, and with the mental faculty absorbed in the object of meditation; BndP_2,53.20 //

Seeing the most eminent lord of yogis, peaceful like a fire garlanded with flames, standing there and reflecting [on the truth], they deliberated among themselves: *cdṛdadyatdadvaḍḍha dyadṛ ḍaddhaṭhṭhaṇthrṭhṭhadaḍḍaṭhṭha-thrṭhṭhaḍḍaṇnrṭhṭhaḍaṇṭhṭhagṭhṭha* (yogīndrapravaraṃ śāntaṃ jvālāmālam ivānalam / vilokya tatra tiṣṭhantaṃ vimṛśantaḥ parasparam //) [Note: The preceding string of characters appears to be a corrupted or encoded transcription of the verse numbers or a placeholder for the Sanskrit text. Having beheld that foremost of lords of yogis, as tranquil as a fire wreathed in flames, standing there, they reflected upon one another.
O King, for a moment they were seized by the utmost trepidation;
then, impelled by Time, the Sāgaras cried out, "This one is the stealer of the horse!"
Those evil-minded men surrounded Kapila, the best of sages;
then, having hemmed him in, they said, "This is a thief, there is no doubt about it."
"Therefore, this evil-minded stealer of horses must be slain by us. Then all those fools, as he sat there like an ordinary man, [attacked him].
Those who were near death quickly assailed the sage.
Then the sage Jaimini, undaunted in spirit though provoked by the interruption of his meditation, spoke:
Then Kapila, overcome by great wrath, became agitated;
though difficult to assail, he trembled when provoked by those evil-minded ones.
And from his body, which was as deep as the ocean, the fire of his wrath burst forth like a conflagration at the end of an aeon fanned by the winds.
Like the fire of Saṃkarṣaṇa wishing to burn the netherworlds,
he shone, inflamed by the indignation of his wrath at being insulted.
Then, O King, opening his eyes which possessed a brilliance equal to the wheel of fire, those two eyes shone for a moment, becoming intensely crimson.
Like the two suns and moon rising together in the sky,
the two princes then emerged from their eyes as they were being turned upward.
And at the turn of time, the profound Kṛtānta gazed upon him;
from the eyes of that enraged one, flames of fire suddenly burst forth.
They issued forth in all directions like continuous streams from the fire of time (Kālāgni),
fierce with mouthfuls of smoke and repeatedly emitting showers of sparks.
The flames of the fire of the Sage’s wrath blazed forth in all directions;
those tongues of flame issued from his eyes, their fierce hollows like the bellies of venomous serpents.
O great king, the fire of his wrath shone forth like the flames of the subterranean fire (vaḍavāgni) within the tranquil ocean, its tongues of flame pervading the intermediate quarters of space.
He reduced them all to ashes, shrouding the very vault of the sky.

The world became intensely distressed, completely enveloped by masses of smoke from fires swirling due to the agitation of the wind accompanied by noise, and by the exceedingly raised dust of the earth.
Then that fire, as if scraping the sky on all sides with its flames driven by the force of the wind,
instantly consumed those enemies of the gods, the sons of the lord of the earth, without exception.
While all the world looked on, he reduced those oceans to ashes without exception, except for that horse, by means of the fire produced from his thigh.
Thus, by that fire of anger, those evil-minded ones were suddenly consumed like sapless trees in a forest fire.
Having witnessed the destruction of those wicked-souled Sāgaras, the gods,
together with the ṛṣis, spoke to one another in amazement.
Alas! The ripening of most cruel sins does not wait long; indeed, the end is wretched for those men in this world who possess such evil natures.
If those cruel and wicked-minded men, as massive as mountains, were to meet their destruction all at once, suddenly like grass consumed by fire; BndP_2,53.42.
These ways of livelihood, which cause terror among living beings and are utterly condemned by the virtuous, have fortunately come to an end; by good fortune, they have reached their destruction.
Having performed unwholesome karma in this world— karma that causes extreme suffering to others and is loathed by all people— what man could find happiness?
Having cried out to all beings, they have departed according to their own deeds;
struck down by the staff of Brahmā, those sinners go to hell for eternal years.
Therefore, wise men should always perform their duty,
and they should avoid from afar anything else that is censured by the world.
An effort toward what is beneficial should be made for as long as one lives by the wise person;
one should not practice malice toward anyone, since life is impermanent.
This body is always impermanent, and worldly fortunes are exceedingly fickle; since cyclic existence is utterly devoid of essence, how could a wise person place their trust in it?
While the gods and the lords of sages were thus conversing with one another,
the sons of Sagara perished, having become fuel for the fire of the sage’s wrath.
Their bodies instantly consumed by fire, the Sāgaras suddenly covered the earth with their ashes and immediately fell into hell along with their own waters.
That fire born of his wrath, having completely consumed those oceans,
was instantly prepared to swiftly burn all the worlds without exception.
Then the gods, terrified with fear, gathered together and remained in the heavens;
desiring to pacify the fire of his wrath, they praised that Great-Souled One.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Destruction of the Ocean," in the *Sagaracarita* (the account of Sagara), within the third section (*upoddhātapāda*) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 53 //
Jaimini said:
O best of Brahmins, you ought to extinguish this fire of anger immediately;
otherwise, at an untimely hour, this entire world will be consumed by it.
The entire world of moving and non-moving beings has been pervaded by your majesty;
forgive us, withdraw your anger, salutations to you, O bull among Brahmins!
Thus being praised, the blessed sage Kapila quickly brought that most terrifying fire of his wrath to an end.
Thereupon the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, became tranquil;
and the gods as well as the ascetics were freed from their distress.
At that very time, O King, the venerable sage Nārada came to Ayodhyā from the world of the gods by chance.
Then, beholding Nārada who had arrived, Sagara duly honored him according to the scriptures with offerings of water for the hands and feet, and other rites.
Having accepted that worship and seated upon an excellent throne, Nārada spoke these words to that tiger among kings: BndP_2,54.7 //
Nārada said: O best of kings, your sons, who had set out for the purpose of driving the horse, were all struck down by the staff of Brahmā and perished.
O King, that sacrificial horse of yours, though guarded by all of them,
was led away by someone unobserved to some place in the heavens by the power of destiny.
Then, O King, while searching for the lost horse upon the surface of the earth, they did not find any news of it anywhere after a long time.
Then, having resolved to search for the horse beneath the earth,
those sons of Sagara began their work and dug into the surface of the ground.
O King, while digging for the earth and the horse, they beheld in the netherworld (pātāla) near that place the lord of yogins, the great sage Kapila.
Seeing him, all those evildoers, impelled by Time, incited Kapila, crying out, "This one is surely a stealer of horses! 54.13.
Then, as the fire from his eyes, born of that wrath, consumed the quarters of the sky,
those sons, their bodies becoming fuel for it, met their destruction.
Since they were cruel, of sinful conduct, and oppressors of all the world,
O Indra among kings, you ought not to grieve because of them.
Therefore, becoming one whose wealth is fortitude regarding what must happen to yourself,
the wise do not grieve for what is lost, dead, or past.
Therefore, O best of kings, appoint this grandson of yours, the high-minded Aṃśumat, for the purpose of bringing back the horse.
Having spoken thus to the tiger among kings, who was accompanied by the assembly and the officiating priests,
the sage Nārada vanished in an instant while they were looking on.
Having heard those words of Nārada, the best of kings,
his soul overcome by pain and grief, reflected for a long time with his noble intellect.
To that king, who was seated in the assembly absorbed in meditation with his face turned downward, Vasiṣṭha, knowing the proper time and place, spoke while consoling him.
How is it that grief finds a place in the hearts of those like you, whose essence is fortitude? O steadfast one, if it has reached you, then its fruit has been attained.
Relaxing all dejection, considering that you have come under the power of destiny,
you ought without doubt to perform the task that follows immediately.
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, the king, who understood the true nature of what was to be done,
summoned fortitude and courage and replied, "So be it."
Having summoned his virtuous grandson Aṃśumat into the midst of the assembly of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, he spoke these words slowly.
"O dear son, all your ancestors, having been struck by the Brahma-staff for their sinful deeds,
have fallen into hell for eternal years."
You alone are my lineage and the protector of this kingdom;
everything pertaining to my welfare, both in this world and in the next, depends entirely upon you.
Therefore, at my command, go to the presence of Kapila in Pātāla,
endowed with great effort for the purpose of bringing back the horse.
Having petitioned him according to the prescribed rites and having especially gratified him,
O child, you should take the horse and return quickly.
Jaimini said: Thus addressed by him, the highly intelligent Aṃśumat bowed to his father’s father, said "So be it," and went into the presence of Kapila.
Having approached him and paid homage according to the prescribed rites, he bowed down with humility and spoke these words slowly, according to his understanding.
Be gracious, O tiger among Brahmins; I have come to you for refuge.
Quickly withdraw your anger, which brings about the destruction of the world.
When you are enraged, the entire world will go to destruction;
therefore, quickly attain tranquility so that the worlds may be free from suffering.
"O illustrious one, be gracious and look upon us with a gentle eye;
know me to be the offspring of those who were consumed by the fire of your wrath."
"I am he who, by the command of that grandson of King Sagara named Aṃśumat, and out of a desire for your favor," [have come here].
"O Brahman, if you have arrived, you shall give [me] for the purpose of bringing the horse.
Having heard those words, Jaimini, the preeminent sage among the lords of yogis, spoke.
Beholding Aṃśumān, he was pleased and said this:
"Welcome to you, my child; by good fortune have you come here."
"Go quickly, and let this horse be led back to the presence of Sagara;
his sacrifice, which was interrupted, should now proceed as it began."
And let a boon be chosen by you from me, whatever is in your heart;
being satisfied by your devotion, I shall grant it even if it be very difficult to obtain.
"Having indeed gone to their complete destruction, speak to the Grandfather; for this is the death of these evildoers, and you ought not to grieve."
Then, having prostrated before the Lord of Yogins, Aṃśumān spoke as follows:
"O Great Sage, if you grant me a boon, I choose this from you."
If you are pleased with me, it would be a boon if you would grant this:
that all my ancestors, who have been scorched by the fire of your wrath, [may be restored].
O Brahmin, they shall go to hell for eternal years;
for those struck down by the Brahman’s staff, there is indeed no performance of funeral offerings or water libations.
O Great Sage, for those in this world who are deprived of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and the water libation (udaka),
co-residence with the ancestors (pitṛsālokya) certainly does not exist, as it is not enjoined by the Vedas.
"By your grace, O Blessed One, may their residence in heaven be imperishable;
by this boon, I shall have accomplished my purpose."
Therefore, be gracious and you yourself tell them the cause for their ascent to heaven,
by which their deliverance from the fire of your wrath may indeed come to pass.
Then the Lord of Yogins, with a very gracious mind, said to him:
"O child, it is not possible for you to deliver them from hell."
Those who have committed evil deeds must also dwell in hell for that long;
let them wait for the time until the birth of your grandson.
At the end of time, O child, there shall be a high-minded grandson of yours,
a king named Bhagīratha, who knows the true essence of all dharma and artha.
But he, constrained by reverence for his father, will certainly bring the Gaṅgā down from heaven after performing great austerities with immense effort.
When the bones and ashes of their bodies have been purified by that water,
all your ancestors shall attain a destination in heaven.
"So be it," [said Brahmā]. O prince, such shall be the majesty of that Gaṅgā;
she will attain renown in this world as Bhāgīrathī.
Even when his bones, ashes, hair, and nails are washed away by water,
the embodied soul goes from even hell to the imperishable heavenly world.
Therefore, go; may it be well with you. You ought not to grieve. Deliver this horse to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Jaimini said:
Then, having bowed to him with devotion and saying "So be it," the high-minded one,
permitted by him, departed toward the city of Sāketa.
Having reached the ocean and bowed to it in due order,
he reported the news of those sages and their state of mind.
He also gave him the horse that had been brought with great effort,
and asked, "What else is to be performed by me after this?"

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Bringing of the Horse from Kapilāśrama," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 54 //
Having greeted him with an exceedingly joyful blessing, he praised him while caressing him.
Then that best of kings, accompanied by the officiating priests and the members of the assembly— all of whom had mastered the Vedas— proceeded with that sacrifice according to the prescribed rites.
Then the sacrifice commenced, endowed with all prosperity and virtues,
duly conducted by the sages headed by Aurva and Vasiṣṭha.
The sacrificial altar was made of gold, as were the various vessels;
everything at the sacrifice was perfectly abundant and performed exactly according to the scriptures.
Thus set in motion, all those officiating priests, led by the sacrificer, completed the sacrifice in due order.
Having completed that sacrifice, the king, the best among those who know the ritual ordinances,
then bestowed the sacrificial fees upon the officiating priests exactly as prescribed.

Then he bestowed wealth in every way upon the officiating priests, the members of the assembly, the Brahmins, and likewise upon those who had come as supplicants, giving them even more than they had desired.
Having thus satisfied the Brahmins and others with sacrificial fees in due order,
he prostrated himself before his gurus and the members of the assembly and asked for their forgiveness.
Then he was accompanied by the social classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as well as by officiating priests,
and by hosts of Vārakīyas, Akadaṃbas, Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards.
Followed by his women, resplendent with a white parasol,
with yak-tail whisks being waved and adorned with chowries, he proceeded.
The quarters of the sky deafened by the sounds of various musical instruments,
he went to the bank of the Sarayū according to the scriptures and according to the prescribed rite.
He joyfully performed the avabhṛtha bath along with his kinsmen;
having thus bathed together with his wife, his friends, and the brāhmaṇas.
Accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments such as the lute, flute,
and drum, and by auspicious Vedic chants uttered by the Brahmins.
Being praised on all sides by *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, and bards,
he entered the beautiful city, which was filled with joyful and well-nourished people.
It was adorned with white fans, umbrellas, banners, and garlands of flags;
its ground had been sprinkled and swept, and it was endowed with the splendor of well-arranged market stalls.
There, with rows of palaces as radiant as Mount Kailāsa,
he beheld the quarters of the sky made fragrant by the scent arising from incense of agallochum.
He was repeatedly showered from all sides with handfuls of parched grain by the women of the city,
while being joyfully gazed upon by the citizens.
Being provided with various kinds of merchandise at every place by merchants,
he gradually proceeded toward his own city.
Having entered his beautiful home, which was adorned with every kind of ornament,
he properly honored his friends as well as the Brahmins.
And being attended then by kings who were lords of various lands,
that tiger among kings rejoiced in his assembly like a second Śakra.
Thus, having fulfilled his heart's desire together with his friends,
Sagara, the most excellent of kings, took his delight along with his two wives.
Then, with joy and in accordance with the approval of Vasiṣṭha, the king consecrated his grandson Aṃśumān, who was endowed with humility, as the crown prince.
Moreover, by virtue of his noble qualities, that king became exceedingly dear to the people of the city and the countryside, as well as to his kinsmen and friends.
The subjects were devoted to him, though he was but a child of immeasurable splendor,
just as they are to the newly risen moon at the beginning of the bright fortnight.
Accompanied by him, that illustrious and best of kings dwelt for a long time, delighting with his sons and his two suitable wives.
Even while still young, that tiger among kings, like another Dharma incarnate,
protected the earth with its mountains, forests, and groves.

Thus, the lord of Uttarakosala, whose body was like that of Yama, rejoiced greatly together with all his subjects— like the full moon, delightful to the minds of all people— as the crest-jewel of the solar dynasty, which is as great as the sun.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Sovereignty by Āṣumā," in the Ocean Narrative, within the third introductory section (upoddhātapāda) of the Middle Portion of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Jaimini said:
"This entire life-story of the high-souled Sagara has been told to you."
Thus has been told, both in brief and in detail, that which destroys all evil.
This region named Bhārata extends from south to north for nine thousand yojanas, with a circular circumference of equal width.
While the sons of that lord of men were searching for the horse,
they dug eight thousand *yojanas* and struck down [the demons].
Because the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, was increased by the sons of Sāgara,
from that time forward it acquired the name "Sāgara" (the Ocean) among the worlds.
Having surrounded the earth, from its very foundations up to the realm of Brahmā— including its sacred fords, holy fields, and forests—
the ocean submerged it with its own waters.
Then all those inhabitants of that place, including gods, asuras, and humans,
fled here and there, overcome by great suffering.
The famous sacred field named Gokarṇa, worshipped by all the gods,
extends for one and a half yojanas on the shore of the western ocean.
O King, in that sacred field there were formerly innumerable holy fords (tīrtha), hermitages of sages and gods, and hosts of perfected beings (siddha) who dwelt there.
That auspicious field, renowned throughout the world and the remover of all sins,
is that sacred ford (tīrtha) which fell upon the south-western quarter of the ocean.
There, all the sages of rigid vows, having performed ascetic penance,
attained supreme nirvāṇa, which is free from rebirth.
There, by the power of this place, Śaṅkara dwells eternally with the hosts of spirits, the Goddess, and all the gods, out of affection.
The sins of those men who undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords with this very purpose perish quickly, like dry leaves in a strong wind.
Delight in serving that field never arises even for those evil-minded men who dwell in its vicinity.
O King, it is only through great merit that men develop a desire to go to that sacred field; it can never happen otherwise.
But those creatures, whether stationary or moving, O King, who die there by force, shall immediately attain eternal heaven.
Even by remembering it, a human being is liberated from all sins;
it is the most excellent of sacred fields, the abode of all holy fords.
Having bathed in these sacred fords and constantly worshipping Sadāśiva,
certain sages who desired spiritual perfection resided there.
Those who are completely freed from desire and anger, and who dwell there free from envy,
indeed attain that perfection in no time at all.
Those who are devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, who are peaceful, free from deceit, and celibate—
they who dwell there shall indeed attain their desired perfection.

O King, acts such as giving gifts, performing fire-sacrifices, reciting prayers, and the worship of ancestors, gods, and the twice-born performed there yield fruit ten million times greater than when done elsewhere.
When that most sacred field was submerged in the waters of the ocean,
the sages dwelling there remained endowed with great ascetic power.
Having consulted with one another, they all ascended Sahya, the best of mountains, for the sake of a dwelling, and took up residence there.
They set out to go to Rāma, who was performing austerities on Mount Indrādra.
The king said:
"When the waters of the ocean had been drunk by Agastya, [the princes] were surrounded on all sides by the sons of kings."
When the field has been dug and cast down below, along with its sacred fords, hermitages, and groves,
as well as upon other such portions of land such as cities, villages, mines, and so forth.
O best of sages, when those regions situated along the shores of the ocean had been destroyed, what did the people who lived there do?
O Brahman, tell me this: how long did they dwell right there, or having set out from there, how much time passed until the ocean was filled, and by what means did it happen?
Jaimini said:
"When the marshy regions have been destroyed by the evil-minded ones..."
All the people residing there departed hither and thither;
however, some inhabitants of that field remained right there, dwelling in great hardship.
At that very time, O King, there was on earth a son of Aṃśumat,
a righteous soul renowned as Dilīpa.
Having duly consecrated him in the kingdom and having fully enjoyed his pleasures, King Aṃśumat,
the wise one, went to the forest with a mind resolved upon asceticism.
Then the illustrious Dilīpa, having conquered all his enemies, ruled this entire earth with righteousness.
He had a son named Bhagīratha, world-renowned,
skilled in all matters of dharma and worldly affairs, illustrious, and of immeasurable valor.
Having consecrated him in the kingdom, King Dilīpa also departed for the forest;
and he, in turn, protected the earth, which was thoroughly cleared of all thorns.
He rejoiced in various enjoyments like the lord of the gods in heaven;
that lord of the earth heard [the accounts] of his own former ancestors.
Having heard from his father that all those struck by the *brahmadaṇḍa* suffer a terrible fall into hell arising from the wrath of the Brahmins, he was deeply distressed.
He attained supreme world-weariness regarding his kingdom, kinsmen, and enjoyments;
having entrusted the kingdom to his chief minister, he went to the forest for asceticism.
Desiring to lead his ancestors to heaven, that best of kings first approached the Lotus-born One with great austerity for the sake of long life.
Therefore, having propitiated him, he obtained his own desired [boon] for as long as his life lasted;
thereafter, O great king, having propitiated and gratified Gaṅgā, he [attained his goal].
She chose as her boon the descent from heaven to the earth;
thereafter, she propitiated Śiva with ascetic penance in order to bear him upon her head.
And he, who is affectionate toward his devotees, granted that boon to him;
then, from the summit of Mount Meru, he caused the Gaṅgā to fall from his own head.
The Lord of the worlds seized her, who was performing the act of grasping;
having reached his head, she flowed forth with great velocity.
She dissolved into that bright, exceedingly deep circle of matted hair on the head of the Lord Śambhu, merging like a handful of water.
Having observed that, he again propitiated Hara for her release;
and by the grace of Śarva, he regained her once she had returned to the earth.
She was led toward that very direction where the oceans had been consumed by fire;
following the king along the path of the royal seer as he performed the sacrifice.
It flooded that entire sacrificial enclosure on all sides;
and that royal sage became enraged because of her throughout the whole sacrificial ground.
Like a child drinking a mouthful of water, Magne drank that [teaching] entirely;
then, remaining unwearied, he served him for a hundred years.
Therefore, the king obtained Gaṅgā from that great-souled one when he was pleased;
for she had dwelt within him for a very long time and issued forth from his matted locks.
Consequently, her name became celebrated on earth as Jāhnavī;
having followed Bhagīratha, she [delivered] all of his ancestors without exception.
The celestial river sprinkled his own waters upon the bones and ashes;
then, as soon as the bones and ashes were sprinkled with that water, at that very moment—
All the Sāgaras, their sins destroyed, went from hell to heaven;
thus that great river, having led all the Sāgaras to heaven, [attained its goal].
Proceeding swiftly by that very same path toward the eastern ocean, the army—
divided into four divisions— went forth in the four directions from the head of the wave.
And due to its fourfold division, it came to have four names:
Sītā, Alakanandā, Sucakṣus, and Bhadravatī.
The four oceans, though long dried up after their waters were drunk by Agastya,
became full once again through the waters of the Gaṅgā.
But when the eastern ocean was further increased by the other seas,
many regions situated near it became submerged.
O King, the fields situated all around the vicinity of the ocean were likewise deserted,
as the people dwelling there had fled hither and thither.
And that sacred field which was previously described to you as Gokarṇa has gone to its disappearance in the ocean because it was swallowed up by the waves.
Then, O King, all those inhabitants of that place, desiring his rescue and wishing to see Bhṛguśārdūla on Mount Sahya, set out.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Bringing of the Gaṅgā," in the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Jaimini said:
Then the sages, beginning with Śuṣka and Sumitra, who were firm in their celebrated vows, [spoke].
Desirous of seeing Rāma, they went toward Mount Mahendra.
Having traversed very many countries, forests, and likewise rivers,
those bulls among sages reached the best of mountains in due course.
Having ascended it slowly, he beheld the renowned circle of hermitages belonging to him,
an auspicious place situated in the midst of the penance grove, abounding in peaceful and non-cruel creatures.
It was enchanting with groves of trees rich in fruits and flowers of every season;
it possessed incomparable, glossy shade and a pleasant breeze fragrant with its own natural scent.
Having reached that hermitage, which resounded with the chanting of the Vedas,
they entered it with joyful minds, proceeding according to seniority.
Those whose wealth was their asceticism beheld him seated comfortably in the Brahma-posture upon a soft black antelope skin, peaceful and surrounded by his disciples.
Like the fire of time having previously consumed the three worlds by its own will,
he appeared like an embodied being engaged in ascetic penance for the sake of quelling that very defect.
Having gathered together, those who were endowed with humility and proper conduct paid homage to the great sage of profound silence, their necks bowed in devotion.
Then, seeing that the sages had arrived, the scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage duly honored them with respectful offerings of water for the hands and feet and other rites.

Then that hundred of brothers belonging to that righteous, high-souled one,
being struck by iron arrows, fled in fear toward the various quarters.
O best of the twice-born, as those kṣatriyas fled, overcome by fear of them, their lineage became very extensive in various places.
Renowned in all directions as the Śāryātas, they were righteous;
indeed, everything that was bold became the boldness of Dhṛṣṭa, for he was fierce in battle.
That assembly consisted of three thousand high-souled Kṣatriyas; and the heir of Nabhaga was the powerful one named Nābhāga.
Ambarīṣa was the son of Nābhāgi, and Virūpa was his son;
Pṛṣadaśva was the son of Virūpa, and Rathītara was his son.
These, born of the Kṣatriya lineage, are indeed remembered as belonging to the Aṅgirasas;
they are the foremost among the Rathītaras, twice-born men endowed with the status of the field.
As Manu was sneezing, Ikṣvāku first emerged;
that Ikṣvāku had a hundred sons who were exceedingly skillful.
Among them, Vikukṣi was the eldest; Nimī and Daṇḍa were the other two.
He had fifty sons, headed by Śakuni.
The protectors of the land of Uttarāpatha are forty-eight kings, and likewise in the southern direction there are [the same number].
And Virāṭa and the others were appointed as protectors of the southern region;
then, at the Aṣṭakā festival, Ikṣvāku indeed bestowed the kingdom upon Vikukṣi.
The king said:
"O mighty one, having slain deer, bring meat for the śrāddha;
my śrāddha must indeed be performed on the Aṣṭakā days, of this there is no doubt."
At the command of that wise man, he went out on a hunt;
having slain thousands of deer, the valiant one became exhausted.
While Vikukṣi was out hunting, he ate a hare there; however, when Vikukṣi returned with his great army and the meat, [he found it gone].
He urged Vasiṣṭha, saying, "Let the meat be sprinkled [with water].
Having been thus urged by the king, he replied, "So be it," and that [meat] was presented according to the prescribed ritual.
Seeing that the meat had been spoiled, he became angry and said to the king:
"O King, this meat has been ruined by your son."
"O one of great splendor, meat is certainly not defiled by the eating of a hare;
O sinless one, it was previously eaten by that evil-minded man out of a lack of mindfulness."
"Therefore, O best of kings, this meat is unfit for the ancestors.
Then Ikṣvāku, becoming enraged, spoke thus to Vikukṣi:
"Appointed by me for the ancestral rites, you went out hunting;
yet today, O pitiless one, you have eaten a hare in the forest."
"Therefore, I renounce you; go according to your own karma.
Thus was the son abandoned by Ikṣvāku at the word of Vasiṣṭha.
When that Ikṣvāku had passed away, Śaśāda,
whose nature was supremely righteous, obtained this earth and became the sovereign of Ayodhyā.
Urged by Vasiṣṭha, he indeed ruled that kingdom;
yet, filled with that very sin, the lord of the earth remained in the state of kingship.
