The heir of Śaśāda was the heroic Kakutstha;
in ancient times, Kakutstha was born from Indra when he had taken the form of a bull.
In the former battle with Āḍibaka, Kakutstha was remembered by him; Anenas was remembered by Kakutstha, and Pṛthu was remembered by Anenas.
Dṛṣadaśva was the son of Pṛthu; from him came the heroic Andhra.
From Andhra came Yuvanāśva, and Śāvasta was his son.
From him was born King Śrāvastaka, by whom Śrāvastī was founded;
the heir of Śrāvastaka was the highly illustrious Bṛhadaśva.
The son of Bṛhadaśva was known as Kuvalāśva,
who, through the slaying of Dhundhu, attained the status of King Dhundhumāra.
The sages said:
"O one of great wisdom, we wish to hear in detail the slaying of Dhundhu,
and for what purpose Kuvalāśva attained the name Dhundhumāra."
Sūta said:
Kuvalāśva had twenty-one thousand sons;
they were all proficient in the sciences, powerful, and difficult to overcome.
All were righteous, performers of sacrifices, and givers of abundant sacrificial fees;
[they had as their son] the highly heroic and supremely virtuous Śūra, Kuvalāśva.
For Bṛhadaśva, the lord of men, consecrated him in that kingdom;
having transferred his royal fortune to his son, the king entered the forest.
But the brahmin seer Uttaṅka restrained the great king Bṛhadaśva, who was a hero and supremely righteous, as he was about to depart.
Uttaṅka said:
"O King, you ought to perform that protection which must be done;
for even Indra himself, O ruler of the earth, is not able to practice penance free from anxiety."
O King, near my hermitage and indeed all around Meru,
there stands an ocean filled with sand.
Invulnerable to the gods, possessing a massive body and great strength,
that great being remained there within the earth, hidden beneath the sands.
The son of the Rākṣasa Madhu, a great Asura named Dhundhu,
lies performing a terrible penance for the destruction of the worlds.
At the end of each year, he releases a breath;
whenever that happens, the earth, together with its forests, trembles there.
By the wind of his breath, a great cloud of dust is raised,
obscuring the path of the sun for seven days, and the earth trembles.
O King, because it was accompanied by sparks, flames, and smoke, and was exceedingly terrible, I am unable to remain in my own hermitage there.
Restrain him, O mighty-armed one, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
he will augment your exceedingly great splendor with his own splendor.
"O Lord of the Earth, let the worlds be at peace today once that god has been slain; for you alone are capable of his destruction."
"O sinless one, a boon was granted to me by Viṣṇu in the past,
for Dhundhu is of great heroism and cannot be subdued by one of little splendor."
For his prowess is truly immense, difficult even for the gods to overcome, and cannot be consumed by the protectors of the earth even in a hundred years.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Uttaṅka,
the royal sage gave Kuvalāśva to him for the purpose of warding off Dhundhu.
"O Blessed One, I have laid down my weapons; however, this son of mine, O best of the twice-born, will become Dhundhumāra, there is no doubt."
Having instructed his son Dhundhumāra, who was steadfast and unwavering,
he, whose vows were celebrated, departed for the forest for the sake of asceticism.
But the righteous King Kuvalāśva, abiding by the word of his father,
[departed] together with twenty-one thousand sons.
Accompanied by Uttaṅka, he set out to subdue that Dhundhu;
then the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu entered into him with his own splendor.
At the command of Uttaṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
when that invincible one had departed, a great sound arose in heaven.
"From this day forward, this king shall be Dhundhumāra";
and the gods, being well-pleased, showered him with divine flowers.
And then the divine drums resounded loudly;
that tiger among men, the valiant one, having gone there together with his sons, [beheld him].
He caused an inexhaustible ocean filled with sand to be dug;
while his sons were digging it, he was then hidden beneath the sand.
There, Dhundhu, having taken his stand in the western direction,
became enraged and, as if overturning the worlds, [consumed them] with the fire born from his mouth.
Like the great ocean at the rising of the moon, that best of asuras forcefully emitted a vast torrent of water, turbulent with waves and streams.
His sons were consumed by fire, yet three remained in the battle;
then that exceedingly powerful king [confronted] that mighty Rākṣasa.
The king of great splendor encountered Dhundhu, the destroyer of his kinsmen;
O child, that lord of men [withstood] even his water-based force.
By means of yoga, the yogi extinguished the fire with water,
forcefully casting away the massive-bodied water-demon who was discharging it.
Having accomplished his task, the lord of men showed himself to Uttaṅka;
and Uttaṅka bestowed a boon upon that high-souled king.
May there be inexhaustible wealth for those who give, may they never be oppressed by enemies,
may they have constant delight in dharma, and likewise may there be an imperishable residence in heaven.
And for his sons who were slain by the Rākṣasa in heaven, he secured imperishable worlds.
Of his sons, three remained; the eldest is called Dṛḍhāśva.
Bhadrāśva and Kapilāśva are recorded as his two younger sons;
Dhaindhumāri and Dṛḍhāśva were his [other] sons, and Haryaśva was his offspring.
Haryaśva’s son was Nikuṃbha, who was always devoted to the duties of a kṣatriya;
Nikuṃbha’s son was Saṃhatāśva, who was skilled in battle.
Kṛśāśva and Akṛtāśva were both sons of Saṃhatāśva;
his wife was Haimavatī, and Satī was the mother of Dṛṣadvatī.
He was renowned throughout the three worlds, and his son was Prasenajit;
the son of Yuvanāśva was famous in the three worlds.
His wife was Gaurī, exceedingly virtuous and devoted to her husband;
yet, having been accused by her husband, she was transformed into the river Bāhudā.
Her son was Gaurika, who became a universal monarch (cakravartin);
indeed, Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, was a king who conquered the three worlds.
Regarding this, the twice-born reciters of the Purāṇas cite this verse:
"As long as the sun rises, and as long as it sets..."
All that is called the domain of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva;
his wife was Caitrarathī, the daughter of Śaśabindu.
She was a virtuous woman named Bindumatī, peerless in beauty upon the earth;
she was devoted to her husband and the eldest of ten thousand brothers.
In her, the lord Māndhātṛ begot three sons:
Purukutsa, Ambarīṣa, and the renowned Mucukunda.
The heir of Ambarīṣa is remembered as another Yuvanāśva;
he was born of Narmadā, and Saṃbhūta was his son.
The son born of Saṃbhūta was the powerful Aṅgāraṇya,
by whom Rāvaṇa was slain and the three worlds were conquered in ancient times.
From him was born Dṛśya, the son of Naraṇya; and Haryaśva was his son. From Haryaśva, by Dṛṣadvatī, King Sumati was born.
His son was the righteous king named Tridhanvan;
and the learned and powerful Trayyāruṇi was the son of Tridhanvan.
He had a son, a prince named Satyavrata, who possessed great strength;
by him, having slain the gods, the wife of the King of Vidarbha was carried off.
When the mantras for taking the hand have been completed here,
[the union occurs] through desire, force, delusion, exultation, and power.
And by the power of a future event, that wise man committed that act; his father, Bhayyāruṇa, abandoned him who was thus joined with unrighteousness.
Uttering "Begone! many times, filled with rage, he spoke alone to his father, asking repeatedly, "Where indeed shall I go?"
Then his father said to him: "Live among the dog-cookers;
I no longer desire you as a son, O defiler of my lineage! (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.63.81)
Thus addressed, he departed from the city at the word of his lord;
and the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him.
But that wise and firm Satyavrata, having been abandoned by his father, lived near the dwellings of the dog-cookers; meanwhile, his father departed for the forest.
But in that region, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, did not rain for twelve full years because of that unrighteousness.
But having entrusted his wife to the care of Viśvāmitra in that region,
the great ascetic practiced intense penance on the shore of the ocean.
His wife, having tied her own biological middle son around the neck,
sold him for a hundred cows indeed, for the sake of maintaining the remaining sons.
Seeing that son of a great seer bound by the neck for the purpose of sale, that best of men, righteous in soul and firm in his vows, set him free.
Satyavrata, possessed of great intelligence,
provided for his maintenance both for the sake of pleasing Viśvāmitra and out of pure compassion.
O dear one, that great ascetic and eminent sage Kauśika, whose throat was bound, became known by the name Gālava after being liberated by that hero.
Abiding in discipline, he supported Viśvāmitra’s wife through his vow, devotion, compassion, and promise.
Having killed deer, boars, buffaloes, and aquatic creatures,
he then brought their meat to the vicinity of Viśvāmitra’s hermitage.
Having undertaken a twelve-year initiation and observed the vow of silence,
they lived according to their father's command after the king had retired to the forest.
Vasiṣṭha protected Ayodhyā, the kingdom, and likewise the inner apartments,
by means of his sacrificial rites and through his connection with righteousness.
But Satyavrata, due to his extreme youth and by the force of what was destined to happen,
maintained an even greater wrath toward Vasiṣṭha because of that very anger.
But at that time, the sage Vasiṣṭha did not restrain his own son, who had been abandoned by his father from the kingdom, for a certain reason.
"The completion of the mantras for taking the hand occurs at the seventh step;
since this is so, Satyavrata indeed carried her away at the seventh step."
"Knowing the dharmas, Vasiṣṭha does not desire the nine mantras here";
thus Satyavrata conceived anger toward Vasiṣṭha in his mind.
Out of regard for his virtues, the venerable Vasiṣṭha performed austerities;
however, Satyavrata did not perceive that he was indeed observing a silent vow.
But at that, the high-souled father felt supreme wrath;
because of that, Pākaśāsana did not send rain for twelve years.
"Therefore, by now carrying out that initiation which is so difficult to bear on earth,
this shall become the atonement for his own lineage, and she too shall be delivered."
Then the venerable Vasiṣṭha did not restrain him, who had been abandoned by his father; for the powerful sage thought, "I shall consecrate him later once [the current king] has perished."
But that powerful one, carrying out that initiation for twelve years,
found no meat available for the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
The prince beheld that cow who milks all desires;
yet, overcome by anger, delusion, exhaustion, and hunger, he [acted toward her].
Seeing that he had adopted the conduct of a bandit, the best of the strong killed him,
as well as his own flesh and the sons of Viśvāmitra.
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha then caused him to be fed and abandoned him;
and the venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke thus to that prince.
"O cruel one, I would indeed cast you down, removing your stake,
were it not for the fact that you, O lowest of men, possess three stakes."

"Through failing to satisfy your father, through the killing of your preceptor’s cow, and through the consumption of what has not been consecrated by sprinkling— these are your threefold transgressions."
Thus, having seen those three stakes, that great ascetic said to him, "Triśaṅku"; for that reason, he is remembered as Triśaṅku.
When Viśvāmitra had been provided with the maintenance of his wives,
he was then pleased and granted a boon to Triśaṅku.
Then, being invited to choose a boon, the prince requested a boon from the Guru;
he thus asked for this boon: "May I go to heaven in my physical body."
When that twelve-year period of fear due to drought had arisen,
the sage, having consecrated him, established him in his paternal kingdom.
While the deities and Vasiṣṭha were looking on, the powerful Kauśika then indeed caused him to ascend to heaven in his physical body.

While Vasiṣṭha looked on, that appeared like a marvel; regarding this, people learned in the Purāṇas cite this verse: BndP_2,63.113: "While Vasiṣṭha looked on, that appeared like a marvel; regarding this, people learned in the Purāṇas cite this verse."
By the grace of Viśvāmitra, the highly resplendent Triśaṅku shines in heaven together with the gods, through the favor of that wise one.
His wife, named Satyavatī, born of the Kaikeya lineage,
gave birth to a sinless prince named Hariścandra.
That king Hariścandra was known as Traiśaṅkava;
he was celebrated as a sovereign emperor who had performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
The son of Hariścandra was the powerful Rohita;
the son of Rohita was Harita, and the son of Harita is said to be Cañcu.
Vinaya and Sudeva were the two sons of Cañcu;
because he conquered the entire kṣatriya class, he is remembered as Vijaya.
His son was Ruruka, a king skilled in the matters of dharma and artha;
from Ruruka was born a son, Vṛka, and from him Bāhu was born.
The king, being addicted to vices, was expelled by the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas,
as well as by the Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and Pahlavas.
In that age when dharma was thus established, he was not excessively devoted to righteousness;
however, Sagara was born as the son of Bāhu, indeed together with poison (gara).
Having reached the hermitage of Bhṛgu and being protected by Aurva,
King Sagara obtained the Agneya weapon from the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Having gone to the earth, Acyuta slew the Tālajaṅghas along with the Haihayas; he also abolished the law of the Śakas and the Pahlavas.
The sages, who knew the dharma of those Kṣatriyas and the Pāradas, asked:
"How was that King Sagara born together with poison?"
For what reason did the indomitable king, filled with wrath, cast out the Śakas and other Kṣatriyas of great prowess from their duties appropriate to their lineage?
Sūta said:
It is said that in former times, the kingdom of that addicted Bāhu was seized by the Haihayas and the Tālajaṅghas, who had arrived together with the Śakas.
The Yavanas, the Pāradas, the Kāmbojas, the Pahlavas,
and the Haihayas— these five tribes then exerted their prowess for his sake.
Then, having renounced his kingdom and his home,
that righteous-souled Bahula entered the forest with his wife and practiced austerities.
Once, that king, being unprepared and having set out for the sake of water,
died along the way due to his old age and weakness.
His Yādava wife, however, followed behind him while pregnant;
her co-wife had administered poison to her with the intent of destroying the fetus.
Having prepared her husband’s funeral pyre, she ascended that fire;
but Aurva Bhārgava, seeing this, turned her back out of compassion.
In his hermitage, she then gave birth to a righteous son of mighty arms named Sagara, together with the poison.
Aurva, having performed for that high-souled one the birth-rites and other ceremonies,
taught him the Vedas and the Shastras, and then bestowed upon him the divine weapons.
Then the king resolved to utterly exterminate the Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, and Pahlavas as well.
Being struck down by the heroic and high-souled Sagara,
they all, seeking refuge, approached Vasiṣṭha for protection.
Having seen them thus addressed, the great sage Vasiṣṭha, with humility,
granted them safety and restrained Sagara.
Having heard his own promise and the words of his preceptor,
Sagara indeed destroyed their dharma and changed their appearance.
Having shaved half of the heads of the Śākas, he released them;
but for the Yavanas and likewise for the Kāmbojas, he shaved the entire head.
The Pāradas have their hair disheveled, and the Pahlavas wear beards;
by that Great-Souled One, they were rendered devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of the vaṣaṭ-call.
The Śakas, Yavanas, Kāmbojas, Pahlavas along with the Pāradas, the Kali-sparśas, Mahiṣikas, Dārvaścolas, and likewise the Khaśas; 2,63.140.
All those groups of Kṣatriyas had their dharma cast aside by the high-souled Sagara, following the earlier words of Vasiṣṭha.
That king, a conqueror by righteousness, having conquered this earth,
being initiated for the horse sacrifice, caused a horse to be grazed.
As he was driving it, that horse was carried away near the shore in the south-eastern ocean and made to enter the very earth.
The king had that entire region excavated by all his sons;
and as they were digging there, they reached a great ocean.
To that primordial Person, the divine Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Prajāpati,
Viṣṇu in the form of Kapila, the Swan, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord.
Having encountered his eye, that splendor was absorbed;
at that time, all his sons were consumed, with only four remaining.
Barhiketu, Suketu, as well as Dharmaratha,
and the heroic Pañcajana— these were the progenitors of that lord’s lineage.
And the Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa granted him boons:
the imperishability of his own lineage, as well as a hundred horse sacrifices.
The Lord granted his son Samudra an imperishable residence in heaven;
then Samudra, the lord of rivers, took the horse and paid him homage.
By that very deed of his, he indeed attained the state of being the ocean;
and the king, having recovered that horse of the Aśvamedha sacrifice from the sea, [returned].
O Lord, he performed a hundred horse-sacrifices again and again;
yet sixty thousand sons of his were consumed by his wrath.
The splendor of those high-souled ones entered Nārāyaṇa;
we have heard that there were sixty thousand sons.
The sages said:
"How were the sons of Sagara born, those of great strength and prowess, sixty thousand in number? Tell us by what rite they were produced."
Sūta said: Sagara had two wives whose sins were consumed by ascetic penance;
the elder was the daughter of Vidarbha, known by the name Keśinī.
But his younger wife was most virtuous,
the daughter of Ariṣṭanemi, peerless on earth in her beauty.
The Lord Aurva, propitiated by their ascetic penance, granted them a boon:
"One of you shall give birth to a desired son who will be the founder of a lineage."
"The second wife shall give birth to sixty thousand sons.
Having heard the words of the Sage, Keśinī [gave birth] to one son.
In the assembly of kings, the king accepted the excellent cause for the lineage;
likewise, Suparṇa’s sister [granted] sixty thousand sons.
The highly fortunate Sumati likewise conceived with great joy;
then, after some time had passed, the eldest wife gave birth to an eldest son.
The illustrious Sumati gave birth to a gourd-vessel containing the sons of Sagara, among whom was the one known as Asamañja, a descendant of Kakutstha.
Then, sixty thousand sons emerged from within the gourd;
she subsequently placed those embryos into jars filled with clarified butter.
The king provided that many nurses, one for each child, for their nourishment;
thereafter, after nine months, they emerged comfortably.
Those highly fortunate princes, who increased the joy of Sagara,
eventually retired to the forest after a long period of time.
The other son born to Keśinī from Sagara was known as Asamañja, whose banner bore the peacock; he was possessed of great strength.
Devoted to the welfare of the citizens, he was banished from the city by his father;
that son of Asamañja was the powerful one named Aṃśumat.
His son was the righteous-souled one renowned as Dilīpa;
from Dilīpa was born the heroic and highly resplendent Bhagīratha.
By him, the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, adorned with celestial chariots,
was indeed brought here from the Lord of the Gods and appointed as his daughter.
Regarding this, people well-versed in the Purāṇas cite this verse:
"Bhagīratha, however, brought down that Gaṅgā by means of his ritual acts."
Therefore, she is called Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā by those most knowledgeable in the lineage;
and Bhagīratha’s son was also known by the name Śruta.
Nābhāga was his heir, ever devoted to righteousness;
Ambarīṣa was his son, and from him Siṃdhudvīpa was born.
It is heard that in former times, those learned in the Purāṇas used to sing:
"The earth was protected by the two arms of Nābhāga and Ambarīṣa."
The earth became exceedingly free from the three types of suffering;
and the valiant Sindhudvīpa had a son named Ayutāyus.
The heir of Ayuta was the highly illustrious Ṛtuparṇa;
that powerful king was a friend of Nala and knew the secret heart of divine dice.
Two Nalas are renowned in the Purāṇas as being firm in their vows:
one was the son of Vīrasena, and the other was the upholder of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
R̥tuparṇa had a son named Sarvakāma, a lord of men;
his son was King Sudāsa, who became a friend of Indra.
The son of Sudāsa is declared to be the king named Saudāsa;
he is indeed renowned by the names Kalmāṣapāda and Mitrasaha.
But the highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha begot Aśmaka upon the wife of Kalmāṣapāda for the sake of increasing the Ikṣvāku lineage.
The legitimate son of Aśmaka was Mūlaka, and he became his [Aśmaka's] son;
regarding this King Mūlaka, they also cite this traditional account.
For out of fear of Rāma, that king lived surrounded by women;
the lord, desiring protection, was indeed without clothes, having the women as his armor.
The righteous King Śataratha is also remembered as the son of Mūlaka;
from that Śataratha was born the powerful King Iḍaviḍa.
The illustrious and powerful Kṛśaśarman was born as the son of Viśvasahasra through his wife Putrikā; he was indeed known as Aiḍaviḍa.
Dilīpa was his son, renowned as Khaṭvāṅga;
he, having come here from heaven and obtained life for but a moment, [acted thus].
Indeed, three worlds were attained through his intellect and truthfulness;
from him was born a long-armed son, Raghu.
From Aja was born that heroic son Raghu;
from him was born the king named Daśaratha, the delighter of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
The heroic Rāma, son of Daśaratha, who knows the dharma and is world-renowned,
as well as Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and the mighty Śatrughna.
Having slain Lavaṇa Mādhava and gone to that Madhuvana forest,
Śatrughna established the city of Mathurā there.
Subāhu and Śūrasena, both sons of Śatrughna,
protected the city of Mathurā along with those two princesses of Videha.
Both Aṅgada and Candraketu were the two sons of Lakṣmaṇa;
at the foot of the Himavat mountain lay their two prosperous provinces.
In the region described by Aṅgada, he shall cause a city to be built named Aṅgadā;
and for Candraketu, there shall be the famous and auspicious city named Candracakrā.
The two heroic sons of Bharata were Takṣa and Puṣkara;
the cities of those two high-souled ones were established in the region of Gāndhāra.
The city of Takṣaśilā was renowned in all directions by the name of Takṣa;
likewise, the city of Puṣkarāvatī was renowned after the heroic Puṣkara.
And regarding this, those people who are knowers of the Purāṇas sing a verse, which was composed by Rāma for the sake of truth, owing to the majesty of that wise one: BndP_2,63.192 //
Dark-complexioned, youthful, with red eyes, a radiant face, and measured speech; his arms reached down to his knees, he had a handsome countenance, lion-like shoulders, and mighty arms.
For ten thousand years Rāma ruled the kingdom;
there was the sound of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus, and that great, resonant roar.
Remaining in Janasthāna, he ensured that the affairs of the thirty gods were carried out, saying, "Let it be given; let it be enjoyed," so that there was no interruption in the kingdom.
The highly illustrious bull among men, seeking the trail of Sītā, slew that descendant of Pulastya who had previously committed an offense against him.
Endowed with courage and perfected in virtue, blazing with his own splendor,
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, shone more brightly than the sun and the fire.
In this way, two sons were born to that mighty-armed one, renowned as Kuśa and Lava; learn now of their two kingdoms.
Kuśa established the kingdom of Kośala and the city of Kuśasthalī;
he settled that delightful place upon the ridges of the Vindhya mountains.
The kingdom of Uttarākośala belonged to the high-souled Lava; Śrāvastī is world-renowned—now learn of the lineage of Kuśa.
Kuśa’s son was the righteous-souled Atithi, who was very fond of guests;
and from Atithi was born the famous king named Niṣadha.
Nala was the son of Niṣadha, and Nābhā was the son of Nala; Puṇḍarīka was the son of Nabhas, and Kṣemadhanvan is recorded as his successor.
The powerful King Devānīka was the son of Kṣemadhanvan;
the lord named Ahīnagu was the son of Devānīka.
Ahīnagotra’s heir was the highly illustrious Pāriyātra; Dalas was his son, and from him was born King Bala.
The righteous-souled Ulūka was the son of Bala;
his son was Vajranābha, and Śaṅkhaṇa was his offspring.
The learned son of Śaṅkhaṇa was known as Vyuṣitāśva;
and the son of Vyuṣitāśva was indeed King Viśvasaha.
Hiraṇyanābha was the son of Kauśalya and was most excellent;
he was indeed known as the disciple of Pauṣyañji among the Sāmans of the Easterners.
From him, the wise Yājñavalkya subsequently mastered yoga after having studied five hundred Saṃhitās.
Puṣpa was his son, a learned man, and Dhruvasandhi was his son;
Sudarśana was his son, and from Sudarśana came Agnivarma.
The son of Agnivarṇa was Śīghra, and the son of Śīghra is recorded as Maru;
Maru, having undertaken a yogic practice, settled in the village of Kalāpa.
In the nineteenth yuga, there was a lord who initiated the Kṣatra lineage;
his son was Prabhu, and Susandhi was the son of that Maru.
From Susandhi was born Marṣa, whose name was Sahasvat;
from Sahasvat was born a son, the king known as Viśrutavat.
The son of that renowned king was King Bṛhadbala;
these are remembered as the hundreds of kings who were the heirs of Ikṣvāku.
Those who were the foremost in that lineage have been proclaimed here according to their preeminence;
one who recites this creation of the radiant Āditya Vivasvat correctly [attains these benefits].
He attains union with Manu Vaivasvata,
the god who bestows progeny and the nourisher of living beings.
Free from sin and free from passion, he is born long-lived and imperishable.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Ikṣvāku Dynasty," in the Bhārgava-carita, within the third section (Upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as narrated by Vāyu. Sūta said: Now learn of the lineage of Nimi, the younger brother of Vikukṣi.
He who founded that city which was like the city of the gods.
It was known as Jayanta, situated near the hermitage of Gautama; in his lineage was indeed born Janaka, the best of kings.
O Great King, the son of the Ikṣvāku king of vast splendor was named Nimi, a man of pure nature who was honored by all beings.
By the curse of Vasiṣṭha, he became bodiless (videha);
his son, named Mithi, was born from three joints of his body.
While the fire-drill was being rubbed in the forest, the one of great renown appeared;
known by the name Mithi, he became Janaka because of his birth.
There was a king of great prowess named Mithi, from whom this city of Mithilā derived its name; his son was Janaka, and from Janaka came Udāvasu.
From Udāvasu was born that righteous Nandivardhana;
from Nandivardhana came the virtuous Śūra, whose name was Suketu.
The son of Suketu was the righteous and mighty Devarāta;
and the son of Devarāta was known as the righteous Bṛhaduktha.
The son of Bṛhaduktha was Mahāvīrya, who was powerful and majestic;
the son of Mahāvīrya was Dhṛtimat, and Sudhṛti was his offspring.
From Sudhṛti was born Dhṛṣṭaketu, a righteous soul and scorcher of foes;
and the son of Dhṛṣṭaketu was the renowned Haryaśva.
Maru was the son of Haryaśva; Maru’s son was Pratiṃbaka;
and the son of Pratiṃbaka is remembered as the righteous King Kīrttiratha.
The son of Kīrttiratha was known as Devamīḍha;
the son of Devamīḍha was Vibudha, and the son of Vibudha was Mahādhṛti.
The son of Mahādhṛti was the powerful King Kīrttirāta;
the learned son of Kīrttirāta was renowned as Mahāroma.
From Mahāromṇa was born the renowned Svarṇaromā;
and the son of Svarṇaromā was King Hrasvaromā.
The wise son of Hrasvaroman was known as Saridhvaja;
it was by that illustrious king, while ploughing, that the glorious Sītā was brought forth.
Rāma’s wife was high-minded, virtuous, firm in her vows, and self-restrained.
Vaiśampāyana said:
How was the illustrious Sītā produced while the earth was being ploughed? *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 2.64.16.
"For what purpose did the king plow the field in which [the horse] was born?
Sūta said:
"While the sacrificial fire-pit of the high-souled one was being plowed during the Aśvamedha sacrifice..."
Therefore, she arose through ritual and great effort;
and from Sīradhvaja was born the son of Maithila named Bhānumat.
His brother was Kuśadhvaja, the king who was the lord of Kāśī;
and the son of that Bhānumat was the majestic Pradyumna.
Muni was his son, and from him Ūrjavaha is remembered;
from Ūrjavaha came Sanadvāja, and Śakuni was his son.
Svāgata was the son of Śakuni; Suvarcas is recorded as his son.
Sutopa was his heir, and Suśruta was his offspring.
Suśruta’s son was Jaya; Jaya’s son was Vijaya;
Vijaya’s son was Kratu; and Kratu’s son is remembered as Sunaya.
From Sunaya was born Vītahavya; Vītahavya’s son was Dhṛti. From Dhṛti was born Bahulāśva, and Bahulāśva’s son was Kṛti.
In him the lineage of the high-souled Cānakas is established.
Thus have these Maithilas been described; now learn also of those of Soma.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Lineage of Nimi," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
O brahmins, the venerable sage Atri was born as the father of Soma;
there, Atri stood encompassed by his own splendor over all the worlds.
Performing only auspicious deeds through action, mind, and speech, he—
of great splendor— stood with arms upraised, as motionless as wood, a wall, or a stone.
We have heard that in ancient times a great ascetic performed a penance called Suduścara for three thousand divine years.
While that man of great intelligence remained there with his vital energy drawn upward and his eyes unblinking, his body indeed attained the state of the moon, O twice-born one.
As his self was thus purified, Soma ascended upwards;
from his two eyes, Soma flowed forth in ten streams, illuminating the quarters of the sky.
Then the ten goddesses, being delighted, received that embryo according to the prescribed rite;
having come together, they bore it, yet they were not able to sustain it individually.
Then, from those directions, that perfected embryo suddenly fell, illuminating the worlds— the cool-rayed moon, the creator of all things.
When those women were no longer able to bear that embryo,
then the cool-rayed moon fell to the earth along with the waters.
Beholding Soma falling, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
placed him upon his chariot out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
For we have heard that he, O brahmins, consisting of the Vedas, righteous in soul and true to his promise,
mounted a chariot yoked with a thousand horses.
When that son of Atri, who was the Supreme Self, had descended, the gods—
the seven renowned mind-born sons of Brahmā— offered praise.
Right there, the sons of Aṅgiras and likewise those of Bhṛgu [worshipped] with many Ṛg-verses, Yajus-formulas, and Atharvāṅgiras hymns.
Then, as he was being praised, the radiant splendor of Soma, being nourished,
sustained the three worlds in every way.
With that preeminent chariot, he of exceeding fame circumambulated the earth, bounded by the oceans,
twenty-one times.
That energy of his which increased and descended upon the earth became the medicinal herbs; moreover, the sky blazes with that very energy.
Through them, O best of the twice-born, the Lord Soma nourishes the worlds when their merit is exhausted, as well as the fourfold classes of beings; for he is indeed the sustainer of the universe.
Having gained splendor through those penances, praises, and his own deeds,
that illustrious one performed austerities for one thousand years.
Those goddesses who are golden-hued and sustain the world by their own power—
among them, Soma is renowned for his own deeds as the one who bestows joy.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Brahmā, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, bestowed upon him sovereignty over seeds,
medicinal herbs, brāhmaṇas, and the waters.
Thus consecrated in the great sovereignty as the king of kings, that majestic lord of monarchs,
radiant and the best among those who shine, indeed brought the worlds into being.
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave twenty-seven daughters of great vows to Indu; they are known as the Nakṣatras.
Having obtained that great kingdom, Soma, the lord of those who possess the *soma* plant,
commenced the Rājasūya sacrifice, for which the sacrificial fee consisted of a hundred thousand [cows].
Hiraṇyagarbha was the Udgātṛ priest, and Brahmā attained the office of Brahman;
there, the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa was the sovereign Sadasya.
He was surrounded by the primordial Brahman-sages, headed by Sanatkumāra.
O twice-born ones, we have heard that Soma gave the three worlds as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those foremost brahmin-sages and to the members of the assembly.
Sinī, Kuhū, Vapu, Puṣṭi, Prabhā, Vasu,
Kīrti, Dhṛti, and Lakṣmī— these nine goddesses attended upon him.
Having performed the final ablution unperturbed and being honored by all the gods and sages,
that lord of kings shone resplendently, illuminating the ten directions.
O Brahmins, having attained that sovereignty so difficult to obtain and praised by the sages, his mind strayed, being obscured by a lack of discipline and led astray by misconduct.
He suddenly carried off Bṛhaspati’s illustrious wife, named Tārā, disregarding all the sons of Aṅgiras.
Though he was entreated by the gods and likewise by the celestial sages,
he did not at that time release Tārā to Aṅgiras.
Uśanas, who was born of Aṅgiras, took his place at the rear;
for he, possessed of great splendor, had previously been the disciple of his father, Bṛhaspati.
Out of that affection, the Lord Rudra,
having taken up his Ājagava bow, became the protector of Bṛhaspati's flank.
By that high-souled one, the supreme weapon named Brahmaśiras was discharged against the gods, by which their glory was destroyed.
There, that great battle known as Tārakāmaya took place between the gods and the Dānavas, causing the destruction of the worlds.
Thereupon, those gods who remained there, known as the Tuṣitas,
went for refuge to Brahmā, the primordial god and the Grandfather.
Then, having restrained Uśanas, Rudra, and the eldest Śaṅkara,
the Grandfather himself approached and gave Tārā back to Aṅgiras.
And seeing that Tārā, whose face was like the lord of stars,
was pregnant, the brahmin Bṛhaspati said, "Relinquish the fetus immediately!"
"A fetus must not be held by you in my womb under any circumstances.
Then Tārā conceived a fetus that was like a blazing fire.
Then, as soon as he was born, the Blessed One eclipsed the splendor of the gods;
thereupon, fallen into doubt, the deities spoke to Tārā.
"Tell the truth: whose son are you—Soma's or Bṛhaspati's?
When she was thus being pressed by the gods, she said neither "yes" nor "no," whether it was right or wrong.
Then the prince, the greatest slayer of robbers, began to curse her;
Brahmā, having restrained him, then questioned Tārā regarding his doubt.
"Tell me the truth in this matter, O Tārā: whose son is this?
With palms joined in reverence, she spoke thus to the Lord Brahmā, the granter of boons.
Then Soma, the King and Lord of Creatures, smelled the head of his son, the great-souled Kumāra, the greatest slayer of Dasyus.
He gave the name Budha to that wise son;
and Budha rises in the sky at the end of the day.
Then that princess indeed gave birth to a son;
his son was the highly resplendent Purūravas, known as Aila.
Upon Urvaśī, six sons of great majesty were born to him;
there, he was forcibly overcome and rendered helpless by consumption.
Then Soma, overcome by consumption and with his orb diminished,
went for refuge to his father Atri.
The highly illustrious Atri performed the pacification of that sin for him;
freed from consumption, he blazed forth with splendor in every way.
O best of the twice-born, this birth of Soma has indeed been proclaimed;
O most excellent of the twice-born, now learn his lineage as it is being narrated.
Blessed, health-bestowing, life-prolonging, meritorious, and a purifier of sins—
by merely hearing this account of Saumya, one is liberated from all evils.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Account of the Births of Soma and Saumya," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu. // 65 //
Sūta said:
Budha was the son of Soma, and Purūravas was the son of Budha;
he was radiant, charitable by nature, a performer of sacrifices, and one who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
A proponent of Brahman, valiant, and invincible by enemies in battle,
he was a sovereign of the earth who maintained the sacred fire and performed sacrifices.
Truthful in speech, righteous in mind, beloved, and having ceased from sexual intercourse,
he became peerless in beauty throughout the three worlds.
The illustrious Urvaśī, casting aside her pride, chose him as her husband— he who was a proponent of Brahman, self-controlled, a knower of dharma, and a speaker of truth.
The valiant king lived with her for eighteen years, and then for seven, six, seven, eight, ten, and eight more.
In the delightful Caitraratha forest, likewise on the banks of the Mandākinī,
in the vast city of Alakā, and in the Nandana, the most excellent of groves.
At the foot of Gandhamādana, on the peak of Meru, that best of mountains, having reached the northern Kurus and the village of Kalāpa as well; BndP_2,66.7 //
In these preeminent forests frequented by the gods,
the king, honored by Urvaśī, took delight with supreme joy.
The sages said:
"How did the divine Gandharvī Urvaśī abandon that human king and come here? Tell us that, for it was a difficult deed."
Sūta said:
Overcome by the curse of Brahmā, she entered the human state;
for the sake of liberation from her own curse, she undertook a vow of religious observance.
Beholding her naked, having sexual intercourse against her will,
and two rams near her bed— she remains there for that long.
"O King, if this is your agreement, O ruler, and if your resolve remains firm for as long as time permits, then let food consist of nothing but ghee for one period of time."
"I shall dwell for that length of time; this is the agreement we have made. The king observed that entire agreement of hers.
Thus, deluded by that curse, she dwelt together with Saha for sixty-four years out of devotion to him.
When Urvaśī had reached the human world, the Gandharvas were filled with anxiety.
The Gandharvas said:
"O highly fortunate ones, consider how that excellent woman may [be recovered]."
Then, O gods, Urvaśī, the ornament of heaven, shall return;
thereafter, a Gandharva of great intelligence named Viśvāvasu will appear.
After she had taken away her two anklets, she departed for heaven;
then, wandering about in separation from her, he [sought] Urvaśī.
And he saw him at Kurukṣetra; though addressed by her, [he said], "Run after the Gandharvas," and he did so, and then they gave it to him.
By means of that fire-vessel, the great chariot-warrior king went to heaven;
for there was originally but one fire, which Aila divided into three.
Such was the power of King Aila, O best of the twice-born,
in that most holy land adorned by great seers.
That lord of the earth, possessed of great fame, ruled his kingdom at Prayāga, on the northern bank of the Yamunā, in the city of Pratiṣṭhāna.
He indeed had six sons, equal in splendor to Indra,
who were known in the world of the Gandharvas as Āyu, Dhīmat, and Amāvasu.
Viśvāvasu, Śrutāyu, and Ghṛtāyu were the sons of Uśij;
and when Amāvasu was born, Bhīma became king, and then Viśvacit.
The illustrious Bhīma had a son, King Kāñcanaprabha;
and the learned Suhotra was the son of Kāñcana, possessed of great strength.
Jahnu was born as the son of Suhotra from the womb of Keśinī;
thereafter, Gaṅgā returned to him during the performance of a vast sacrificial rite.
He settled in that place because he foresaw a future event,
having seen the sacrificial ground flooded on all sides by the Gaṅgā.
O best of the twice-born, King Sauhotri was also filled with rage;
then the celestial sages saw that the Gaṅgā had been drunk by the royal seer.
The highly fortunate Jahnu brought the daughter of Jāhnavi as his own daughter;
he took Kāverī, the granddaughter of Yuvanāśva, as his wife.
By the curse of Yuvanāśva, he fashioned from half of Gaṅgā the Kāverī,
the best of rivers, the blameless wife of Jahnu.
Jahnu begot a beloved and righteous son named Sunaha upon Kāverī; Ajaka was his son.
The heir of Ajaka was the highly illustrious Balākāśva;
his son was known as Mṛgaśīla, who was well-praised.
And Kuśa had four sons of divine splendor:
Kuśāmba, Kuśānābha, Amūrtarayas, and Vasu.
Kuśika, that best of kings, performed austerities seeking a son;
when a full thousand years had passed, Śatakratu appeared before him.
Seeing him engaged in such fierce asceticism, the thousand-eyed Purandara,
the eternal one himself, became capable of fathering a son for him.
Purandara himself conceived the thought of becoming his son;
thus the subduer of Paka, Kauśika, became the son named Gādhi.
The daughter of Purukutsa became his wife; from her was born to Gādhi a highly fortunate maiden in former times, auspicious by name, Satyavatī.
The lord Gādhi gave her to Ṛcīka, who was desirous of a son;
and her husband, the descendant of Bhṛgu, the joy of the Bhṛgus, was indeed delighted with her.
He prepared a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) for the sake of a son for both Gādhi and himself;
then, at that time, Ṛcīka of the Bhṛgu lineage spoke to his beloved wife there.
"This sacrificial porridge (caru) is to be consumed by you and by your auspicious mother;
from her shall be born a radiant son, a bull among kṣatriyas."
Invincible in battle by Kṣatriyas, the slayer of the bull among Kṣatriyas,
he shall have a son for you as well, O blessed lady— one who is steadfast and rich in ascetic merit.
"O best of the twice-born, this sacrificial oblation shall produce one whose nature is tranquility.
Having spoken thus to his wife, Ṛcīka, the descendant of Bhṛgu, [departed].
Constantly devoted to asceticism, Gādhi entered the forest;
then, accompanied by his wife, he went to the hermitage of Ṛcīka.
Then, on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, the lord of men took two portions of sacrificial charu from the sage in order to see his daughter, Styavatī.
With a joyful and undistracted mind, she reported her husband’s words to her mother;
the mother, however, by fate, gave her own sacrificial oblation to that daughter.
Out of ignorance, she prepared that sacrificial pap for herself;
then Satyavatī conceived a glorious embryo destined to bring about the end of the Kṣatriyas.
She, of terrible appearance, held [the fetus] with her blazing body;
then Ṛcīka, having seen her and having examined her through yoga, [acted].
Then that best of the twice-born said to his own wife of excellent complexion:
"O blessed lady, you have been deceived by your mother through the exchange of the sacrificial porridge."
"For you shall give birth to a son of cruel deeds and exceedingly terrible nature;
likewise, O Mother, such a one rich in asceticism shall be born."
"For the entire universe has been offered there by me through my Brahmanic austerity.
Thus was the highly fortunate Satyavatī addressed by her husband at that time.
He propitiated his husband, saying, "May my son not become such a base Brahmin from you"; thus addressed, he spoke to the sage.
"O blessed lady, such a desire was not even conceived by me, nor by you;
yet a son of fierce deeds might arise for the sake of his father and mother."
Satyavatī, having been addressed with these words, spoke again as follows:
"O Sage, you could create even the worlds if you so desired; how much more so a son?"
"O you of noble vows, it behoves you to grant me a son for my husband who is composed in tranquility and upright;
indeed, may I have a grandson of such a nature as this."
"O best of the twice-born, if it is truly impossible to act otherwise,
then he granted her grace through the power of her asceticism."
"O woman of excellent complexion, there is no distinction for me between a son and a grandson;
O auspicious lady, it shall be exactly as you have spoken."
Therefore, Satyavatī gave birth to a son of the Bhṛgu lineage,
Jamadagni, who was devoted to austerity, self-controlled, and composed in spirit.
In ancient times, due to a reversal of the sacrificial offerings (caru) between the rites of Rudra and Viṣṇu performed by Bhṛgu,
Jamadagni was born from the Vaiṣṇava fire.
Having obtained Viśvāmitra as his heir, Gādhi, the descendant of Kuśika, attained equality with the Brahman-sages and was honored by Brahmā.
For she is indeed Satyavatī, meritorious and devoted to the vow of truth;
she is celebrated as Kauśikī, and thus this great river has come into being.
The highly fortunate Kauśikī, the best of rivers, flows nearby;
there lived a king named Reṇuka, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage.
His highly fortunate daughter was named Kamalī Reṇukā;
and through austerity, fortitude, and meditative concentration, [he begot] upon Kamalī Reṇukā—
Ārcīka begot Jamadagni, who was exceedingly formidable,
the foremost among those who have reached the end of all sciences, and one who had mastered the science of archery.
Thus was the high-minded Rāma, the slayer of kṣatriyas and like a blazing fire, born to Satyavatī by Aurva’s son Ṛcīka.
Jamadagni, the best among the knowers of Brahman, was born from the power of asceticism;
his middle son was Śunaḥśepha, and his youngest was Śunaḥpuccha.
The righteous-souled Viśvāmitra was known by the name Viśvaratha;
through the grace of Bhṛgu, he was born as the enhancer of the Kauśika lineage.
The son of Viśvāmitra was the sage Śunaḥśepha;
he was indeed destined to serve as the sacrificial animal at the sacrifice of Hariścandra.
Śunaḥśepha was indeed given back to Viśvāmitra by the gods;
because he was given by the gods (devaiḥ), he therefore became Devarāta.
Śunaḥśepha is remembered as the eldest son of Viśvāmitra; Madhucchandas and the others, as well as Kṛtadeva, Dhruva, and Aṣṭaka, were also his sons.
Kacchapa and Pūraṇa were indeed the sons of Viśvāmitra;
the lineages of those high-souled Kauśikas are manifold.
The Pārthivas, Devarātas, Jājñavalkyas, Samarpaṇas, Uduṃbaras, Vātaḍyas, Talakāyanas, and Cāndravas; BndP_2,66.70.
The Lohiṇyas, the Reṇus, and likewise the Kāriṣavas are recorded; as are the Babhruvas, the Paṇins, and similarly the Dhyānajapyas.
The Śyāmāyanas, Hiraṇyākṣas, Sāṃkṛtas, and Gālavas are recorded; as well as the Devalas, Yāmadūtas, Śālaṅkāyanas, and Bāṣkalas.
The Lālāḍhyas and the Bādaras were others belonging to the wise Viśvāmitra; many Kauśikas are recorded as being those for whom marriage with other sages is prescribed.
The Kauśikas, the Sauśrutas, and likewise the others, the Saindhavāyanas,
are known as the sons of the holy Brahmarṣi Viśvāmitra,
the lord of Yoga; among them, Śunaḥśepha is remembered as the eldest.
And likewise, Aṣṭaka was the son of Viśvāmitra and Dṛṣadvatī;
Lauhi was the son of Aṣṭaka. Thus, the lineage of Jahnu has been described by me.
The sages said:
By what kind of dharma, or by austerity, or by sacred learning, does one attain this?
Brahminhood was attained by kings such as Viśvāmitra and others;
by whichever specific name [is used], it is through that very means that Kṣatriyas reached the status of Brahmins.

"I wish to know the distinction between austerity and likewise between giving. Being addressed thus, he then spoke these meaningful words: BndP_2,66.78: "I wish to know the distinction between austerity and likewise between giving. Being addressed thus, he then spoke these meaningful words.
One who desires righteousness but performs a sacrifice by summoning the best of the twice-born with wealth acquired through unjust means does not enjoy the fruit of that righteousness.
Having performed such intense recitation out of unrestrained greed for wealth, he who, filled with passion and delusion, gives it at the end merely for the sake of purification; ||| BndP_2,66.80 |||
Indeed, the gifts given by that wicked-souled person who, though engaged in religious practice, is harmful, become fruitless.
Thus, having acquired wealth through delusion,
the gift of a wicked-souled person who gives and sacrifices with a defiled mind does not endure.
He bestows wealth acquired through righteous means upon those worthy of it; and he performs sacrifices and gives gifts without regard for sensual desires.
He obtains the fruit of giving, and that gift results in happiness;
through giving one attains enjoyments, and through truth one goes to heaven.
By means of well-performed austerity, one stands supporting the worlds;
truth is superior to austerity, and therefore knowledge is remembered as the highest teacher.
For it is heard that there were twice-born ones who attained perfection through austerity and were joined with the status of Kṣatriyas:
Viśvāmitra, King Māndhātṛ, Saṃkṛti, and Kapi.
Kāśya, Purukutsa, Śala, the lord Gṛtsamada, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Ajamīḍha, and likewise Bhārgavyoma; // BndP_2,66.87 //
Kakṣīvat, Auśija, King Śiśira,
Rathāntara, Śaunaka, Viṣṇuvṛddha, and other kings likewise [performed sacrifices].
For these are remembered as being endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas, yet they attained the state of Ṛṣis through austerity;
all these royal seers (rājarṣis) have indeed reached great perfection.
Therefore, O wise ones, I shall now proclaim the lineage of the high-souled Āyu.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Genealogy of the Amāvasu Lineage," in the *Bhārgava-carita*, within the third section (*Uddhāta-pāda*) of the middle part of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The high-souled sons of Āyu were five in number, all possessed of great strength;
those kings were born of Prabhā, the daughter of Svarbhānu.
Nahuṣa was the first among them, and after him Kṣatravṛddha is remembered;
Rambha, Raji, and Anenas were renowned throughout the three worlds.
And the son of Kṣatravṛddha was the highly illustrious Sunahotra;
Sunahotra had three heirs who were supremely righteous.
Kāśa and Śala—these two—as well as the lord Gṛtsamada;
the son of Gṛtsamada was Śunaka, from whom Śaunaka descended.
O twice-born ones, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras were born in his lineage through their various deeds.
Śala’s son was Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and Śiśira was his son;
the Śaunakas and the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas are twice-born men endowed with the status of Kṣatriyas.
Kāśya was the son of King Kāśipa, and likewise Dīrghatapas was his son; Dhanva was the son of Dīrghatapas, and from him came the learned Dhanvantari.
At the conclusion of his ascetic penance, one of great splendor was born to the wise and aged king;
then the ṛṣis spoke these words again to Sūta.
The sages said:
"Who was the god Dhanvantari who took birth here among humans? We wish to know this; tell it to us, O scorcher of the foe."
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, let this birth of Dhanvantari be heard here;
he was born in ancient times at the shore of the ocean while the nectar was being churned.
Having arisen from the pitcher, he was surrounded on all sides by splendor;
seeing him whose task was instantly accomplished, Viṣṇu stood before him.
"You are born from the lotus," he said; therefore, he is remembered as Abja.
Abja spoke to that Viṣṇu: "O Lord, I am your son."
"O best of gods, grant me a portion and a place in your world.
Having been addressed thus, the Lord, seeing that it was true, spoke.
The distribution of sacrificial portions was indeed established by the Daityas and likewise by the gods;
and the ritual of the fire-oblation was prescribed according to the rules in the Vedas by the great seers.
"O descendant of Kadru, I am indeed unable to perform a fire sacrifice for you here;
for you are a charioteer [of limited scope], O God, and your mantra is not known, O Lord. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 2.67.15)
But in the second birth, you will attain renown in the world;
having attained the perfection endowed with *aṇimā* and the other powers, you will exist there.
O Lord, you shall attain divinity with this very body;
the twice-born shall sacrifice to you with four mantras and with clarified butter derived from cows.
Or rather, you shall indeed establish the science of Ayurveda once again;
for this matter was necessarily destined to occur, as it was foreseen of old by the Lotus-born One.
"Upon reaching the Dvāpara age, you will become [the Kali age], of this there is no doubt.
Having granted him that boon, Viṣṇu then vanished from that place.
When the second Dvāpara age arrived, that king of Kāśī, the son of Sunahotra,
as well as King Dīrghatapas, performed austerities, desiring a son.
Desiring to propitiate the lotus-born god for the sake of a son,
the king then invited Dhanvantari to choose a boon.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, may my son attain a state of liberation.
Having granted permission, saying "So be it," the Lord vanished on that very spot.
Then, in his house, the god Dhanvantari was born as the great king Kāśirāja, the destroyer of all diseases.
Having received Āyurveda, along with its medical practices, from Bharadvāja,
he divided it again into eight parts and imparted it to his disciples.
The son of Dhanvantari was also renowned as Ketumān;
then, from Ketumān, King Bhīmaratha was born.
The son of Bhīmaratha was born as the wise lord of subjects, renowned as Divodāsa; he became the sovereign of Vārāṇasī.
At that very time, however, a Rākṣasa named Kṣemaka settled the ancient city of Vārāṇasī, which had been deserted.
For that city had previously been cursed by the high-souled Nikumbha, who said again and again: "It shall indeed remain empty for a thousand years."
As soon as she had been cursed, Divodāsa, the lord of subjects,
established a beautiful city on the Gomatī at the edge of his territory.
The sages said:
For what reason did Nikuṃbha curse Vārāṇasī in the past—
that righteous-souled Nikuṃbha who cursed the field of the Siddhas?
Sūta said:
Having reached the city, the royal sage Divodāsa,
that king of great splendor, dwelt there in that prosperous place, O lord of men.
At that very time, however, Maheśvara,
having taken a wife and desiring to please the Goddess, was dwelling indeed in the presence of his father-in-law.
By the command of the God, the attendants, who possess universal forms and are rich in ascetic merit,
gratify Maheśvarī with the dress and appearance previously described.
Mahādeva rejoiced because of them, but Menā was not at all pleased;
she constantly felt loathing for both the god and the goddess.
"By my side is your husband Maheśvara, who is ill-behaved; he is utterly destitute here in every way. Alas, what misery! He truly has no shame. (BndP 2.67.35)
Mātrā, having been addressed thus with these words, could not endure it due to her feminine nature;
yet, smiling, the boon-granting goddess then approached the side of Hara.
With a dejected countenance, the goddess spoke to Mahādeva:
"I will not dwell here, O Lord; take me to your own abode."
Thus addressed, O best of the twice-born, Mahādeva surveyed all the worlds and chose a place upon the earth for his residence.
The great-splendored Maheśvara, having learned that Vārāṇasī—the field of spiritual perfection—had been settled as a city by Divodāsa, [proceeded there]. BndP_2,67.39.
Having summoned Gaṇeśa, who was standing by his side, he said to Kṣema:
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, go to the city and make Vārāṇasī desolate."
Then, by means of gentle methods, that exceedingly powerful king,
Nikumbha, went to the ancient city of Vārāṇasī.
In a dream, he revealed himself as a twice-born man named Maṅkaṇaka and said:
"O sinless one, I shall bring you prosperity; choose a place for my residence."
"Having fashioned an image in my likeness, install it at the edge of the city.
The twice-born man then had everything executed exactly as it had been seen in the dream.
Having formally requested permission from the king at the city gate according to the prescribed rites,
a great and constant worship is indeed performed.
With perfumes, incenses, garlands, and likewise with spectacles,
as well as with offerings of food, it became truly extraordinary.
Thus Gaṇeśvara is constantly worshipped there;
consequently, he bestows thousands of boons upon the Nāgas.
She granted sons, gold, long life, and likewise all desired objects;
she was the preeminent queen of the king, renowned by the name Suyaśas.
The virtuous queen, having been urged by the king, arrived for the sake of a son;
and after performing extensive worship, the queen requested a son.
Having come again and again on many occasions for the sake of his son,
Nikumbha nevertheless did not grant him the sons for a specific reason.
If the king were to become angry, then something would proceed from that;
however, after a long time, anger took possession of the king.
Indeed, this great being bestows hundreds of boons upon the citizens at his gate out of affection, yet he gives us nothing at all.
"He is constantly worshipped by my people within my very city;
moreover, he has been entreated many times by my queen for the sake of a son."
"And that ungrateful man, who eats his fill, does not give me my son;
therefore, he does not deserve honor from me in any way whatsoever."
"Therefore, I shall destroy the abode of that evil-minded one.
Having thus resolved, that wicked-souled sinner against the king [acted].
The evil-minded one destroyed that abode of Gaṇapati;
seeing his shrine shattered, the Lord cursed the king.
"O lord of men, because you have destroyed my dwelling without cause,
this city shall suddenly become empty."
Then, by that curse, Vārāṇasī became desolate;
having cursed the city, Nikumbha then led Mahādeva away.
The great god, high-minded, created an empty city as his own abode,
equal in divine splendor to that of the goddess.
The goddess indeed took delight there, amazed by her own sovereignty;
then, for the sake of the goddess's sport, the Lord Īśāna spoke these words.
"I shall certainly not leave this dwelling, for my home is indeed unrenounced.
Laughing, he then said to her: "My home is indeed unrenounced;
O Goddess, I will not go elsewhere after abandoning this place."
"O beautiful woman, sport with me here in this unsurpassed field;
therefore, it has indeed been declared by the Lord himself as 'Avimukta' (the Unforsaken)."
Thus Vārāṇasī was cursed, yet it is celebrated as Avimukta,
wherein dwells the god Bhava, who is saluted by all the gods.
Throughout the three ages, the righteous Maheśvara remains together with the Goddess;
however, in the Kali age, that city of the Great-Souled One vanishes from sight.
When that city had vanished, that city Vārāṇasī dwelt there once again; thus, having been cursed, it returned to its habitation.
Having slain the hundred sons of Bhadrasena, all of whom were excellent archers, King Divodāsa established [the city].
The kingdom of Bhadrasena was indeed seized by that powerful one;
Bhadrasena’s son, however, was named Durmada by name.
Out of compassion for his childhood, he was released by Divodāsa;
from Divodāsa and Ṛṣadvatī, the hero Pratardana was born.
O Great King, that boy, his son, struck him once again, desiring thereby to bring an end to their enmity.
Pratardana had two sons, the renowned Vatsa and Garga;
Vatsa’s son was Alarka, and Sannati was his son.
Regarding the royal sage Alarka, a verse was sung by the ancients:
"For sixty thousand and sixty hundred years..."
Indeed, Alarka, the best of the Kāśis, endowed with youth and beauty,
attained a supreme lifespan through the grace of Lopāmudrā.
At the end of the curse, the mighty-armed king, having slain the Rākṣasa Kṣemaka,
caused the beautiful city of Vārāṇasī to be inhabited once more.
The heir of Sannati was the righteous one named Sunītha;
the heir of Sunītha was the righteous one named Kṣaima.
Kṣema’s son was Ketumān, and his son was Suketu;
the son of Suketu was known as Dharmaketu.
The heir of Dharmaketu was the great chariot-warrior Satyaketu;
and the son of Satyaketu was the lord of subjects named Vibhu.
Suvibhu was the son of Vibhu, and from him Sukumāra is remembered;
the son of Sukumāra was the very righteous Dhṛṣṭaketu.
The heir of Dhṛṣṭaketu was Veṇuhotra, a lord of subjects;
and the son of Veṇuhotra was indeed the renowned Gārgya by name.
Gārgya’s lineage was Gargabhūmi, while that of the wise Vatsa was [the same];
their sons were both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, and they were all very righteous.
"Valiant and powerful, with prowess equal to that of lions—these are declared to be the Kāśyapas; now learn also of those of the Rajas [lineage]."
The son of Raji was the heroic Raji, who had five hundred sons on earth; they were renowned as the Rajeyas, a lion-like kshatriya clan that struck fear into its enemies.
Then, when a most terrible war between the gods and the asuras had broken out,
both the gods and the asuras spoke to the Grandfather.
"O Blessed One, who will be the victor in the battle between us two?
Tell us, O Lord of all worlds; we wish to hear it."
Brahmā said:
"Those for whose sake the lord Raji, having taken up his weapons, shall fight in battle—they will conquer the three worlds; of this there is no doubt."
Where there is royal splendor, there is prosperity; where there is prosperity, there is fortitude;
where there is fortitude, there is dharma; and where there is dharma, there is victory.
Then all those gods and dānavas, having heard of Raji’s victory,
approached him desiring victory themselves, praising that best of kings.
With joyful minds, all those kings—the gods and the dānavas—said to the king:
"For our victory, take up your excellent bow!"
Raji said:
"O Daityas, I shall conquer the gods led by Śakra;
I shall become the righteous Indra, and thereafter I will fight on the field of battle."
The Dānavas said:
"Prahlāda is our Indra; for his sake we fight for victory.
At this time, O King, you should remain here as directed by the gods."
Saying "So be it," even as he was being urged by the gods,
he was invited by the gods, saying, "Having conquered [them], you shall become Indra."

He, the self-controlled one of supreme glory, slew all the Dānavas who were otherwise invincible even to those who wield the thunderbolt, and he brought under his power the lost prosperity of the gods.
Having slain all the Dānavas, the lord Raji did not take [the earth];
then Śatakratu, together with the gods, spoke thus to Raji there.
Having said, "I am the son of Raji," he spoke these words once more:
"O King, you are Indra among all the gods; of this there is no doubt."
"O slayer of enemies, you shall attain fame as Indra, whose son I am.
Having heard Śakra’s words, he was deceived by that illusion.
"Be it so," the king, being well-pleased, said indeed to Śatakratu;
and when that lord of the earth, who resembled a god, had ascended to heaven.

those hundreds of sons of his [inherited] that very station of the Lord of Śacī.
They ascended in many ways to the heavenly world, Triviṣṭapa;
then, after a great deal of time had passed, the one of great strength [reappeared].
Śakra, his kingdom destroyed and his sacrificial portion lost, said to Bṛhaspati:
"Prepare for me a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) the size of a jujube fruit."
"O Brahmarṣi, may I be invigorated by that splendor so that I may endure;
for, O Brahman, I am emaciated and despondent, having been deprived of my kingdom and my throne."
