The sages said:
How was the maiden given by the high-souled Maruta to the king?
And what were the powers of the great-souled sons born of Maruta’s daughter?
Sūta said: O King, desiring food, that lord of creatures, possessed of great luster, used to consume the Marut-soma month after month for sixty years.
Thereupon, those Maruts, gratified by that Marutsoma,
being pleased, gave him inexhaustible food and all kinds of desirable articles.
The food he has eaten once does not diminish for a day and night,
even if it is being given away by the millions from the very rising of the sun.
From that wise Marīci and the daughter of Mitra-jyotis were born great beings who knew the Dharma and perceived liberation.
Having renounced the duties of household life and attained dispassion, they reached the state of asceticism here and departed for union with Brahman.
From Anenas was born the powerful Kṣatradharman;
from Kṣatradharman was born Pratipakṣa, who was a great ascetic.
And the son of Pratīpa was the famous Sṛñjaya;
Jaya was the son of Sṛñjaya, and Vijaya was born as his [Jaya’s] son.
Vijaya’s son was Jaya; his son is remembered as Haryaśvaka.
The son of Haryaśva was the powerful King Sahadeva.
The righteous-souled Sahadeva was renowned as Ahīna;
Ahīna’s son was Yatsena, and his son was Saṃkṛti.
Saṃkṛti, Dharmātman, Kṛtadharman, and Mahāyaśas— learn of these sons of Nahuṣa who were devoted to the duties of the kṣatriyas.
The heirs of Nahuṣa were six, possessing splendor equal to that of Indra:
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Āyāti, Viyati, and Kṛti.
Among them, Yati was indeed the eldest, and Yayāti was younger than him;
at that time, Yati obtained Gā, the daughter of Kakutstha, as his wife.
That ascetic, having established himself in liberation, became a sage who had become one with Brahman;
among those five, however, was Yayāti, the lord of the earth.
He obtained Devayānī, the daughter of Uśanas, as his wife,
as well as Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of the Asura Vṛṣaparvan.
Devayānī gave birth to Yadu and Turvasu, while Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, gave birth to Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.
He begot sons of great prowess, resembling the sons of gods;
Śakra, being pleased, gave him a most resplendent chariot.
With unattached, divine gold, two inexhaustible great quivers,
and yoked with horses swift as thought, he carried away the maiden.
With that preeminent chariot,
Yayāti— who was invincible in battle by gods, dānavas, and humans— continually conquered the earth.
He became the foremost charioteer among all the Paurava kings,
down to Janamejaya the Kaurava, who was born in the land of Sudeśa.
The chariot of King Parīkṣit, the grandson of Kuru, went to its destruction through the curse of the wise Gārgya.
For that evil-minded King Janamejaya, the lord of men, who smelled of iron, sought to harm the young son of Gārgya.
That royal sage, smelling of iron, ran hither and thither; abandoned by the people of the city and the countryside, he found no peace anywhere at all.
Then, tormented by sorrow, he could not find peace anywhere;
distressed, he then went for refuge to the sage Śaunaka.
That renowned sage Indrota, who was of noble intellect,
had Śaunaka engage Janamejaya [in sacrifice].
O best of the twice-born, through the horse sacrifice performed for the sake of purification,
that king’s iron-like odor vanished as he reached the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
That divine chariot was indeed given by the gratified Śakra to Vasu, the lord of Cedi; from him, Bṛhadratha obtained it.
Then, having slain Jarāsaṃdha, Bhīma, the joy of the Kauravas, affectionately presented that excellent chariot to Vāsudeva.
Having reached old age, that royal sage Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, spoke these words to his eldest and most excellent son, Yadu: Bṛhaddevatā 2.68.29.
O dear one, wrinkles and grey hairs have come upon me due to the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, yet I am not yet satiated with youth.
"O Yadu, take upon yourself my evil along with old age;
accept my old age. To him, Yadu replied: ||| BndP_2,68.31 |||
"For the alms I promised to the brahmin were not specifically defined; they must indeed be earned through exertion. Therefore, I will not accept your old age."
"In old age there are many defects concerning the consumption of food and drink;
therefore, O King, I am not willing to accept your old age."
With white hair and beard, dejected and made frail by old age,
his body covered in wrinkles, he was hopeless and of weak appearance.
Incapable of performing one's duties and humiliated in one's youth, I do not desire that old age, even when accompanied by those who wear the sacred thread.
"O King, you have many sons who are dearer to you than I;
O knower of dharma, let them accept him, or indeed choose another son."
Thus addressed by Yadu,
he, the best among speakers, filled with intense anger, spoke to his eldest son while censuring him.
"O evil-minded one, what other stage of life (āśrama) do you have, or what rule of dharma is yours, since you disregard me, who am your teacher? (Bṛhannārada Purāṇa 2.68.38)
Having spoken thus to Yadu, the king, filled with wrath, cursed him:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not yield your youth to me."
"Therefore, O fool Turvasu, your subjects shall not partake in the kingdom; accept this evil along with my old age."
Turvasu said:
"O father, I do not desire old age, which destroys the enjoyment of desires;
for in old age there are many defects regarding food and drink."
"Therefore, O King, I do not venture to accept your old age.
Yayāti said:
"Since you, though born from my own heart, do not grant me your youth."
Therefore, O Turvasu, your progeny shall undergo extinction among those who are confused regarding dharma and among men born in the inverse order.
O fool, you shall become a king among other flesh-eaters,
or among those addicted to the wives of their gurus, or even among those born of animal wombs;
O sinner, your dwelling shall be among the Mlecchas, of this there is no doubt.
Sūta said:
Having thus cursed his own son Turvasu, Yayāti—
He spoke these words to Druhyu, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā:
"Druhyu, you must take up this [duty] which destroys one's complexion and form."
"O Jarā, give me your own youth for a thousand years;
when those thousand years are complete, I shall restore your youth to you."
"I shall take back my own sin along with old age.
Druhyu said:
"An old man should not mount a chariot, nor a horse, nor should he enjoy women."
There is no happiness for him, nor does he desire old age because of that.
Yayāti said:
"O you who were born from my heart, yet do not grant me your own youth!"
Therefore, O Druhyu, your beloved desire shall never be fulfilled;
you will not always possess the power to move about upon a boat.
Though you are not a king, you shall dwell there eternally in the lineage of kings;
O Anu, hand over your sin along with old age.
"In this way, for a thousand years, I would live with your youth.
The aged man replied: "I am like a child, rendered powerless by old age; indeed, I am always impure due to my decrepitude."
He who does not offer oblations into the fire at the proper time—may I not desire such old age.
Yayāti said:
"You, who were born from my own heart, do not grant me your youth."
"This defect of old age has been described by you; therefore, you yourself will experience it, and your offspring, having reached youth, will perish before your very eyes."
"Or you too shall become like one who leaps into fire;
therefore, O Pūru, take upon yourself this evil along with my old age."
O dear one, old age, wrinkles, and gray hair have come upon me;
yet, due to the curse of Kāvya Uśanas, I am not yet satiated with youth.
For a certain time, I shall indeed enjoy the objects of your senses;
when a thousand years are complete, I will restore your youth to you.
"I shall indeed take my own sin upon myself along with old age.
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus, the son immediately replied to his father.
But as you think, O dear one, so shall I do;
and I shall take upon myself, O King, your evil along with your old age.
"Take my youth from me and enjoy sensual pleasures as you desire;
I shall remain concealed by old age, merely maintaining the appearance of your current age."
"Having given my youth to you, I shall practice according to the truth.
Yayāti said:
"O Pūru, I am pleased; may it be well with you. Since I am pleased, I grant this to you."
"The subjects in your kingdom shall have all their desires fulfilled.
Sūta said:
With Pūru’s consent, King Yayāti then [transferred] his own old age.
Then Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, out of respect for his age, transferred [his infirmity] from the palace to Bhārgava.
Filled with joy, that best of men moved through his own domains according to his desire, according to his energy, according to the season, and according to his pleasure.
That lord of kings, who was indeed never at variance with dharma,
gratified the gods with sacrifices according to his ability, and likewise the ancestors with śrāddha rites.
He gratified the best of the twice-born with desired gifts and cherished objects,
guests with food and drink, and the Vaiśyas with protection.
He should gratify the Śūdras with kindness, the Dasyus by means of restraint,
and all his subjects according to righteousness, each in their proper manner.
Yayāti protected [the earth] like another Indra in person;
that king, possessing the prowess of a lion, was young and devoted to the objects of the senses.
Without contradicting the Dharma, he lived in supreme happiness,
seeking after desires while perceiving their faults.
Accompanied by Viśvācī, he took delight in the Nandana grove of Vaibhrāja;
however, when the king saw that they were indeed increasing in number, then—
Having gone into the presence of Pūru, he indeed took back his own old age;
and having attained those desires, the king was both satisfied and weary.
The lord of men indeed remembered the time for a thousand years,
having calculated the divisions of time, both the *kalās* and the *kāṣṭhās*.
Then, considering the time to be complete, O subduer of enemies, he spoke to his son Pūru according to his pleasure, his energy, and the proper occasion.
"O son Pūru, I have enjoyed the objects of the senses during my youth;
I am pleased with you—blessings be upon you—take back your own youth."
"Accept this kingdom, for you are my beloved son.
Thus King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, took upon himself old age.
And Pūru regained his own youth once again;
meanwhile, the king desired to consecrate his youngest son, Pūru.
The social classes, headed by the Brāhmaṇas, spoke these words:
"O Lord, how [could you abandon] the grandson of Śukra and the son of Devayānī?"
If you bypass your eldest son Yadu and bestow the kingdom upon Pūru,
then Yadu is your eldest-born son, and after him was born Turvasu.
Druhyu was the son of Śarmiṣṭhā, and after him came Anu and Pūru.
How is it that, bypassing the elder sons, the youngest deserves the kingdom? We address you for your enlightenment; uphold the dharma.
Yayāti said: "Let all the social orders, with the Brāhmaṇas at their head, hear my words."
"Just as the kingdom must never be given by me to the eldest,
so too is a son praised who carries out the word of his mother and father, O hero."
My eldest son Yadu did not obey my command,
and he who acts contrary to his father's will is not considered a true son by the virtuous.
That son, who behaves toward his father and mother like a son,
has been treated with contempt by Yadu as well as by Turvasu.
Druhyu and Anu both showed me great contempt,
whereas Pūru followed my word and honored me especially.
My youngest heir, by whom my old age was assumed,
has fulfilled all my desires through his meritorious deeds, O Pūru.
And Śukra, Kāvya Uśanas himself, granted this boon:
"O high-minded one, he who follows you shall indeed be king."
The subjects said: "With your permission, let Pūru likewise be consecrated in the kingdom—
he who is a son endowed with virtues and always devoted to the welfare of his mother and father."
Even the youngest is a lord who deserves every blessing;
Pūru is worthy of this kingdom, for he is dear to you and does what is pleasing to you.
When the citizens and the people of the city, being well-pleased, said, "It is not possible to give an answer other than by granting Śukra's boon," Nahuṣa then [consented].
Then, having consecrated his own son Pūru upon the throne,
he established Turvasu in the southeastern quarter.
To the southwest, the king settled his eldest son, Yadu;
and to the west and the north, he settled both Druhyu and Anu.
Having conquered the earth together with its oceans and its seven islands,
King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, then divided it into five parts for his sons.
By those knowers of the Dharma, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its cities— is governed according to the law, each according to its respective region.
Having thus divided the earth among his sons, King Nāhuṣa,
whose royal glory had been transferred to his offspring, became filled with joy.
Having laid aside his bow and arrows, as well as his kingdom, upon his sons,
the king became filled with joy after entrusting the burden to his kinsmen.
In this regard, there is a verse formerly sung by the great king Yayāti,
by which one may withdraw all desires from oneself just as a tortoise draws in its limbs from every side.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter.
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist on earth—all that is not enough for even one person; seeing this, one is not deluded.
When one no longer harbors ill-will toward any living being through action,
thought, or speech, then one attains Brahman.
When one does not fear others, when others do not fear him,
and when he neither desires nor hates, then he attains Brahman.
That which is difficult for the foolish to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays,
and which is a disease that ends only with life— happiness belongs to him who renounces that craving.
The hair of an aging person decays; the teeth of an aging person decay;
but the hope for life and the hope for wealth do not decay even as one ages.
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine happiness there may be,
these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the inexhaustible happiness of Kṛṣṇa.
Having spoken thus, that royal sage, together with his wife, set out for the forest;
and having performed austerities there on Bhṛgutuṅga, he of great renown remained in that very place.
Having observed the vow of the sages, he attained heaven right there;
his five lineages are meritorious and honored by the celestial rishis.
By those [virtues] the entire earth is pervaded, as by the rays of the sun;
such a man shall become blessed, possessed of progeny, long-lived, and renowned.
O best of the twice-born, by reading or hearing the entire life-story of Yayāti, one attains [the highest goal].
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter in the third introductory section (upoddhāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim the lineage of Yadu, the eldest son of supreme splendor;
listen as I describe it to you in detail and in proper sequence.
Yadu had five sons who were like the offspring of gods:
Sahasrajit was the eldest, followed by Kroṣṭu, Nīla, Añjika, and Laghu.
The son of Sahasrajit was the illustrious king named Śatajit;
the sons of Śatajit were three renowned and most righteous men.
Haihaya, Haya, and likewise King Veṇuhaya;
the heir of Haihaya is known as Dharmanetra.
The son of Dharmanetra was Kunti, and his son was Saṃkṣeya;
the heir of Saṃkṣeya was the king named Mahiṣmān.
The powerful Bhadramena was the son of Mahiṣmat;
he was indeed previously mentioned as the king who ruled over Vārāṇasī.
The heir of Bhadra was the king named Durmada;
the son of Durmada was the wise and renowned Kanaka.
The heirs of Kanaka were four, world-renowned:
Kṛtavīrya, Kṛtāgni, and likewise Kṛtavarmā.
And Kṛtaujas was the fourth;
Arjuna, the son of Kṛtavīrya, was born with a thousand arms as a king who ruled over the seven continents.
For having performed most difficult austerities for ten thousand years, Kārtavīrya propitiated Datta, who was born of Atri.
To him, Datta granted four boons;
first, that one of immense splendor chose a thousand arms as his initial boon.
The sudden prevention of one who is contemplating unrighteousness,
and the conquest of the earth through righteousness and its protection likewise through righteousness alone.
"Having won many battles and slain thousands of enemies,
may my death occur while I am fighting in battle, in the midst of the fray."
Thus, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its cities,
and surrounded by the seven oceans— was conquered by him through his sovereign power and according to the prescribed rites.
As he fought by means of his illusory power, a thousand arms appeared for him through yoga, just like those of the Lord of Yoga himself.
O best of sages, it is heard that seven hundred sacrifices were performed according to the prescribed rites by that king across the seven continents.
All the sacrifices of that mighty-armed one of vast splendor were performed with golden altars and all with golden sacrificial posts.
They are adorned by all the highly fortunate gods dwelling in celestial chariots,
and are eternally graced by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Then the Gandharva Nārada sang a verse concerning that king,
having observed the life and majesty of that royal sage.
Verily, men shall not attain the state of Kārtavīrya through sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valor, or sacred learning.
On the seven continents, that king— armed with bow, sword, and quiver,
and mounted on his chariot along with his followers— is indeed seen through the power of yoga.
No property was lost, there was no affliction, and no delusion;
by the power of the great king, the subjects were protected according to the Dharma.
For eighty-five thousand years,
that lord of men became a sovereign wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), a master of all jewels.
He became this very Paśupāla and likewise Kṣetrapāla;
through his state of yoga, he became Arjuna and Parjanya by means of rain.
With his thousand arms, hardened by the striking of bowstrings,
he shines like the autumnal sun with its thousand rays.
For that lord of men, having conquered the assembly hall of Karkoṭaka with an army of elephants in Māhiṣmatī, established his city there.
That lotus-eyed one, while sporting and becoming weary of his ease, indeed brought about the rainy season with the very force of the ocean during the monsoon.
Agitated by him as he sports, the Narmadā— garlanded with wreaths of golden chains, her cry of distress like that of escaping waves— approaches in fear.
In ancient times, with his thousand arms, he plunged into the great ocean,
which had its tides overflowing at an untimely hour, agitated by the wind.
When the great ocean was agitated by his thousand arms,
the great asuras dwelling in the netherworld became motionless and hid themselves away.
The great poison of the fish submerged in the Mahāvīci hell was ground to powder;
unbearable waves of foam fell and were scattered, while the eddies tossed it about.
The king, agitating the ocean with his thousand arms,
made it resemble the Ocean of Milk when it was surrounded by the gods and asuras.
Seeing that most excellent of kings, who was as formidable as the churning of Mount Mandara for the sake of producing the nectar of immortality, they suddenly fled in fear.
The great serpents, their heads bowed down,
became motionless like plantain trees or reeds withered by the wind at the close of day.
Having strung his firm bow with five hundred arrows,
he forcibly bewildered Rāvaṇa, the lord of Laṅkā, along with his army.
Having conquered him and brought him under his control, he bound him in Māhiṣmatī;
then Pulastya went there and subdued both him and Arjuna.
Requested by Pulastya, the king released Paulastya;
the sound of the bowstring upon that thousand arms became like the roar of thunder.
Oh, how great was the prowess of that descendant of Bhṛgu in battle, who severed the head of him who was like a mass of clouds at the end of an eon, or like a thunderbolt bursting asunder!
Once, in the midst of battle, he was begged for food by the thirsty Agni, who saw his thousand arms resembling a grove of golden palm trees.
The lord of the people gave the seven islands as alms to the Fire-god,
including cities, cowherd settlements, villages, and towns in every direction.
Desirous of consuming him, the fire of variegated luster blazed within his arrows;
yet that highly illustrious one [remained] by the power of that lord of men.
He burned the mountains and forests of Kārtavīrya,
and indeed the entire empty hermitage of Varuṇa’s son.
That Haihaya, Citrabhānu,
who had obtained as his son in former times the most excellent and radiant Varuṇa, burned with the arrogance of his sacrificial rites.
That sage named Vasiṣṭha was also known as Āpava;
thereupon, the powerful Āpava, out of anger, cursed Arjuna.
"O Haihaya, because this forest has been abandoned by you,
another shall perform that difficult task for me."
The son of Kuntī named Arjuna shall become that king;
and Rāma, the most heroic among strikers, [shall give] Arjuna [the bow].
Having indeed severed his thousand arms and having violently crushed him with his might,
that ascetic and brahmin of great strength will slay him.
At that time, Rāma indeed became subject to death by the curse of that wise king,
for he himself had previously chosen that boon.
He had a hundred sons, five of whom were great chariot-warriors;
they were skilled in weapons, powerful, heroic, righteous, and illustrious.
Śūra, Śūrasena, Vṛṣāsya, and Vṛṣa himself—
Jayadhvaja, the founder of the lineage, was the lord of the people in Avanti.
The son of Jayadhvaja was the powerful Tālajaṅgha;
he had a hundred sons who were likewise known as the Tālajaṅghas.
Five clans of those high-souled Haihayas are renowned:
the Vītihotras, the Saṃjātas, the Bhojas, and likewise the Āvantyas.
The Tuṇḍikeras were valiant, as were the Tālajaṅghas;
and there was also a king named Ananta, the son of Vītihotra.
His son was Durjaya, the subduer of enemies;
indeed, that king possessed the quality of never losing his wealth.
By his power, the great king protected those subjects;
he would suffer no loss of wealth, and whatever was lost he would recover.
Whoever here recounts the birth of the wise Kārtavīrya,
his riches shall increase perpetually and his dharma shall flourish.
O Lord of the Earth, as one sacrifices and as one gives, so does one find [recompense] in heaven.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Birth of Kārtavīrya," in the *Bhārgavacarita* within the third *Upodghāta-pāda* of the middle section of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
"For what reason was the forest of the high-souled Āpava burnt?"
Tell that to us who ask, as it was accomplished through the prowess of Kārtavīrya.
We have heard that this royal sage was a protector of his subjects;
how, having been their protector, could he destroy the penance grove?
Sūta said:
From Sātvata, sons of great strength were born to Kauśalyā.
The divine Bhaji, the bull-like Devāvṛdh, and Andhaka were devoted to him.
And there was the renowned Mahābhoja, devoted to Brahman and true to his promise;
indeed, their four lineages—listen to them in detail.
To Bhajamāna were born two daughters, Sṛñjayī and Bāhyakā; the latter was the mother of Upavāhyaka. Sṛñjaya had two sons, and Bāhyakā bore them both.
His two wives, who were sisters, gave birth to many sons:
Nimloci, Kiṅkaṇa, Dhṛṣṭi, and Para-purañjaya.
From Bhajamāna, those sons of the outer Sṛñjaya lineage were born,
known by the names Ayutājit, Sahasrājit, and Śatājit.
They were born from their sister Bāhyakā as she was being enjoyed by them.
Among them, King Devāvṛdha performed supreme austerity, thinking, "May I have a son endowed with all virtues. (Bṛhaddevatā 2.71.6)
Having thus composed himself, he touched the waters of the Parṇāśā river.
And because of his bathing,
that best of rivers, owing to the king's auspiciousness, did what was pleasing to him.
Her limbs overwhelmed by anxiety, she then reached this conclusion:
"I do not know of that woman from whom such a son could have been born."
Indeed, he shall be endowed with all virtues, for he is King Devāvṛdha;
therefore, today I myself shall become his companion in religious observances.
The disposition that resided within his heart arose from her just as it had been described;
then she became a young maiden, yet remained entirely absorbed in thought.
He chose the king as his suitor, and that monarch desired her;
with a joyful mind, he conceived a radiant embryo within her.
Then, in her ninth month, that excellent river gave birth to a son endowed with all virtues; he was Babhru, and he was Devāvṛdha at that time.
In that lineage, the twice-born who are knowers of the Purāṇas indeed sing this verse,
praising the virtues of the high-souled Devāvṛdha.
Just as we hear him from afar, so do we behold him when near;
Babhru is the best among men, equal to Devāvṛdha among the gods.
Seventy-six thousand and sixty-five men attained immortality through Babhru Devāvṛdha as well.
A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, wise, devoted to the Brahmins, truthful in speech, and learned;
he was renowned, a great patron, and a mighty chariot-warrior among the Sātvatas.
His lineage was very great; those known on earth as the Bhojas were his descendants.
And Gāndhārī and Mādrī became his two spirited wives.
Gāndhārī gave birth to Sumitra, the delighter of his friends;
Sādrī bore a son named Yudhājit, and from him was born Mīḍhvāṃsa.
Anamitra and Śini were both excellent men;
Nighna was the son of Anamitra, and Nighna had two sons.
The illustrious Prasena and Satrājit were both his sons;
and Sūrya became a friend to that Satrājit, as dear to him as his own life.
Once, at the end of the night, that best of chariot-warriors went in his chariot to the river Āravī to draw up water from the bank for the sake of performing his morning rites.
As he was standing there worshipping the sun, the Lord Vivasvat stood before him,
his form clearly manifest, the all-pervading one endowed with a circle of radiance.
Then the king spoke to Vivasvat, who stood before him:
"O Lord of the luminaries, I behold you just as I see [the sun] in the sky."
And what indeed is the distinction between you, O Vivasvat, who are merely standing before me as a circle of light, and one who has approached through friendship?
Having heard this, the Blessed One then unfastened the Syamantaka jewel from his own neck and bound it upon the king.
Then the king beheld him in embodied form;
having seen him with joy, he conversed with him for a moment.
As Vivasvat was setting out once more, Satrajit addressed him:
"You are of the same color as fire, by whom the world perceives."
"Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to give this jewel to me.
To him, Bhāskara gave the jewel named Syamantaka.
Having fastened that [garland], the lord of the earth entered the city;
then, having caused the city to marvel, he proceeded to the inner apartments.
Out of affection, King Satrājit gave that supreme and divine jewel, the Syamantaka, to his brother Prasena.
There is a jewel named Syamantaka; in whatever kingdom it may reside, the rain-cloud pours forth according to desire, and likewise there is no fear of disease.
Govinda desired the Syamantaka jewel from Prasena;
however, although he was capable, he did not obtain it, nor did he take it by force.
Once, while adorned with that [jewel], Prasena went out hunting;
for the sake of the Syamantaka, he met a most terrible death at the hands of a lion.
Jāmbavān, the king of the bears, indeed slew that lion and,
taking the divine jewel, entered his own cave.
Then the elders of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, perceiving that deed of Kṛṣṇa as being motivated by greed for the jewel, suspected him alone.
Unable to endure that false accusation from them, the powerful Lord, the slayer of enemies, wandered through the forest.
But Prasena went out on a hunt; meanwhile, the city officials took up his tracks and reached the city.
Searching through the excellent mountain Ṛkṣavanta and the supreme mountain Vindhya, the high-minded one, becoming exhausted, beheld [it].
He did not find Prasena there, slain along with his horse, nor indeed the jewel;
then, near the body of Prasena, a lion appeared.
He was seen struck down by a bear; indicated by the tracks of the bear, the Yādava searched for the cave by following those footprints.
O twice-born ones, within a great cavern he heard a voice uttered by a woman intoxicated with joy; it was the nurse, who, having taken the infant son of Jāmbavat,
was saying, "Do not cry," while playing with a jewel.
The nurse said: "A lion killed Prasena; that lion was slain by Jāmbavān."
"O Sukumāra, Māra has indeed been seen; Syamantaka has been revealed, and that sound has been made clear. Having said this, he quickly entered his hole.
And he saw Prasena torn apart near the cave;
then the Blessed One entered the bear’s cave with ease.
The noble-minded Vāsudeva beheld Jāmbavān, the king of bears; he then fought with Jāmbavān inside the cave.
Govinda entered the cave on foot for twenty-one days;
and once Kṛṣṇa had entered the cave, Vasudeva and the others followed behind him.
Then, returning to Dvāravatī, they reported that Kṛṣṇa had been slain;
meanwhile, Vāsudeva, having conquered the mighty Jāmbavanta, [returned].
He obtained the maiden Jāmbavatī, the daughter of the king of bears who shared his name;
for Jāmbavān, overcome by the Blessed One’s splendor, had been forcibly seized [by him] for the sake of the jewel.
He quickly gave his daughter Jāmbavatī to Viṣvaksena,
and he took the Syamantaka jewel for the sake of purifying himself.
Having conciliated that king of the bears, he then emerged from the cave;
thus, having recovered the jewel, he purified himself by his own effort.
In the presence of Sāttvata, Madhusūdana gave the jewel-gem to Satrājit;
he then married Jāmbavatī, who was born again.
Therefore, Madhusūdana was purified from that false accusation;
and he who here removes this false accusation against Kṛṣṇa [is likewise purified].
He knew that false accusation would never touch him;
Satrajit had ten wives and ten thousand sons.
Among them, three were renowned: the eldest was Bhaṅgakāra, then Vīra, and Vātapati; the last was Tapasvin, who was very dear to many.
Then Vīramatī, the mother of Bhaṅgakāra,
gave birth to three daughters endowed with beauty and virtue.
Satyabhāmā, the most excellent of women, observant of vows and firm in her resolve, was likewise an ascetic; her father gave her to Kṛṣṇa.
And having heard that the jewel-gem Syamantaka had been taken by Śatadhanvan of the Bhoja clan, Kṛṣṇa did not seize it from Satrājit.
For at that time, Akrūra, seeking wealth, requested the blameless Satyabhāmā as well as the Syamantaka jewel.
Then, having killed Satrājit, the mighty Śatadhanvan took that jewel at night and gave it to Akrūra.
Then Akrūra, that bull among men, taking that jewel,
made a compact that it was not to be shown to anyone else.
"We shall advance against you who have assailed Kṛṣṇa;
my entire Dvārakā undoubtedly stands within my power. (Bhaviṣya Purāṇa 2.71.62)
When her father was dead, the illustrious Satyabhāmā, afflicted with grief,
mounted her chariot and departed for the city of Vāraṇāvata.
But Satyabhāmā, having reported that conduct of her husband Śatadhanvan the Bhoja to him,
stood by his side, afflicted with grief, and shed tears.
After performing the water-libation rites for the deceased Pāṇḍavas,
Hari appointed Sātyaki to attend to the welfare of his brothers.
Then, having arrived swiftly at Dvārakā, the glorious Madhusūdana spoke these words to his elder brother, the wielder of the plow:
Prasena was killed by a lion, and Satrājit by Śatadhanvan; the Syamantaka must be sought, for I am its rightful owner, O Lord.
"O mighty-armed one, ascend the chariot quickly; having slain the exceedingly powerful Bhoja, the Syamantaka jewel shall become common property for all of you."
Then, as the tumultuous battle between the Bhoja and Kṛṣṇa proceeded,
Śatadhanvan gazed toward Akrūra from every direction.
But having failed to seize Akrūra and Uddhava,
Hārdikya, though capable, did not come forward out of deceit, O tormentor of enemies.
Then, filled with fear, he again applied his mind to escaping from there;
he mentally traversed more than a hundred yojanas.
The divine mare of the Bhoja king, renowned by the name Hṛdayā and capable of traveling a hundred yojanas, was the one with which he fought Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing that increase of the chariot’s speed as it traversed the hundred-yojana path, Śatadhanvan became like the surging ocean.
Then, O twice-born ones, because of the horse's exhaustion and distress, its life-breaths ascended into the sky; thereupon Kṛṣṇa spoke to Rāma.
"Stay here, O mighty-armed one; I have seen the fault of the mare.
I shall go on foot and seize the Syamantaka jewel."
Then, having gone on foot from there, Acyuta, the supreme knower of weapons, indeed slew Śatadhanvan in the grove near Mithilā.
Having killed the mighty Bhoja, he did not see the Syamantaka;
and as he was returning, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) said to Kṛṣṇa, "Give me the jewel."
Then Kṛṣṇa said, "It does not exist," whereupon Rāma, filled with rage,
repeatedly replied to Janārdana with the exclamation, "Fie!"
"Because you are my brother, I forgive this; may it be well with you, I am departing.
I have no concern for Dvārakā, nor for you, nor for the Vṛṣṇis."
Then Rāma, the crusher of enemies, entered Mithilā,
having been honored by the King of Mithilā with all desired offerings.
At that very time, Babhru, the best among the wise,
performed all kinds of sacrifices without restraint.
For the sake of the Syamantaka jewel, the wise and high-minded son of Kāndinī entered into a consecration accompanied by armor for the purpose of protection.
These sacrifices of that high-souled one were known as the Akūras;
they all provided abundant food and sacrificial fees, and granted every desire.
Then King Duryodhana, the lord, having gone to Mithilā,
obtained divine instruction in the use of the mace from Balabhadra.
Then, having been propitiated by the great chariot-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas, Rāma was brought back to Dvārakā by the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
Then the powerful Akrūra,
that bull among men, having slain Śatrughna along with Bandhumat in battle, arrived together with the Andhakas.
In Narā, the daughter of Suyajña, were born two sons of Bhaṅgakāra, the best of men, who were renowned and possessed of great strength.
Bandhumat and Śakraghna were born as the foremost sons of Andhaka;
yet, upon the killing of Bhaṅgakāra, Kṛṣṇa was not pleased.
Then, fearing the dissension among his kinsmen, he looked upon him;
and when Akrūra had departed from there, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, ceased to rain.
Since the kingdom had been devastated in many ways by drought,
the Kukuras and Andhakas then sought to appease Akrūra.
Then, when the lord of charity had likewise reached Dvāravatī,
the thousand-eyed Indra rained down [water] into the belly of the ocean.
O best of sages, the illustrious Akrūra gave his sister, a maiden renowned for her virtue, to Vāsudeva out of affection.
Then, having discerned through his yogic power that the jewel was with Babhru, Janārdana Kṛṣṇa spoke to Akrūra in the midst of the assembly hall.
O Lord, that jewel, that most excellent gem which has come into your hands—give it to me, who am worthy of your honor; do not act with ignoble pride toward me.
When sixty years had passed, the resentment that arose within me grew deeply rooted;
having encountered it repeatedly, a great lapse of time then occurred.
Then, at the word of Kṛṣṇa, the high-minded Babhru delivered that jewel without any difficulty in the assembly of all the Sātvatas.
Then, O subduer of enemies, being pleased and joyful in heart, he gave back that jewel to Babhru, who had obtained it through his honesty, from Babhru’s own hand.
Having received the Syamantaka jewel from the hand of Kṛṣṇa and fastened it on,
the son of Gāndinī shone like the sun.
He who understands both this false accusation and even the highest purity knows that he shall never, under any circumstances, suffer from a false accusation.
From Anamitra, the youngest son of Vṛṣṇi, was born Śini;
Satyavān, endowed with truthfulness, was his [Śini’s] son, and Satyaka was his offspring.
Satyaki and Yuyudhana were his [sons], and Bhūti was his son;
Bhūti’s son was Yugandhara, who is celebrated as Bhautya.
To Māḍī was born a son, Yudhājit, whose son was Vṛṣṇi;
from Vṛṣṇi were born two sons, Śvaphalka and Citraka.
Wherever the righteous great king Śvaphalka resides,
there is no fear of disease, nor likewise any fear of drought.
O best of the twice-born, once it happened that Indra,
the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain for three years within the realm of the lordly King Āśīra.
There he caused Śvaphalka, who was highly honored, to dwell;
and because of Śvaphalka’s residence there, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, sent down rain.
Śvaphalka obtained as his wife the daughter of the King of Kāśī, named Gāndinī; for she used to give cows constantly to the Brahmins.
Indeed, while staying within her mother’s womb for many hundreds of years, she did not give birth; and as she remained thus in the womb, her father spoke to her.
"Be born quickly; may it be well with you; for what reason do you remain thus?
To him, that maiden dwelling within the womb spoke every day: "The cow. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 2.71.108)
"If you would grant this, then after three years I shall emerge from the womb.
"So be it," her father said to her, and he fulfilled her wish.
Her son is remembered as Akrūra, the son of Śvaphalka, who was a donor, a performer of sacrifices, a hero, learned in the scriptures, fond of guests, and one who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees.
Upamaṅgu, Maṅgu, Mṛdura, Cārimejaya,
Girirakṣas, Yakṣa, Śatrughna, and Arimardana.
Dharmavṛddha, Sukarman, and another named Gandhamāda;
Āvāha and Prativāha; and Vasudevā was their excellent wife.
From Akrūra, by the wife of Ugrasena, two sons who brought joy to their lineage were born:
Devavān and Upadeva, both resembling gods.
Citraka had sons, namely Pṛthu and Vipṛthu,
as well as Aśvagrīva, Aśvavāha, Supārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa.
Ariṣṭanemi, Aśvāsya, Suvārmā, and likewise Varmabhṛt;
Abhūmi and Bahubhūmi; and Śraviṣṭhā and Śravaṇā are the two women.
Satyakā, the daughter of Kāśi, obtained four sons:
Kukura, Bhajamāna, Śuci, and Kambalabarhiṣa.
Kukura’s son was Vṛṣṇi, and Vṛṣṇi’s son was Kapotaroman; his son, in turn, was Viloman.
He had a learned son named Andhaka, who was indeed a friend of Tuṃburu;
he is also known by another name, Candanodakadundubhi.
From him was born a son named Abhijit, and from him in turn was born Punarvasu;
that best of men performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son.
In the midst of that *atirātra* sacrifice, he was highly elevated from the middle of the *sadas* hall;
thereupon, the learned Punarvasu, a knower of dharma, a donor, and a performer of sacrifices, [emerged].
Then, it is said, a pair of children was born to that Abhijit;
they were Āhuka and Āhukī, both renowned as the best among the wise.
And regarding that Āhuka, they cite these verses here concerning his chariots,
which were equipped with seats, side-boards, and undercarriages, and were adorned with banners and protective fenders.
There were indeed ten thousand chariots with a roar like thunderclouds;
moreover, there was no one who spoke untruth, no one who failed to perform sacrifice, and no one who did not give a thousandfold.
We have heard it told that the son of Ārdraka was never impure, nor unrighteous, nor ignorant, nor emaciated; such was his steadfastness.
Accompanied by that retinue,
the peerless Āhuka traveled with eighty million horses, steeds resembling young colts.
In the eastern direction, while intensely contemplating the enjoyment of the Nāgas,

he who lies forever in the northern region of the ocean, the Ocean of Milk, the sea of nectar,

These two states follow the flavors, and the moon and fire reside in their potency;
semen belongs to the category of phlegm, and blood to the category of bile.
The seat of phlegm is the heart; bile is established at the navel;
and the seat of the mind is known to be the heart in the middle of the body.
The navel is situated within the abdomen, and there resides the god Hutāśana (Fire);
the mind is to be known as Prajāpati, and phlegm is perceived as Soma.
For bile is known as fire; indeed, this world consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
When the embryo has thus developed and reached the stage resembling a jujube fruit, [it proceeds further].

Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—
prāṇa, increasing the supreme self (paramātman), circulates throughout him.

Apāna moves through the posterior part of the body, udāna through the upper half of the embodied being; vyāna is that by which [the breath] is distributed throughout, while samāna resides in all the joints.
From that, his attainment of the elements arises as objects of the senses:

O wise one, how did Viṣṇu attain human status in this world of mortals?

O Viṣṇu, we wish to hear of his deeds in their proper sequence.
"O Great-minded One, it is said in the Vedas that Viṣṇu is the supreme wonder and the god; tell me the wondrous origin of Viṣṇu."

This wonder has been recounted; now let that which brings happiness be told—the manifestation of the Great-Souled One, whose strength and heroism are renowned, and who is Viṣṇu, whose deeds are truly marvelous; his essential nature is here being described.
Sūta said:
I shall proclaim to you the manifestation of the Great-Souled One.
Just as the Blessed One of great asceticism became a human among men through the fault of killing a woman, so too did Bhṛgu [become a man] by the curse of Bhṛgu.

When the dharma of the age has been overturned and time has become lax, a lord is born here among men to establish the order of dharma,
due to the cause of Bhṛgu’s curse and the deeds of the gods and asuras.
The sages said:
"How did he obtain that discourse for the sake of the gods and asuras?
We wish to know this; how did the event concerning the gods and asuras unfold?"
Sūta said:
Listen as I relate that account of the war between the gods and the asuras exactly as it occurred.
Formerly, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu ruled the three worlds;
subsequently, the sovereignty over the three worlds was held by Bali in succession.
There was a supreme friendship between those gods and the asuras; indeed, ten full cycles known as yugas passed while the world remained unimpeded.
The gods and asuras became followers of those two instructions;
then, once Bali was bound, a most terrible dispute broke out between them.
Then, for the sake of providing an island of refuge for them, there occurred many terrible and great battles between the gods and the asuras, which caused a vast destruction.
In this Varāha [Kalpa], twelve Daṇḍas are recorded as ending with Ṣaṇḍa and Marka;
listen now to their names as I intend to speak of them in brief.
The first was Nārasiṃha, and the second was Vāmana;
the third was Vārāha, and the fourth was Amṛtamanthana.
The fifth battle was indeed the most terrible, Tārakāmaya;
the sixth was Āḍībaka among them, and the seventh is remembered as Traipura.
Andhakāra is the eighth among them, and Dhvaja is remembered as the ninth;
Vārtra is the tenth, terrible, and after that Hālāhala is remembered.
The twelfth among them is remembered as the terrible Kolāhala;
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Narasiṃha.
When the three worlds had been overrun, Bali was bound by Vāmana;
Hiraṇyākṣa was slain in single combat during the divine dispute.
The mighty being of great strength, undefeated in battles,
that Daitya was split in two by the boar with its tusk.
During the churning for the nectar of immortality, Prahlāda was defeated in battle by Indra;
however, Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, was constantly intent on slaying Indra.
Having obtained immunity from being slain by anyone other than you through special weapons and the like, he was nevertheless overcome by Indra’s prowess and slain during the Tārakāmaya war.
When the gods were unable to withstand that supreme non-divine being, Viṣṇu, possessed by Śakra, slew Jaṃbha in the sixth [encounter].
All the Dānavas were slain in Tripura by Tryambaka;
then, in the battle against Andhaka, both the Daityas and the Suras as well as the Rākṣasas were destroyed.
They were conquered by the gods and humans, and likewise joined with the ancestors;
they completely overcame all those Dānavas together with Vṛtra.
Strengthened by Viṣṇu as his ally, Mahendra slew him;
and the one who was skilled in yoga had his banner destroyed by Mahendra and his umbrella by me.
Having entered Dhvajalakṣa, the younger brother of Vipracitti gathered together all those Daityas and Dānavas in their entirety.
Surrounded by all the gods, Vṛṣa conquered Hālāhala;
surrounded by all the Daityas, Raji conquered Kolāhala.
Having won at the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the sacrifice through the Ṣaṇḍāmarkas and the deities,
these twelve battles between the gods and the asuras took place.
Causing the destruction of both gods and asuras, and bringing misfortune to all creatures,
King Hiraṇyakaśipu reigned for a hundred million years.
Likewise, he became the lord of the three worlds for two hundred and eighty thousand years plus an additional one hundred thousand.
Furthermore, King Bali ruled for sixty-three million and one hundred billion years in succession.
For as long as Bali held the authority of the kingdom,
for that long was Prahlāda defeated along with the asuras.
Those three Indrāstras were indeed renowned as the most powerful among the Asuras;
for ten yugas, it is said, this entire world remained under the dominion of the Daityas.
Then Śukra cursed the kingdom for ten yugas;
indeed, Mahendra then entered this undisturbed triple-world of Bali.
When that [kingdom] had been taken from Prahlāda by the turn of time,
the three worlds were, in due course, obtained by Pākaśāsana.
Then, having abandoned the Asuras, the sacrifice went over to the gods;
when the sacrifice had thus gone to the gods, those Asuras spoke to Kāvya.
"What is this? While we look on, the sacrifice has abandoned our kingdom and gone to the gods;
indeed, we are unable to remain here today, so we shall enter the netherworld."
Thus addressed, he spoke to them, dejected yet consoling them with his voice:
"Do not fear, O gods; I shall sustain you by my own splendor."
May rain, the herbs, the essences, and whatever else is the supreme substance—
may all these indeed abide within you, O gods, as your very sin.
"I shall bestow everything for your sake; all that is being held by me.
Then, having seen the gods and asuras held captive by the wise Kāvya, [the gods spoke].
Then, desiring victory, they were indeed greatly distressed and addressed one another:
"This Kāvya is forcibly turning all of this away from us."
"Let us go quickly, before they can recover their strength;
having forcibly slain them, let us send the survivors to Pātāla."
Then the gods, being highly incensed, rushed toward the Dānavas and struck them; being slaughtered by them, the Dānavas fled toward Kāvya himself.
Then Kāvya, seeing those sons of Diti pursued by the gods, quickly protected them from the gods as they were terrified.
Having seen the gods standing there, Kāvya reflected upon destiny;
then, having meditated and recollecting former events, he spoke to them.
The entire three worlds were conquered by Vāmana with his three strides;
Bali was bound, Jambha was slain, and Virocana was struck down.
In twelve battles, the great asuras were slain by the gods;
the majority of them, those who were most prominent, were killed by various means.
"Indeed, you are but a few remaining in this battle;
I myself shall provide you with counsel. Wait for a short time."
"I shall go to Mahādeva for the sake of the mantra and for victory;
let the Hotṛ priest nourish the fire with these mantras, and it will consume him."
"Then, O Lord, I shall go to the deity Nīlalohita for the sake of counsel;
having returned here afterwards, I will bestow grace upon you once more."
"You must indeed perform austerities in the forest, clothed in bark garments;
the gods will certainly not trouble you until my return."
Then, having obtained from the god Maheśvara mantras that are irresistible, we shall fight the gods again; thus you will indeed attain victory.
Then, having reached an agreement, those asuras said to the gods:
"We have all laid down our weapons; you may indeed traverse the worlds."
"Having heard Prahlāda’s words, which were indeed consistent with truth, we shall practice austerities in the forest, clothed in bark garments."
Then the gods, freed from fever and filled with joy, withdrew;
when the Daityas had laid down their weapons, they returned to their own abodes just as they had come.
Then Kāvya said to them: "Wait for some time;
remain free from anxiety and devoted to austerity, for time is that which accomplishes the purpose of one's task."
"O Dānavas, wait here in my father’s hermitage!
Having thus instructed the Asuras, Kāvya approached Mahādeva.
Having thus bowed down to the Lord, the source of the universe, he spoke:
"O God, I desire those mantras which do not exist with Bṛhaspati."
"O twice-born one, since you have spoken thus, you truly desire the mantras that bring fearlessness among the Asuras for the defeat of the gods. Thus addressed, the god spoke.
"Perform the vow prescribed by me, remaining composed as a celibate student for a full thousand years, with head hanging downwards, inhaling the smoke from a sacrificial pit."
"If you drink it, may it be well with you; from me you shall obtain the mantra.
Thus was Śukra, the great ascetic, addressed by the God of gods.
Touching the feet of the God, he replied, "So be it.
"O Lord, O Vaibhra, I shall observe the vow as I have been instructed by you, O God."
Then, after Śukra had departed, Kuṇḍadhāra was appointed by the Lord to produce smoke for that [purpose] for the benefit of the Asuras.
He dwelt there for the sake of the mantra, practicing celibacy under Maheśvara;
having understood that, the kingdom was then entrusted to him by the Asuras according to the principles of policy.
At that opening, all the gods, led by Bṛhaspati and brandishing their weapons, then rushed toward them in indignation.

When the weapon was laid down, when safety was granted, and while the preceptor remained established in his vow,
those gods, desiring to slay their rivals, abandoned their agreement.
But those who are without a teacher— may you be blessed— remaining confident in their asceticism,
wearing garments of bark, rags, and skins, free from ritual action, and possessing no worldly attachments.
"We shall certainly not be able to defeat the gods in battle by any means;
therefore, let us seek refuge with the mother of Kāvya through non-violence."
Then, being terrified, they sought refuge with her;

Seeing those Asuras thus supported by her, the gods then assailed them with force, having deliberated upon their relative strengths and weaknesses.
Then, seeing those asuras being slaughtered by the gods, the goddess, filled with rage, said to them: "I shall deprive you of Indrahood."
Then, having quickly paralyzed Indra through his fury, he pursued him;
and seeing Śakra thus paralyzed, the gods became as if bewildered.
Then, seeing Śakra brought under control, they fled in fear;
when the hosts of gods had departed, Viṣṇu spoke to Indra.
"Enter me; may it be well with you; I shall lead you forth, O Lord of the Gods.
Thus addressed, Viṣṇu then entered Purandara.
Seeing that he had been protected by Viṣṇu, the goddess became enraged and spoke these words:
"O Maghavan, together with Viṣṇu, I shall forcibly burn you to ashes!"
"While all beings look on, let the power of my asceticism be seen.
Overwhelmed by that, those two gods, Indra and Viṣṇu, spoke together.
"How can we two together be released? Viṣṇu said to Indra.
Indra replied, "Kill her indeed, before the two of us are consumed by her."
"I have been especially overcome by this; therefore, abandon it without delay.
Then Viṣṇu, having reflected upon that, resolved to carry out the killing of the woman.
Then, perceiving that Śakra had become possessed by covetousness, the Lord, the slayer of Mura’s enemies, quickly acted with haste against her as she was rushing forward.
Then the god Viṣṇu, having perceived the cruel intent he wished to carry out, became enraged;
Mādhava brandished that weapon and severed his head.
Seeing that terrible murder of his wife, Bhṛgu, the lord, became enraged;
then Viṣṇu was cursed by Bhṛgu for the slaying of his wife.
"Since you, knowing the law, have slain this woman who was not to be killed,
therefore you shall indeed enter among human beings seven times."
Then, when dharma has been destroyed again and again by that curse,
he is born here among humans for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds.
Having invoked Viṣṇu, he himself took that head, brought it there, joined it to the body, and then spoke these words: *Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa* 2.72.144.
I shall restore you to life, who have been truly slain by Viṣṇu,
if indeed the entirety of dharma has been practiced by me, or even if it is known to me.
"By that truth, live on, if what I speak is true. Then, by the utterance of that truth, the goddess was restored to life.
Then, having sprinkled her with cool water, he said, "Live!
Thereupon, seeing her like one who has just awakened from sleep, she was perceived by all living beings.
"Excellent! Excellent!"—thus did the voices of the invisible deities resound through the quarters of the sky upon seeing that the goddess had been thus restored to life by Bhṛgu at that time.
While all living beings looked on, it was as if a miracle had occurred,
for Bhṛgu, remaining unperturbed, then restored his wife to life.
Having seen this, Śakra found no peace thereafter due to the fear of Kāvya;
consequently, Indra, while awake, [summoned] his own daughter Jayantī.
The wise Indra, the subduer of Pāka, spoke these words to his own daughter:
"This son of Kavi is indeed performing severe penance for the sake of becoming the one who is not Indra."
Therefore, O daughter, I have been made deeply anxious; yet, with a firm mind, I say:
go, O auspicious one, and attend to him with means that dispel his fatigue.
Undistracted by those various services that were agreeable to her mind,
the goddess Jayantī, daughter of Sārīndra, moved with auspicious conduct.
Then she, assuming her own beautiful form, undertook that difficult vow and carried out the words spoken by her father exactly as they were told.
And with agreeable words, she who speaks so sweetly praised him,
while at the proper time she served him by massaging his limbs, providing pleasures to the skin.
She lived for many years, serving him and acting in accordance with his will;
she also completed the full, terrible vow of smoke for a thousand years.
Delighted, he then invited Kāvya to choose a boon, saying:

Therefore, by means of austerity, intelligence, sacred learning, strength,
and even through your splendor, you shall surpass all the gods.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, whatever Vedic knowledge belongs to me exists here,
along with its auxiliary branches, its secret doctrines, as well as the sacrificial manuals and the Upaniṣads.
All that appears to you must not be spoken of to anyone;
by that, O best of the twice-born, you shall become a conqueror of all.
Having thus granted her that boon, Bhava further bestowed upon the descendant of Bhṛgu the lordship over progeny, the lordship over wealth, and indeed invincibility.
Having obtained these boons, Kāvya’s hair stood on end with joy;
out of delight, a divine hymn to the Great Lord manifested within him.
Then, standing sideways, he thus praised Nīlalohita:
