salutations be to you, who exists within the four [worlds] beginning with Mahas and ending with Satya.
O Lord, whatever improper words have been uttered by me in this hymn of praise,
you ought to forgive it all, O friend of Brahmanas, because I am your devotee.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Hymn," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as narrated by Vāyu.
Sūta said: Having thus propitiated Īśāna, the Lord of Gods, who is blue-and-red (Nīlalohita),
he, bowing low and deeply prostrating with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to him.
Having touched the body of Kāvya with his hand,
the joyful Bhava granted him a full vision and vanished right there.
Then, when that god and his retinue had vanished,
he stood with palms joined in reverence and spoke thus to Jayantī:
"Whose are you, O fortunate one? Or who are you that, being sorrowful, are sorrowful for me?
Why do you, endowed with ascetic power, desire to conquer me?"
"O lady of beautiful hips, O woman of excellent complexion, I am constantly pleased by this devotion, humility, self-restraint, and affection."
"What do you desire, O lady of beautiful limbs? What wish of yours may be fulfilled?
I shall fulfill it for you today, even if it should be very difficult to attain."
Thus addressed, she said to him: "O most excellent of Brahmins, you ought to know through your ascetic power what I intend to do; for you indeed know it exactly as it is."
Thus addressed, he spoke to her after seeing her with his divine eye:
"O lady of beautiful limbs, you are Māhendrī; you have come here for my benefit."
"O beautiful-hipped one, O passionate lady, you desire to enjoy union with me here for ten years, remaining invisible to all beings."
"O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips with the luster of sapphire, O fair-eyed one,
O sweet-spoken woman, choose this desire from me."
"So be it; let us go home, O lady with the gait of a rutting elephant.
Then, having arrived at his own home, the lord was reunited with Jayantī.
And that descendant of Bhṛgu lived with that goddess for ten years,
concealed by her illusory power (māyā) so as to be invisible to all beings.
Knowing that he had attained his purpose, all the sons of Diti,
filled with joy and desiring to see him, went to his house.
When they had gone and did not see their preceptor concealed by Jayantī,
they realized his deception and returned the way they had come.
But Bṛhaspati, having learned that Kāvya was restrained by the boon,
remained for ten years out of affection and with a desire for Jayantī’s welfare.
Then, having perceived that opportunity and impelled by the counsel of the gods,
he assumed the form of Kāvya and addressed the asuras.
Then, seeing that they had arrived, Bṛhaspati said to them: "Welcome! I have come for the benefit of my patrons."
"I shall teach you whatever sciences have been acquired by me. Thereupon, with joyful minds, they approached him for the sake of knowledge.
When ten years had thus been completed,
at the end of that period, Devayājī then immediately became possessed of wisdom.
Then he also set his mind upon inspecting his patrons.
Śukra said:
"O Goddess of pure smiles, I shall go to see your patrons."
"O virtuous lady, O you with wide eyes of three colors and a wandering gaze!"—being thus addressed, the goddess said: "Devote yourself to me, O observer of great vows!
This, O Brahmin, is the duty of the righteous; I do not violate your dharma."
Sūta said:
Then, having gone there and seen the gods, [he was addressed] by the wise preceptor of the gods.
Having deceived them with words in the form of poetry, he spoke again:
"Grant me permission for this poem, for this is the sage Aṅgiras."
"Alas, you Dānavas have been deceived while I was occupied!"—
hearing him speaking thus, the sons of Diti were then thrown into confusion.
There, both of them sat firmly with pure smiles, gazing at one another; all who were present stood utterly bewildered, not knowing what to do.
Then, while they were thus bewildered, Kāvya spoke to them again:
"This teacher who is Kāvya is indeed the noble Aṅgiras, a deity."
"Follow me all of you; abandon this Bṛhaspati!
When this was said, they all looked intently at those two.
At that time, the Asuras did not distinguish the difference between those two;
Bṛhaspati said to them, "O brothers, this is Aṅgiras."
"O Daityas, I am your preceptor Kāvya; this Bṛhaspati is merely my own form. O Asuras, he is deluding you with my appearance."
Having heard his words and deliberated among themselves, they then spoke these words:
"This lord has indeed ruled us constantly for ten years."
"O twice-born ones, this man indeed desires to create a rift between us; he is our guru.
Then all those Dānavas, having prostrated and offered their salutations, [spoke].
Deluded by the practice of their sciences, all those asuras accepted his words; with eyes bloodshot and enraged, they spoke to him.
"This teacher is beneficial to us; go away, you are not our teacher.
Whether he be Bhārgava or Āṅgirasa, let him alone be our teacher."
"We abide by his command; go, do not delay.
Having spoken thus, all the gods approached Bṛhaspati.
When they did not comply, he spoke those words of great benefit;
then Bhārgava indeed became enraged at their arrogance.
"Since you, O Dānavas, do not serve me even though I have instructed you,
therefore, having lost your senses, you shall surely meet with defeat."
Having spoken thus to them, Kāvya then departed as he had come;
for Bṛhaspati, having learned that those Asuras had been cursed by Kāvya.
Having achieved his purpose, he then became joyful and resumed his own form;
perceiving that the Asuras were now terrified, he, having accomplished his aim, vanished from sight.
Then, when he had vanished, those Dānavas were bewildered;
"Alas! Woe! they said to one another, deceived by their affection.
We have been made by the Creator not averse to our duty,
yet we have been burnt by the application of deceitful means through illusion in our respective tasks.
Then the asuras, terrified of the gods, fled in haste,
placing Prahlāda at their head and once again following Kāvya.
Then, having approached Kāvya, they stood facing him;
seeing them returned, Kāvya spoke again to those for whom he was the officiating priest.
Since you did not welcome me when I awakened you at the proper time,
you have fallen into ruin because of that arrogance.
Then Prahlāda said to him: "O Bhārgava, abandon your pride toward those who offer you their own oblations, and especially toward your devotees."
While you were not seen, we were deluded by that teacher of the gods; it behooves you, having perceived us with your far-reaching vision, to protect us who are devoted to you.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, if you do not show us favor,
we shall enter the netherworld this very day, cursed by you.
Sūta said:
Having understood the truth of the matter, Śukra, out of great compassion,
was thus entreated and thereupon withdrew his anger.
He said this: "Fear not; you must not go to the netherworld (rasātala).
For this inevitable event has arrived for you while I am yet awake."
It is not possible to act otherwise, for destiny is indeed most powerful;
as for this consciousness that has been lost, you shall surely regain it.
"The time for the transition has arrived," Brahmā declared;
"and by my grace, you have enjoyed the exalted three worlds."
Having ascended to the heads of the gods, he remained there for ten complete ages known as yugas;
for that same duration of time, Brahmā indeed proclaimed his sovereignty.
Furthermore, in the Sāvarṇika [Manvantara], the kingdom shall indeed belong to you;
moreover, your grandson Bali will become the lord of the worlds.
Thus was Kālamaya described by Brahmā himself as your grandson;
and when the worlds had been withdrawn in that manner, there was indeed neither sorrow nor lamentation.
Since his activities were not motivated by desires,
therefore he was granted [this boon] by the pleased Aja during the Sāvarṇika interval.
"The lord said to me, 'The kingdom of the gods shall belong to Bali';
therefore, he remains invisible to all beings, awaiting his time."
"Out of affection, the Self-Existent One indeed granted you the state of immortality;
therefore, you should remain free from anxiety, for you are suddenly distressed by this change of circumstances."
"O Lord, I am not able to glide before you;
I have been forbidden by Brahmā, who knows what is to come."
And these two disciples of mine are equal to Bṛhaspati;
they shall sustain all of you when you are embroiled with the gods.
Sūta said:
Having been thus addressed by Kāvya of unwearied deeds, the Daityas,
headed by Prahlāda, then departed together with those two.
Having heard that inevitable matter, the Daityas and Dānavas suddenly proclaimed the victory spoken by Kāvya.
All of them, armored and equipped with weapons, then challenged the gods;
then, seeing the gods and asuras standing ready for battle, [the Lord spoke].

Then, having donned their armor, the gods fought them. While that battle between the gods and asuras was thus proceeding for a hundred years, the asuras were conquering the gods; then the gods, being overwhelmed, held a council.
The gods said:
"By the power of Śaṇḍa and Marka, we have been defeated by the asuras;
therefore, for the sake of the sacrifice and whatever is for our own benefit, [an action must be taken]."
"We shall invoke them through sacrifice; then we will conquer the Asuras.
Then the gods invoked both Śaṇḍa and Marka.
And at the sacrifice, having summoned those two, he said: "O twice-born ones, abandon the Asuras!"
"We shall indeed seize you both after having conquered the Dānavas.
Thus did those two then abandon the gods by means of that deceptive stratagem.
Then the gods attained victory and the Dānavas met with defeat;
having vanquished the gods and asuras, Śaṇḍa and Marka approached [the enemy].
Overcome by the curse of the poet and left without support,
they were then harassed by the gods and entered the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
Thus were those Dānavas rendered devoid of effort by Śakra through the curse occasioned by Bhṛgu; from that time forward, they remained so.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu, the Lord, repeatedly enters into the sacrifice when the sacrifice has become lax,
in order to establish the system of dharma and to bring about the destruction of adharma.
The Lord Brahmā declared that all those asuras who did not abide by the command of Prahrāda were to be slain by humans.
From Dharma, Nārāyaṇa was born during the Cākṣuṣa interval;
he, as the son of Vena, inaugurated the sacrifice during the Vaivasvata interval.
At the manifestation of Vainya, Brahmā himself was his domestic priest;
then, when the fourth age had arrived, the gods fell into distress.
Born within the ocean for the sake of slaying Hiraṇyakaśipu,
he became a second Narasiṃha, fierce and preceded by his sons.
Having become a twice-born brahmin at an auspicious time, the delighter of Aditi’s lineage addressed Bali, the son of Virocana and lord of the Daityas, as he was performing a sacrifice.
“You are the king of the three worlds; everything is established in you.
O King, you ought to grant me three strides,” said the Lord.
"I give," King Bali, the son of Virocana, said to him;
and recognizing him as the dwarf, he then gave it himself with great joy.
O best of the twice-born, that Lord Vāmana traversed this entire universe— both heaven and space and the earth— with three strides.
The great-souled one of immense fame surpassed the sun with his own splendor, illuminating all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having seized the demonic splendor as well as the three worlds, that mighty-armed Janārdana shone forth, illuminating all the worlds.
Namuci, Śambara, and Prahrāda, along with their sons and grandsons, were brought down to the depths of Pātāla by Viṣṇu.
The cruel ones were slain and driven out; they fled in all directions, while Mādhava absorbed the great elements along with the individual souls and their specific qualities.
And there, O brahmins, Bali, together with his army, displayed a marvel:
he beheld the entire world within his own body.
There is nothing in the worlds that is not pervaded by the Great-Souled One;
such indeed is the form of Upendra, [perceived] by gods, dānavas, and humans.
Seeing this, everyone was utterly bewildered, stupefied by the splendor of Viṣṇu;
Bali, along with his kinsmen, sons, and hosts of grandsons, was bound with great nooses.
The entire lineage of Virocana was established in Pātāla;
then, having bestowed the sovereignty over all the immortals upon the high-souled Indra, [he departed].
The mighty-armed Janārdana manifested among human beings;
these three were his auspicious and divine manifestations.
Learn now those seven foremost among his human incarnations;
in the tenth Tretā Yuga, Dattātreya indeed appeared.
When the Dharma had perished, the fourth [incarnation] was Mārkaṇḍeya;
and on the fifteenth day of the month, he appeared as the fifth during the Tretā age.
In his status as a universal monarch (cakravartin), Māndhātṛ was preceded by Utathya;
in the nineteenth Tretā age, the Lord brought an end to all the kṣatriyas.
Then, in the twenty-fourth yuga, during the sixth [turyayuga], Rāma Jāmadagnya appeared with Viśvāmitra at his head, accompanied by Vasiṣṭha as his domestic priest.
The seventh was born as the son of Daśaratha for the sake of Rāvaṇa;
the eighth was Viṣṇu, born from Parāśara in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age.
From him was born Vedavyāsa, preceded by Jātūkarṇya;
likewise, in the ninth [manvantara], Viṣṇu was born as the son of Kaśyapa from Aditi.
Born of Devakī from Vasudeva, preceded by Gārgya,
he is immeasurable, possessed of self-restraint, the fulfiller of desires, and self-controlled.
The Blessed One sports in the world like a child with toys;
this mighty-armed Madhusūdana cannot be measured.
Indeed, there exists nothing higher than this Viśvarūpa;
likewise, when the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age comes to an end.
When dharma had perished, the Lord Viṣṇu was then born in the Vṛṣṇi clan to establish the order of dharma and to destroy the asuras,
deluding all beings through his yoga-māyā, he whose self is yoga.
Having entered a human womb, he wanders the earth in disguise.
For the sake of dwelling among men, preceded by Sāṃdīpani,
[he went] where he [slain] Kaṃsa, Śālva, and the great asura Dvivida.
Ariṣṭha, Vṛṣabha, Pūtanā, the horse Keśin,
the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, and the wrestler who was the lord of Rājagṛha.
The heroic one slew the Daityas dwelling within human bodies,
and by means of his wondrous deeds, he cut off the thousand arms of Bāṇa.
Naraka was slain in battle, as was the mighty Yavana;
and by his splendor, all the jewels of the kings were seized.
And the Kuru heroes and those kings who dwell in the netherworld (rasātala) have been slain;
these were the manifestations of the Great-Souled One for the sake of the welfare of the world.
When this very Yuga has waned and only its twilight remains,
there will appear the powerful Kalki, named Viṣṇuyaśas, the son of Parāśara.
The tenth [incarnation], born of Bhavya, was preceded by Yājñavalkya;
he indeed led an army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
He was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of brahmins who held weapons in their hands—
some who were exceedingly righteous and some who were, in certain respects, haters of dharma.
[He conquered] the northern regions and the Middle Country, as well as those bordering the Vindhya mountains;
likewise, the southerners and the Dravidians together with the Siṃhalas.
The Gāndhāras, the Pāradas, the Pahlavas, the Pāvanas, the Śakas, the Tubaras, the Śabaras, the Pulindas, and the Baradas.
That powerful lord, whose wheel of dominion has been set in motion, will be the mighty destroyer of the Mlecchas, including the Laṃpakas, Aṅghrikas, Puṇḍras, and Kirātas.
Invisible to all beings, he shall wander the earth;
that man was born as the son of the wise Devasena.
In a previous birth, he who was the heroic Viṣṇu named Pramiti became,
in the full Kali age, a descendant of the lunar lineage.
Thus, these are recorded as the origins of that god,
each directed toward its respective time, body, and specific cause.
In part, he shall enter various wombs throughout the three worlds;
established in the twenty-fifth kalpa, he shall indeed remain for twenty-five years.
Having slaughtered all beings, indeed all human beings in every way,
he made the earth have only seeds remaining through his cruel deed.
Having pacified those mostly unrighteous *vṛṣalas*,
Kalki, having then accomplished his purpose, will depart together with his army.
But those who have been struck down by their own karma, though they were once perfected beings,
will themselves suddenly become enraged with one another and fall into delusion.
But having destroyed them all, impelled by his destined purpose,
he shall reach his end along with his followers in the middle of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Then, when that eon had passed and the king along with his army had perished, the subjects were left without a ruler.
But when their protection had failed and they were slain by one another in battle,
they were deprived of each other's sight, joyless, and deeply afflicted by suffering.
Having abandoned their cities and villages, they were equal [to one another] and free from possessions;
the sacred scriptures and the Dharma had perished, and likewise the stages of life (āśramas) and their duties had vanished.
The forest-dwellers will become short-statured and short-lived;
they will dwell by rivers and mountains, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits.
Wearing garments of bark, leaves, and skins, they will resort to terrible impurity;
short-lived, deprived of news, beset by many afflictions, and deeply distressed.
Thus, when the Kali-yuga has reached its ultimate limit during the period of the twilight (saṃdhyāṃśaka), the people shall go to their destruction along with the Kali age itself.
When that Kali Yuga has waned and the Kṛta Yuga has set in again,
they will attain [their goals] according to the proper rule through their very nature, and not otherwise.
Thus has all this activity of the gods and asuras been recounted; and in connection with the lineage of Yadu, your great Vaiṣṇava glory has indeed been told.
Now I shall proclaim [the lineage] of Turvasu, as well as that of Pūru, Druhyu, and Anu.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Viṣṇu," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
The son of Turvasu was Vahni; the son of Vahni was Gobhānu;
and the son of Gobhānu, O hero, was the unconquered Trisānu.
Karandhama was the son of Trisānu, and Marutta was his son;
however, another King Marutta, who was unknown [to you], was mentioned previously.
It is heard that King Marutta was childless;
he indeed adopted Duṣkanta, the descendant of Puru, as his son.
Thus, it is said that in ancient times, due to the curse of Yayāti regarding the transfer of his old age,
Turvasu formerly entered the Paurava lineage.
The heir of Duṣkanta was the king named Sarūpya;
from Sarūpya likewise came Aṇḍīra, and he had four sons.
The Pāṇḍyas, the Keralas, the Colas, and likewise the Kulyas—
their territories were the Kulyas, the Pāṇḍyas, and the Colas together with the Keralas.
The two renowned and heroic sons of Druhyu were Babhru and Setu; Aruddha was the son of Setu, and the son of Babhru is called Ripu.
The powerful [ruler] was slain with great difficulty by Yauvanāśva in battle;
indeed, that great war lasted for fourteen months.
The heir of Aruddha was the king named Gāndhāra,
after whose name the great region of Gāndhāra became renowned.
There were also horses born in the land of Gāndhāra, the best among steeds; Dharmasuta was the son of Gāndhāraputra, and Dhṛta was his son.
From Dhṛta was born Durdamana, and Pracetas was his son;
the hundred sons of Pracetas were all kings.
All the rulers of the Mleccha kingdoms were established in the northern direction;
and the three heroic sons of Anu were supremely righteous.
Sabhānara, Kālacakṣu, and Parākṣa are thus renowned.
The son of Sabhānara was the wise king Kālānala.
The virtuous son of Kālānala was the renowned Sṛñjaya;
Sṛñjaya’s son was the hero named Purañjaya.
There was a king equal to Indra, whose fame was established in heaven;
he was high-minded, righteous, and the son of Mahāśāla.
The king, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) of great fame and lord of the seven continents,
begot two sons of noble mind who were renowned throughout the world.
And [he begat] Uśīnara, who was a knower of dharma, and likewise the righteous Titikṣu;
the wives of Uśīnara were five, born from the lineages of royal sages.
Nṛgā, Kṛmī, Navā, Darvā, and Dṛṣadvatī as the fifth—
these were the five daughters of Uśīnara, and among them were those who carried on the lineage.
To Nṛgā were born virtuous sons from the great ascetic Nṛga as he grew old; and to Navā was born a son named Nava.
O twice-born ones, from Kṛmi was born Kṛmi, and from Darvā was born the righteous one named Suvrata; and Śibi, the son of Ṛṣadvatī, was also born of Auśīnara, O brahmins.
Śibapura is known as the city of Śibi, while Yaudheya is the city of Nṛga; Navarāṣṭra belongs to Nava, and Kṛmilā is the city of Kṛmi.
Likewise, learn of the sons of Śibi from Aṃbaṣṭha, the son of Suvrata;
Śibi’s sons were the four Śibis, esteemed by the world.
Vṛṣadarbha was the heroic Suvīra, as well as Kekaya and Madraka;
their flourishing territories were known as Kekaya and Madraka.
O Vṛṣadarbhas and Suvīras, O subjects, listen to Titikṣu!
Titikṣu became the renowned king in the eastern quarter.
Uśadratha, the mighty-armed, had a son named Hema;
Hema’s son was Sutapas, and from Sutapas was born Bali.
Having been born in human form when his lineage had perished,
that great yogi Bali, who was high-minded, was bound by his desire for progeny.
He begot sons who established the four castes upon the earth;
he likewise fathered Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Suhma.
Yuddha, Kaliṅga, and likewise Vāleya are said to be the Kṣatriyas; and the Brāhmaṇas known as the Vāleyas were the progenitors of that lord’s lineage.
To the wise Bali, the gratified Brahmā granted boons:
the status of a great yogi and a lifespan equal to the duration of a kalpa.
Invincibility in battle, as well as power through righteousness,
the vision of the three worlds, and likewise preeminence in procreation.
"You shall indeed possess incomparable strength, you shall perceive the true meaning of the principles of Dharma,
and you shall establish the four fixed social orders."
Thus addressed by the Lord, King Bali attained peace;
after a long time, the wise one returned to his own station.
Their prosperous territories were Aṅga, Vaṅga, Suhma, Puṇḍra, and Kaliṅga; now learn of their lineage.
All those sons of his, born of the field and produced from the sage,
were of great luster, born to Dīrghatamas through Sudeṣṇā.
The sages said:
"O Lord, how were the five sons of Bali begotten as *kṣetraja* offspring by the seer Dīrghatamas? Pray, tell this to us who ask."
Sūta said:
In ancient times, there was a celebrated and wise sage named Uśija;
that great-souled one had a wife named Mamata.
But the younger brother of Uśija, the priest of the dwellers of heaven,
Bṛhaspati of great splendor, approached Mamatā.
But Mamatā, being unwilling, said to Bṛhaspati:
"O beautiful one, I am pregnant by your elder brother."
"For this great embryo of mine, O Bṛhaspati, cries out piteously as he incessantly practices the sacred word and pours forth the Veda with its six limbs."
O you whose power is unfailing, it is not fitting for you to consort with me;
rather, O Lord, do so at this very time, or whenever you deem appropriate.
Thus addressed by her, the great-splendored Bṛhaspati,
though himself a high-souled being, could not restrain his own self, which was possessed by desire.
O Bṛhaspati, that righteous-souled one indeed united with her;
as he was then emitting his seed, the child within the womb spoke to him.
"You have discharged your semen; do not live! There is no possibility for both of us here. You are one whose seed is never in vain, and I too have arrived here previously."
Thus addressed, the venerable sage Bṛhaspati, filled with anger, then cursed the son of Uśija who was still in his brother’s womb.
"Since you have spoken thus to me out of delusion at such a time, when all beings desire [it], you shall behold a long-lasting darkness."
From him was born the ṛṣi named Dīrghatamas due to a curse;
then came Auśija Bṛhatkīrti, who was like Bṛhaspati in his splendor.
Thereafter, with his vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), he dwelt in the hermitage of his brother;
from the lordly bull, the son of Surabhi, he learned the dharma of cattle.
Then his brother, who was his paternal uncle, built a dwelling for him;
for there, while he was living, a bull arrived by chance.
The son of Surabhi moved among the darbha grass spread out for the sake of the sacrifice;
then Dīrghatamas seized him, who was quivering at his horns.
Though restrained by him, he did not move even a single step from his place;
then the bull said to him, "O best among the strong, release me!"
"O father, since I was born upon the earth from the god Tryambaka, I have never encountered anyone anywhere who is as powerful as he."
"Release me, O best of the strong; choose a boon out of affection.
Thus addressed, he said to him: "Where will you go while I am still alive?"
"Therefore, I shall not release you, a four-footed beast who tastes the property of another.
Then that bull replied to Dīrghatamas:
"O dear one, we possess neither sin nor theft;
we know nothing at all of what should or should not be eaten, nor of what should or should not be drunk."
O Brahmin, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, as well as what may be approached and what may not, we are indeed not sinful; for this is the dharma of cows as it has been heard.
Upon hearing the name of the cows, he was struck with agitation and released him;
indeed, through traditional devotion, he sought to appease the son of the cow.
Then, through the grace of the Lord of Bulls (Śiva), he took up the dharma of cows;
being devoted to that and possessing such a nature, he then maintained it by means of his mind alone.
Then, his mind deluded by fate, he lusted after the wife of his younger brother Autathya, even as she struggled and wept.
But Suradvan could not endure that arrogance,
for he considered the cow's nature to be his strength and thus insulted his daughter-in-law.
But having observed that reversal and reflected upon it, the high-souled Śaradvat, knowing the future destiny, disregarded him.
With eyes bloodshot from anger, he said to Dīrghatamas:
"You do not know what is to be approached and what is not, since you seek your daughter-in-law out of a lust for cattle."
"I abandon you, who are of evil conduct; go now according to your own karma, since you are blind, aged, and difficult to maintain due to your misdeeds."
"Therefore you have been abandoned by me; in my opinion, you are one of evil conduct.
Sūta said:
Then, his mind became intent upon that cruel deed.
Having rebuked him many times and seized him with both arms,
he threw him into the belly of the ocean and cast him into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Then, for seven days, the ocean was swept away by the current;
at that time, a king named Bali, who was accompanied by his wife and was a knower of the true principles of dharma and artha, [remained there].
Then the righteous Bali, son of Virocana, seeing him being submerged as he was carried along by the current, seized him.

The Kṣatriya portion occupies three parts, while from the fourth part onwards, it extends in each direction;
among those who have passed away and are equal [to them], listen as I describe them.
There were indeed a hundred Prativindhya kings, a hundred Nāgas together with the Haihayas,
one hundred and one Dhṛtarāṣṭras, and eighty Janamejayas.
There will be a hundred Brahmadattas, a hundred Śāris, and a hundred Viris;
thereafter, O Śvetakāśya, there will be a hundred Paulas, beginning with Kuśa.
After that, another thousand Śaśavindus who had passed away likewise performed horse sacrifices, all of them giving a hundred thousand as sacrificial fees.
In this same manner, hundreds and thousands of royal sages have passed away during this current interval of Vaivasvata Manu.
Learn now of the lineages that are recorded as having arisen from them in this world.
It is not possible to describe in detail the mutual succession of those lineages.
Even in hundreds of years, it is impossible to describe [them] by means of their preceding and succeeding conjunctions;
twenty-eight cycles known as yugas have passed within the Vaivasvata interval.
Learn now of those sixty-three future kings who, together with these royal sages, shall exist along with the kings.
Then follow the accounts of the Yugas, and after that, the end of the Vaivasvata Manvantara;
all this has been told to you, both in brief and in detail.
Moreover, due to the great abundance of repetitions, it is not possible [to recount them] even in the course of ages;
these five lineages of the sons of Yayāti are for the benefit of the people.
And those who have passed away, as well as those who sustain the worlds, are glorified;
he obtains five boons here that are difficult to attain in this world.
Through the retention and hearing of this wise lineage of five, one attains infinite longevity, fame, wealth, sons, and heaven.
Thus, O twice-born ones, this third quarter has been recounted to you by me in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I describe?
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage," in the third section (Upodghāta-pāda) of the middle part of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, as proclaimed by Vāyu.
And this third section is completed.
